questions.prompt: A hospital group's requirement says its site-to-site VPN to Azure must keep working even if one entire datacenter within the Azure region goes offline. Which design choice directly meets this requirement?
choices: Add a second on-premises VPN device on a different internet line.
Choose a zone-redundant gateway SKU (an AZ variant), so the gateway instances are spread across availability zones.
Keep the default active-standby gateway, because planned maintenance fails over in seconds.
Enable BGP on the existing tunnel so routes are withdrawn when it drops.
questions.why: Only a zone-redundant (AZ) SKU places the gateway instances in physically separate availability zones within the region. That lets the gateway survive the loss of one datacenter.

questions.prompt: A retail chain enables active-active on its Azure VPN gateway. Its head office still uses a single VPN device connected over a single internet line. One morning that internet line goes down. What happens to the site-to-site VPN?
choices: Every tunnel goes down, because the single office device and line are still a single point of failure.
Traffic briefly pauses, then fails over to the standby Azure instance within seconds.
Nothing is interrupted, because BGP reroutes traffic to the second Azure instance's public IP.
Only one of the two tunnels goes down, because active-active gives each Azure instance its own tunnel.
questions.why: Active-active removes the single point of failure on the Azure side only. Both tunnels end at the same office device and line, so losing that line takes down every tunnel.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would make a site-to-site VPN to Azure highly available. Walk from the default setup to the most resilient one, and name one tradeoff or limit of going further.
lessons.modelAnswer: A site-to-site VPN is an encrypted IPsec tunnel between our office VPN device and an Azure VPN gateway. The default gateway is active-standby: two instances, but only one carries traffic, so an unplanned failure can interrupt us for a minute or more. Turning on active-active gives each instance its own public IP and tunnel, so both carry traffic. That only protects the Azure side, though. We also need two office devices, ideally on separate internet links, each defined as its own local network gateway. Combining both gives a full mesh of four tunnels, and BGP lets routes shift automatically when a tunnel drops. A zone-redundant gateway SKU adds protection against losing one datacenter in the region. The tradeoff is cost and complexity: more public IPs, more devices to maintain, and BGP to configure and troubleshoot. It is also still the public internet, so performance is never guaranteed.
rubricPoints: Defines the VPN as an IPsec tunnel between an on-premises device and an Azure VPN gateway.
Contrasts the default active-standby gateway with active-active and notes the failover impact.
Points out that on-premises redundancy, meaning two devices and links, is also needed.
Describes dual-redundancy as a full mesh of tunnels and explains BGP's role in rerouting.
Mentions zone-redundant gateway SKUs for surviving the loss of an availability zone.
Names a tradeoff, such as cost, complexity, or reliance on the public internet.

suggested.rationale: High-availability VPN design is tested as scenario reasoning about which failure each topology survives, so working through exam-style situations adds the most.

lessons.plain: A virtual network gateway is the managed VPN endpoint that Azure runs at the edge of your virtual network, the private network you build in the cloud. A site-to-site VPN is an encrypted tunnel over the internet that links that network to an office or datacenter. The SKU is the size and feature tier of the gateway, much like choosing a delivery van: you pick it by how much it must carry, how many stops it makes, and whether it needs extras. A van that is too small means a slow, painful swap later.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company has 25 branch offices that must connect to Azure over VPN, and together they push about 800 Mbps at peak. Which two numbers would you check first on a gateway size before picking it, and why?
lessons.teach:
A gateway SKU is a named size of Azure VPN gateway that fixes three things: maximum aggregate throughput, which is the combined encrypted traffic across all tunnels; the maximum number of site-to-site tunnels; and supported features. Choose it by matching each requirement to a limit.

The families are Basic, a legacy entry tier, and VpnGw1 through VpnGw5. Each VpnGw size also has an AZ variant, such as VpnGw2AZ, which spreads the gateway across availability zones, meaning separate datacenters within one region. Basic lacks BGP (Border Gateway Protocol, which lets the two ends exchange routes automatically), active-active mode, zone redundancy, and custom IPsec policies, and it is limited to a handful of tunnels. Treat Basic as dev or test only. As rough figures, VpnGw1 to VpnGw3 allow about 30 tunnels. VpnGw4 and VpnGw5 allow about 100 tunnels and several Gbps. Generation 2 sizes give more throughput at the same number. Always confirm current figures in Microsoft's published table, because they change.

Why this works: each SKU reserves fixed compute for encryption. Throughput and tunnel count are therefore hard ceilings, not soft targets.

Worked example. Requirement: 25 branches, 800 Mbps peak, BGP, survive a zone failure. Step 1: BGP rules out Basic. Step 2: zone survival means an AZ SKU. Step 3: 25 tunnels fits under the roughly 30-tunnel limit of VpnGw1 to VpnGw3. Step 4: 800 Mbps exceeds VpnGw1's roughly 650 Mbps, so pick VpnGw2AZ, at about 1.25 Gbps on Generation 2. Step 5: if each branch later needs two tunnels for redundancy, that becomes 50 tunnels, which pushes you to VpnGw4AZ.

Common mistake: sizing on throughput alone and forgetting tunnel count, or picking Basic to save money. Resizing within a family is usually quick. Moving off Basic, or between families, typically means deleting and recreating the gateway. In a running system that causes an outage for every connected site. It can also force a new public IP that every branch device must be reconfigured to use.

questions.prompt: A logistics company is connecting 12 warehouses to Azure over site-to-site VPN. Each warehouse will run two tunnels for redundancy. Peak combined encrypted traffic is 400 Mbps. The design needs BGP (automatic route exchange) and must survive the loss of one availability zone. Step 1: BGP is required, so Basic is ruled out. Step 2: surviving a zone failure means choosing an AZ variant. Step 3: ??? Step 4: 400 Mbps is under VpnGw1's roughly 650 Mbps, so VpnGw1AZ is the smallest size that meets every requirement. Which statement correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Two tunnels per warehouse gives 24 tunnels, which is close to the limit, so VpnGw4AZ should be chosen to stay safe.
Tunnel count only matters on Basic, so on VpnGw sizes only throughput needs to be checked.
Count one tunnel per warehouse, giving 12 tunnels, which is well under every VpnGw limit, so tunnel count can be skipped.
Two tunnels per warehouse gives 24 tunnels, which fits under the roughly 30-tunnel limit of VpnGw1 to VpnGw3, so VpnGw4 or VpnGw5 is not needed.
questions.why: The tunnel count is 12 sites times 2 tunnels, which is 24, and that fits under the roughly 30-tunnel ceiling of VpnGw1 to VpnGw3, so the choice can then be settled on throughput.

questions.prompt: An Azure VPN gateway SKU fixes a maximum aggregate throughput. What does aggregate throughput mean here?
choices: The unencrypted traffic the gateway forwards between virtual networks inside Azure.
The highest speed any single tunnel can reach, with each tunnel getting its own full allowance.
The combined encrypted traffic across all of the gateway's tunnels added together.
The average traffic per branch, multiplied by the number of availability zones the gateway uses.
questions.why: Aggregate throughput is the total encrypted traffic across every tunnel, and it is a hard ceiling because each SKU reserves a fixed amount of compute for encryption.

questions.prompt: A retail chain needs site-to-site VPN for 60 stores with one tunnel each. Peak combined traffic is only 300 Mbps. BGP is required, but there is no requirement to survive a zone failure. Using the rough figures, which SKU is the best fit?
choices: VpnGw1, because 300 Mbps is well under its roughly 650 Mbps limit.
Basic, because the traffic is low and it is the cheapest option.
VpnGw4, because 60 tunnels exceeds the roughly 30-tunnel limit of VpnGw1 to VpnGw3.
VpnGw2AZ, because BGP is only available on AZ variants.
questions.why: Tunnel count is the binding limit here: 60 tunnels exceeds the roughly 30 allowed by VpnGw1 to VpnGw3, so VpnGw4 with about 100 tunnels is needed even though throughput is low.

questions.prompt: A clinic network deployed a Basic VPN gateway in production to save money. It is now live with 4 branch sites, and the team needs to add BGP. What is the most likely consequence of fixing this?
choices: BGP can be switched on as a setting on the existing Basic gateway, so only the branch routers need updating.
Nothing needs to change on the gateway, because BGP is optional and the branches can keep static routes indefinitely.
The gateway can be resized in place within a few minutes with no effect on the branches, because changing a SKU is always quick.

The gateway typically has to be deleted and recreated on a VpnGw SKU, which causes an outage for every connected site and may require a new public IP that each branch device must be reconfigured to use.
questions.why: Basic does not support BGP, and moving off Basic usually means deleting and recreating the gateway, which disconnects all sites and can force a new public IP onto every branch device.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would pick a VPN gateway SKU for a new site-to-site design, and name one tradeoff or limit that could bite you later.
lessons.modelAnswer: I list the requirements and match each one to a SKU limit. First, I count the tunnels, including any extra tunnels added for redundancy. Second, I add up peak traffic across all sites, because throughput is aggregate across tunnels, not per tunnel. Third, I check features. Needing BGP, active-active mode or custom IPsec policies rules out Basic. Needing to survive a zone failure means an AZ variant like VpnGw2AZ. Then I pick the smallest size that clears every ceiling, with some headroom, and confirm the numbers against the current published table. The tradeoff is cost against future pain. A bigger SKU costs more every hour. Undersizing, or picking Basic, can force a delete-and-recreate later, because you can't always resize across families. That means an outage for all connected sites, and possibly a new public IP that every branch device has to be reconfigured with.
rubricPoints: Defines a SKU as a gateway size that sets throughput, tunnel count and features.
Checks tunnel count, including redundant tunnels, and aggregate throughput against the SKU limits.
Notes that Basic lacks BGP, active-active and zone redundancy, so it suits only dev or test.
Chooses an AZ variant when zone-level resilience is required.
Names the risk that changing families or leaving Basic means recreating the gateway and causing downtime.
Recommends confirming current figures in the official table and leaving headroom.

suggested.rationale: SKU selection is a matching exercise against requirements, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios with tunnel counts, throughput and feature needs builds the skill better than any existing mission.

lessons.plain: A site-to-site VPN is an encrypted tunnel across the public internet that joins a whole office network to a private network in Azure. Once it is up, servers in the office and virtual machines in Azure talk as if they shared one building, even though the traffic crosses the open internet. Think of two locked post rooms in different cities that agree on one secret seal: every parcel is sealed before it leaves and opened only at the other end. Implementing it means building both ends and linking them, so each side knows the other's address and the shared secret.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your office router and your Azure network gateway are both online, but the tunnel between them will not come up. What is one simple setting that must be exactly the same on both ends for them to trust each other?
lessons.teach:
Implementing a site-to-site (S2S) VPN means creating the Azure-side pieces, linking them with a connection, and setting up the on-premises device to match. A VPN is a virtual private network: traffic is encrypted inside a tunnel over the internet. IPsec is the standard suite that does this encryption. IKE (Internet Key Exchange) is the handshake the two ends use to agree on keys.

You need four Azure pieces. A virtual network (VNet) is your private address space in Azure. It must contain a subnet named exactly GatewaySubnet, reserved for the gateway. A virtual network gateway is the managed VPN endpoint, with a public IP address, deployed into that subnet. A local network gateway is an Azure record describing the office: its VPN device's public IP and the office address ranges. A connection of type IPsec (site-to-site) joins the virtual network gateway to the local network gateway and holds a pre-shared key (PSK), a secret string both ends must hold.

Worked example. Azure VNet 10.1.0.0/16, office 192.168.0.0/24, office router public IP 203.0.113.10. First, create GatewaySubnet 10.1.255.0/27. Second, deploy the VPN gateway, which takes a while, and note its public IP, say 198.51.100.5. Third, create a local network gateway with 203.0.113.10 and prefix 192.168.0.0/24. Fourth, create the connection with PSK "Blue-River-77". Fifth, configure the office router: peer 198.51.100.5, the same PSK, matching IPsec/IKE settings, and route 10.1.0.0/16 into the tunnel. When the status shows Connected, a VM at 10.1.0.4 can reach 192.168.0.20.

A common mistake is a typo in the PSK, or wrong prefixes in the local network gateway. Another is office and Azure ranges that overlap. With a PSK mismatch, the tunnel never connects. With wrong or overlapping prefixes, it may show Connected, yet Azure sends office-bound packets nowhere. Users then see timeouts even though the dashboard looks healthy.

questions.prompt: Harbor Logistics is linking its Azure VNet 10.40.0.0/16 to a depot whose LAN is 172.20.8.0/24. Most of the work is already done. GatewaySubnet 10.40.255.0/27 exists. The VPN gateway is deployed with public IP 192.0.2.80. A local network gateway records the depot router's public IP 203.0.113.200 and the prefix 172.20.8.0/24. An IPsec connection exists with the PSK "Gull-Tide-42". On the depot router, the engineer sets the peer to 192.0.2.80, enters the same PSK and matches the IPsec/IKE settings. One step remains on the depot router before a depot PC at 172.20.8.15 can reach an Azure VM at 10.40.1.9. What is it?
choices: Change the peer to 203.0.113.200, so the router points at its own public IP.
Route 172.20.8.0/24 into the tunnel, so the depot's own LAN range is advertised.
Route only 10.40.255.0/27 into the tunnel, because that is where the gateway lives.
Route 10.40.0.0/16 into the tunnel, so traffic bound for the Azure VNet is encrypted toward Azure.
questions.why: The depot router must send traffic for the whole Azure VNet range (10.40.0.0/16) into the tunnel; otherwise packets for 10.40.1.9 never enter it.

questions.prompt: In an Azure site-to-site VPN, what does the local network gateway represent?
choices: An Azure record of the on-premises site: its VPN device's public IP and its address ranges.
The link object that joins the two ends and holds the pre-shared key.
The handshake the two ends use to agree on encryption keys.
The managed VPN endpoint in Azure, deployed into GatewaySubnet with its own public IP.
questions.why: The local network gateway describes the remote office (its device's public IP and its prefixes); the virtual network gateway is the Azure endpoint, and the connection holds the PSK.

questions.prompt: Pinecrest Clinic's Azure VNet is 10.0.0.0/16, and its clinic LAN is also 10.0.0.0/16. After the S2S VPN is built, the connection status shows Connected, but staff get timeouts when they try to reach Azure VMs. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The VPN gateway is still deploying.
The office and Azure address ranges overlap, so Azure cannot send office-bound packets to the right place.
GatewaySubnet is too small for the gateway.
The pre-shared key has a typo on one side.
questions.why: Overlapping ranges can leave the tunnel showing Connected while traffic is misrouted, which gives timeouts behind a healthy-looking dashboard. A PSK typo would stop the tunnel from connecting at all.

questions.prompt: Northwind Brewing finishes its S2S VPN setup, but the connection never reaches the Connected status. The prefixes are correct and do not overlap. Which problem best explains this?
choices: The Azure VM it wants to reach has not been started yet.
The pre-shared key on the office router does not exactly match the PSK on the Azure connection.
The local network gateway lists an extra office prefix that is not in use.
The office router routes the Azure VNet range into the tunnel.
questions.why: Both ends must hold the identical PSK. If it does not match, authentication fails and the tunnel never connects.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, what you must build on each side to bring up a site-to-site VPN, and name one limit or tradeoff of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: On Azure, we need a VNet with a subnet named GatewaySubnet. Into it goes a virtual network gateway, the managed VPN endpoint with a public IP. We also create a local network gateway, which is just Azure's description of our office: the router's public IP and our office address ranges. Then a site-to-site connection links the two and holds a pre-shared key. On our side, we set the office router to point at the Azure gateway's public IP, with the same key and matching IPsec/IKE settings. We also route the Azure ranges into the tunnel. The address ranges must not overlap. If the prefixes are wrong, the tunnel can look Connected while traffic still fails. The tradeoff: the traffic rides the public internet. It is encrypted, but speed and latency are not guaranteed the way a private circuit would be.
rubricPoints: Names the Azure pieces: VNet with GatewaySubnet, virtual network gateway, local network gateway, and connection.
Explains that the local network gateway describes the on-premises device's public IP and address ranges.
States that the pre-shared key and IPsec/IKE settings must match on both ends.
Notes that the on-premises device must be configured and the address spaces must not overlap.
Names a limit, such as traffic crossing the public internet with no guaranteed performance, or a tunnel showing Connected while routing still fails.

suggested.rationale: Tracing a packet from an Azure VM to an office address shows how each piece matters: the gateway, the local network gateway prefixes, and the connection. That makes the build order and the common failures concrete.

lessons.plain: A site-to-site VPN is an encrypted tunnel across the internet between your office network and an Azure virtual network. Azure offers two styles. A policy-based VPN works like a guest list: you write down exact pairs of address ranges that may talk, and only traffic matching a pair goes through. A route-based VPN works like a road with a signpost: the tunnel acts as a network interface, and the routing table decides what traffic drives down it. Route-based is the flexible, modern default. Policy-based exists mainly for older on-premises devices that only understand guest lists.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your office VPN tunnel to Azure works, and then a new office subnet is added. In which style would you expect that subnet's traffic to be silently dropped until someone edits a fixed list of allowed address pairs on both ends: the guest-list style or the signpost style?
lessons.teach:
A policy-based VPN decides what to encrypt using traffic selectors. A traffic selector is a fixed pair of address prefixes, such as on-premises 10.1.0.0/16 and Azure 10.20.0.0/16. A route-based VPN instead creates a virtual tunnel interface, which is a logical network port. Its selector is any-to-any, and the routing table steers traffic into it. Those routes come from static prefixes or from BGP (Border Gateway Protocol), a protocol where the two ends exchange routes automatically.

In Azure, policy-based gateways are limited. They only work on the legacy Basic SKU, which is the gateway size or tier. They support one site-to-site tunnel and only IKEv1. IKE (Internet Key Exchange) is the protocol that negotiates the tunnel's encryption keys. They have no BGP, no point-to-site client connections, and no VNet-to-VNet links. Route-based gateways support IKEv2, BGP, multiple tunnels, point-to-site, VNet-to-VNet, and active-active high availability.

Here is a worked example. With a policy-based tunnel, a packet goes from 10.1.5.4 to 10.20.3.7. The gateway checks it against the pair 10.1.0.0/16 to 10.20.0.0/16, finds a match, and encrypts it. Later the office adds 192.168.50.0/24. Its packets match no pair, so they are dropped until both devices are edited. With a route-based tunnel, you add 192.168.50.0/24 to the routes, or BGP learns it automatically, and the traffic flows.

Use policy-based only when an older on-premises device supports nothing else and you need just one tunnel. Choose route-based in every other case. If you need several sites that each use policy-based devices, use a route-based gateway with its policy-based traffic selector option turned on.

A common mistake is deploying a policy-based gateway and planning to switch later. You cannot change a gateway's VPN type. You must delete the gateway and recreate it, which causes downtime, and the gateway's public IP may change, forcing every peer device to be reconfigured.

questions.prompt: A logistics company has three warehouses. Each warehouse has an older firewall that can only do policy-based VPN, and all three must connect to the same Azure virtual network. An engineer reasons it through. Step 1: A policy-based Azure gateway supports only one site-to-site tunnel, and this design needs three, so a policy-based gateway is ruled out. Step 2: ______. Step 3: Each warehouse firewall keeps its fixed address-prefix pairs, and the Azure side matches them, so all three tunnels can come up. Which statement completes Step 2?
choices: Deploy three separate policy-based gateways in the one virtual network, one for each warehouse firewall.
Deploy a policy-based gateway now and change its VPN type to route-based once the second warehouse connects.
Deploy a route-based gateway and turn on its policy-based traffic selector option so it can match the old firewalls.
Deploy a route-based gateway and enable BGP, because the old firewalls will then learn the routes automatically.
questions.why: When several sites each use policy-based devices, the fit is a route-based gateway with its policy-based traffic selector option turned on, which supports multiple tunnels while matching each device's fixed prefix pairs.

questions.prompt: In a route-based VPN, what decides which traffic is sent into the encrypted tunnel?
choices: A fixed pair of address prefixes configured identically on both VPN devices
The gateway SKU, which sets a limit on which subnets are allowed to be encrypted
The IKEv1 negotiation, which lists every allowed source and destination address
The routing table, which steers traffic to a virtual tunnel interface whose selector is any-to-any
questions.why: A route-based VPN creates a virtual tunnel interface (a logical network port) with an any-to-any selector, and routes, either static or learned via BGP, steer traffic into it.

questions.prompt: A design firm needs a site-to-site link from its head office that exchanges routes automatically with BGP (Border Gateway Protocol), and it also needs remote staff to connect from laptops using point-to-site connections. The head-office router is modern and supports IKEv2. Which gateway VPN type fits?
choices: Policy-based, because the firm needs only one site-to-site tunnel from the head office
Either type works, because both support BGP and point-to-site in Azure
Route-based, because policy-based gateways support neither BGP nor point-to-site
Policy-based on the Basic SKU, with point-to-site added once the tunnel is up
questions.why: Policy-based gateways have no BGP and no point-to-site client connections, while route-based gateways support both, so route-based is the only fit.

questions.prompt: A retailer deployed a policy-based VPN gateway on the Basic SKU for one store. Now a second store needs its own tunnel. What must the retailer do, and what is the impact?
choices: Delete the gateway and recreate it as route-based; expect downtime, and the public IP may change so peers need reconfiguring
Upgrade the gateway's SKU in place; the VPN type changes automatically and the public IP is kept
Edit the gateway's VPN type from policy-based to route-based; the existing tunnel stays up throughout
Add a second traffic selector pair to the existing gateway; the second store then connects without any downtime
questions.why: A gateway's VPN type cannot be changed, so it must be deleted and recreated, which causes downtime and may change the public IP, forcing every peer device to be reconfigured.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how policy-based and route-based VPNs decide what traffic to send through the tunnel, when you would ever pick policy-based in Azure, and what you give up by choosing it.
lessons.modelAnswer: Both styles build an encrypted IPsec tunnel to Azure. They differ in how they pick the traffic to send. Policy-based uses fixed traffic selectors: exact pairs of on-premises and Azure prefixes. Anything outside those pairs is dropped. Route-based treats the tunnel as a virtual interface with any-to-any selectors and lets the routing table decide. Those routes can be static or learned through BGP, so adding a subnet is just a route change. In Azure, I'd only pick policy-based for a single tunnel to an older device that can't do route-based. The tradeoff is big. You are stuck on the Basic SKU with one tunnel and IKEv1, with no BGP, no point-to-site, no VNet-to-VNet, and no active-active. You also can't convert the gateway later; you must delete and recreate it, which means downtime. If several legacy devices are involved, I'd use a route-based gateway with policy-based traffic selectors enabled.
rubricPoints: Policy-based uses fixed prefix-pair traffic selectors; route-based uses a tunnel interface plus the routing table.
Route-based supports BGP, IKEv2, multiple tunnels, point-to-site, VNet-to-VNet and active-active.
Policy-based in Azure is limited to the Basic SKU, a single site-to-site tunnel and IKEv1.
Policy-based is chosen only for legacy on-premises devices that cannot do route-based.
The VPN type cannot be changed after creation; changing it means recreating the gateway, with downtime.
For multiple policy-based devices, use a route-based gateway with policy-based traffic selectors.

suggested.rationale: Exam questions present a device or requirement and ask which VPN type fits, so reasoning through scenario-style situations builds this decision skill best.

lessons.plain: A local network gateway is an Azure record that describes the far end of a VPN: your office or data centre. Azure cannot see your building, so you tell it two things: the public internet address of your on-premises VPN device, and which private address ranges live behind that device. Think of it as an address-book entry for a branch office: the street address (public IP) plus the list of departments reachable there (address ranges). Azure's own VPN endpoint uses this entry to know where to build the encrypted tunnel and which traffic should be sent down it.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your office network uses 10.10.0.0/16, and you later add a new lab subnet, 10.20.0.0/24, behind the same VPN device. Nothing else changes. Will Azure virtual machines automatically be able to reach the lab subnet over the VPN? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
A local network gateway is an Azure resource that represents your on-premises VPN device and network. It is not a device you deploy; it is configuration. Its main settings are: the public IP address or a fully qualified domain name (FQDN, a DNS name that resolves to the device's address); the address space, meaning the on-premises IP prefixes (ranges written like 10.10.0.0/16) that should be reached through the tunnel; and optional BGP settings. BGP, Border Gateway Protocol, lets the two sides exchange routes automatically; if used, you enter the on-premises autonomous system number (ASN, an ID for a routing domain) and the BGP peer IP of the device.

Why it works: the virtual network gateway (Azure's managed VPN endpoint in your virtual network) is paired with the local network gateway through a connection object. Azure turns the local network gateway's prefixes into routes for the virtual network, all pointing at the VPN gateway, and uses the public IP as the tunnel destination.

Worked example: the VNet is 10.1.0.0/16. The office device has public IP 203.0.113.10 and serves 10.10.0.0/16 and 10.20.0.0/24. You create a local network gateway with that IP and both prefixes, then create a site-to-site connection to it. A VM at 10.1.0.4 sends a packet to 10.20.0.5. Azure checks its routes, finds 10.20.0.0/24 pointing at the VPN gateway, encrypts the packet, and sends it to 203.0.113.10, which delivers it inside the office.

Common mistake: leaving out a prefix, or entering the Azure VNet's own range. A missing prefix means packets fall to the default internet route and never reach the office; overlapping ranges cause conflicting routes. You can edit the address space later without rebuilding the tunnel. With BGP enabled, you usually list only the device's BGP peer address (as a /32) because the other prefixes are learned dynamically.

questions.prompt: Northwind Logistics has a virtual network (VNet) at 10.50.0.0/16. Its warehouse VPN device has public IP 198.51.100.20 and serves 192.168.10.0/24 and 192.168.20.0/24. Step 1: Create a local network gateway with public IP 198.51.100.20 and both 192.168.x prefixes in its address space. Step 2: Create a site-to-site connection between the VNet's virtual network gateway and that local network gateway. Step 3: A VM at 10.50.1.4 sends a packet to 192.168.20.9. Step 4: ??? Step 5: The warehouse device receives the packet and delivers it to 192.168.20.9 inside the warehouse. Which choice correctly fills in Step 4?
choices: Azure forwards the packet to the local network gateway, which runs as a VM inside the VNet, decrypts it there, and passes it on.
Azure finds a route for 192.168.20.0/24 that points at the VPN gateway, encrypts the packet, and sends it through the tunnel to 198.51.100.20.
Azure matches 192.168.20.0/24 and sends the encrypted packet straight to the device's inside address, 192.168.20.1.
Azure has no route for 192.168.20.9 because BGP is not enabled, so the packet leaves through the default internet route.
questions.why: The local network gateway's prefixes become VNet routes pointing at the VPN gateway, and its public IP, 198.51.100.20, is used as the tunnel destination.

questions.prompt: In Azure, what is a local network gateway?
choices: Azure's managed VPN endpoint, which you deploy inside your virtual network to terminate tunnels.
A physical or virtual appliance that you install in your office so it can build a tunnel to Azure.
A configuration resource in Azure that describes your on-premises VPN device: its public address and the on-premises IP ranges behind it.
The object that links two gateways together and holds the settings for the tunnel between them.
questions.why: A local network gateway is configuration, not a deployed device, and it represents the on-premises VPN device and network. The managed endpoint is the virtual network gateway, and the linking object is the connection.

questions.prompt: Fabrikam's local network gateway lists 172.16.0.0/16 in its address space. Azure VMs can reach on-premises servers at 172.16.4.10. However, they cannot reach a newer on-premises subnet, 172.17.5.0/24, which sits behind the same VPN device. BGP is not used. What is the most likely cause, and what is the fix?
choices: 172.17.5.0/24 is missing from the address space, so that traffic follows the default internet route. Add the prefix to the local network gateway; the tunnel does not need rebuilding.
A static local network gateway supports only one prefix, so BGP must be enabled before a second range can be added.
The Azure VNet's own address range is missing from the local network gateway, so it must be added to the address space.
The tunnel only learns new prefixes when it is built, so the connection must be deleted and created again.
questions.why: A missing prefix means Azure has no route to the VPN gateway for that range, so traffic falls to the internet route. The address space can be edited later without rebuilding the tunnel.

questions.prompt: Tailspin Toys is creating a local network gateway with BGP enabled. The on-premises device has ASN 65010 (ASN means autonomous system number, an ID for a routing domain) and BGP peer IP 10.200.255.1. The on-premises network uses several 10.200.x.x subnets. What should usually go in the local network gateway's address space?
choices: Only 10.200.255.1/32, because the other on-premises prefixes are learned dynamically through BGP.
The device's public IP as a /32, because that is the address BGP peers with.
Every on-premises subnet must be listed, because BGP only shares routes that are already entered.
The Azure VNet's own address range, so BGP knows which routes to advertise to the office.
questions.why: With BGP enabled, you usually list only the device's BGP peer address as a /32, since BGP exchanges the remaining routes automatically.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a local network gateway is, what you must put into it, and what goes wrong in a running VPN if its address space is incomplete or wrong. Mention how BGP changes what you need to enter.
lessons.modelAnswer: A local network gateway is just Azure's description of our on-premises side; nothing runs there. It holds the public IP or FQDN of our office VPN device, so Azure knows where to aim the tunnel, and the list of on-prem prefixes that should travel through it. When we connect it to the virtual network gateway, Azure creates routes for those prefixes pointing at the VPN gateway. The limit is that static prefixes are only as good as our upkeep: if we add a new office subnet and forget to add it, Azure VMs send that traffic to the internet route and it fails, and if we accidentally overlap the VNet's range we get route conflicts. If we enable BGP, we enter our ASN and the device's BGP peer IP, and routes are learned automatically, which reduces that maintenance risk at the cost of configuring BGP on the device.
rubricPoints: States it is a configuration object representing the on-premises VPN device and network, not a deployed appliance.
Names the public IP or FQDN as the tunnel destination.
Names the address space as the on-premises prefixes routed through the tunnel.
Explains that a missing or overlapping prefix breaks or misroutes traffic.
Notes that BGP settings (ASN, peer IP) allow routes to be learned instead of listed manually.

suggested.rationale: Tracing a packet's path shows directly how the prefixes in a local network gateway decide whether traffic enters the VPN tunnel or falls to the internet route.

lessons.plain: An IPsec/IKE policy is the agreed list of security settings two VPN devices use to build an encrypted tunnel between them. IPsec is the set of rules that encrypts traffic between networks, and IKE (Internet Key Exchange) is how the two ends prove who they are and agree on secret keys. Think of two embassies agreeing on which lock, which seal, and how often to change keys before they send any diplomatic bags. On an Azure VPN gateway, a managed VPN endpoint in a virtual network, you can accept Azure's default settings or set a custom policy so it matches exactly what your office firewall requires.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your office firewall only accepts one exact set of encryption settings. If you set Azure to use a different set, do you think the tunnel would still come up with weaker settings, or not come up at all?
lessons.teach:
A custom IPsec/IKE policy is a fixed set of cryptographic choices attached to one site-to-site connection on an Azure VPN gateway. Without one, Azure offers a list of default combinations and accepts whichever one the on-premises device proposes. With one, Azure offers and accepts only that single combination.

The policy covers two phases. Phase 1 (the IKE security association, a temporary trust agreement) authenticates the two peers and builds a protected control channel. You pick its encryption (for example AES256), its integrity check, a hash that detects tampering (for example SHA256), and a Diffie-Hellman (DH) group, a method for two parties to agree on a shared secret over an open network; a higher group number usually means a stronger key. Phase 2 (the IPsec security association) protects the actual data. You pick its encryption, its integrity, and a PFS group. PFS (Perfect Forward Secrecy) means each rekey performs a fresh DH exchange, so stealing one key does not unlock older traffic. You also set SA lifetimes, meaning how long, in seconds or kilobytes, a key is used before being replaced.

Worked example: the network team says the office firewall requires AES256, SHA256 and DH group 14 for phase 1, and AES256, SHA256 and PFS group 2048 (equivalent to group 14) for phase 2, with a 27,000-second lifetime. You open the connection resource, choose a custom policy, enter those exact values on both phases, and save. The gateway then rekeys the tunnel using only that combination. Note that custom policies need a VPN gateway SKU above Basic, and each connection holds one policy.

The common mistake is a single mismatch, such as PFS set to None in Azure while the firewall demands PFS. Because a custom policy gives Azure no fallback, phase 2 negotiation fails and the connection stays down, so on-premises users lose access to Azure workloads until both sides match exactly.

questions.prompt: A logistics company, Northgate Freight, is connecting its warehouse firewall to Azure with a site-to-site VPN. The firewall team states its requirements. Phase 1: AES192 encryption, SHA384 integrity, DH group 24. Phase 2: AES192 encryption, SHA256 integrity, PFS group 24. SA lifetime: 3,600 seconds. The engineer works through the setup. Step 1: confirm the Azure VPN gateway uses a SKU above Basic. Step 2: open the warehouse connection resource and choose a custom IPsec/IKE policy. Step 3: enter AES192, SHA384 and DH group 24 for phase 1. Step 4: ??? Step 5: save, so the gateway negotiates only this one combination. What belongs in Step 4?
choices: Set phase 2 to AES192, SHA384 and PFS group 24, because phase 2 should reuse the phase 1 integrity setting, with a 3,600-second lifetime
Set phase 2 to AES192, SHA256 and PFS None, because phase 1 already performed a DH exchange
Set phase 2 to AES192, SHA256 and PFS group 24, with an SA lifetime of 3,600 seconds
Leave phase 2 at Azure's defaults, so Azure can accept whatever data-protection settings the firewall proposes
questions.why: A custom policy has no fallback, so phase 2 must match the firewall's stated values exactly: AES192, SHA256, PFS group 24 and a 3,600-second lifetime.

questions.prompt: A university links its campus VPN device to an Azure VPN gateway. At first it uses no custom IPsec/IKE policy. Later an engineer attaches a custom policy to that connection. What changes in how Azure negotiates the tunnel?
choices: Azure now accepts any combination the campus device proposes, including weaker ones
Azure keeps its list of default combinations and adds the custom one as the preferred first option
Azure now offers and accepts only the single combination defined in the custom policy
The custom policy is applied to every connection on the gateway, not just this one
questions.why: Without a custom policy Azure accepts any of its default combinations. With one, it offers and accepts only that one combination for that connection.

questions.prompt: A small retailer, Bramble Books, runs an Azure VPN gateway on the Basic SKU. Its security auditor requires a specific custom IPsec/IKE policy on the store's site-to-site connection. What must happen before the policy can be applied?
choices: Create a second connection, because each connection can hold only one policy
Set the SA lifetime in kilobytes rather than seconds, because Basic supports only kilobyte lifetimes
Enable PFS on the on-premises firewall, because that unlocks custom policies on Basic
Move the gateway to a SKU above Basic, because Basic does not support custom policies
questions.why: Custom IPsec/IKE policies need a VPN gateway SKU above Basic, so the gateway must be upgraded first.

questions.prompt: A hospital applies a custom IPsec/IKE policy on its Azure connection. The policy sets phase 2 encryption to AES128. The on-premises firewall requires AES256 for phase 2, and every other setting matches. What is the most likely result?
choices: Azure falls back to its default combinations, and the tunnel comes up using AES256
The tunnel comes up using AES128, because Azure's setting takes priority
Phase 1 fails, because encryption mismatches always break the IKE security association
Phase 2 negotiation fails and the connection stays down until both sides match
questions.why: A custom policy gives Azure no fallback, so a single phase 2 mismatch makes phase 2 fail. The tunnel stays down, and on-premises users lose access to Azure workloads.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a custom IPsec/IKE policy on an Azure VPN connection controls and why you might set one, including the main risk or limitation of using it instead of the defaults.
lessons.modelAnswer: A custom IPsec/IKE policy pins the exact cryptography for one site-to-site connection. Phase 1, the IKE part, authenticates the two gateways and sets up a protected control channel using a chosen encryption, integrity hash and Diffie-Hellman group. Phase 2, the IPsec part, protects the real traffic with its own encryption, integrity and PFS group, so every rekey gets fresh key material. We also set how long keys live before they are replaced. We use it when compliance or the on-premises device demands specific algorithms, or to block weaker defaults. The tradeoff is strictness: with a custom policy Azure offers only that one combination, so any mismatch with the firewall, even just the PFS setting, stops the tunnel from coming up. It also requires a gateway SKU above Basic, and each connection holds only one policy.
rubricPoints: States the policy fixes the cryptographic settings for one site-to-site connection.
Distinguishes phase 1 (IKE: authenticate peers, control channel) from phase 2 (IPsec: protect data).
Names the settings involved: encryption, integrity, DH group, PFS group, and SA lifetime.
Explains why to use it: compliance or matching a specific on-premises device.
Names the risk: no fallback, so any mismatch prevents the tunnel from connecting.
Mentions a limit such as the Basic SKU lacking support or one policy per connection.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine configures VPN cryptography, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios about matching phase 1 and phase 2 settings to a device's requirements builds the needed judgment best.

lessons.plain: A virtual network gateway is the doorway between a private network you build in Azure, called a virtual network or VNet, and networks outside it, such as your office or another cloud network. Think of a guarded loading dock on a warehouse. The dock is built into one specially marked bay and has a public street address. A guard checks and seals every shipment that passes through. You build the dock once, choosing its size and style. Later you add the individual delivery routes, which are the connections. Creating the gateway means picking that bay, the address, the dock's type and its capacity.
lessons.guessPrompt: Azure insists the gateway lives in its own dedicated subnet with an exact, fixed name. Why do you think the platform would refuse to let you place it in an ordinary subnet alongside your virtual machines?
lessons.teach:
A virtual network gateway is a managed set of Azure-run machines that carries encrypted or private traffic between a VNet and outside networks. You never log in to these machines. You only set their options.

The key settings:

GatewaySubnet is a subnet that must use exactly this name. Azure places the gateway instances in it and nothing else may go there. Size it at /27 or larger so the gateway can scale and can sit alongside an ExpressRoute gateway later.

Gateway type is VPN for encrypted tunnels over the internet, or ExpressRoute for private circuits. This lesson covers VPN.

VPN type is usually route-based. In a route-based gateway, the routing table decides which traffic enters the tunnel. The older policy-based type is far more limited.

The SKU is the size tier, for example VpnGw2AZ. It sets throughput, tunnel count and features. The AZ suffix means the gateway is spread across availability zones, which are separate datacenters in one region.

The public IP address is the gateway's internet-facing address. It should be a Standard, static address.

Active-active mode runs two live instances, each with its own public IP. The alternative is active-standby, where one instance waits for the other to fail.

BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) lets routers exchange routes automatically. Enabling it requires an ASN, which is a routing identity number. Azure's default ASN is 65515.

Worked example. Your VNet is 10.1.0.0/16. First, add a subnet named GatewaySubnet at 10.1.255.0/27. Next, create the gateway with type VPN, route-based, SKU VpnGw2AZ, and a new Standard static public IP. Leave active-active off and enable BGP with ASN 65515. Deployment then runs for roughly 30 to 45 minutes. After that, site connections can be attached.

Common mistake: naming the subnet "gateway-subnet" or making it /29. A misnamed subnet blocks creation. An undersized one blocks later growth and forces a rebuild. Also avoid attaching network security groups, or a default route sending all traffic elsewhere, to GatewaySubnet. Either can silently break tunnels in a running system.

questions.prompt: A clinic network, Harbourview Health, has a VNet at 172.20.0.0/16 and wants both gateway instances to carry traffic at the same time. Steps so far: (1) add a subnet named GatewaySubnet at 172.20.250.0/27; (2) choose gateway type VPN, VPN type route-based, SKU VpnGw3AZ; (3) turn active-active mode on; (4) ??? ; (5) enable BGP and start the deployment, then wait roughly 30 to 45 minutes before attaching site connections. What belongs in step 4?
choices: Skip the public IP, because the GatewaySubnet already gives the gateway an address
Create one Standard, static public IP and let both instances share it
Create two Basic, dynamic public IPs so each instance can pick up a new address
Create two Standard, static public IPs, one for each live instance
questions.why: Active-active runs two live instances that each need their own public IP, and gateway public IPs should be Standard and static.

questions.prompt: Northwind Freight's VNet is 192.168.0.0/16. They expect to add an ExpressRoute gateway next to their VPN gateway next year. Which subnet setup for the VPN gateway is valid and leaves room to grow?
choices: A subnet named GatewaySubnet at 192.168.10.0/29
A subnet named GatewaySubnet at 192.168.10.0/27 that also hosts a small management VM
A subnet named gateway-subnet at 192.168.10.0/27
A subnet named GatewaySubnet at 192.168.10.0/26
questions.why: The subnet must be named exactly GatewaySubnet, must be /27 or larger (a /26 is larger), and must hold nothing except the gateway.

questions.prompt: Contoso Bakeries had working VPN tunnels for months. This week an administrator applied a route table to every subnet in the VNet, including GatewaySubnet, that sends all traffic (0.0.0.0/0) to a firewall appliance. Shortly afterwards the tunnels stopped passing traffic, with no deployment error shown. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The gateway's public IP was converted from static to dynamic
The default route applied to GatewaySubnet sent gateway traffic elsewhere and silently broke the tunnels
BGP was disabled automatically when the route table changed
The gateway SKU is too small for the new firewall's throughput
questions.why: A default route sending all traffic elsewhere, attached to GatewaySubnet, can silently break tunnels on a running gateway.

questions.prompt: Fabrikam Logistics needs its VPN gateway to keep working even if one datacenter in its Azure region goes offline. Which gateway setting most directly meets this requirement?
choices: Choose a SKU with the AZ suffix, such as VpnGw2AZ
Enable BGP using Azure's default ASN of 65515
Set the VPN type to policy-based instead of route-based
Use active-standby mode so one instance waits for the other to fail
questions.why: The AZ suffix spreads the gateway across availability zones, which are separate datacenters in one region, so the loss of one datacenter does not take the gateway down.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what you must decide when creating a VPN virtual network gateway, and name one choice that is costly to get wrong because it is slow or hard to change later.
lessons.modelAnswer: A virtual network gateway is the managed doorway Azure runs so our VNet can reach on-premises or other networks over encrypted tunnels. Before creating it, we need a subnet named exactly GatewaySubnet, ideally /27 or bigger, with nothing else in it. Then we choose gateway type VPN and VPN type route-based, so routing decides what enters the tunnel. We also pick a SKU for throughput and tunnel count, preferably a zone-redundant AZ one, and give it a Standard static public IP. Two more choices are active-active versus active-standby, and whether to enable BGP with an ASN. The tradeoff is time and rigidity. Creation takes 30 to 45 minutes. An undersized GatewaySubnet can't simply be grown while the gateway sits in it, so we'd face a rebuild and downtime. It's worth sizing generously up front.
rubricPoints: Defines the gateway as a managed Azure resource linking a VNet to outside networks.
States the GatewaySubnet must have that exact name, be dedicated, and be /27 or larger.
Names gateway type VPN, route-based VPN type, SKU and public IP as core settings.
Mentions active-active versus active-standby and optional BGP with an ASN.
Names a limit such as long deployment time or the cost of an undersized subnet.

suggested.rationale: Creating a gateway is mostly a set of configuration facts and fixed rules, such as the subnet name, sizing and setting choices, that no current mission or planned engine exercises directly.

lessons.plain: A virtual network gateway is the managed VPN endpoint that Azure runs at the edge of your virtual network (VNet, your private network in the cloud). It builds an encrypted tunnel to a VPN device in your office. When that tunnel fails, diagnosing means working out which layer broke: the two ends cannot reach each other, they cannot agree how to encrypt, or the tunnel is up but traffic is not routed into it. Think of two people with a locked box. Either the courier cannot find the address, the keys do not match, or the box arrives but nobody knows which room it belongs in.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your Azure VPN connection shows as connected, yet an office server still cannot reach an Azure virtual machine. Is the problem more likely the encryption settings or the routing settings, and why?
lessons.teach:
Diagnosing a virtual network gateway connection means isolating the failure to one of three layers. Reachability: the two public IP addresses must be able to exchange IKE traffic (Internet Key Exchange, the handshake that negotiates keys) on UDP ports 500 and 4500, plus encrypted ESP packets. Negotiation: both sides must use the same pre-shared key (a password both ends know) and matching IPsec/IKE settings such as encryption algorithm, integrity check, Diffie-Hellman group and lifetimes. Routing: once the tunnel is up, each side must know which address ranges belong on the other side.

This split works because the connection status tells you which layer to look at. "Not connected" or "Connecting" points to reachability or negotiation. "Connected" with no traffic points to routing. Azure Network Watcher's VPN troubleshoot tool runs checks against the gateway and connection and writes logs, and gateway diagnostic logs (IKE and tunnel logs) record why a handshake failed, such as a key or proposal mismatch.

Worked example: status shows Connected, but on-premises 10.20.5.0/24 cannot reach a VM. Step one, the tunnel is up, so keys and IKE are fine. Step two, open the local network gateway (Azure's record of the on-premises site: its public IP and address prefixes). It lists only 10.20.0.0/24. Step three, Azure does not route 10.20.5.0/24 into the tunnel, so replies go nowhere. Fix: add the missing prefix, or use BGP (a routing protocol that exchanges routes automatically).

Other checks: the local network gateway has the device's correct public IP; address spaces do not overlap; the device type matches the gateway (policy-based versus route-based); no user-defined route on GatewaySubnet sends traffic away; network security groups on the VMs allow the flow. As a last resort, resetting the gateway restarts its instances and briefly drops every tunnel.

Common mistake: changing encryption settings when the tunnel already shows Connected. That cannot fix a routing gap and may break a working tunnel, causing an outage for every site on that gateway.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's site-to-site connection from its Lisbon warehouse to Azure shows the status "Connecting" and never reaches "Connected". Step 1: The tunnel is not up, so routing is not the problem yet. The fault is in reachability or negotiation. Step 2: The engineer confirms that the local network gateway (Azure's record of the on-premises site) holds the warehouse device's correct public IP. The engineer also confirms that UDP 500 and 4500 traffic arrives at the Azure gateway, so reachability looks fine. Step 3: The gateway's IKE diagnostic log reports that authentication failed because the shared secret did not match. Step 4: ??? Which action correctly completes Step 4?
choices: Add the warehouse address range to the local network gateway so traffic is routed into the tunnel
Set the same pre-shared key on both the Azure connection and the warehouse device
Reset the Azure gateway so its instances restart and retry the handshake
Add a network security group rule allowing the warehouse range to reach the VMs
questions.why: The log points to a negotiation failure caused by mismatched shared secrets, so the fix is to make the pre-shared key identical on both ends; routing and NSG changes only matter once the tunnel is up.

questions.prompt: In Azure VPN troubleshooting, what is a local network gateway?
choices: Azure's record of the on-premises site, holding its public IP and address prefixes
A Network Watcher tool that runs checks against a connection and writes logs
A routing protocol that exchanges address prefixes automatically between sites
The Azure-side gateway instance that terminates IPsec tunnels in GatewaySubnet
questions.why: A local network gateway represents the on-premises side in Azure, so a wrong public IP or a missing prefix there breaks reachability or routing.

questions.prompt: A hospital's VPN connection to Azure shows "Connected". All the on-premises clinic ranges are listed correctly on the local network gateway. Clinic staff can reach every VM in the app subnet except one, called rx-vm-07. What is the most sensible next check?
choices: The network security group rules that apply to rx-vm-07
Whether UDP ports 500 and 4500 are open between the two public IPs
Whether the clinic device is policy-based or route-based
The IKE encryption algorithm and Diffie-Hellman group on both sides
questions.why: The tunnel is up and the other VMs in the same subnet are reachable, so the fault is specific to that one VM. A network security group (a set of allow and deny rules for traffic) on that VM blocking the flow fits best.

questions.prompt: An Azure VPN gateway serves six branch offices. Only the Denver branch reports a problem: its tunnel shows "Connected", but no traffic passes. A colleague suggests resetting the gateway first. Why is that a poor first move?
choices: A reset only clears Network Watcher logs and does nothing to the tunnels
A reset restarts the gateway instances and briefly drops all six tunnels, without targeting the routing gap
A reset permanently deletes the pre-shared keys, so every connection must be rebuilt
A reset changes the gateway from route-based to policy-based
questions.why: Resetting is a last resort: it interrupts every site on the gateway. A Connected tunnel with no traffic points to routing, which a reset does not fix.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would work through a broken site-to-site VPN to Azure, starting from the connection status, and name one limit or tradeoff of a fix you might use.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with the connection status because it tells me which layer to check. If it says Not connected, the problem is reachability or negotiation: I confirm the local network gateway has the office device's right public IP, that UDP 500 and 4500 and ESP are allowed, that the pre-shared key matches exactly, and that the IKE and IPsec settings agree on both sides. Network Watcher's VPN troubleshoot and the IKE diagnostic logs usually name the mismatch. If it says Connected but traffic fails, encryption is fine, so I look at routing: missing address prefixes in the local network gateway, overlapping ranges, a route table on GatewaySubnet, or a network security group blocking the VM. One tradeoff: resetting the gateway can clear a stuck state, but it drops every tunnel on that gateway for a short while, so it affects other sites too.
rubricPoints: Uses connection status to separate reachability/negotiation problems from routing problems.
Names negotiation causes such as a mismatched pre-shared key or IKE/IPsec settings.
Names routing causes such as missing local network gateway prefixes or overlapping address spaces.
Mentions a diagnostic tool such as Network Watcher VPN troubleshoot or gateway diagnostic logs.
States a tradeoff, such as a gateway reset briefly dropping all tunnels.

suggested.rationale: Tracing a packet across the virtual network and tunnel and seeing exactly where it stops is the core skill of telling a negotiation failure from a routing gap.

lessons.plain: Azure Extended Network is a way to stretch one of your on-premises subnets into Azure, so a server you move to the cloud can keep the exact same IP address it had in your data center. Think of it like an extension cord between two rooms: the outlet in the new room is still on the same circuit as the old one. Two small helper virtual machines, one on each side, pass traffic for that subnet back and forth through a tunnel. Other machines keep reaching the moved server at its old address, so nothing has to be renumbered during a migration.
lessons.guessPrompt: You are moving a server to Azure, but dozens of old applications have its IP address hard-coded. What would you need so the server keeps that same address in Azure and its on-premises neighbours can still reach it as if nothing moved?
lessons.teach:
Azure Extended Network is a feature that extends a layer 2 subnet from on-premises into an Azure virtual network (VNet, Azure's private network). A layer 2 subnet is one where machines reach each other directly by hardware address, without passing through a router. Its main use is migration: a workload can move to Azure and keep its original IP address.

How it works: you deploy two appliance virtual machines running Windows Server 2022 Datacenter: Azure Edition, one in your data center and one in Azure, and configure them with Windows Admin Center, a browser-based server management tool. Each appliance has two network interfaces: an internal one attached to the subnet being extended, and an external one on a routable network. The appliances wrap subnet traffic in VXLAN (Virtual Extensible LAN), a protocol that carries layer 2 frames inside ordinary UDP packets, and send it between their external addresses. That transport rides on hybrid connectivity you must already have: a site-to-site VPN (an encrypted tunnel over the internet) or ExpressRoute (a private circuit to Azure). In Azure you create a subnet with the same address range as the on-premises one, plus a separate subnet for the Azure appliance's external interface.

Worked example: on-premises subnet 10.10.1.0/24 holds an app at 10.10.1.20 and a database at 10.10.1.30. You migrate the app into the matching Azure subnet, keeping 10.10.1.20. The database sends to 10.10.1.20; since it is the same subnet, no router is involved. The on-premises appliance picks up the frame on its internal interface, encapsulates it in VXLAN, and sends it over the VPN to the Azure appliance's external address. The Azure appliance unwraps it and delivers it to the app. Replies follow the reverse path.

Common mistake: treating it as a connectivity option that replaces VPN or ExpressRoute. It does not; it sits on top of one. The consequence in a running system: every frame for the stretched subnet hops through two appliances and a tunnel, adding latency and making those appliances a bottleneck and single point of failure, so it is meant as a temporary bridge, removed once migration finishes and addresses can be changed.

questions.prompt:
A logistics company, Harbor Freight Lines, is migrating servers from its on-premises subnet 192.168.40.0/24 into Azure. It already has an ExpressRoute circuit (a private connection to Azure) and has deployed Azure Extended Network appliances: two Windows Server 2022 Datacenter: Azure Edition virtual machines, one on-premises and one in Azure. A file server has moved into the matching Azure subnet and kept its address, 192.168.40.15. A print server that is still on-premises at 192.168.40.50 sends a frame to 192.168.40.15.

Step 1: The print server sees that 192.168.40.15 is in its own subnet, so it sends the frame directly, with no router involved.
Step 2: The on-premises appliance picks up the frame on its internal interface, the one attached to the stretched subnet.
Step 3: ???
Step 4: The Azure appliance receives the traffic on its external interface, unwraps it, and delivers the original frame to the file server.

Which action belongs in step 3?
choices: The appliance sends the frame straight across the public internet to the Azure appliance, with no VPN or ExpressRoute involved.
The appliance changes the destination to a new Azure address so the file server can be reached.
The appliance wraps the frame in VXLAN and sends it over ExpressRoute to the Azure appliance's external address.
The appliance hands the frame to the on-premises router, which routes it to Azure as an ordinary packet for 192.168.40.15.
questions.why: The appliances carry layer 2 frames between sites by wrapping them in VXLAN, which puts each frame inside ordinary UDP packets, and sending them between their external addresses over the hybrid link that already exists, here ExpressRoute.

questions.prompt: A hospital wants to move a legacy scheduling application to Azure. Other systems reach the application by a hard-coded IP address in subnet 172.20.5.0/24, so the application must keep that address during the move. Which statement best describes how Azure Extended Network helps?
choices: It assigns the application a new Azure address and translates traffic from the old address to the new one.
It replaces the need for a site-to-site VPN or ExpressRoute by creating its own private circuit to Azure.
It stretches the on-premises layer 2 subnet into an Azure virtual network, so the application can move and keep its original IP address.
It places a router between the on-premises and Azure halves of the subnet so traffic is routed rather than switched.
questions.why: Extended Network extends a layer 2 subnet into Azure, so machines on both sides reach each other directly as one subnet and migrated workloads can keep their IP addresses.

questions.prompt: A retailer has a site-to-site VPN to Azure and wants to use Azure Extended Network to stretch its on-premises subnet 10.50.8.0/24 into an Azure virtual network. Which subnet design does it need in Azure?
choices: A subnet with the same range, 10.50.8.0/24, plus a separate subnet for the Azure appliance's external interface.
A single subnet with a different address range, such as 10.60.8.0/24, used by both the migrated workloads and the appliance.
Only a subnet for the appliance's external interface, because the stretched address range stays on-premises.
A subnet with the same range, 10.50.8.0/24, and nothing else, because the appliance's external interface also connects to that subnet.
questions.why: Azure needs a subnet matching the on-premises address range for the migrated workloads, plus a separate routable subnet for the Azure appliance's external interface, which carries the VXLAN traffic.

questions.prompt: A bank finished migrating every server from its stretched subnet into Azure six months ago. It still runs its Azure Extended Network appliances and plans to keep them as the permanent design. What is the main risk of this plan?
choices: None, because Extended Network is built to be a long-term replacement for VPN and ExpressRoute.
The migrated servers will lose their original IP addresses once the appliances have run for more than a few months.
The appliances will stop encrypting traffic, because VXLAN takes over from the VPN after the migration ends.
Every frame for the stretched subnet passes through two appliances and a tunnel, adding latency and making the appliances a bottleneck and single point of failure.
questions.why: Extended Network is meant as a temporary bridge; kept in place, it leaves all traffic for the stretched subnet depending on two appliances and a tunnel, which adds latency and creates a bottleneck and a single point of failure.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what Azure Extended Network does, what it depends on, and why you would not leave it running forever.
lessons.modelAnswer: Azure Extended Network stretches an on-premises subnet into an Azure VNet so a migrated server keeps its original IP address. We run two appliance VMs on Windows Server 2022 Datacenter: Azure Edition, one on-prem and one in Azure, set up through Windows Admin Center. Each has an internal interface on the extended subnet and an external one on a routable network. They wrap the subnet's traffic in VXLAN and send it between them. It needs a site-to-site VPN or ExpressRoute already in place; it doesn't replace that link. In Azure we create a subnet with the same range as on-prem plus a subnet for the appliance's external side. The tradeoff is that all traffic for that subnet goes through two appliances and a tunnel, which adds latency and creates a bottleneck and single point of failure. So it's a migration bridge: once apps stop depending on fixed addresses, we re-IP and remove it.
rubricPoints: States that it extends an on-premises subnet into Azure so migrated workloads keep their IP addresses.
Mentions the pair of appliance VMs, one on each side, tunneling traffic with VXLAN.
Notes it requires existing site-to-site VPN or ExpressRoute connectivity rather than replacing it.
Mentions the matching subnet range in Azure and a separate subnet for the external interface.
Names a limit such as added latency, appliance bottleneck, or single point of failure, making it a temporary migration tool.

suggested.rationale: Tracing a frame from an on-premises host through both appliances and the VXLAN tunnel to the migrated server is the clearest way to see what the extended network does and where its latency and failure points sit.

lessons.plain: A point-to-site VPN lets individual devices, such as a remote worker's laptop, open their own encrypted tunnel into a private network in Azure. The tunnels end on a virtual network gateway, a managed service that Azure runs for you. That gateway comes in sizes called SKUs, short for stock-keeping units, meaning product tiers. Picking a SKU is like choosing a building entrance: a small door is cheap but admits few people at once, while a wider set of doors costs more and handles a crowd. The SKU you choose sets how many people can be connected at once, how much total traffic flows, and which connection features are available.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose 400 remote employees may all be connected at the same moment, and the gateway sizes you can buy allow 250, 500 or 1,000 simultaneous user connections. Which size would you pick, and why not the smallest?
lessons.teach:
Selecting a gateway SKU for point-to-site (P2S) VPN means matching a gateway tier to four needs: how many clients connect at once, total bandwidth, which tunnel protocols and sign-in methods clients use, and whether the gateway must survive a datacenter failure. A virtual network gateway is Azure's managed VPN endpoint, and P2S requires it to be route-based, meaning it forwards traffic using a routing table.

The tiers grow in steps. Basic is a legacy tier: it allows about 128 connections and supports only SSTP, a tunnel protocol that runs over the web port 443. It does not support IKEv2 or OpenVPN, two other tunnel protocols, and it does not support RADIUS, a central sign-in server, or Microsoft Entra ID, Microsoft's cloud identity service. VpnGw1 to VpnGw5 add capacity: roughly 250, 500, 1,000, 5,000 and 10,000 P2S connections, with aggregate throughput rising from about 650 Mbps to about 10 Gbps. An AZ suffix, as in VpnGw2AZ, makes the gateway zone-redundant, meaning it is spread across availability zones, which are separate datacenters in a region.

Worked example: 700 staff use OpenVPN with Entra ID sign-in and the gateway must survive a zone outage. Step one, Basic is out because it lacks OpenVPN and Entra ID. Step two, VpnGw1 at 250 and VpnGw2 at 500 are too small. Step three, VpnGw3 at 1,000 fits with headroom. Step four, zone survival adds AZ. Answer: VpnGw3AZ.

A common mistake is ignoring the protocol cap: SSTP is limited to about 128 connections on every SKU, so a large VpnGw4 still turns away the 129th SSTP user. Choose IKEv2 or OpenVPN for large groups. In a running system, an undersized gateway rejects new users once full, and moving from Basic to a VpnGw tier requires deleting and recreating the gateway, which causes downtime, while resizing between VpnGw tiers of the same generation is far less disruptive.

questions.prompt: A logistics company has 3,200 field contractors who connect with IKEv2 and sign in through the company's RADIUS server. There is no requirement to survive an availability zone outage. Step one: Basic is ruled out because it supports neither IKEv2 nor RADIUS. Step two: VpnGw1 (about 250), VpnGw2 (about 500) and VpnGw3 (about 1,000) are all too small for 3,200 simultaneous clients. Step three: ???. Step four: no zone survival is needed, so no AZ suffix is added. Which statement completes step three?
choices: VpnGw3 at about 1,000 is enough if the contractors connect in shifts rather than all at once
VpnGw4AZ is required, because any gateway above 1,000 clients must be zone-redundant
VpnGw5 at about 10,000 is needed, because RADIUS sign-in is only offered on the largest tier
VpnGw4 at about 5,000 connections is the smallest tier that fits 3,200 with headroom
questions.why: VpnGw4 allows roughly 5,000 P2S connections, the first step above 3,200, and RADIUS is available on all VpnGw tiers, so the larger VpnGw5 and the AZ variant are unnecessary.

questions.prompt: A design firm runs a VpnGw3 gateway, which allows about 1,000 point-to-site connections. All 400 of its remote designers connect using SSTP. What happens when they all try to connect, and what is the fix?
choices: All 400 connect, because VpnGw3 supports about 1,000 connections of any protocol
About 250 connect and the rest are refused, so the gateway should be resized to VpnGw4
All 400 connect, but only if the gateway is switched to the zone-redundant VpnGw3AZ
About 128 connect and the rest are refused, so clients should move to IKEv2 or OpenVPN
questions.why: SSTP is capped at about 128 connections on every SKU, so the larger gateway does not help; using IKEv2 or OpenVPN removes that cap.

questions.prompt: A small charity has 180 volunteers who connect with OpenVPN and sign in with Microsoft Entra ID. Zone redundancy is not required. Which is the smallest suitable gateway SKU?
choices: Basic, because 180 users is close to its limit of about 128 connections
VpnGw1AZ, because OpenVPN gateways must always be zone-redundant
VpnGw2, because Entra ID sign-in needs at least about 500 connections
VpnGw1, because it fits about 250 clients and supports OpenVPN and Entra ID
questions.why: Basic lacks OpenVPN and Entra ID support, and VpnGw1 is the next tier with roughly 250 connections, enough for 180 clients.

questions.prompt: A clinic's point-to-site gateway is on the legacy Basic SKU, and it now needs IKEv2 for 300 staff, so it must move to VpnGw2. What should the team plan for during this change?
choices: A simple in-place resize with almost no interruption, just like moving from VpnGw1 to VpnGw2
No change at all, because Basic can be given IKEv2 support by editing its settings
Only adding an AZ suffix, since zone redundancy is what unlocks IKEv2 on Basic
Deleting and recreating the gateway, which means a period of VPN downtime for users
questions.why: Moving from Basic to a VpnGw tier requires deleting and recreating the gateway, causing downtime, unlike resizing between VpnGw tiers of the same generation.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would pick a virtual network gateway SKU for a point-to-site VPN, including at least one limit or tradeoff that could catch them out.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with the requirement, not the price. First, how many users might be connected at the same time: VpnGw1 handles about 250, VpnGw2 about 500, VpnGw3 about 1,000, and VpnGw4 and VpnGw5 go to 5,000 and 10,000. Second, total bandwidth, since aggregate throughput also rises by tier. Third, protocols and sign-in: Basic only does SSTP and cannot use IKEv2, OpenVPN, RADIUS or Entra ID, so it is rarely the right choice. Fourth, if we need to survive a datacenter outage, I pick the AZ version. The tradeoffs: bigger tiers cost more, and SSTP caps at about 128 users no matter how big the gateway is, so large groups should use IKEv2 or OpenVPN. Also, upgrading from Basic means rebuilding the gateway with downtime, so I size with headroom up front.
rubricPoints: Concurrent connection count drives the minimum tier.
Aggregate throughput must cover expected total traffic.
Basic lacks IKEv2, OpenVPN, RADIUS and Entra ID support.
SSTP is capped near 128 connections on every SKU.
AZ variants add zone redundancy for resilience.
Leaving Basic requires recreating the gateway, so plan headroom.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine sizes VPN gateways, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios that weigh user count, protocol and resilience builds the selection skill best.

lessons.plain: When a single laptop connects to an Azure virtual network over a point-to-site VPN (a private, encrypted link from one device into the cloud network), the data travels inside a tunnel. The tunnel type is the protocol that builds that tunnel. Azure offers three: OpenVPN, SSTP and IKEv2. Picking one is like choosing a shipping company for parcels. Each company accepts different kinds of senders (operating systems), uses different roads (network ports), and some roads are closed in certain places, such as hotel or airport Wi-Fi that blocks unusual traffic. You pick the tunnel types that every user can actually use from where they work.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your staff use Windows, Mac and Linux laptops and often work from hotels whose Wi-Fi only allows ordinary web traffic. What would you look for in a VPN protocol so all of them can connect?
lessons.teach:
A tunnel type is the protocol a point-to-site VPN uses to wrap and encrypt traffic between a user's device and the Azure virtual network gateway, the managed service that terminates VPN connections for a virtual network. You set it in the gateway's point-to-site configuration.

The three options differ in transport and client support. SSTP (Secure Socket Tunneling Protocol) is a Microsoft protocol that runs over TLS (the same encryption used by HTTPS) on TCP port 443. Because it looks like web traffic it passes most firewalls, but it is supported only on Windows. IKEv2 (Internet Key Exchange version 2) sets up an IPsec tunnel, IPsec being a standard suite for encrypting IP packets. It uses UDP ports 500 and 4500 and has built-in clients on Windows, macOS, iOS and Android, but restrictive networks often block those UDP ports. OpenVPN is an open TLS-based protocol that typically uses TCP 443, so it also passes firewalls, and it runs on Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS and Android through the OpenVPN client or the Azure VPN Client. OpenVPN is also the tunnel type required if users sign in with Microsoft Entra ID, Microsoft's cloud identity service.

You can enable one type or a supported pair: IKEv2 with SSTP, or IKEv2 with OpenVPN. SSTP and OpenVPN cannot be combined. The Basic gateway tier does not support IKEv2 or OpenVPN.

Worked example: users have Windows, Mac and Linux laptops and travel. Step 1, Linux rules out SSTP-only and IKEv2-only, so OpenVPN is needed. Step 2, hotels block UDP, so a TCP 443 option must be present, and OpenVPN covers that. Step 3, Macs can also use their built-in IKEv2 client, so you enable IKEv2 and OpenVPN together. Step 4, users download a fresh VPN client configuration package.

A common mistake is choosing IKEv2 alone. It works in the office, then travelling users time out because their network drops UDP 500 and 4500. Another mistake is changing the tunnel type without reissuing client profiles, which leaves existing clients unable to connect until they are updated.

questions.prompt: A design agency with 40 staff is setting up a point-to-site VPN, a VPN connection from each user's own device into an Azure virtual network. Staff use Windows laptops and Android phones and must sign in with Microsoft Entra ID, Microsoft's cloud identity service. The existing virtual network gateway, the managed service that ends VPN connections for the network, is on the Basic tier. Step 1: Sign-in with Entra ID requires the OpenVPN tunnel type, so OpenVPN must be enabled.
