Its parts: a frontend IP is the address clients connect to; a backend pool is the set of virtual machines that do the work; a health probe is a regular check that marks a backend unhealthy if it stops answering, so traffic skips it. To choose a backend, it hashes the 5-tuple (source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port, protocol), which keeps one connection's packets on the same server. Because it only forwards packets and never terminates or inspects them, it adds very little delay and handles huge volumes.

Typical use cases: non-HTTP traffic (UDP gaming, DNS, custom TCP apps, databases); an internal tier, such as spreading app servers' calls across a private database or API tier inside a virtual network; very high throughput, low-latency needs; giving VMs outbound internet access; and sending all ports to a pair of network appliances for high availability.

Worked example: a game listens on UDP port 7777 on three VMs. A player's packet reaches the frontend IP. The probe reports VM2 down, so only VM1 and VM3 are eligible. The 5-tuple hash picks VM3. The packet is forwarded unchanged, and later packets from that player keep landing on VM3.

Common mistake: picking Load Balancer when the requirement says route /images to one pool, offload TLS (the encryption on HTTPS) or block web attacks with a WAF (web application firewall). It cannot see URLs or decrypt traffic; those needs point to Application Gateway regionally or Front Door globally. Choosing wrongly in production leaves you unable to do path routing or web filtering at all.

questions.prompt: A logistics company runs a custom TCP telemetry service on port 9200 on four virtual machines (VM-A, VM-B, VM-C and VM-D) behind an internal Azure Load Balancer inside its virtual network. Trace one sensor's connection. Step 1: the sensor's first packet arrives at the frontend IP 10.1.0.10. Step 2: ______. Step 3: the 5-tuple hash, applied across VM-A, VM-B and VM-D only, selects VM-B. Step 4: the packet is forwarded unchanged to VM-B, and the rest of that sensor's connection keeps landing on VM-B. Which statement correctly fills Step 2?
choices: The load balancer decrypts the traffic, checks the request path, and leaves VM-C out because it does not serve that path.
The load balancer measures each VM's current CPU load and leaves VM-C out because it is currently the busiest of the four.
The load balancer reads the packet payload, sees which sensor sent it, and leaves VM-C out because it serves a different sensor type.
The health probe has stopped getting answers from VM-C, so VM-C is marked unhealthy and only VM-A, VM-B and VM-D are eligible.
questions.why: A layer 4 load balancer never reads or decrypts packet content, so it removes a backend from the eligible set only when the health probe marks that backend unhealthy.

questions.prompt: An Azure Load Balancer receives a new packet and must decide which healthy backend virtual machine gets it. What information does it use to make that choice?
choices: The HTTP URL path and host header inside the request
The decrypted contents of the HTTPS request body
A hash of source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port and protocol
A cookie set by the application on the client's browser
questions.why: Azure Load Balancer works at layer 4, so it hashes the 5-tuple, which keeps all packets of one connection on the same server; it cannot see URLs, cookies or decrypted content.

questions.prompt: A video-conferencing startup needs to spread real-time audio traffic, sent over UDP on port 3478, across a pool of virtual machines with as little added delay as possible. Which Azure service fits this requirement?
choices: Front Door, because its web application firewall can filter the audio packets for attacks
Application Gateway, because it can offload TLS encryption before the audio reaches the VMs
Application Gateway, because it can route the audio by URL path to the correct pool
Azure Load Balancer, because it forwards UDP packets without inspecting them and adds very little delay
questions.why: The traffic is non-HTTP UDP needing low latency, which is exactly what a layer 4 load balancer that only forwards packets is built for.

questions.prompt: An online retailer requires that requests to /checkout go to one group of servers and requests to /catalog go to another, and that HTTPS encryption be removed at the entry point. An engineer proposes Azure Load Balancer. What is the problem with this choice?
choices: Load Balancer can do path routing but only for UDP traffic, and this site uses TCP
Load Balancer works at layer 4, so it cannot read URL paths or decrypt HTTPS, leaving both requirements unmet
Load Balancer can only send traffic to network appliances, never to web servers
Load Balancer meets both needs but adds too much delay because it inspects every request
questions.why: Path routing and TLS offload need a service that reads layer 7 content, such as Application Gateway regionally or Front Door globally, while Load Balancer only sees IPs, ports and protocol.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when Azure Load Balancer is the right choice, and name one thing it cannot do that would push you toward Application Gateway or Front Door instead.
lessons.modelAnswer: Azure Load Balancer works at layer 4, so it balances connections using only IP addresses, ports and the TCP or UDP protocol. It hashes the connection's 5-tuple to pick a healthy backend, uses health probes to skip failed servers, and forwards packets without inspecting them, which makes it very fast and protocol-agnostic. I'd pick it for non-HTTP workloads like UDP game servers, DNS or database traffic, for internal tiers inside a virtual network, for high-throughput low-latency needs, and for outbound access or spreading traffic across network appliances. The tradeoff is that it never reads the request content: it can't route by URL path or host header, can't terminate TLS and has no web application firewall. If a requirement needs any of those, I'd look at Application Gateway for regional web traffic or Front Door for global web traffic.
rubricPoints: States that Azure Load Balancer operates at layer 4 using IPs, ports and TCP/UDP.
Mentions health probes removing unhealthy backends from rotation.
Gives at least one fitting use case such as non-HTTP traffic, an internal tier or high-throughput low-latency needs.
Names a limit: no URL/path routing, TLS termination or WAF because it does not inspect content.
Points to Application Gateway or Front Door when layer 7 features are required.

suggested.rationale: The skill is recognizing from a requirement whether layer 4 balancing fits versus a layer 7 service, which is best practiced by reasoning through exam-style scenarios.

lessons.plain: A load balancer is a traffic spreader: it takes connections arriving at one address and hands them out across several servers so no single one is swamped. Azure Load Balancer comes in versions called SKUs (stock-keeping units, meaning product editions) and tiers (meaning how wide an area it covers). Choosing a SKU is like choosing between a basic and a commercial grade of door lock: the commercial one costs money but survives more, is locked until you grant access, and comes with a guarantee. The tier decides whether the door serves one building or a whole city of buildings.
lessons.guessPrompt: If one load balancer edition is free but has no uptime guarantee and cannot spread servers across separate datacenters, and another costs money but has a guarantee and can, which would you pick for a production web shop, and what extra setup might the safer one need?
lessons.teach:
Azure Load Balancer is a layer 4 load balancer: it forwards TCP and UDP connections based on IP address and port, without looking inside web requests. You choose it along two axes.

The SKU is the product edition. Basic was the free, older edition. It supported up to 300 backend instances, limited to one availability set or scale set, could not use availability zones (physically separate datacenters within a region), was open to inbound traffic by default, and carried no SLA (service level agreement, a published uptime commitment). Microsoft retired Basic on 30 September 2025, so new designs should not use it. Standard is the paid production edition: up to 1,000 instances drawn from any VMs in one virtual network, zone-redundant or zonal frontends, a 99.99% SLA, HA ports (one internal rule that balances all ports at once), outbound rules for controlling SNAT, and detailed metrics. Gateway is a special SKU for chaining network virtual appliances such as third-party firewalls into a traffic path; it is covered separately.

The tier is the scope. Regional balances across servers in one Azure region. Global (cross-region) sits in front of several regional Standard load balancers and gives one static public address for worldwide failover. Global requires Standard SKU underneath.

Why Standard is safer: it is secure by default, meaning inbound traffic is blocked unless a network security group (NSG, a list of allow and deny rules) permits it.

Worked example. Requirement: an internal app tier of 600 VMs must survive a datacenter outage with a guaranteed SLA, in one region. Step 1: 600 exceeds Basic's 300 limit, so Standard. Step 2: surviving a datacenter outage needs availability zones, which also means Standard. Step 3: one region means the Regional tier. Answer: Standard, Regional, with zone-redundant frontend.

Common mistake: assuming Standard behaves like the old Basic and leaving out the NSG. Every client connection is silently dropped, and the app looks down even though health probes pass. A related trap: SKUs must match, so a Standard load balancer needs Standard public IP addresses.

questions.prompt: A ticket-booking company runs 150 web VMs in East US and 150 in West Europe. It wants one static public IP address that customers everywhere use, with automatic failover if a whole region goes down. Step 1: SKU. Basic is retired, and a cross-region design needs Standard underneath, so choose Standard. Step 2: tier. [missing] Step 3: use Standard public IP addresses to match the SKU, and add an NSG (network security group, a list of allow and deny rules) that permits the web ports, because Standard blocks inbound traffic by default. Which choice correctly completes Step 2?
choices: Regional tier: one regional load balancer can include the VMs from both regions in its backend
Global tier placed in front of a Regional Standard load balancer in each region
Gateway SKU, because it chains the two regions together into one traffic path
Basic Regional in each region, since each region holds fewer than 300 VMs
questions.why: The Global (cross-region) tier sits in front of several Regional Standard load balancers and provides the single static public address and worldwide failover the requirement asks for.

questions.prompt: A team at a logistics firm replaces an old setup with a new Standard Azure Load Balancer, the layer 4 service that spreads TCP and UDP connections across servers. The health probes show every backend VM as healthy, but every client connection times out. What is the most likely cause?
choices: No NSG allows the inbound traffic, and Standard blocks inbound traffic by default
The health probes are checking the wrong layer 7 web path
The backend pool has more than 300 VMs, which is over the Standard limit
Standard needs the Global tier before it accepts any client traffic
questions.why: Standard is secure by default, so client connections are dropped until a network security group permits them, even though the probes report healthy.

questions.prompt: An insurance company sends all traffic in one region through a cluster of network virtual appliances behind an internal load balancer. It wants a single rule that balances every port and protocol, so it does not have to write one rule per port. Which choice fits?
choices: Basic SKU with a separate rule for each port
Global tier with outbound rules
Regional tier on the Basic SKU with zone-redundant frontends
HA ports on an internal Standard load balancer
questions.why: HA ports is a Standard feature: one internal rule that balances all ports at once.

questions.prompt: A small design agency is building a new internal app on 80 VMs in one region. To save money, an engineer suggests the free Basic SKU because 80 is well under its 300-instance limit. What is the best response?
choices: Use Basic, because the instance count fits within its limit
Use Basic Global, so that the app can fail over across regions later
Use the Gateway SKU, because it is meant for small internal apps
Use Standard, because Basic was retired on 30 September 2025 and new designs should not use it
questions.why: Basic was retired on 30 September 2025, so any new design should use Standard no matter how few VMs it has.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would pick the SKU and tier for a new Azure Load Balancer, and name one tradeoff or gotcha of the choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I pick the SKU, the product edition. Basic is retired and lacked zones, an SLA, and had a 300-instance cap, so for anything new I choose Standard: up to 1,000 instances in a VNet, availability-zone support, a 99.99% SLA, HA ports and outbound rules. Gateway SKU is only for inserting network appliances like firewalls into a path. Then I pick the tier: Regional if all backends live in one region, Global if I need one static IP that fails over between regional Standard load balancers in several regions. The tradeoff is that Standard costs money and is secure by default, so inbound traffic is blocked until an NSG allows it; forgetting that makes the service look dead. It also needs matching Standard public IPs.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes SKU (edition) from tier (regional versus global scope).
States that Basic is retired and lacked zones, SLA and scale, so Standard is the production choice.
Names Standard capabilities such as availability zones, 99.99% SLA, 1,000 instances, HA ports or outbound rules.
Explains that Standard is secure by default and needs an NSG to allow inbound traffic.
Notes that the Global tier sits over regional Standard load balancers.
Mentions SKU matching with public IP addresses or the cost tradeoff.

suggested.rationale: No mission or engine builds Azure load balancers, so reasoning through exam-style requirement scenarios to land on a SKU and tier is the most useful practice.

lessons.plain: A load balancer is a traffic spreader: it takes incoming connections and shares them across several identical servers so no single one gets swamped. Azure Load Balancer comes in two flavours based on where the traffic comes from. A public load balancer has an address on the internet, so anyone online can reach it. An internal load balancer has a private address that only exists inside your own Azure network, so only your own machines can reach it. Think of a shop's front door that faces the street versus a staff-only door in the back corridor. Both lead to working counters, but different people can use each.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your web servers must be reachable by customers on the internet, but the database-facing app servers behind them should only ever be called by the web servers. Which tier would you put behind an internet-facing load balancer, and which behind a private one?
lessons.teach:
Azure Load Balancer is a layer 4 load balancer, meaning it spreads TCP and UDP connections based on IP address and port, without reading web content such as URLs. Its frontend IP configuration is the address clients connect to. The backend pool is the group of virtual machines that actually receive the traffic. The choice between public and internal comes down to that frontend.

A public load balancer uses a public IP address, one that is routable on the internet. Use it when outside users must reach a service, such as a public website. An internal (private) load balancer uses a private IP address taken from a subnet in your virtual network (VNet, your isolated private network in Azure). The internet cannot route to that address at all, which is why it suits services only your own systems should call. An internal frontend is still reachable from peered VNets and from on-premises networks connected through VPN or ExpressRoute, because those paths carry private traffic.

One load balancer is either public or internal; all of its frontend addresses are of the same kind. If you need both, you deploy two.

Worked example, a three-tier app. Step 1: customers on the internet must reach the web tier, so put the web VMs behind a public load balancer with a public IP. Step 2: the web VMs call an API tier. Nobody outside should reach it, so put the API VMs behind an internal load balancer with a private IP such as 10.0.2.10 in the app subnet. Step 3: an on-premises reporting server connected by VPN also calls 10.0.2.10, which works because it arrives over private routing.

A common mistake is putting an internal tier behind a public load balancer and relying only on firewall rules to hide it. That gives the tier an internet-facing address, enlarging the attack surface; one misconfigured rule exposes the backend to the world. Choosing internal removes the public address entirely.

questions.prompt: A logistics company, Northway Freight, is planning its Azure load balancing. Step 1: delivery drivers use phones on the public internet to send location updates to a tracking service. The tracking VMs go behind a public load balancer whose frontend is a public IP address. Step 2: the tracking VMs call a rate-calculation service on its own VMs. Only Northway's systems should ever reach it. An engineer asks whether the existing public load balancer can also serve as the entry point for the rate service. Step 3: a warehouse office, connected to the VNet by ExpressRoute (a private dedicated link into Azure), calls the rate service at its private address and succeeds because the traffic arrives over private routing. Which choice correctly completes Step 2?
choices: Deploy a separate internal load balancer with a private frontend IP such as 172.16.4.20 from the rate subnet, and put the rate VMs in its backend pool.
Keep the rate VMs behind the public load balancer and add firewall rules that block all internet sources, so only Northway's systems get through.
Use the public load balancer to route requests by URL path, so that only calls to the /rates path reach the rate-calculation VMs.
Add a second frontend IP to the existing public load balancer, choose a private address such as 172.16.4.20 for it, and point it at the rate VMs.
questions.why: One load balancer is either entirely public or entirely internal, so a service that must have no internet-facing address needs its own internal load balancer with a private frontend IP.

questions.prompt: An engineer is setting up an Azure Load Balancer (a layer 4 load balancer that spreads TCP and UDP connections by IP address and port). Which part of its configuration decides whether it is a public or an internal load balancer?
choices: The number of virtual machines placed in the backend pool
Whether the frontend IP configuration uses a public IP or a private IP from a VNet subnet
Whether the backend VMs run a web server or a database
The TCP or UDP port numbers that the load balancer forwards
questions.why: The frontend IP configuration is the address clients connect to, and its type, public or private, is what makes a load balancer public or internal.

questions.prompt: A university hosts a student-records service on Azure VMs. It must be called only by VMs in a peered VNet (another virtual network linked privately to this one) and by campus servers connected through ExpressRoute. No one on the internet should reach it. Which load balancer fits?
choices: An internal load balancer with a private frontend IP, which peered VNets and ExpressRoute can reach over private routing
A public load balancer, because campus servers sit outside Azure and need an internet-routable address
A public load balancer for the campus servers plus private frontend IPs on the same load balancer for the peered VNet
No load balancer, because private traffic from peered VNets and ExpressRoute cannot reach a load balancer frontend
questions.why: An internal frontend is unreachable from the internet but still reachable from peered VNets and from on-premises networks over VPN or ExpressRoute, because those paths carry private traffic.

questions.prompt: A retail company places its internal inventory-database VMs behind a public load balancer and relies on network security rules to deny all internet traffic. Months later, an engineer edits one rule incorrectly. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: The inventory backend becomes reachable from the internet, because the tier was given an internet-facing address
On-premises servers connected by VPN lose access, while internet users still cannot connect
The load balancer automatically converts to internal and assigns a private IP from the subnet
Nothing changes, because a public load balancer only accepts traffic from peered VNets
questions.why: Putting an internal tier behind a public load balancer gives it a public address, so a single misconfigured rule exposes it to the world, whereas an internal load balancer has no public address to expose.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you decide between a public and an internal Azure Load Balancer for a tier of an application, including who can and cannot reach an internal one and one limit of the choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: I look at who the clients are. If the callers are on the internet, like customers hitting our website, I use a public load balancer, whose frontend is a public IP address. If the callers are only our own systems, like web servers calling an API tier, I use an internal load balancer, whose frontend is a private IP from a subnet in our VNet. The internet simply cannot route to that address, so the service has no public exposure to defend. An internal one is still reachable from peered VNets and from on-premises over VPN or ExpressRoute, since that's private traffic. One limit: a single load balancer is either public or internal, so a three-tier app usually needs two of them. And because it's layer 4, either type only spreads TCP/UDP connections; it doesn't route by URL.
rubricPoints: The decision is driven by where the clients are: internet versus inside private networks.
A public load balancer's frontend is a public IP reachable from the internet.
An internal load balancer's frontend is a private IP from a VNet subnet and is not reachable from the internet.
Internal frontends are reachable from peered VNets and on-premises over VPN or ExpressRoute.
One load balancer is either public or internal, so mixed needs require two.
Using a public load balancer for a private tier needlessly enlarges the attack surface.

suggested.rationale: The skill is reading a scenario's client locations and picking the right frontend type, which is best practised by reasoning through exam-style multi-tier situations.

lessons.plain: A load balancer is a traffic director: it receives incoming connections at one address and spreads them across several servers so that no single server is overloaded or becomes a single point of failure. A regional load balancer does this inside one Azure region, which is one geographic group of datacenters. A cross-region load balancer sits one level higher. It has one address that works worldwide, and it spreads traffic across several regional load balancers in different parts of the world. Think of one national phone number that rings the nearest branch office, and automatically rings a different branch if the nearest one is closed.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your app runs on servers in one region, spread across three datacenter buildings. A storm takes the whole region offline. Would a load balancer that only works inside that region keep the app reachable? What would you need to add?
lessons.teach:
Azure Load Balancer is a layer 4 load balancer. Layer 4 means it forwards TCP and UDP connections, which are the basic network transport protocols, without reading web content such as URLs. It comes in two tiers. The regional tier is the default. It lives in one Azure region and spreads traffic across backend virtual machines in that region. With the Standard SKU, which is the current product version, it can be zone-redundant, meaning it keeps working if one availability zone (one datacenter building or group of buildings inside the region) fails. It can be public, facing the internet, or internal, with a private address inside a virtual network.

The global tier, called the cross-region load balancer, is a public Standard load balancer whose frontend is a single static anycast IP address. Anycast means the same address is announced from many Microsoft network edge locations, so a client enters the nearest one. Its backend pool does not contain virtual machines. It contains the frontends of regional public Standard load balancers. It sends each client to the closest healthy region, and it keeps the client's original IP address.

Worked example: a game studio runs UDP servers behind a regional load balancer in East US and another in West Europe. A cross-region load balancer puts both behind one IP. Step 1: a player in Paris connects to that IP. Step 2: traffic enters a nearby Microsoft edge and goes to the West Europe regional load balancer. Step 3: that load balancer picks a healthy virtual machine. Now suppose every West Europe virtual machine fails its health probe, which is a regular check that a backend is responding. The regional load balancer reports itself unhealthy, and the cross-region load balancer sends the Paris player to East US. The IP does not change and no DNS record has to expire, so failover is fast.

A common mistake is to treat zone redundancy as disaster recovery. A zone-redundant regional load balancer survives the loss of a building, but it does not survive the loss of a whole region. The reverse also matters. The cross-region tier is public only, so it cannot balance private internal traffic, and it adds a global layer you do not need if the app lives in one region.

questions.prompt:
A ticketing company runs a TCP booking service (no URL-based routing needed) in Canada Central and in UK South. It wants one fixed public IP for customers worldwide and automatic failover if a whole region goes down. Here is the design, worked through.

Step 1: The service only needs TCP connections forwarded, so a layer 4 Azure Load Balancer fits.
Step 2: In each region, place the virtual machines behind a public Standard regional load balancer, with health probes checking each machine.
Step 3: ???
Step 4: Customers connect to one static anycast IP. If every machine in UK South fails its probe, traffic shifts to Canada Central without the IP changing and without waiting for a DNS record to expire.

Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Make each regional load balancer zone-redundant; that alone gives region-level failover behind one IP
Create a cross-region load balancer whose backend pool contains the frontends of the two regional public Standard load balancers
Create a cross-region load balancer and put the virtual machines from both regions directly into its backend pool
Create a cross-region load balancer whose backend pool contains two internal regional load balancers with private addresses
questions.why: The cross-region tier balances across regional public Standard load balancer frontends, not virtual machines or internal load balancers, and that is what gives one anycast IP with fast region failover.

questions.prompt: A hospital runs an internal patient-records service (TCP) on virtual machines in a single Azure region. Only clients inside its virtual network should reach it, and it must keep working if one availability zone fails. Which choice fits best?
choices: A public regional load balancer placed behind a cross-region load balancer
A regional load balancer in each of two regions, joined by a cross-region load balancer
A zone-redundant internal regional Standard load balancer
A cross-region load balancer with a private frontend address
questions.why: The app lives in one region and needs private access plus zone survival, which a zone-redundant internal regional Standard load balancer gives; the cross-region tier is public only and would add a global layer the app does not need.

questions.prompt: An engineer puts a logistics app behind a zone-redundant regional Standard load balancer in South Central US and tells the manager this covers disaster recovery. Later the entire South Central US region goes offline. What happens to the app?
choices: Clients keep reaching the app, because zone redundancy protects against region loss
The app becomes unreachable, because zone redundancy only survives losing a zone within the region
Traffic moves to another availability zone in a different region automatically
The load balancer's anycast IP sends clients to the nearest other region
questions.why: Zone redundancy protects against losing a building or group of buildings inside one region, not the whole region, so region failover needs something like a cross-region load balancer in front of regional load balancers in more than one region.

questions.prompt: What does the backend pool of an Azure cross-region load balancer contain?
choices: Virtual machines from several regions
The frontends of regional public Standard load balancers
Availability zones within one region
Internal load balancers with private addresses
questions.why: The cross-region tier does not hold virtual machines; its backends are the public frontends of regional Standard load balancers, and it sends each client to the closest healthy one.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would use a regional load balancer and when you would use a cross-region load balancer. Include at least one limit of the cross-region option.
lessons.modelAnswer: A regional load balancer spreads TCP and UDP traffic across virtual machines inside one Azure region. With the Standard SKU it can span availability zones, so it survives losing a datacenter, but not losing the whole region. It can be public or internal. A cross-region load balancer is the global tier. It gives you one static anycast public IP, and its backend pool contains regional public load balancers, not virtual machines. Clients reach the nearest healthy region. If a region's regional load balancer has no healthy backends, traffic shifts to another region on the same IP, with no DNS change to wait for. I would pick regional for a single-region or internal app. I would pick cross-region for a public layer 4 app that runs in several regions and needs fast regional failover. The limits are that cross-region is public only, it requires Standard regional load balancers underneath, and it still works at layer 4, with no URL-based routing.
rubricPoints: A regional load balancer distributes layer 4 traffic within one region and can be public or internal.
Zone redundancy protects against a zone failure but not a full region outage.
A cross-region load balancer uses one global static anycast public IP and routes to the nearest healthy region.
The cross-region backend pool contains regional Standard public load balancers, not virtual machines.
Cross-region failover keeps the same IP, so it does not wait for DNS changes.
Cross-region is public only and still works at layer 4.

suggested.rationale: The skill is recognizing from a scenario's scope (one region versus many, public versus internal, layer 4) which tier fits, so reasoning through exam-style situations adds the most.

lessons.plain: An Azure Load Balancer is a managed traffic spreader that works at the network level. It takes connections arriving at one address and hands each one to one of several servers behind it, skipping any server that looks unhealthy. Think of a receptionist at a clinic. Patients come to one front desk. The receptionist sends each patient to a doctor who is in and free, and never to an empty room. Creating one means setting up four pieces: the front desk address, the list of servers, the health check, and the rule that ties them together.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a load balancer sits in front of two web servers, and it checks each server's health every few seconds. What do you think it should do with new visitors when one server stops answering those checks, and what if both stop?
lessons.teach:
Azure Load Balancer is a layer-4 load balancer. Layer 4 means it decides using only IP addresses, ports and protocol (TCP or UDP), and never reads web content. You build one from four parts.

The frontend IP configuration is the address clients connect to. On a public load balancer it is a public IP. On an internal load balancer it is a private IP from a subnet in your virtual network (VNet), which is your private network in Azure. The backend pool is the group of targets that receive traffic, either virtual machine network interfaces or IP addresses in one VNet. The health probe is a repeated check, such as a TCP connect or an HTTP request to a path, run on a port at a set interval. A target that fails enough checks in a row is taken out of rotation. The load-balancing rule joins these together. It says that traffic arriving on frontend port X with protocol Y goes to backend port Z for pool members that pass probe P.

Worked example: you want port 80 spread across VM1 and VM2. First, create a Standard SKU load balancer in the VMs' region. Second, add a public frontend IP. Third, add both VM network interfaces to a backend pool. Fourth, create an HTTP probe on port 80 for the path /health. Fifth, create a rule from frontend TCP 80 to backend port 80 that uses that probe. A client then hits the frontend IP. The rule matches, the probe shows both VMs healthy, and the connection goes to one of them. If VM2 stops answering /health, new connections go only to VM1.

A common mistake involves the Standard SKU, which is closed by default. A network security group (NSG), a set of allow and deny traffic filters, must allow the client traffic. It must also allow the probes, which come from the AzureLoadBalancer service tag. If the probes are blocked, or nothing answers on the probe path, every backend is marked unhealthy. The load balancer then drops new connections, even though the VMs themselves are running fine.

questions.prompt: Harbor Logistics runs an order API on three virtual machines (VMs), OrdA, OrdB and OrdC, listening on TCP port 8443. Only other servers inside their virtual network (VNet) should reach it. An engineer builds an Azure Load Balancer like this. Step 1: create a Standard SKU load balancer in the VMs' region. Step 2: add an internal frontend IP configuration using the private address 10.20.1.10 from a subnet in the VNet. Step 3: add the network interfaces of OrdA, OrdB and OrdC to a backend pool. Step 4: ______. Step 5: create a load-balancing rule from frontend TCP 8443 to backend port 8443 for pool members that pass that probe. Which step 4 completes the build?
choices: Add a network security group rule that denies the AzureLoadBalancer service tag so only clients reach the VMs
Add a public IP to the frontend so the health checks can reach the three VMs from the internet
Create a probe that reads each request's URL path and picks the VM that serves that path
Create a health probe that does a TCP connect to port 8443 on each pool member at a set interval
questions.why: Step 5's rule uses a probe that does not exist yet, so step 4 must create a health probe (here a repeated TCP connect on 8443) that decides which pool members stay in rotation.

questions.prompt: A team at Pinecrest Media wants requests for /video to go to one group of servers and requests for /api to go to another, chosen by reading the web address. Why can't Azure Load Balancer make that choice on its own?
choices: It only works with UDP traffic, and web requests use TCP
It needs a separate backend pool for each VNet, and the two server groups are in one VNet
It can read web paths only on an internal load balancer, not on a public one
It is a layer-4 load balancer that decides using only IP addresses, ports and protocol, and never reads web content
questions.why: Layer 4 means the load balancer sees only IP addresses, ports and TCP or UDP, so it cannot read a path like /video or /api.

questions.prompt: Northgate Bank needs a load balancer for a reporting service on TCP 5000 that must be reachable only from inside its Azure virtual network, never from the internet. What should the frontend IP configuration use?
choices: No frontend IP at all, because clients connect to the backend pool members directly
The private IP of one of the backend VMs, so traffic lands there first
A private IP taken from a subnet in the virtual network, making it an internal load balancer
A public IP, with the backend pool limited to private addresses
questions.why: An internal load balancer's frontend is a private IP from a subnet in your VNet, so only clients inside the private network can reach it.

questions.prompt: At Riverbend Clinic, a Standard SKU public load balancer sends TCP 3000 to four running VMs using an HTTP probe on /status. The VMs' network security group allows client traffic on port 3000 but has no rule allowing the AzureLoadBalancer service tag. What happens when a new client connects?
choices: The connection is dropped, because the blocked probes mark every backend unhealthy
The connection goes to a random VM, because the probe is ignored when it cannot reach a target
The connection succeeds, because the VMs are running and port 3000 is allowed
The connection succeeds only on the first VM in the backend pool
questions.why: Standard SKU is closed by default, so blocked probes from the AzureLoadBalancer tag fail, every backend is taken out of rotation, and new connections are dropped even though the VMs are fine.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the pieces you configure when creating an Azure Load Balancer and how one client connection flows through them. Include one limit of what it can do, or one way a correct-looking setup can still fail.
lessons.modelAnswer: Azure Load Balancer spreads TCP or UDP connections across servers using only addresses and ports. You configure a frontend IP, which is public or private depending on who the clients are. You add a backend pool of VM network interfaces or IPs in one VNet, and a health probe that keeps checking each backend on a port or HTTP path. Then a load-balancing rule maps a frontend port and protocol to a backend port and attaches the probe. When a client connects, the rule matches, and the connection goes to a backend the probe currently marks healthy. One limit is that it works at layer 4, so it cannot route by URL or inspect HTTP. One failure mode is that the Standard SKU is closed by default. If an NSG blocks the probe traffic, or the app doesn't answer the probe path, every backend looks down and traffic is dropped even though the VMs are running.
rubricPoints: Names the frontend IP, backend pool, health probe and load-balancing rule.
Explains that the rule maps a frontend port and protocol to a backend port using a probe.
Describes unhealthy backends being removed from rotation.
States that it is layer 4 and does not inspect HTTP content.
Mentions that NSGs must allow both client traffic and probe traffic on the Standard SKU.

suggested.rationale: Tracing a connection from the frontend through the rule, the probe state and the NSG to a backend shows how each configured piece decides the outcome.

lessons.plain: Azure Traffic Manager is a global traffic director that works through DNS, the internet's phone book that turns names like app.contoso.com into IP addresses. When a user's device asks for your app's address, Traffic Manager picks which copy of your app to hand back, for example the nearest healthy region or a backup region if the main one is down. It is like a receptionist who gives callers the right branch office number. The receptionist never carries the conversation, though. After that, the user talks directly to the chosen site.
lessons.guessPrompt: If Traffic Manager only gives a user's device an address and then steps aside, what do you think happens to that user's connection when the region they were sent to suddenly fails?
lessons.teach:
Azure Traffic Manager is a DNS-based load balancer. DNS (Domain Name System) translates names into IP addresses. A Traffic Manager profile is the configuration object. It gets a name ending in trafficmanager.net. You point your own domain at that name with a CNAME record, which is a DNS alias from one name to another. The profile lists endpoints, meaning the destinations it may hand out. These can be Azure endpoints such as a public IP or app service, external endpoints such as any internet address, or nested endpoints, which are other Traffic Manager profiles.

A routing method decides which endpoint each DNS answer contains. Priority sends everyone to the top endpoint and fails over down the list. Weighted splits traffic by ratio. Performance picks the lowest-latency region for the user. Geographic picks by the user's location. Multivalue returns several healthy addresses. Subnet maps client IP ranges to endpoints. Endpoint monitoring regularly probes each endpoint over HTTP, HTTPS or TCP. Unhealthy endpoints are dropped from answers.

Here is a worked example using the priority method. Endpoint 1 is East US and endpoint 2 is West Europe, and the TTL is 60 seconds. TTL (time to live) is how long resolvers may cache an answer. Step 1: a user resolves app.contoso.com and gets East US. Step 2: East US fails, and probes miss the tolerated number of checks. Step 3: Traffic Manager marks it degraded and starts answering with West Europe. Step 4: the user's cached answer expires after up to 60 seconds, the user resolves again, and now reaches West Europe.

A common mistake is thinking traffic flows through Traffic Manager. It does not. Traffic Manager cannot terminate TLS, cache content, inspect requests or apply a web application firewall. It also works for any protocol, not just HTTP. The consequence in a running system is that failover is never instant. Probe intervals plus DNS caching, including clients that ignore TTL, mean some users keep hitting a dead region for a while. Lowering TTL speeds failover but increases DNS query volume.

questions.prompt: Northwind Games puts a TCP-based game API behind a Traffic Manager profile that uses the weighted routing method. The Canada Central endpoint has weight 80 and the UK South endpoint has weight 20. The TTL (how long resolvers may cache a DNS answer) is 300 seconds, and endpoint monitoring probes each endpoint over TCP. Step 1: roughly 80% of DNS answers contain Canada Central, so most players connect there. Step 2: Canada Central stops responding, and the probes miss the tolerated number of checks. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: a player whose resolver cached the Canada Central answer keeps trying it for up to 300 seconds, then resolves again and connects to UK South. Which choice correctly fills Step 3?
choices: Traffic Manager takes over the player's open TCP connections and forwards them to UK South right away, because all game traffic passes through the profile.
Traffic Manager stops answering DNS queries for the game's name until Canada Central passes its probes again.
Traffic Manager marks Canada Central unhealthy and drops it from DNS answers, so every new answer now contains UK South.
Traffic Manager keeps the 80/20 split, because the weights are fixed settings, so about 80% of answers still point players at Canada Central.
questions.why: Endpoint monitoring removes unhealthy endpoints from DNS answers, so only the healthy UK South endpoint is handed out, and players reach it once their cached answer expires.

questions.prompt: Tailspin Health must make sure that users located in Germany are always sent to its Germany West Central deployment so their data stays in that country, even if another region would respond faster. Which Traffic Manager routing method fits this requirement?
choices: Multivalue, because it returns several healthy addresses in each DNS answer
Performance, because it sends each user to the region with the lowest latency for that user
Geographic, because it chooses the endpoint based on where the user is located
Priority, because it sends everyone to the top endpoint and fails over down the list
questions.why: Geographic routing picks the endpoint by the user's location, which enforces where users land; performance routing would pick by latency and could send German users elsewhere.

questions.prompt: An engineer at Adatum plans to use Azure Traffic Manager in front of two web apps so that it terminates TLS (decrypts HTTPS) and applies a web application firewall to block malicious requests. Why will this plan not work?
choices: Traffic Manager only handles TCP traffic, so it cannot see HTTPS requests at all.
Traffic Manager can terminate TLS but must first be switched to the performance routing method before a firewall can be applied.
Traffic Manager can only do these things for external endpoints, not for Azure endpoints such as an app service.
Traffic Manager only answers DNS queries with an endpoint address; the user's traffic then goes straight to the endpoint and never passes through Traffic Manager.
questions.why: Because Traffic Manager is DNS-based, application traffic never flows through it, so it cannot decrypt, inspect or filter requests.

questions.prompt: Litware's Traffic Manager profile has a TTL of 300 seconds. After a regional outage, users complained that some of them kept reaching the failed region for several minutes. The team lowers the TTL to 30 seconds. What is the most likely result?
choices: Failover becomes instant for every user, because no client can keep an answer longer than 30 seconds.
Failover gets faster and DNS query volume drops, because resolvers keep their cached answers for less time.
Failover speed stays the same, because TTL only controls how often endpoints are probed.
Failover gets faster for most users, but resolvers query Traffic Manager more often, so DNS query volume rises.
questions.why: A shorter TTL means cached answers expire sooner, which speeds failover but causes more DNS lookups, and failover is still not instant because of probe intervals and clients that ignore TTL.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how Traffic Manager decides where users go and why failover with it is not instant, naming one tradeoff you would tune.
lessons.modelAnswer: Traffic Manager is a global load balancer that works only at the DNS layer. Our domain is a CNAME to the profile. When a client resolves it, Traffic Manager returns one endpoint's address. It chooses that endpoint using a routing method such as priority for active-passive failover, weighted for a split, performance for the lowest latency, or geographic for data residency. It also checks health probes and skips unhealthy endpoints. After that, the client connects directly to the endpoint, so Traffic Manager never sees the actual traffic. That means no TLS offload, caching or WAF, but it does work for any protocol. The limit is failover speed. Probes must detect the failure first, and then cached DNS answers must expire. Lowering the TTL makes failover faster but means more DNS queries and slightly more cost, and some clients ignore TTL anyway.
rubricPoints: States that Traffic Manager routes by answering DNS queries, not by proxying traffic.
Names at least two routing methods and when to use them.
Explains that health probes remove unhealthy endpoints from answers.
Explains that failover is delayed by probe detection and DNS TTL caching.
Notes the TTL tradeoff or the lack of TLS offload, caching and WAF.

suggested.rationale: The exam skill is reasoning through scenarios about DNS-based routing methods and failover timing, and picking Traffic Manager over proxy-based options, so a situation to work through adds the most.

lessons.plain: Gateway Load Balancer is an Azure load balancer built for one job: quietly slipping a set of security or inspection appliances into the path of traffic headed to your application, without changing how the application or its users see that traffic. Think of an airport security checkpoint built into the jet bridge. Passengers walk the same route to the plane and never take a detour, yet everyone gets screened along the way. If more screeners are needed, you add lanes, and nobody has to rebuild the terminal. The appliances can belong to a separate team or vendor, and the application team only has to point at them.
lessons.guessPrompt: You run a web app behind a public load balancer, and the security team wants every incoming packet inspected by a firewall appliance, with the app still seeing each user's real IP address. Should the firewall sit in front as a new destination users connect to, or somewhere that users never address directly? Why?
lessons.teach:
Gateway Load Balancer is a special SKU (product version) of Azure Load Balancer that inserts network virtual appliances, or NVAs, into a traffic path transparently. An NVA is a virtual machine running network software such as a firewall, intrusion detection system or packet inspector. Transparent means neither the client nor the application has to know the appliance exists. Source and destination addresses stay as they were, so the app still sees the real client IP. People often call this bump-in-the-wire.

It works through chaining. You create the Gateway Load Balancer with a frontend IP, which is the address it receives traffic on, and a backend pool of NVAs. You then reference that frontend from a consumer resource. The consumer can be the frontend IP configuration of a Standard public load balancer, or a Standard public IP attached to a single VM's network interface. Traffic reaching the consumer gets wrapped in VXLAN, a tunneling format that puts the original packet inside an outer packet, and is sent to an NVA. Each backend uses tunnel interfaces. The internal interface handles one direction and the external interface handles the other, each with its own port and identifier. A health probe checks that each NVA is alive, and a load-balancing rule spreads flows across healthy NVAs. The same flow always returns through the same NVA, which keeps inspection symmetric. The provider (the NVA owner) and the consumer can live in different subscriptions.

Worked example: a user at 203.0.113.5 connects to 20.1.1.1:443, a public load balancer frontend chained to a Gateway Load Balancer. First, the packet arrives at 20.1.1.1. Second, it is VXLAN-encapsulated and forwarded to a healthy firewall NVA. Third, the firewall inspects it, allows it, and returns it through the tunnel. Fourth, the public load balancer delivers it to a web VM, which sees source 203.0.113.5. The reply travels back through the same firewall.

A common mistake is trying to chain to a Basic SKU load balancer or to an internal load balancer. Chaining supports only Standard public frontends and Standard VM public IPs. A second mistake is deploying appliances that are not set up for VXLAN tunnels. In a running system, those appliances drop the traffic and the application becomes unreachable even though every VM looks healthy.

questions.prompt: Larkspur Analytics runs one reporting VM with a Standard public IP of 52.160.10.20 attached to its network interface. A security team in a separate subscription wants every inbound connection inspected by intrusion detection appliances, without changing the VM or its clients. The engineer works through it. Step 1: create a Gateway Load Balancer with frontend IP 10.50.0.4 and a backend pool of two intrusion detection NVAs, each set up with VXLAN internal and external tunnel interfaces. Step 2: add a health probe and a load-balancing rule so flows are spread across healthy NVAs. Step 3: (missing). Step 4: a client at 198.51.100.77 connects to 52.160.10.20, the packet is VXLAN-encapsulated and sent to a healthy NVA, inspected, returned, and delivered to the VM, which sees source 198.51.100.77. What is Step 3?
choices: Place an internal Standard load balancer in front of the VM and chain its frontend to 10.50.0.4
Configure the VM's Standard public IP 52.160.10.20 to reference the Gateway Load Balancer frontend 10.50.0.4
Change the client DNS record so users connect to 10.50.0.4 instead of 52.160.10.20
Add a route table to the VM's subnet that sends all inbound traffic to the NVA's private IP address
questions.why: Chaining works by having a supported consumer, here a Standard public IP on a single VM's network interface, reference the Gateway Load Balancer frontend, so traffic is diverted transparently without route or client changes.

questions.prompt: Pinecrest Retail inserts firewall NVAs in front of its web servers using a Gateway Load Balancer chained to its public load balancer. A developer worries that the web server logs will now show the firewall's address instead of the shopper's address. What source IP will the web servers actually see for a shopper connecting from 192.0.2.44?
choices: The private IP of whichever firewall NVA inspected the flow
The frontend IP of the Gateway Load Balancer
192.0.2.44, because the insertion is transparent and addresses are kept
The frontend IP of the public load balancer
questions.why: Gateway Load Balancer is bump-in-the-wire: traffic is tunneled with VXLAN rather than rewritten, so original source and destination addresses stay intact and the app sees the real client IP.

questions.prompt: Orbit Media has four candidate resources and wants to chain one of them to a Gateway Load Balancer so traffic passes through packet inspection appliances. Which one can be chained?
choices: A Standard public load balancer frontend IP configuration
A Basic SKU public load balancer frontend
An internal Standard load balancer frontend
A Basic SKU public IP attached to a VM
questions.why: Chaining supports only Standard public load balancer frontends and Standard public IPs on a single VM's network interface; Basic SKU and internal load balancers are not supported.

questions.prompt: After chaining a Gateway Load Balancer in front of its API servers, Tidewater Bank finds the API unreachable. The appliance VMs and API VMs all report healthy and the chaining configuration is in place. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The appliances were not set up with VXLAN tunnel interfaces, so they drop the encapsulated traffic
The Gateway Load Balancer sends reply traffic through a different appliance than the request
The provider and consumer resources sit in different subscriptions, which blocks chaining
The API servers reject traffic because they now see the appliance's IP as the source
questions.why: Traffic arrives at the NVAs wrapped in VXLAN, and appliances not configured for those tunnels drop it, making the app unreachable even though every VM looks healthy.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what Gateway Load Balancer does and how it is wired to an application, and name at least one limit or tradeoff of using it.
lessons.modelAnswer: Gateway Load Balancer lets us put firewalls or other inspection appliances in the path of our app's traffic without changing addresses or routing. We build a Gateway Load Balancer whose backend pool holds the appliances, add a health probe and a load-balancing rule, and then chain its frontend to our Standard public load balancer frontend or to a VM's Standard public IP. Traffic hitting that public address is wrapped in VXLAN, sent to a healthy appliance, inspected, and returned along the same path. The app still sees the real client IP, and each flow stays on one appliance in both directions. The appliances can live in another team's subscription. There are limits. It only chains to Standard public frontends, not Basic or internal load balancers. The appliances must support VXLAN tunneling. It also adds a hop, so a misconfigured or unhealthy appliance pool can take the whole app offline.
rubricPoints: Defines it as a load balancer SKU that transparently inserts network virtual appliances into a traffic path.
Explains chaining from a Standard public load balancer frontend or a VM's Standard public IP.
Mentions VXLAN tunneling with internal and external tunnel interfaces, plus health probes across the appliance pool.
Notes that the client IP is preserved and flows stay symmetric through one appliance.
Names a limit, such as no Basic or internal load balancer chaining, the need for VXLAN-capable appliances, or the added dependency.

suggested.rationale: Tracing a packet from a chained public frontend through the VXLAN tunnel to an appliance and back makes the invisible insertion concrete.

lessons.plain: A load balancing rule is the instruction that tells a load balancer what to do with incoming traffic. It says: when traffic arrives at this address on this port using this protocol, share it out among this group of servers on that port, but only to servers that have recently proved they are healthy. Think of a restaurant host with a note saying "guests at the front door go to any open table in the main room, but skip tables the waiter has marked closed." Without the rule, the load balancer has an address and a list of servers but no instructions connecting them.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your load balancer listens on port 80, but your web app on each server listens on port 8080. How do you think the load balancer could still deliver the traffic correctly?
lessons.teach:
In Azure Load Balancer, a layer-4 service that spreads TCP and UDP traffic, a load balancing rule links four things. The frontend IP is the address clients connect to. The backend pool is the group of virtual machines that receive traffic. The health probe is a repeated check, such as a TCP connection or an HTTP request to a path, that marks each backend healthy or unhealthy. The protocol, frontend port and backend port say which traffic matches and where it goes. Ports may differ, so 80 outside can map to 8080 inside.

It works because new flows are sent only to healthy pool members, chosen by a hash of the five-tuple: source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port and protocol. Session persistence changes this hash. Client IP sends one client to the same backend. Client IP and protocol does the same per protocol. Other settings include idle timeout, which sets how long a quiet connection stays open. TCP reset tells both ends when that timeout closes a connection. Floating IP lets the backend see the frontend address as the destination. HA ports, on an internal Standard load balancer, balances all ports in one rule.

Worked example. The rule is frontend 20.1.1.1 TCP 80, backend pool web, backend port 8080, probe HTTP 8080 /health. First, a client connects to 20.1.1.1:80. Second, the rule matches TCP 80. Third, the probe lists vm1 and vm2 as healthy and vm3 as failed. Fourth, the hash picks vm2. Fifth, the packet reaches vm2 on port 8080.

A common mistake is pointing the probe at the wrong port or path, or letting a network security group block probe traffic. A network security group is a set of allow and deny filters. Probes come from the AzureLoadBalancer service tag, address 168.63.129.16. If every probe fails, every backend is marked down and the rule delivers nothing, so the application looks offline even though the servers are running.

questions.prompt:
Northwind Clinic runs an internal Azure Load Balancer (a layer-4 service that spreads TCP and UDP traffic) in front of its booking API. The load balancing rule has frontend IP 10.4.0.50, protocol TCP, frontend port 443, backend pool booking (VMs app-a, app-b and app-c), backend port 9443, and a health probe (a repeated check that marks each backend healthy or unhealthy) doing an HTTP request to port 9443 at path /ready. Session persistence is set to None.

Step 1: A staff laptop at 10.4.8.21, source port 51122, opens a TCP connection to 10.4.0.50:443.
Step 2: The rule matches because the protocol is TCP and the destination port is 443.
Step 3: The latest probe results show app-a and app-b answering /ready successfully, and app-c failing.
Step 4: ???
Step 5: The packet is delivered to app-b on port 9443.

Which choice correctly fills in Step 4?
choices: The load balancer sends the flow to app-c so that the failed VM gets a chance to recover before the next probe.
A hash of the five-tuple (source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port, protocol) picks app-b from the healthy members, app-a and app-b.
The load balancer sends the flow to whichever of the three VMs currently has the fewest open connections, which turns out to be app-b.
A hash of only the client's source IP picks app-b from all three pool members, because each client is always pinned to one VM.
questions.why: New flows go only to healthy pool members, and with persistence set to None the backend is chosen by a hash of the full five-tuple, so app-b is picked from app-a and app-b.

questions.prompt: A retail company's checkout VMs sit behind an Azure Load Balancer. Each VM keeps a shopper's cart in local memory, so the business needs every new connection from the same shopper's IP address to reach the same VM, even when the shopper's source port changes. Which load balancing rule setting meets this need?
choices: Set session persistence to Client IP
Enable floating IP so the backend sees the frontend address as the destination
Enable TCP reset so both ends are told when the connection closes
Increase the idle timeout so that quiet connections stay open longer
questions.why: Client IP session persistence changes the hash so that it is based on the client's IP address, which sends that client to the same backend regardless of source port.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm puts a public Azure Load Balancer in front of three VMs that run a tracking web app listening on port 8443. Customers must reach the app at the load balancer's frontend IP on port 443 over TCP. Which load balancing rule settings are correct?
choices: Protocol UDP, frontend port 443, backend port 8443, health probe on port 8443
Protocol TCP, frontend port 443, backend port 8443, health probe on port 8443
Protocol TCP, frontend port 443, backend port 443, health probe on port 8443
Protocol TCP, frontend port 8443, backend port 443, health probe on port 443
questions.why: Clients connect on the frontend port (443) over TCP, the rule forwards to the port the app listens on (8443), and the probe should check that same backend port, since frontend and backend ports are allowed to differ.

questions.prompt: An engineer at a media company adds a new network security group (a set of allow and deny filters) to the subnet of the VMs behind an Azure Load Balancer. The group denies all inbound traffic except from the company's office range. Minutes later the website stops responding, yet every VM is running and its web service answers when tested directly from the office. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The NSG change reset the five-tuple hash, so clients are now being sent to a backend port that the load balancer has not mapped.
The NSG blocks probe traffic from the AzureLoadBalancer service tag (168.63.129.16), so every backend is marked unhealthy and the rule delivers nothing.
The NSG shortened the idle timeout, so every new connection is closed with a TCP reset before it can complete.
The NSG automatically turned on session persistence, so all clients are pinned to a single VM that is now overloaded.
questions.why: Health probes come from 168.63.129.16 (the AzureLoadBalancer tag); if the NSG blocks them, all probes fail, every backend is marked down, and the application looks offline even though the servers are running.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a load balancing rule ties together and how it decides which server gets a connection. Include one limit or tradeoff, such as what session persistence costs or what happens when the health probe is misconfigured.
lessons.modelAnswer: A load balancing rule connects the load balancer's frontend IP and port to a backend pool and a backend port, for a chosen protocol. It also attaches a health probe. When a new flow arrives that matches the rule, the load balancer picks one healthy backend using a hash of the five-tuple, so one connection stays on one server. The frontend and backend ports can differ, for example 80 outside and 8080 inside. Session persistence by client IP keeps a user on the same server, which helps apps that keep state locally. The tradeoff is less even spreading, especially when many users share one IP behind a NAT. The biggest risk is the probe. If it targets the wrong port, or a network security group blocks the AzureLoadBalancer tag, every backend is marked down and traffic stops even though the VMs are fine.
rubricPoints: States that the rule maps a frontend IP, protocol and port to a backend pool and backend port.
Explains that a health probe decides which backends are eligible.
Mentions five-tuple hash distribution and that session persistence can change it.
Notes that frontend and backend ports can differ.
Names a tradeoff, such as uneven spread from persistence or a total outage from a failing probe.

suggested.rationale: The skill is reasoning through a scenario's ports, probes and persistence to choose correct rule settings, which an exam-style situation exercises better than any current mission.

lessons.plain: An inbound NAT rule tells a load balancer to send traffic arriving on one specific public port straight to one specific machine behind it, instead of spreading it across many machines. NAT means network address translation: rewriting the destination address and port of a packet as it passes through. Think of an office building with one street address. The receptionist normally sends visitors to whichever clerk is free, but if you say extension 501, you go to Alice's desk and nobody else's. Admins use this to reach one particular virtual machine, for example to log in remotely, while sharing a single public address across the whole group.
lessons.guessPrompt: Three virtual machines sit behind one load balancer with a single public IP address, and all three listen for remote logins on port 22. How could an admin on the internet reach exactly the second machine, and not whichever one the load balancer picks?
lessons.teach:
An inbound NAT rule on Azure Load Balancer (Microsoft's managed layer-4 traffic distributor, working on IP addresses and ports rather than web content) maps a frontend IP address and port to one backend virtual machine's private IP address and port. The frontend is the address clients connect to; the backend is the VM's network interface inside the virtual network. A load-balancing rule spreads connections across a pool; a NAT rule pins a connection to one target.

There are two forms. The single-VM form maps one frontend port to one VM. The backend-pool form gives a frontend port range plus a backend port, and the load balancer assigns each VM in the pool its own frontend port from that range, which scales better when VMs are added.

Worked example: frontend IP 20.1.2.3, rule frontend ports 50001 to 50003, backend port 22, pool of VM1 (10.0.1.4), VM2 (10.0.1.5), VM3 (10.0.1.6). The load balancer assigns 50001 to VM1, 50002 to VM2, 50003 to VM3. An admin connects to 20.1.2.3:50002. Step one, the load balancer matches port 50002 to VM2. Step two, it rewrites the destination to 10.0.1.5:22. Step three, VM2 answers, and the load balancer translates the reply so it appears to come from 20.1.2.3:50002. The admin is now on VM2.

Other settings: protocol (TCP or UDP), idle timeout (how long a quiet connection stays open), TCP reset on idle, and floating IP (keeps the frontend address as the destination instead of rewriting it). Note that NAT rules do not use health probes; traffic is forwarded even if the VM is unhealthy.

Common mistake: forgetting the network security group, a list of allow and deny rules on the subnet or interface. The Standard SKU is closed by default, so without an NSG rule allowing port 22 to the VM, the NAT rule exists but every connection times out. Also, a frontend port cannot be reused by a load-balancing rule on the same frontend IP and protocol. Finally, exposing management ports publicly invites brute-force attempts, so restrict source addresses.

questions.prompt: Larkspur Analytics uses a Standard SKU Azure Load Balancer (a managed layer-4 distributor that works on IP addresses and ports). It has an inbound NAT rule mapping frontend 40.5.6.7, TCP port 4022, to the virtual machine db-01 at private address 10.20.0.8, port 22. An engineer's SSH connection to 40.5.6.7:4022 times out, so the team troubleshoots. Step 1: they confirm that the NAT rule exists and points to 10.20.0.8:22. Step 2: they confirm that db-01 is running. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the engineer retries, the load balancer rewrites the destination to 10.20.0.8:22, and the session opens. Which action is Step 3?
choices: Add a health probe on port 22 so that the NAT rule knows db-01 is healthy enough to receive traffic
Add a network security group rule that allows TCP port 22 to db-01, limited to the engineer's source address
Enable floating IP on the NAT rule so that the destination address is no longer rewritten
Raise the idle timeout on the NAT rule so that the connection has more time to open
questions.why: A Standard SKU load balancer is closed by default, so a NAT rule only works once a network security group (a list of allow and deny rules on the subnet or interface) permits the backend port, and limiting the source address reduces brute-force exposure.

questions.prompt: Meridian Freight runs six identical web servers behind one Azure Load Balancer. It wants public HTTPS traffic shared across all six, and its admins also need to reach one particular server, app-04, on its own for maintenance. Which feature handles the admins' requirement?
choices: An inbound NAT rule, because it maps a frontend IP and port to one specific backend VM's private IP and port
A health probe, because it routes admin connections to whichever VM is currently healthy
Floating IP, because it gives app-04 its own public address inside the virtual network
A load-balancing rule, because it spreads connections across every VM in the backend pool
questions.why: A load-balancing rule spreads connections across a pool, while an inbound NAT rule pins a connection to one chosen target VM.

questions.prompt: Brightwater Clinics creates a backend-pool inbound NAT rule. The frontend is 52.14.9.30, the frontend port range is 61001 to 61004, and the backend port is 3389. The load balancer has assigned frontend port 61003 to VM ward-c, whose private address is 10.8.2.12. An admin connects to 52.14.9.30:61003. With floating IP turned off, which destination does the load balancer rewrite the traffic to?
questions.why: The load balancer matches the frontend port to ward-c and rewrites the destination to that VM's private IP and the rule's backend port, 3389.

questions.prompt: Tidewell Games has an inbound NAT rule that forwards frontend port 50110 to VM build-02 on port 22. The operating system on build-02 hangs and stops answering, but nobody changes the load balancer. What happens to new connections that arrive on frontend port 50110?
choices: They are automatically redirected to another healthy VM in the same backend pool
They are still forwarded to build-02, because inbound NAT rules do not use health probes
They are moved to a load-balancing rule that shares the same frontend port
They are rejected at the load balancer, because its health probe marks build-02 as down
questions.why: NAT rules ignore health probes, so traffic keeps going to the one mapped VM even when that VM is unhealthy.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what an inbound NAT rule does on Azure Load Balancer, how it differs from a load-balancing rule, and name at least one limit or risk they should keep in mind when using it.
lessons.modelAnswer: An inbound NAT rule maps a frontend IP and port on the load balancer to one specific backend VM's private IP and port. So instead of the load balancer choosing a VM, like a load-balancing rule does, the port number decides which VM you land on. For example, 20.1.2.3:50002 goes to VM2 on port 22. The backend-pool version takes a port range and hands each VM its own frontend port, so it grows as you add VMs. Limits: NAT rules ignore health probes, so traffic goes to the VM even if it is down. On the Standard SKU you also need an NSG rule allowing the port, or connections just time out. You cannot reuse a frontend port already used by a load-balancing rule on the same IP and protocol. And publishing management ports to the internet is risky, so restrict source IPs or prefer a safer remote-access path.
rubricPoints: States that a NAT rule maps a frontend IP and port to one specific backend VM and port.
Contrasts it with a load-balancing rule that spreads traffic across a pool.
Mentions the backend-pool form that assigns each VM its own port from a range.
Notes an NSG must allow the traffic on the Standard SKU.
Names a limit such as no health probes, port conflicts, or exposure of management ports.

suggested.rationale: Tracing a packet from a frontend port through the address rewrite and NSG check to one backend VM is exactly what a virtual network path tracer would let the learner practise.

lessons.plain: When servers inside a private network reach out to the internet, they need a public address to speak from, because their private addresses are not routable outside. Source network address translation (SNAT) swaps each server's private address for a shared public one on the way out and swaps it back on the reply. An explicit outbound rule is the setting on a load balancer that says which servers share which public addresses, and how many connection slots each one gets. Think of an office switchboard: many staff share a few outside phone lines, and someone decides how many lines each desk may use at once.
lessons.guessPrompt: If one public IP address gives you roughly 64,000 outgoing connection slots, and you want ten virtual machines to share it fairly, about how many slots would you hand each machine, and what happens if an eleventh machine joins?
lessons.teach:
An outbound rule on an Azure Standard Load Balancer is an explicit setting that maps a backend pool (the group of virtual machines behind the load balancer) to one or more frontend public IP addresses for traffic the machines start themselves. It performs SNAT: the load balancer rewrites each outgoing packet's private source address and port to a public address and a SNAT port, then reverses the swap for the reply.

Why ports matter: each public IP offers about 64,000 SNAT ports. Every simultaneous connection to the same destination address and port uses one. An outbound rule lets you set exactly how many ports each machine receives, in multiples of 8, along with the protocol (TCP, UDP or both) and an idle timeout (4 to 120 minutes) after which unused connections are released. You can also enable TCP reset on idle so both ends learn the connection closed.

Worked example: one frontend IP gives about 64,000 ports. The pool may grow to 10 machines, so you allocate 6,400 ports each (6,400 is divisible by 8). Ten machines use 64,000 ports, the full supply. If an eleventh machine joins, no ports remain, so it gets no outbound access. Adding a second public IP doubles the supply to about 128,000, enough for 20 machines at 6,400 each.

Without an outbound rule, a load-balancing rule can provide outbound SNAT automatically, but it allocates a small default number of ports based on pool size, which is hard to predict. Best practice is to turn off outbound SNAT on the load-balancing rule and define an explicit outbound rule instead.

Common mistake: allocating ports for today's pool size rather than the maximum. Running out of SNAT ports, called SNAT port exhaustion, shows up as intermittent outbound connection failures and timeouts under load, often to one busy destination such as a database or API, while inbound traffic still looks healthy.

questions.prompt: Harbourline Logistics runs a fleet-tracking service behind an Azure Standard Load Balancer. Its backend pool (the group of virtual machines behind the load balancer) has 10 machines today and is capped at 16 machines at peak. The team attaches two frontend public IP addresses and writes an explicit outbound rule so each machine's self-started traffic gets SNAT (its private source address and port rewritten to a public address and a SNAT port). Step 1: two public IPs give about 2 × 64,000 = 128,000 SNAT ports in total. Step 2: ??? Step 3: confirm the per-machine number is a multiple of 8, as outbound rules require. Step 4: save the outbound rule with protocol TCP and a 15-minute idle timeout. Which choice correctly completes Step 2?
choices: Divide the total by today's pool size: 128,000 ÷ 10 = 12,800 ports per machine.
Divide the total by the maximum pool size: 128,000 ÷ 16 = 8,000 ports per machine.
Give each machine one full public IP's supply: 64,000 ports per machine.
Divide one IP's ports by the maximum pool size: 64,000 ÷ 16 = 4,000 ports per machine.
questions.why: Sizing against the maximum of 16 machines with both IPs' 128,000 ports gives 8,000 each, a multiple of 8, so every machine still has outbound access when the pool is full.

questions.prompt: On an Azure Standard Load Balancer, what does the SNAT (source network address translation) performed by an outbound rule actually do?
choices: It spreads incoming client connections evenly across all machines in the backend pool.
It rewrites the private source address and port of traffic a backend machine starts to a public IP and a SNAT port, then reverses the swap for the reply.
It rewrites the destination address of incoming requests so they reach a chosen backend virtual machine.
It blocks any outbound connection that has been idle for longer than the configured timeout.
questions.why: SNAT changes the source side of machine-initiated outbound packets to a public address and SNAT port and translates the replies back, which is what lets private machines reach the internet.

questions.prompt: Brightwell Pharmacy's order-processing virtual machines sit behind an Azure Standard Load Balancer. During a weekend sale, calls from those machines to an external payment API fail intermittently and time out, yet customers reaching the site through the load balancer see normal, healthy responses. Nothing else changed. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The backend machines have run out of SNAT ports, known as SNAT port exhaustion.
The load balancer's health probe is marking the backend machines as unhealthy.
The frontend public IP address was removed from the load balancer.
TCP reset on idle is enabled on the outbound rule.
questions.why: Intermittent outbound failures under load to one busy destination while inbound traffic stays healthy is the typical sign that too few SNAT ports were allocated.

questions.prompt: Corvane Studios relies on a load-balancing rule's automatic outbound SNAT for its render farm, and engineers can't predict how many SNAT ports each machine receives as the pool changes size. Which change follows best practice?
choices: Keep the automatic SNAT and add more machines to the pool so the ports spread further.
