Shorten the idle timeout on the load-balancing rule to 2 minutes so ports are freed faster.
Turn off outbound SNAT on the load-balancing rule and define an explicit outbound rule that sets ports per machine.
Create an outbound rule but leave outbound SNAT switched on in the load-balancing rule too, so both supply ports.
questions.why: An explicit outbound rule, with outbound SNAT disabled on the load-balancing rule, lets you set a predictable number of ports per machine instead of relying on a small, pool-size-based default.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what an explicit outbound rule on a Standard Load Balancer does and how you would size its SNAT port allocation, naming the tradeoff between ports per machine and how far the pool can scale.
lessons.modelAnswer: An outbound rule tells the Standard Load Balancer which public IPs the backend pool uses when its machines start connections to the internet. It does SNAT: it swaps each machine's private address and port for a public IP and a SNAT port, then swaps back on replies. Each public IP gives about 64,000 ports, and each concurrent connection to the same destination uses one. I set ports per machine in multiples of 8, plus protocol and idle timeout. The tradeoff is fixed supply: more ports per machine means fewer machines fit. With one IP and 6,400 ports each, only ten machines get outbound access, and an eleventh gets none. So I size for the maximum pool, add public IPs if needed, and disable default SNAT on the load-balancing rule so allocation is predictable rather than automatic and small. Exhaustion shows as intermittent outbound timeouts.
rubricPoints: States that an outbound rule maps the backend pool to frontend public IPs for connections the machines start.
Explains SNAT as rewriting private source address and port to a public address and SNAT port, reversed on replies.
Notes each public IP supplies about 64,000 ports, allocated per machine in multiples of 8.
Names the tradeoff that more ports per machine means fewer machines can scale into the pool, and adding IPs raises the supply.
Recommends disabling default SNAT on the load-balancing rule in favour of the explicit rule.
Describes SNAT exhaustion symptoms as intermittent outbound failures or timeouts.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine exercises SNAT port math, so reasoning through exam-style sizing scenarios with pool sizes and public IP counts builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: Azure Application Gateway is a managed web traffic manager that sits in front of your web servers inside one Azure region. Unlike a basic load balancer, which only looks at addresses and ports, it reads each web request: the website name, the path, the headers, the cookies. Think of a hotel receptionist who reads each guest's booking and sends them to the right floor, where a doorman would only count heads at the door. Mapping requirements to its features means hearing a need, such as 'send /images to the image servers', and naming the gateway capability that delivers it.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company hosts shop.contoso.com and blog.contoso.com on separate server groups in one Azure region, behind a single public IP address. Which piece of each request would a traffic manager have to read to send visitors to the right group?
lessons.teach:
Application Gateway is a regional layer 7 load balancer. Layer 7 is the application layer, where HTTP and HTTPS live. Regional means it serves one Azure region, not the globe. Because it understands HTTP, it can decide using request content. These features are the ones to map. Path-based routing sends requests by URL path, so /video goes to one backend pool, meaning a group of servers. Multi-site hosting routes by host name, so one gateway serves several domains. TLS termination decrypts HTTPS at the gateway, which saves server CPU. End-to-end TLS re-encrypts traffic toward the backend when compliance requires encryption all the way. Redirection can turn HTTP into HTTPS. Header and URL rewrite edit requests or responses as they pass through. Cookie-based session affinity keeps one user on the same server. Connection draining lets a server being removed finish its open requests. Web Application Firewall (WAF) is an optional add-on that blocks common web attacks such as SQL injection. The v2 SKU, meaning the product version, adds autoscaling and zone redundancy, which is copies spread across datacenters in a region.

Worked example. The requirement reads: 'One region, HTTPS only, block SQL injection, /api to API servers, everything else to web servers.' Step 1: the traffic is HTTP and stays in one region, so Application Gateway fits. Step 2: HTTPS only maps to a redirect from HTTP to HTTPS plus TLS termination. Step 3: blocking SQL injection maps to WAF. Step 4: the /api split maps to path-based routing with two backend pools. Azure Load Balancer fails because it works at layer 4, the address and port level, and cannot read paths. Front Door fails as the best answer because it is global and edge-based, which this single-region need does not call for.

A common mistake is picking Application Gateway for non-web traffic, such as a database port or UDP game traffic. It only handles web protocols, so that traffic needs Azure Load Balancer. Another mistake is choosing it for users worldwide who need caching near them, which is Front Door's job. Choosing the wrong tool leaves a requirement unmet in production. Typical results are unprotected endpoints, broken sessions, or traffic that simply cannot be routed.

questions.prompt: A city library runs its web apps in one Azure region. The requirement reads: 'Serve catalog.library.example and events.library.example from one gateway, keep each patron on the same server during a session, and let servers finish open requests before they are removed for patching.' Step 1: the traffic is HTTP and stays in one region, so Application Gateway fits. Step 2: ??? Step 3: keeping each patron on the same server maps to cookie-based session affinity. Step 4: letting servers finish open requests before removal maps to connection draining. Which feature completes Step 2?
choices: Serving two domains from one gateway maps to path-based routing, which splits requests by URL path.
Serving two domains from one gateway maps to header rewrite, which edits the host name as requests pass through.
Serving two domains from one gateway maps to multi-site hosting, which routes requests by host name.
Serving two domains from one gateway maps to Front Door, because more than one domain needs a global service.
questions.why: Multi-site hosting routes by host name, so a single regional gateway can serve several domains.

questions.prompt: A health records portal uses Application Gateway in one region. An auditor says patient data must stay encrypted on every hop, including the hop from the gateway to the backend servers. Which feature meets this requirement?
choices: Header and URL rewrite, which edits requests as they pass through
End-to-end TLS, which re-encrypts traffic toward the backend servers
TLS termination only, which decrypts HTTPS at the gateway to save server CPU
Redirection, which turns incoming HTTP requests into HTTPS
questions.why: End-to-end TLS re-encrypts traffic from the gateway to the backend, so data stays encrypted all the way, while TLS termination alone leaves that last hop unencrypted.

questions.prompt: A game studio needs to spread UDP game traffic across a pool of servers in one Azure region. An engineer proposes Application Gateway with WAF. What is the right assessment?
choices: Wrong, because Front Door should be used for any traffic that needs load balancing
Correct, because Application Gateway is regional and the traffic stays in one region
Correct, because WAF protects the UDP game servers from common attacks
Wrong, because Application Gateway only handles web protocols, so Azure Load Balancer fits
questions.why: Application Gateway works only with web traffic such as HTTP and HTTPS, so non-web traffic like UDP needs Azure Load Balancer, which works at layer 4.

questions.prompt: A retailer's Application Gateway must add capacity automatically during holiday sales and keep running if one datacenter in its region fails. Which choice fits?
choices: The v2 SKU, which adds autoscaling and zone redundancy
Cookie-based session affinity, which keeps each shopper on one server
Front Door, which places copies of the service at the global edge
Connection draining, which lets servers finish open requests before removal
questions.why: The v2 SKU adds autoscaling and zone redundancy, which spreads copies across datacenters within one region.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you decide that a requirement calls for Application Gateway, and name at least three features you would map to specific needs. Include one limit that would push you to Azure Load Balancer or Front Door instead.
lessons.modelAnswer: Application Gateway is a regional layer 7 load balancer, so I reach for it when web traffic in one region needs routing based on what is inside the request. If different URL paths must go to different server pools, that's path-based routing. If several domains share one gateway, that's multi-site hosting. If the requirement is HTTPS everywhere, I'd use TLS termination plus an HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect, and end-to-end TLS if traffic must stay encrypted to the backend. If users must stay on one server, that's cookie-based session affinity. If it needs protection from attacks like SQL injection, that's the WAF add-on. If load varies, the v2 SKU autoscales. The limits matter too. It only handles web protocols, so raw TCP or UDP traffic belongs on Azure Load Balancer. It is also regional, so global users who need edge caching and acceleration point to Front Door.
rubricPoints: States that Application Gateway is a regional layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS) load balancer.
Maps at least three requirements to features such as path-based routing, multi-site hosting, TLS termination, session affinity, rewrite, or WAF.
Notes that the WAF add-on handles protection against common web attacks.
Explains that non-web TCP/UDP traffic belongs on Azure Load Balancer.
Explains that global, edge-cached delivery points to Front Door instead.

suggested.rationale: This objective is about reasoning from a written requirement to the right feature and ruling out the alternatives, which exam-style scenarios practise better than any current mission or planned engine.

lessons.plain: Azure Application Gateway is a managed web traffic distributor that sits in front of websites and web APIs inside one Azure region. A basic load balancer only sees addresses and port numbers. Application Gateway reads each web request, including the site name, the URL path and cookies, and decides which group of servers should answer it. Think of a hotel receptionist who reads your booking and sends you to the right floor, compared with a turnstile that simply lets people through one by one. It can also check requests for common attacks using a built-in web application firewall.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company runs one website in a single Azure region. Requests for /images should go to one set of servers and requests for /api should go to another. Would a device that only looks at IP addresses and port numbers be able to make that split? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
Azure Application Gateway is a regional layer 7 load balancer. Layer 7 is the application layer: the gateway understands HTTP and HTTPS, the protocols browsers and web APIs use. Layer 4 is the transport layer, which sees only IP addresses, TCP or UDP ports, and nothing inside the request. Azure Load Balancer works at layer 4. Regional means the gateway is deployed into a subnet of your virtual network in one Azure region. A virtual network is your private network space in Azure.

Because it reads the request, Application Gateway can do several things a layer 4 device cannot. Path-based routing sends different URL paths to different backend pools, where a backend pool is the group of servers that receives the traffic. Multi-site hosting serves several domain names from one gateway. TLS termination decrypts HTTPS at the gateway so the servers do less work. TLS, Transport Layer Security, is the encryption behind HTTPS. Cookie-based session affinity keeps a user on the same server. The Web Application Firewall (WAF) blocks attacks such as SQL injection, which is malicious database commands hidden in input.

Here is a worked example. Shop.example.com runs only in West Europe and needs protection from injection attacks. A user requests https://shop.example.com/api/cart. The gateway decrypts the TLS, and the WAF inspects the request and finds nothing harmful. The gateway sees the path /api/* and forwards the request to the API pool. A request for /images/logo.png goes to the image pool instead.

So why not the other two services? Azure Load Balancer cannot see paths or hostnames. Azure Front Door is a global entry point at Microsoft's edge locations. It suits apps spread across several regions, or apps that need caching close to users. Application Gateway fits a single-region web app, including internal apps reachable only on a private IP address.

A common mistake is picking Application Gateway for traffic that is not web traffic, such as RDP or a UDP game service. That traffic belongs on Azure Load Balancer. Another mistake is relying on Application Gateway for cross-region failover. If its region fails, the gateway fails with it.

questions.prompt: A physiotherapy clinic runs its web app only in the Australia East region. It must serve two domain names, booking.physioclinic.example for patients and staff.physioclinic.example for employees, through one entry point. An engineer reasons through the choice as follows. Step 1: Both sites are HTTPS web traffic, and the routing decision depends on the hostname inside the request. Azure Load Balancer works at layer 4 and sees only IP addresses and ports, so it is ruled out. Step 2: The app runs in one region and has no need for caching near users, so Azure Front Door's global edge is not required. Application Gateway, a regional layer 7 load balancer, fits. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: Each hostname's requests reach its own backend pool, the group of servers for that site. Which Application Gateway feature completes Step 3?
choices: Enable TLS termination so the gateway decrypts HTTPS and the servers do less work
Use path-based routing so that requests for /booking and /staff go to different backend pools
Turn on cookie-based session affinity so each user stays on the same server
Configure multi-site hosting so one gateway serves both domain names and sends each to its own backend pool
questions.why: Multi-site hosting is the feature that lets one gateway serve several domain names and route each hostname to its own backend pool. Path-based routing works on URL paths, not hostnames.

questions.prompt: Why can Azure Application Gateway send /video/* requests to one server group and /docs/* requests to another, while Azure Load Balancer cannot?
choices: Application Gateway works at layer 7 and reads HTTP requests, including the URL path. Load Balancer works at layer 4 and sees only IP addresses and ports.
Application Gateway uses cookie-based session affinity, and that feature is what makes path decisions possible.
Load Balancer can read paths, but only for UDP traffic, so it ignores HTTPS requests.
Application Gateway is deployed at Microsoft's global edge locations, while Load Balancer runs inside one region.
questions.why: Path-based routing requires reading inside the HTTP request, which only a layer 7 device like Application Gateway does. A layer 4 load balancer sees only addresses and ports.

questions.prompt: A logistics company hosts an internal staff timesheet web app in the Canada Central region. The app must be reachable only on a private IP address inside the company's virtual network, and security requires blocking SQL injection attempts. Which choice fits best?
choices: Azure Load Balancer, because internal apps need only layer 4 distribution
Azure Application Gateway with the Web Application Firewall (WAF), deployed with a private IP in the virtual network
Azure Front Door with caching enabled, so staff get faster page loads
Azure Front Door with its WAF, because Front Door is the only service that protects web apps
questions.why: Application Gateway fits single-region web apps, including internal apps on a private IP, and its WAF blocks attacks such as SQL injection. Load Balancer cannot inspect requests, and Front Door is a global edge entry point.

questions.prompt: A media company runs its web app behind a single Application Gateway in North Europe. It assumes that if North Europe has an outage, the gateway will redirect users to a copy of the app in another region. What is wrong with this plan?
choices: The plan fails only because cookie-based session affinity must be turned off before failover can work.
Application Gateway is regional, so if North Europe fails the gateway fails with it. Cross-region entry and failover is a job for Azure Front Door.
Nothing is wrong. Application Gateway automatically fails over to any region with a healthy backend pool.
Azure Load Balancer should be placed in front of the gateway, because layer 4 devices handle global failover.
questions.why: Application Gateway is deployed into one region's virtual network and goes down if that region fails. Front Door is the global entry point suited to multi-region apps.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would choose Azure Application Gateway over Azure Load Balancer or Azure Front Door, and name one limit that would push you to a different service.
lessons.modelAnswer: Application Gateway is a regional, layer 7 load balancer for HTTP and HTTPS traffic. It lives in a subnet of our virtual network and reads each request's hostname, path and cookies. That means it can send /api to one backend pool and /images to another, and host several sites on one gateway. It can also terminate TLS so our servers don't decrypt traffic, keep users on one server with cookie affinity, and block attacks like SQL injection with its WAF. Azure Load Balancer can't do any of that, because it only sees IPs and ports. I'd pick Application Gateway for a web app in one region, including an internal app on a private IP. The limits matter, though. It's built for web traffic, so RDP or UDP belongs on Load Balancer. It's also regional, so if we need global entry, multi-region failover or edge caching, Front Door is the better fit.
rubricPoints: States that Application Gateway is a layer 7 load balancer for HTTP and HTTPS web traffic.
Names at least two request-aware features, such as path-based routing, multi-site hosting, TLS termination, cookie affinity or WAF.
Explains that Azure Load Balancer is layer 4 and cannot route by path or hostname.
Notes that Application Gateway is regional and lives in a virtual network, unlike the global Front Door.
Names a limit: it does not suit non-web traffic, or it cannot provide cross-region failover on its own.

suggested.rationale: This objective is about picking the right service from a requirement, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios that contrast Application Gateway with Load Balancer and Front Door builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: Azure Application Gateway is a managed web traffic front door: it receives HTTP and HTTPS requests and spreads them across your servers. Behind the scenes it runs on a number of instances, meaning copies of the gateway. You decide how that number is set. With manual capacity you pick a fixed count, like booking a set number of checkout staff for every shift. With autoscale you give a minimum and a maximum, and the gateway adds or removes instances as traffic rises and falls, like a shop that calls in extra staff when the queue grows and sends them home when it shrinks.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your web app needs about 3 gateway instances most of the day but sometimes needs 8 during a busy hour. Would you rather fix the gateway at 8 instances all day, or let it move between 3 and 8 on its own, and what could go wrong with each choice?
lessons.teach:
Application Gateway capacity is the number of gateway instances handling traffic. On the v2 SKU (Standard_v2 and WAF_v2; a SKU is a product tier), you choose between two capacity modes. Manual, also called fixed, capacity means you set one instance count and it never changes unless you change it. Autoscale means you set a minimum instance count and a maximum instance count, and the platform adds instances when load grows and removes them when load drops. The older v1 SKU only offers manual capacity.

Why it works: autoscale watches how busy the gateway is and adjusts. You still pay for the minimum all the time, because those instances are always reserved, but you only pay for extra capacity while it is used. The maximum caps both capacity and cost.

Worked example. A shop's site needs 3 instances overnight and up to 8 during a lunchtime rush. Step 1: with manual capacity of 3, lunchtime traffic overwhelms the gateway and users see slow pages or errors. Step 2: with manual capacity of 8, lunchtime is fine, but you pay for 8 instances all night. Step 3: with autoscale, minimum 3 and maximum 10, the gateway runs 3 overnight, grows toward 8 at lunch, and keeps headroom up to 10 for a surprise. Autoscale wins here.

Manual still fits when load is steady and well known, or when you need a strictly predictable bill and capacity that never moves.

Common mistake: setting the autoscale minimum too low, even zero, to save money. Adding instances is not instant; it takes minutes. If traffic jumps suddenly, the gateway is undersized while new instances start, and users get timeouts or 502 errors. In a running system, set the minimum to cover your normal baseline plus a safety margin for sudden spikes, and set the maximum high enough for your worst expected peak.

questions.prompt: A city council runs a parking-permit portal behind an Application Gateway on the WAF_v2 SKU (a SKU is a product tier). On ordinary days the portal needs about 4 gateway instances. When new permits open each quarter, demand jumps within minutes to about 12 instances. Step 1: with manual (fixed) capacity of 4, the quarterly rush overwhelms the gateway and residents see slow pages and errors. Step 2: with manual capacity of 12, the rush is handled, but the council pays for 12 instances every ordinary day. Step 3: the team switches to autoscale, where you set a minimum and a maximum instance count and the platform adds or removes instances between them. [Missing step: which minimum and maximum should they choose?] Step 4: the gateway sits near its minimum on ordinary days, grows during the permit rush, and the bill rises only while the extra instances run.
choices: Minimum 0, maximum 12, so ordinary days cost as little as possible
Minimum 5, maximum 14, covering the normal baseline with a margin and leaving headroom above the expected peak
Minimum 12, maximum 12, so the rush capacity is always ready
Minimum 2, maximum 8, keeping costs low on both quiet days and busy days
questions.why: The minimum should cover the normal baseline of 4 plus a safety margin because new instances take minutes to start, and the maximum should be at least the worst expected peak of 12, with some headroom for surprises.

questions.prompt: A team runs an Application Gateway v2 with autoscale set to minimum 3 and maximum 9. On average it runs 5 instances. Which statement about cost is correct?
choices: They always pay for at least 3 instances, plus extra only while more instances are actually running
Autoscale has a fixed price, so the bill is the same whatever the load
They pay only for the instances in use, so a quiet hour with 1 instance of load costs 1 instance
They pay for 9 instances all the time, because the maximum is reserved
questions.why: The minimum instances are always reserved and billed, while capacity above the minimum is billed only while it is used, and the maximum caps how high capacity and cost can go.

questions.prompt: A company has an existing Application Gateway on the v1 SKU. Its traffic varies a lot during the day, and the team wants the gateway to add and remove instances automatically. What must they understand first?
choices: The v1 SKU supports only manual capacity, so they need a v2 SKU (Standard_v2 or WAF_v2) to use autoscale
On v1 they must set the minimum to zero before autoscale becomes available
Autoscale is available on v1, but only on the WAF tier
On v1 they only need to set a maximum instance count to turn on autoscale
questions.why: Only the v2 SKU offers a choice between manual and autoscale capacity; the older v1 SKU offers manual capacity only.

questions.prompt: To save money, an online ticket reseller sets its Application Gateway v2 autoscale minimum to 0 and its maximum to 20. When a popular concert goes on sale, traffic jumps from almost nothing to heavy load within seconds. What is the most likely result?
choices: The gateway switches itself to manual capacity of 20 for the rest of the day
Users get timeouts or 502 errors for several minutes, because new instances take minutes to start
Nothing goes wrong, because autoscale adds all 20 instances the moment traffic arrives
The bill is capped at zero, because the minimum is zero
questions.why: Adding instances is not instant, so with a minimum set too low the gateway stays undersized while new instances start, and users see timeouts or 502 errors during the sudden spike.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would pick manual capacity versus autoscale for Application Gateway v2, and name one limit or tradeoff of autoscale they should watch for.
lessons.modelAnswer: Application Gateway runs as a number of instances. With manual capacity we fix that number; it never changes on its own, so the cost and capacity are completely predictable, which suits steady, well-understood traffic. With autoscale on the v2 SKU we set a minimum and a maximum, and the gateway grows and shrinks with load. That suits traffic that varies through the day or has peaks, because we pay for the minimum all the time and for extra instances only while they are in use, with the maximum capping cost. The tradeoff is that scaling out takes minutes, not seconds. If we set the minimum too low and traffic spikes suddenly, users can see slow responses or 502 errors before new instances are ready. So the minimum should cover the normal baseline plus a margin, and the maximum should cover the worst peak. The old v1 SKU only supports manual capacity.
rubricPoints: Manual capacity is a fixed instance count that only changes when someone changes it.
Autoscale on v2 uses a minimum and maximum and adjusts instances to load.
Manual suits steady, predictable traffic or a strictly fixed bill; autoscale suits variable or peaky traffic.
The minimum is always paid for and the maximum caps capacity and cost.
Scaling out takes minutes, so a too-low minimum risks errors during sudden spikes.
The v1 SKU supports only manual capacity.

suggested.rationale: Setting minimum and maximum instance counts against a traffic curve and watching scale-out lag cause errors is exactly the judgment an autoscaling policy engine would let the learner practise.

lessons.plain: A backend pool is the list of servers that a load balancer is allowed to hand traffic to. Think of a restaurant host at the door: customers arrive at one entrance, and the host seats them at whichever table is free. The backend pool is the host's list of tables. In Azure, the load balancer has a front door address, and the backend pool names the virtual machines, or the IP addresses, standing behind it. A server that is not on the list never gets traffic, however healthy it is. Creating the pool is one step. Rules and health checks then decide how traffic actually flows.
lessons.guessPrompt: You put three web servers in a load balancer's backend pool, but you have not yet written any rule saying which port to forward. If a user browses to the load balancer's address on port 80, do you think any server receives the request? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
A backend pool is a named group of destinations attached to an Azure Load Balancer, Azure's managed layer-4 traffic distributor. The pool says where traffic may go. It does not say when or how. Two other pieces do that. A load balancing rule maps a frontend IP and port, meaning the address clients connect to, onto the pool. A health probe is a repeated check that marks each member up or down.

You can add members in two ways. NIC-based membership adds a virtual machine's network interface, or more exactly one of its IP configurations; virtual machine scale set instances can join the same way. IP-based membership adds private IP addresses together with the virtual network (VNet), the private Azure network, that they live in. Pick one method per pool, because the two cannot be mixed. With the Standard SKU, which is the current tier, members can be any VMs or scale sets in a single VNet. The older Basic tier, now retired, limited a pool to one availability set or scale set.

Worked example. You run vm1, vm2 and vm3 in VNet app-vnet. Step 1: create a pool named web-pool on the load balancer. Step 2: add the ipconfig of each VM's NIC. Step 3: add a probe that checks TCP port 80. Step 4: add a rule from frontend port 80 to web-pool port 80 using that probe. Step 5: a client connects. The load balancer hashes the connection details, picks a member the probe reports as healthy, say vm2, and forwards the packets.

A common mistake is to stop after step 2 and expect traffic. An empty-rule pool forwards nothing. Another is adding a VM from a different VNet, which is rejected. A third is forgetting that each member's network security group must allow the application port and the probe source, 168.63.129.16. In a running system, a member the probe cannot reach is silently dropped from rotation. Users then see reduced capacity, or a total outage if every member fails.

questions.prompt:
Ledgerline, a small accounting firm, runs a reporting API on two VMs in the VNet ledger-vnet. Their private IPs are 10.4.1.10 and 10.4.1.11, and the API listens on TCP port 5000. An engineer sets up a Standard Azure Load Balancer (a managed layer-4 traffic distributor) as follows.

Step 1: create a backend pool named report-pool using IP-based membership, which adds private IP addresses together with their VNet. Add 10.4.1.10 and 10.4.1.11 with ledger-vnet.
Step 2: add a health probe, a repeated check that marks each member up or down, on TCP port 5000.
Step 3: add a load balancing rule from frontend port 443 to report-pool port 5000 using that probe.
Step 4: ???
Step 5: the probe now reports both members as healthy, and client connections to port 443 reach one of the two VMs.

Before Step 4, the probe marked both members down and nothing was forwarded, even though the API was running. What is Step 4?
choices: Update each VM's network security group to allow TCP port 5000, including traffic from the probe source 168.63.129.16.
Recreate the load balancer on the Basic SKU, which handles health probes more simply.
Change the rule's frontend port from 443 to 5000, so the frontend port matches the backend port.
Also add each VM's network interface ipconfig to report-pool, so the pool has both IP-based and NIC-based members.
questions.why: A member's network security group (its traffic filter) must allow both the application port and the probe source 168.63.129.16; otherwise the probe cannot reach the member and drops it from rotation.

questions.prompt: An Azure Load Balancer setup has three parts: a backend pool, a load balancing rule and a health probe. Which job belongs to the backend pool?
choices: Mapping the frontend IP and port that clients connect to onto a set of destinations.
Naming the group of destinations where traffic is allowed to go.
Repeatedly checking each destination and marking it up or down.
Deciding when and how a client connection should be forwarded.
questions.why: The pool only says where traffic may go; the rule maps the frontend onto the pool and the probe tracks health.

questions.prompt: Northpeak Logistics has a Standard Azure Load Balancer whose backend pool, track-pool, already holds the NICs of two VMs in the VNet hub-vnet. An engineer now tries to add the NIC of a third VM that lives in a different VNet, spoke-vnet. What happens?
choices: It is accepted only if the engineer switches the pool to IP-based membership first.
It is rejected, because all members of a pool must be in a single VNet.
It is accepted, because Standard SKU pools can contain any VMs or scale sets in any VNet.
It is accepted, but the probe will always mark the third VM as down.
questions.why: With the Standard SKU, pool members can be any VMs or scale sets, but they must all be in one VNet, so a VM from another VNet is rejected.

questions.prompt: At Brightwave Media, an engineer creates a backend pool named media-pool, adds the NIC ipconfigs of four healthy VMs and adds a health probe on TCP port 8080. Clients connecting to the load balancer's frontend on port 8080 get no response. The network security groups already allow port 8080 and the probe source. What is the most likely cause?
choices: A pool can hold at most three members, so the fourth VM blocks forwarding.
The health probe must run on a different port from the one the application uses.
No load balancing rule maps the frontend port 8080 onto media-pool, so the pool forwards nothing.
The pool needs IP-based members instead of NIC-based ones before it can forward traffic.
questions.why: A pool only says where traffic may go; without a load balancing rule connecting a frontend IP and port to the pool, no traffic is forwarded.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a backend pool on Azure Load Balancer is, the two ways to add members, and why creating the pool alone does not make traffic flow. Name one limit on which servers can be members.
lessons.modelAnswer: A backend pool is the list of destinations a load balancer may send traffic to. It is just the 'where'. There are two ways to fill it. You can add VM network interfaces, specifically their IP configurations, or scale set instances. Or you can add private IP addresses together with the VNet they sit in. You choose one method per pool and cannot mix them. On its own the pool does nothing. You still need a load balancing rule that maps a frontend IP and port to the pool, and a health probe so the load balancer only picks members that answer. One limit: with the Standard SKU, all members must be in the same virtual network. Another practical catch is that each member's NSG must allow the app port and the probe address 168.63.129.16. Otherwise the VM is marked unhealthy and gets no traffic.
rubricPoints: Defines a backend pool as the set of destinations a load balancer can forward to.
Names both membership methods: NIC/IP configuration based and IP-address based, not mixed in one pool.
States that a load balancing rule and a health probe are required before traffic flows.
Names a limit such as Standard SKU members needing to be in a single VNet.
Mentions that unhealthy or blocked members are taken out of rotation.

suggested.rationale: Creating a backend pool is mainly configuration knowledge about membership options and limits, and no current mission or planned engine has the learner build an Azure load balancer pool.

lessons.plain: A health probe is a small, repeated check that a traffic distributor sends to each server behind it to ask, in effect, "are you able to take work right now?" Servers that answer correctly keep receiving traffic; servers that stop answering are quietly taken out of rotation until they recover. Think of a restaurant host who glances at each waiter every few seconds: a waiter who is slumped over or not responding stops getting new tables, and goes back on the roster once they look ready again. In Azure, Load Balancer, Application Gateway and Front Door all use probes, but each checks at a different depth.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a load balancer only checks whether a server's network port accepts a connection, what could go wrong when the web application on that server is running but returning errors on every page?
lessons.teach:
A health probe is a recurring test sent by a load-balancing service to each member of its backend pool (the set of servers or endpoints that receive traffic). A probe has a protocol, a port, often a path such as /health, an interval (how often it runs), and a threshold (how many consecutive failures, or successes, flip a member's status). Members marked unhealthy get no new traffic; when probes pass again they are added back automatically.

Why it works: the distributor cannot see inside your app, so you give it a cheap question with a clear yes/no answer. The depth of that question matters. A TCP probe only proves a port accepts a connection. An HTTP or HTTPS probe requests a path and judges the status code, so it proves the web app actually responds.

The three services differ. Azure Load Balancer (a layer 4, connection-level distributor) supports TCP, HTTP and HTTPS probes; HTTP and HTTPS probes count only status 200 as healthy. Its probes come from the Azure address 168.63.129.16, which network security group rules must allow (the AzureLoadBalancer service tag covers it). Application Gateway (a layer 7, web request distributor) has a default probe and lets you build custom probes with your own host name, path, interval, timeout, unhealthy threshold and match conditions such as accepted status codes (200 to 399 by default) or text in the response body. Front Door (a global edge service) probes each origin from many edge locations, using HEAD or GET over HTTP or HTTPS, so frequent intervals generate a lot of requests.

Worked example: a Load Balancer HTTP probe hits /health on port 80 every 5 seconds, threshold 2. VM2's app crashes at 10:00:00. The probe at 10:00:03 fails, then 10:00:08 fails: VM2 is marked down and new flows go to VM1 and VM3. The app restarts, the next probe returns 200, VM2 rejoins.

Common mistake: using a TCP probe for a web app, or a health page that checks a shared database. The first misses hung apps; the second marks every server down at once when the database blips, taking the whole site offline.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company puts three web servers (WEB-A, WEB-B, WEB-C) behind an Application Gateway (a layer 7 web request distributor). It uses a custom probe that requests /status over HTTP every 15 seconds, with an unhealthy threshold of 3. WEB-B's app crashes at 09:20:00. Step 1: the probe at 09:20:10 gets no valid response, which is failure 1. Step 2: the probe at 09:20:25 fails, which is failure 2. Step 3: ??? Step 4: new requests are sent only to WEB-A and WEB-C. Step 5: after the app restarts, probes pass again and WEB-B is added back automatically. What is Step 3?
choices: Nothing new happens at 09:20:40. WEB-B was already marked unhealthy at 09:20:10 because any single failed probe removes a member.
The probe at 09:20:40 also fails. That is the third consecutive failure, which meets the threshold of 3, so WEB-B is marked unhealthy.
WEB-B was marked unhealthy at 09:20:25, because two failures in a row are always enough, whatever threshold is configured.
At 09:20:40 an administrator must manually remove WEB-B from the backend pool, because probes only report status and never change routing.
questions.why: The status only flips once the number of consecutive failures reaches the configured threshold, which here is 3, and the third failure comes at 09:20:40.

questions.prompt: A clinic runs its booking site on VMs behind Azure Load Balancer (a layer 4, connection-level distributor). The HTTP probe targets /ping, but that page answers with status 302, a redirect to /ping/. What happens to the VMs?
choices: They are marked unhealthy, because Load Balancer HTTP probes treat only status 200 as healthy.
They are marked unhealthy only if the redirect target also fails to answer.
They stay healthy, because any status from 200 to 399 is accepted by default.
They stay healthy, because Load Balancer only checks that the port accepts a connection.
questions.why: Azure Load Balancer HTTP and HTTPS probes count only status 200 as healthy. The 200 to 399 default range belongs to Application Gateway.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm adds a new network security group (NSG, a set of allow and deny traffic rules) to its backend VMs behind Azure Load Balancer. The NSG denies all inbound traffic except from the company's office range. Right away, every VM shows as unhealthy, even though the apps are running fine. What is the most likely fix?
choices: Change the probe path to the site's home page instead of the health page.
Raise the unhealthy threshold so that more failures are needed before a VM is marked down.
Switch the probe from HTTP to TCP so that it uses a lighter check.
Add an NSG rule that allows inbound traffic from the AzureLoadBalancer service tag, which covers 168.63.129.16.
questions.why: Load Balancer probes come from 168.63.129.16. If the NSG blocks that address, every probe fails no matter what protocol, threshold or path is used.

questions.prompt: An online bookshop's web app sometimes hangs. The process keeps port 443 open but never returns a page. Its load-balancing probe still reports every server as healthy, so customers keep landing on the hung servers. Which change best addresses this?
choices: Keep the TCP probe and shorten its interval so that it runs more often.
Keep the TCP probe and lower its threshold to one failure.
Point the probe at a health page that also checks the shared customer database.
Replace the TCP probe with an HTTPS probe on a lightweight health path that judges the status code.
questions.why: A TCP probe only proves the port accepts connections. An HTTPS probe checks that the app actually returns a valid response. A health page that checks a shared database could mark every server down at once whenever the database has a brief problem.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a health probe does and how you would choose its type and settings, naming at least one tradeoff in how deep or how frequent the check should be.
lessons.modelAnswer: A health probe is a repeated check the load balancer, Application Gateway or Front Door sends to each backend so it only sends traffic to members that answer correctly. Failed probes past the threshold pull a member out; passing probes bring it back. I would pick the depth deliberately: a TCP probe only proves a port is open, so for a web app I prefer an HTTP or HTTPS probe on a dedicated path like /health, which Load Balancer accepts only with a 200 and Application Gateway can match against status ranges or body text. The tradeoff is depth versus blast radius: a health page that checks a shared database can mark every server down at once. Frequency is another tradeoff: short intervals and low thresholds detect failure faster but add load, which is noticeable with Front Door probing from many edge sites. I would also make sure NSGs allow probe traffic from 168.63.129.16.
rubricPoints: A probe is a repeated check that removes unhealthy backends from rotation and restores them when they recover.
TCP probes only test that a port is open, while HTTP/HTTPS probes test that the app returns an accepted status.
Interval and threshold trade detection speed against probe load and false alarms.
A health endpoint that checks shared dependencies can mark all backends down at once.
Load Balancer probes come from 168.63.129.16 and must be allowed by NSG rules.
Application Gateway custom probes and Front Door origin-group probes offer service-specific settings such as match conditions or HEAD/GET.

suggested.rationale: Choosing probe type, path and thresholds for a given failure scenario across three services is best practiced by reasoning through exam-style situations, and no current mission or planned engine simulates load-balancer probing.

lessons.plain: A listener is the front door bell of an Azure Application Gateway, which is a managed web traffic load balancer that understands HTTP. The listener waits on a specific address, port, and protocol, and can also check which website name the visitor asked for. When a request matches, the listener accepts it and passes it on to be routed. Think of an office reception desk with several signs: one receptionist greets visitors for Company A, another for Company B, and a general desk catches everyone else. Each receptionist is a listener.
lessons.guessPrompt: One gateway has a single public IP address on port 443 and must serve two different websites, shop.example.com and blog.example.com, to two different sets of servers. What piece of information in each incoming request do you think the gateway could use to tell the two sites apart?
lessons.teach:
A listener is the part of Application Gateway that decides whether to accept an incoming connection. It combines four things. The frontend IP is the public or private address clients connect to. The port is the number they connect on, such as 80 or 443. The protocol is HTTP (unencrypted) or HTTPS (encrypted with TLS, Transport Layer Security). For HTTPS, the listener holds a certificate, a file that proves the site's identity and lets the gateway decrypt the traffic. Each listener is tied to a routing rule that says where accepted traffic goes next.

There are two listener types. A basic listener matches every request on its IP and port, whatever site name was asked for. A multi-site listener also checks the host name, read from the Host header (the site name the browser sends) or the SNI field (the name sent during the TLS handshake). Multi-site listeners let one gateway and one IP serve many websites. A listener can also show custom error pages.

Worked example: a gateway has public IP 20.1.1.1 on port 443 with three listeners: multi-site for shop.example.com, multi-site for blog.example.com, and a basic listener. A request arrives for blog.example.com. Step one, IP and port match all three. Step two, the gateway checks the host name; the shop listener does not match, the blog listener does. Step three, the blog listener's rule sends it to the blog servers. A request for unknown.example.com matches neither multi-site listener and falls to the basic listener.

Common mistake: letting the basic listener be evaluated first. Listeners are checked in order, set by rule priority on the v2 gateway, and a basic listener matches everything. If it wins first, the multi-site listeners never get traffic, so every site's visitors land on the wrong servers. Give multi-site listener rules higher priority than the basic catch-all.

questions.prompt: Fabrikam runs an Application Gateway v2 on private IP 10.40.0.8, port 443. It has three listeners, checked in this order by rule priority: first a basic listener, then a multi-site listener for api.fabrikam.io, then a multi-site listener for portal.fabrikam.io. A request arrives for api.fabrikam.io. Step one: the IP 10.40.0.8 and port 443 match all three listeners. Step two: ______. Step three: the basic listener's routing rule sends the request to the default servers, and the API servers never see it. Which choice fills step two?
choices: The gateway compares the host name against every listener at once and picks the most specific match, so the api listener accepts the request
The gateway rejects the request, because two listeners on the same IP and port conflict, so it falls back to the basic listener's custom error page
The gateway reads the host name api.fabrikam.io and skips the basic listener, because basic listeners only receive names that no multi-site listener matches
The basic listener is checked first and matches any host name on that IP and port, so it accepts the request before the api listener is checked
questions.why: Listeners are evaluated in priority order and a basic listener matches every host name, so when it comes first it accepts the request before the multi-site api listener is ever checked.

questions.prompt: An Application Gateway has both a basic listener and a multi-site listener on the same frontend IP and port. What extra check does the multi-site listener make that the basic listener does not?
choices: It checks the requested host name, taken from the Host header or the SNI field sent during the TLS handshake
It checks that the backend servers are healthy before deciding whether to accept the request
It checks whether the request uses HTTP or HTTPS and only accepts encrypted traffic
It checks the client's source IP address against an allowed list before accepting the connection
questions.why: A multi-site listener matches on IP, port and host name, reading the name from the Host header or SNI, while a basic listener accepts any host name on its IP and port.

questions.prompt: Northwind Traders wants a single Application Gateway with one public IP, 52.10.4.7, to serve three separate websites, sales.northwind.org, hr.northwind.org and wiki.northwind.org, all over encrypted HTTPS on port 443, with each site going to its own servers. Which listener setup fits?
choices: Three separate gateways, each with its own public IP and one basic listener, because one IP can only serve one site
Three multi-site HTTPS listeners on 52.10.4.7 port 443, one per host name, each holding a certificate and tied to its own routing rule
Three basic HTTP listeners, one on port 80, one on 443 and one on 8080, one for each website
One basic HTTPS listener on 52.10.4.7 port 443, tied to a single routing rule that points at all three sets of servers
questions.why: Multi-site listeners let one gateway and one IP serve many websites by matching on host name, and each HTTPS listener needs a certificate and a routing rule to send its site's traffic to the right servers.

questions.prompt: An engineer creates a new Application Gateway listener with a frontend IP, port 443 and the HTTPS protocol, and ties it to a routing rule. What else must this listener hold so it can prove the site's identity and decrypt the traffic?
choices: A custom error page for the site
A certificate for the site
A Host header value for the site
A second frontend IP for the site
questions.why: An HTTPS listener holds a certificate, the file that proves the site's identity and lets the gateway decrypt the TLS-encrypted traffic.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what an Application Gateway listener does, the difference between basic and multi-site listeners, and one limit or ordering pitfall they must watch for.
lessons.modelAnswer: A listener is how Application Gateway decides which incoming traffic to accept. It is defined by a frontend IP, a port, and a protocol, HTTP or HTTPS, and an HTTPS listener carries a certificate so the gateway can decrypt the traffic. Each listener feeds a routing rule that sends the request onward. A basic listener accepts everything arriving on its IP and port. A multi-site listener also checks the requested host name from the Host header or SNI, which lets one gateway and one IP serve several websites to different backends. The pitfall is ordering: listeners are evaluated in order, by rule priority on v2, and a basic listener matches anything. If it is evaluated before the multi-site listeners, it swallows all traffic and every site goes to the wrong servers, so keep the basic listener as the lowest-priority catch-all.
rubricPoints: A listener is defined by frontend IP, port, and protocol (HTTP or HTTPS).
HTTPS listeners need a certificate so the gateway can decrypt traffic.
Basic listeners match all requests on the IP and port, while multi-site listeners also match the host name.
Multi-site listeners let one gateway and IP host several websites.
Listeners are evaluated in order, so a basic listener placed first catches all traffic, which must be avoided.
Each listener hands accepted traffic to a routing rule.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine configures gateway listeners, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios about listener type and ordering builds the needed judgment best.

lessons.plain: A routing rule on Azure Application Gateway (a managed web traffic manager that understands web requests) is the instruction that says where an incoming request goes. It joins three pieces: the listener that catches the request, the group of servers that should answer it, and the settings used to talk to those servers. Think of a mailroom clerk: the address on the envelope decides the department, and the rule is the clerk's sorting sheet. A simple rule sends everything to one group. A smarter rule reads the web address path, such as /images or /api, and sends each kind of request to its own group.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your website has pictures under /images/ and data requests under /api/, each served by a different set of servers. If one public entry point receives all traffic, what part of the request do you think it should read to decide which set of servers gets it?
lessons.teach:
A request routing rule is the Application Gateway object that binds a listener to a backend target. A listener is the part that accepts traffic on a given frontend IP address, port and, optionally, hostname. A backend pool is the group of servers or services that can answer. Backend HTTP settings say how the gateway connects to that pool, such as the port, protocol and timeout. The rule says: traffic caught by this listener goes to this pool using these settings.

There are two rule types. A basic rule sends every request from its listener to one backend pool. A path-based rule uses a URL path map, which is a list of path patterns, each pointing to its own pool and settings, plus a default pool for anything that matches no pattern. Path-based routing works because Application Gateway works at Layer 7, the application layer, so it can read the URL. A Layer 4 load balancer only sees IP addresses and ports and cannot do this. A rule can also redirect traffic instead of forwarding it. For example, it can send HTTP visitors to an HTTPS listener. Each rule also has a priority from 1 to 20000. Lower numbers are evaluated first.

Worked example: a listener on port 443 for shop.example.com uses a path-based rule. The path map is /images/* to ImagePool, /api/* to ApiPool, and the default is WebPool. A request arrives for shop.example.com/api/orders. The listener accepts it. The rule checks the path, finds that /api/orders matches /api/*, and forwards it to ApiPool using the API's HTTP settings. A request for /checkout matches no pattern, so it goes to WebPool.

A common mistake is writing the pattern /images without /*. That pattern matches only the exact path /images. So /images/cat.png falls through to the default pool. In a running system, the web servers then return errors or missing pictures, even though every server is healthy.

questions.prompt:
A city library runs Application Gateway with a listener on port 443 for portal.libraryhub.org. It uses a path-based rule whose URL path map (the list of path patterns, each pointing to its own backend pool and backend HTTP settings) is: /video/* to MediaPool, /reports/* to ReportPool, and a default of AppPool. A request arrives for portal.libraryhub.org/reports/2024/budget.pdf.

Step 1: The listener accepts the request because the port and hostname match.
Step 2: ???
Step 3: The gateway connects to the chosen pool using that pool's backend HTTP settings (port, protocol, timeout).

Which choice correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: The rule spreads the request across MediaPool, ReportPool and AppPool in turn.
The rule checks the path, sees /reports/2024/budget.pdf matches /reports/*, and picks ReportPool.
The rule finds no exact match for /reports, so it sends the request to the default AppPool.
The rule picks a pool based only on the destination IP address and port 443.
questions.why: The path begins with /reports/ and so matches the /reports/* pattern, which points to ReportPool, and the default pool is only used when no pattern matches.

questions.prompt: On an Application Gateway, which object ties a listener to a backend pool and the backend HTTP settings, so that traffic caught by that listener is sent to that pool in that way?
choices: The URL path map
The listener
The request routing rule
The backend HTTP settings
questions.why: A request routing rule is the object that binds a listener to a backend target and the settings used to reach it.

questions.prompt: A training company's Application Gateway has a path-based rule with the pattern /docs pointing to DocsPool, and a default pool of MainPool. Users report that pages like /docs/setup.html come back broken, yet every server shows as healthy. What is the most likely cause?
choices: DocsPool's servers are failing their health checks, so traffic is being dropped.
/docs matches only that exact path, so /docs/setup.html falls to MainPool.
A Layer 4 load balancer is in front, and it is rewriting the URL paths.
The rule's priority number is too low, so the rule is never evaluated at all.
questions.why: Without /* the pattern matches only the exact path /docs, so deeper paths fall through to the default pool, whose servers do not have that content even though they are healthy.

questions.prompt: An Application Gateway has two request routing rules. RuleRetail has priority 700 and RuleAdmin has priority 25. Which statement about how they are handled is correct?
choices: Priority only applies to redirect rules, so the order here is undefined.
RuleAdmin is evaluated first, because lower priority numbers go first.
RuleRetail is evaluated first, because higher priority numbers go first.
Both rules are evaluated together, and the gateway picks one at random.
questions.why: Rule priority ranges from 1 to 20000 and lower numbers are evaluated first, so priority 25 is checked before priority 700.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what an Application Gateway routing rule connects, how a path-based rule decides where a request goes, and one limit or tradeoff they should watch for when writing path patterns or choosing between basic and path-based rules.
lessons.modelAnswer: A routing rule is the glue in Application Gateway. It takes a listener, which accepts traffic on an IP, port and maybe a hostname. It connects that listener to a backend pool and the HTTP settings used to reach the pool. A basic rule sends everything from the listener to one pool. A path-based rule uses a URL path map instead. For example, /api/* goes to the API servers, /images/* goes to the image servers, and everything else goes to a default pool. This is possible because the gateway works at Layer 7 and reads the URL, which a Layer 4 load balancer cannot do. The tradeoff is precision. If you write /images instead of /images/*, only the exact path matches, so image requests silently land on the default pool. A basic rule is simpler but cannot split traffic by path. Rules also carry a priority, and lower numbers are evaluated first.
rubricPoints: States that a rule binds a listener to a backend pool plus backend HTTP settings.
Distinguishes basic rules (one pool) from path-based rules (URL path map with a default pool).
Explains that path routing relies on Layer 7 awareness of the URL.
Names a pitfall such as a missing /* wildcard sending traffic to the default pool.
Mentions rule priority, with lower numbers evaluated first, or the redirect option.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine exercises Layer 7 routing, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios about which path map or rule type fits a requirement builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: On Azure Application Gateway, a regional web traffic manager, HTTP settings (shown as backend settings in the newer portal) are the instructions the gateway follows when it passes a visitor's request on to your servers. They cover which protocol and port to use, how long to wait for an answer, whether a visitor should keep returning to the same server, and what website name to present. Think of a hotel concierge forwarding your order to the kitchen. The note says which door to use, how long to wait, and whose name the order goes under.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your web app runs on a hosted platform that serves many customers' sites from the same servers and decides which site to show based on the website name in each request. If a traffic manager in front forwards requests using its own name instead of your app's name, what do you think the visitor will see?
lessons.teach:
An HTTP setting (the newer portal calls it a backend setting) is the part of Application Gateway's configuration that controls the hop from the gateway to the backend pool. The gateway is a layer-7 load balancer, meaning it understands web requests. The backend pool is the group of servers or services that do the real work. A routing rule ties a listener (the gateway's front door) to a backend pool and one HTTP setting.

The main fields are these. Protocol and port: HTTP, or HTTPS (encrypted), and the port the backend listens on. Choosing HTTPS gives end-to-end encryption, which TLS lessons cover in depth. Cookie-based affinity: the gateway sets a cookie so one visitor keeps reaching the same server, which is useful when that server holds session data. Connection draining: when a server leaves the pool, requests already in flight get time to finish. Request timeout: how many seconds the gateway waits for a reply before giving up. Override backend path: replaces the start of the URL path before forwarding. Host name override: sets the Host header, which is the website name sent with the request. It can be picked from the backend target or typed in. A custom health probe can also be linked to the setting.

Worked example. A visitor requests https://shop.contoso.com/cart. The listener accepts the request on port 443, and the routing rule picks a pool holding an Azure App Service app, a managed web-hosting service. The HTTP setting says HTTPS, port 443, pick the host name from the backend target, and a 30-second timeout. The gateway opens HTTPS to the app, sends Host set to the app's own name, waits up to 30 seconds, and passes the reply back.

Common mistake: leaving the host name unchanged in front of a multi-tenant service like App Service. That platform hosts many sites and picks one by the Host header, so it receives an unknown name and answers with errors or redirects. A second trap is a timeout shorter than a slow report takes to run. When the gateway gives up waiting, users see 502 Bad Gateway errors even though the backend is healthy.

questions.prompt: Northwind Traders puts an Application Gateway in front of two virtual machines that run an internal reporting app. The app listens on plain HTTP, port 8080, keeps each user's session data in the memory of whichever server they first reach, and its largest reports take up to 90 seconds to build. An engineer fills in the HTTP setting as follows. Step 1: set protocol to HTTP and port to 8080 so the gateway talks to the app where it actually listens. Step 2: (missing). Step 3: turn on cookie-based affinity so each user keeps returning to the server that holds their session. Which choice correctly completes Step 2 so large reports do not end in errors?
choices: Set the request timeout to 20 seconds so stuck requests fail fast
Set the request timeout to 120 seconds, longer than the slowest report
Turn on host name override so the app receives its own name in the Host header
Enable connection draining for 120 seconds so slow reports have time to finish
questions.why: The request timeout is how long the gateway waits for a reply, so it must exceed the 90-second worst case or users get 502 Bad Gateway errors from a healthy backend.

questions.prompt: Adatum runs a web shop behind Application Gateway. The shopping basket is stored only in the memory of the server that first handled each visitor. Which HTTP setting field makes sure a visitor keeps reaching that same server?
choices: Connection draining
Host name override
Cookie-based affinity
Override backend path
questions.why: Cookie-based affinity has the gateway set a cookie that pins a visitor to one server, which is what you need when that server holds session data.

questions.prompt: Tailspin Toys places Application Gateway in front of an Azure App Service app (a managed web-hosting service that hosts many customers' sites on shared infrastructure). The backend health looks fine, but users get errors and unexpected redirects. The HTTP setting uses HTTPS on port 443 and leaves the host name unchanged. What is the most likely fix?
choices: Raise the request timeout from 30 to 60 seconds
Switch the protocol to HTTP so the backend stops redirecting
Use host name override, picking the host name from the backend target
Turn on cookie-based affinity so users stick to one instance
questions.why: App Service chooses which site to serve by the Host header, so the gateway must send the app's own name instead of the original visitor-facing name.

questions.prompt: Fabrikam regularly removes one server at a time from an Application Gateway backend pool to patch it. Users complain that file uploads already in progress get cut off the moment a server is removed. Which HTTP setting field addresses this?
choices: Override backend path
A custom health probe
Connection draining
Request timeout
questions.why: Connection draining gives requests already in flight time to finish when a server leaves the pool, instead of cutting them off.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what an Application Gateway HTTP setting controls and why you would turn on cookie-based affinity or a host name override, including one downside or limit of affinity.
lessons.modelAnswer: A routing rule sends traffic from a listener to a backend pool, and the HTTP setting describes how the gateway talks to that pool. It sets the protocol and port, the request timeout, connection draining, any path override, the Host header, and optionally a custom probe. A host name override matters when the backend is a shared platform like App Service that chooses which site to serve by the Host header. Without it the app gets the wrong name and returns errors or redirects. Cookie-based affinity keeps a visitor on one server, which helps apps that store sessions in memory. The tradeoff is that load spreads less evenly, and if that server fails the user loses the session. It is better to store sessions externally when you can. Also set the timeout longer than your slowest legitimate request, or users get 502 errors.
rubricPoints: States that HTTP settings govern the gateway-to-backend hop and are linked to a pool through a routing rule.
Names key fields such as protocol and port, timeout, affinity, draining, and host or path override.
Explains that a host name override is needed for multi-tenant backends like App Service that route by the Host header.
Explains that cookie-based affinity pins a user to one server and notes uneven load or lost sessions as the tradeoff.
Mentions that too short a request timeout produces 502 errors.

suggested.rationale: No existing mission or planned engine configures gateway backend settings, so the most useful practice is reasoning through exam-style scenarios like a host header mismatch or 502 timeouts.

lessons.plain: Transport Layer Security (TLS) is the encryption behind the padlock in a browser. Azure Application Gateway is a managed web traffic manager, a layer-7 load balancer, that sits in front of your web servers. Configuring TLS on it decides where the encrypted connection is unlocked. Think of a mailroom: sealed letters arrive, the clerk opens them to read the address and check for anything dangerous, then either hands them on open or reseals them before delivery. The gateway can open and inspect the traffic, then pass it on in plain form or re-encrypt it for the journey to your servers.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a gateway decrypts customer traffic so it can read the URL and route it, what new risk exists on the network path between the gateway and your web servers, and how might you remove it?
lessons.teach:
TLS on Application Gateway has two parts. TLS termination, also called SSL offload, means the gateway ends the client's encrypted session itself. You create an HTTPS listener, the component that accepts incoming connections on a port, and attach a server certificate. That certificate is either uploaded as a PFX file, a bundle holding the certificate and its private key, or referenced from Azure Key Vault, a managed secret store. The gateway reads Key Vault through a managed identity, which is an Azure-issued identity for a resource, so no password is stored. Termination works because the gateway must see the decrypted HTTP request to route by URL, apply rewrites, or let the web application firewall inspect it. It also takes cryptographic work off your servers.

End-to-end TLS means the gateway re-encrypts traffic before sending it to the backend. You set the backend HTTP settings, which control how the gateway talks to servers, to HTTPS. On the v2 SKU the gateway checks the backend's certificate. If a public certificate authority signed it, this works automatically. If it is self-signed or from a private authority, you upload a trusted root certificate, the top certificate in that chain. The host name the gateway sends must also match the name on the backend certificate. A TLS policy sets which protocol versions and cipher suites, meaning encryption algorithm sets, are allowed. You can pick a predefined policy or build a custom one, for example with TLS 1.2 as the minimum.

Worked example: a client opens shop.contoso.com. First, the HTTPS listener presents the Key Vault certificate and decrypts the request. Next, the firewall inspects it and the routing rule picks a pool. Then the HTTPS setting opens a new TLS session to 10.0.1.4, sending host shop.contoso.com. Finally, the gateway validates the server's certificate against the uploaded root and forwards the request.

A common mistake is switching backends to HTTPS with a self-signed certificate and no trusted root, or with a mismatched host name. The health probe fails, the backend is marked unhealthy, and users get 502 errors.

questions.prompt: Northwind Health runs a patient portal at care.northwind.org behind an Application Gateway v2. Its two backend servers, 10.20.4.10 and 10.20.4.11, use certificates issued by Northwind's own private certificate authority, and the security team requires traffic to stay encrypted all the way to the servers. The engineer works through the setup. Step 1: create an HTTPS listener on port 443 and reference the care.northwind.org server certificate from Azure Key Vault through the gateway's managed identity. Step 2: set the backend HTTP settings to HTTPS so the gateway re-encrypts traffic toward the servers. Step 3: ??? Step 4: configure the backend setting to send the host name care.northwind.org, which matches the name on the server certificates. Which action belongs in Step 3 so that the health probe passes and users do not get 502 errors?
choices: Upload the servers' PFX files to the listener so it presents the backend certificates to clients
Apply a custom TLS policy that sets TLS 1.2 as the minimum protocol version on the listener
Upload the trusted root certificate of Northwind's private certificate authority to the backend HTTPS settings
Switch the listener back to HTTP so the gateway does not have to decrypt and re-encrypt the request
questions.why: The backend certificates come from a private authority, so the v2 gateway can only validate them if it has that authority's trusted root certificate; without it, the probe fails and the backend is marked unhealthy.

questions.prompt: Litware Retail wants its Application Gateway to send requests for /checkout/* to one backend pool and /catalog/* to another, and to let the web application firewall inspect every request. Clients connect over HTTPS. Why must the gateway perform TLS termination for this design to work?
choices: Termination lets the backend servers skip installing any certificate at all
The gateway must see the decrypted HTTP request to read the URL path and let the firewall inspect it
Termination is required before the gateway can use a managed identity to reach Key Vault
Path-based routing only works when the gateway re-encrypts traffic with the backend's certificate
questions.why: While traffic is still encrypted the gateway cannot read the URL path or request content, so it must end the client's TLS session to route by path and run firewall inspection.

questions.prompt: At Tailspin Logistics, an engineer switches an Application Gateway v2 backend setting to HTTPS. The server at 10.30.2.5 has a certificate from a public certificate authority issued for api.tailspin.com, but the backend setting sends the host name 10.30.2.5. What happens, and what fixes it?
choices: The listener rejects clients; uploading a new PFX to the listener fixes it
The health probe fails and users get 502 errors; send api.tailspin.com as the host name
Traffic flows normally because publicly signed certificates are trusted without further checks
The gateway falls back to HTTP; enabling a stricter TLS policy forces HTTPS
questions.why: The host name the gateway sends must match the name on the backend certificate, so the mismatch fails the probe, marks the backend unhealthy, and causes 502 errors until the matching name is sent.

questions.prompt: Adatum Bank's compliance team says its Application Gateway must reject any client that tries to connect with TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1. Which Application Gateway setting addresses this requirement?
choices: A TLS policy, predefined or custom, that sets TLS 1.2 as the minimum version
A managed identity granted access to the bank's Key Vault
A backend HTTP setting changed from HTTP to HTTPS
A trusted root certificate uploaded to the backend HTTP settings
questions.why: A TLS policy controls which protocol versions and cipher suites the gateway allows, so setting TLS 1.2 as the minimum blocks older versions.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between TLS termination and end-to-end TLS on Application Gateway, which settings each needs, and the tradeoff of choosing one over the other.
lessons.modelAnswer: TLS termination means the gateway's HTTPS listener holds our certificate, either an uploaded PFX file or a Key Vault reference read through a managed identity. Clients' encrypted sessions end at the gateway. Because it can then read the decrypted request, it can route by path, rewrite headers, and run the web application firewall, and our servers skip the encryption work. The tradeoff is that traffic from the gateway to the backends travels unencrypted inside the virtual network. If compliance needs encryption all the way, we use end-to-end TLS. We set the backend HTTP settings to HTTPS, and on v2 the gateway validates the backend certificate. For a private or self-signed certificate we upload its trusted root, and the host name must match the certificate. Otherwise probes fail and users see 502 errors. End-to-end costs extra CPU and certificate management. A TLS policy controls the minimum version and cipher suites.
rubricPoints: Termination happens on an HTTPS listener with a certificate from a PFX file or Key Vault.
Decrypting at the gateway allows path routing, rewrites, and web application firewall inspection.
End-to-end TLS re-encrypts to backends using HTTPS backend HTTP settings.
Private or self-signed backend certificates need a trusted root, and the host name must match.
A wrong root certificate or mismatched host name causes unhealthy backends and 502 errors.
A TLS policy sets the minimum protocol version and cipher suites, and end-to-end adds overhead.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine configures gateway certificates, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios builds the most useful skill, such as compliance requiring encryption to the backend or a 502 after switching to HTTPS.

lessons.plain: A rewrite rule set is a saved list of small edits that Azure Application Gateway (a managed web traffic distributor for one region) makes to requests and responses as they pass through it. It can add, change or remove headers, and it can alter the web address path or query string before the request reaches your servers. Think of a mailroom clerk who re-labels envelopes as they go by. The letter still arrives, and neither the sender nor the receiver is told it was touched. The website visitor never sees the edit happen.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your backend web server sends every reply with a header announcing its exact software version, and the security team wants that hidden from visitors. If the traffic passes through a gateway that can edit messages in flight, what single change would you ask the gateway to make, and would you apply it to the request or to the response?
lessons.teach:
A rewrite rule set is a named collection of rewrite rules on Application Gateway v2, the current generation of Azure's regional layer-7 (HTTP-aware) load balancer. The set does nothing until you associate it with one or more routing rules. A routing rule ties a listener, which is the IP, port and hostname the gateway accepts traffic on, to a backend pool.

Each rewrite rule has three parts. The rule sequence is a number, and lower numbers run first. Conditions are optional tests, written as regular-expression patterns (text-matching patterns), checked against request headers, response headers, or server variables. Server variables are values the gateway knows about the connection, such as the client IP or the URL path. Actions are the edits themselves: set or delete a request header, set or delete a response header, or change the URL path or query string. If a rule has conditions, all of them must match before its actions run.

This works because the gateway terminates the HTTP conversation, so it can read and rebuild each message before forwarding it.

Worked example: a backend app service redirects users to its internal name. First, the backend replies with the response header Location: https://app1.azurewebsites.net/login. Second, a rule's condition checks that the Location response header matches a pattern that captures the path. Third, its action sets Location to https://www.contoso.com plus the captured path. Fourth, the browser receives the public address and stays on your domain.

A common mistake is confusing a rewrite with a redirect. A redirect tells the browser to go somewhere else, using an HTTP 3xx status. A rewrite silently edits the message and the browser never knows. Another frequent miss is building the set but never associating it with a routing rule, so the edits never run.

In a running system, a wrong path rewrite can send every request to a page that does not exist. Test changes on one routing rule first.

questions.prompt: Fabrikam runs an online shop behind Application Gateway v2, Azure's regional layer-7 (HTTP-aware) load balancer. A security review asks that every response stop showing the X-Powered-By header, which reveals the backend software. The engineer works through it like this. Step 1: create a rewrite rule set (a named collection of rewrite rules) called strip-tech-headers. Step 2: add a rule with rule sequence 100 and no conditions, so it applies to every message. Step 3: ???
