Step 4: associate strip-tech-headers with the routing rule that ties the HTTPS listener for shop.fabrikam.com on port 443 to the backend pool, then load a page and confirm the header is gone. What belongs in Step 3?
choices: Add an action that deletes the request header X-Powered-By
Add an action that deletes the response header X-Powered-By
Configure the gateway to send an HTTP 301 redirect whenever X-Powered-By is present
Add an action that changes the URL path to remove X-Powered-By
questions.why: X-Powered-By comes back from the backend in its reply, so the action must delete a response header; a rule with no conditions runs that edit on every response.

questions.prompt: At Northwind Traders, an engineer builds a rewrite rule set on Application Gateway v2 called add-hsts. It contains one rule, sequence 40, with no conditions, and an action that sets the response header Strict-Transport-Security. After saving, responses from the site still have no Strict-Transport-Security header. What is the most likely cause?
choices: A rule with no conditions never runs its actions
Response headers can only be deleted by a rewrite rule, never set
Rule sequence 40 is too low, and rewrite rules only run at sequence 100 or higher
The rewrite rule set was never associated with a routing rule, so it never runs
questions.why: A rewrite rule set does nothing until it is associated with at least one routing rule; low sequence numbers and missing conditions do not stop a rule from running.

questions.prompt: On Contoso Pharma's Application Gateway v2, one rewrite rule set has two rules. Rule A has sequence 120 and no conditions. Rule B has sequence 300 and two conditions: the client IP server variable matches the pattern 10.4.*, and the request header User-Agent matches the pattern Mobile. A request arrives from client IP 10.4.7.20 sent by a desktop browser whose User-Agent does not contain Mobile. Which statement is correct?
choices: Rule B runs first, but its actions are skipped because not every condition matched
Rule A runs first, and Rule B's actions are skipped because not every one of its conditions matched
Rule B runs first because it has the higher sequence number, and its actions run because one condition matched
Rule A runs first, and Rule B's actions also run because at least one of its conditions matched
questions.why: Lower sequence numbers run first, so Rule A goes before Rule B, and a rule's actions run only when all of its conditions match, which fails here because the User-Agent test does not match.

questions.prompt: Tailspin Travel moved its catalogue app, and the backend now serves the page at /legacy/catalog. Customers keep typing /catalog, and the team wants the backend to receive /legacy/catalog while the browser address bar still shows /catalog and the browser never learns anything changed. What should they configure on Application Gateway v2?
choices: A rewrite rule whose action changes the URL path from /catalog to /legacy/catalog, in a set associated with the relevant routing rule
A redirect that answers /catalog with an HTTP 302 status pointing to /legacy/catalog
A rewrite rule whose action deletes the request header Host so the backend picks the right page
A rewrite rule whose action sets the Location response header to /legacy/catalog
questions.why: A URL path rewrite silently edits the request before the gateway forwards it, so the backend sees /legacy/catalog and the browser never knows, whereas a redirect uses an HTTP 3xx status that sends the browser to the new address.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what an Application Gateway rewrite rule set is, how its rules decide what to change, and one limit or tradeoff of using it instead of fixing the behaviour in the application itself.
lessons.modelAnswer: A rewrite rule set is a bundle of edit instructions that Application Gateway v2 applies to traffic passing through it. It only takes effect once it is associated with a routing rule. Each rule in the set has a sequence number, and lower numbers run first. It can have conditions, which are regex tests on headers or server variables like the client IP or URL path, and all of them must match. It also has actions: set or delete request or response headers, or change the URL path or query string. It is not a redirect, because the browser never learns anything changed. A typical use is fixing a backend's Location header so users stay on the public domain, or stripping a header that reveals the server version. The tradeoff is that the fix lives in the network layer, not the code. That hides the real behaviour from developers, and a bad path rewrite can break every request on that route.
rubricPoints: States that a rewrite rule set is a collection of rules that edit headers, URL path or query string in transit on Application Gateway v2.
Notes the set must be associated with a routing rule to take effect.
Explains rule sequence, optional conditions on headers or server variables, and actions.
Distinguishes rewrite (invisible edit) from redirect (client told to go elsewhere).
Names a limit or tradeoff, such as hiding app behaviour or a bad rewrite breaking a route.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine edits HTTP headers in flight, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios that ask for rewrite versus redirect, and request versus response edits, builds the judgement this objective tests.

lessons.plain: Azure Front Door is a global front entrance for websites and web APIs. Users do not connect straight to your servers in one region. They connect to the nearest of many Microsoft edge sites around the world, and that edge passes the request over Microsoft's own network to the best healthy copy of your app. Think of a hotel chain with one phone number that always rings at the closest open front desk. On the way, Front Door can keep copies of files nearby, block attacks, and send different web addresses to different servers. It handles only web traffic, meaning HTTP and HTTPS.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your shop's website runs in two Azure regions, one in Europe and one in Asia. Shoppers worldwide should reach the closer copy, and everyone should be moved automatically if one region goes down. Should the service that spreads this traffic sit inside one region or at a global level, and why?
lessons.teach:
Azure Front Door is a global, layer 7 entry point. Layer 7 means it reads the web request itself, including the host name, the path and the headers. It does not just forward network packets. It runs at many edge locations, which are Microsoft sites close to users. It uses anycast, so one public address is announced from all of those sites at once, and each user lands on the nearest one. The backends it sends traffic to are called origins. Origins are grouped into origin groups. Health probes are small test requests that tell Front Door which origins are working.

To match a requirement to a feature: users spread across the world, or failover between regions, points to global routing. Within that, latency routing picks the fastest healthy origin. Priority routing keeps a standby origin unused until the main one fails. Weighted routing splits traffic by percentages. Different paths going to different backends points to path-based routing. Slow static files point to caching at the edge. Blocking attacks such as SQL injection points to the web application firewall (WAF), a filter for malicious web requests. Keeping the origin off the public internet points to Private Link, a private connection from Front Door to the origin. Changing or redirecting URLs points to the rules engine.

Worked example: a retailer serves Europe and Asia and needs fast images, region failover and attack blocking. First, a shopper in Tokyo hits the Tokyo edge. Second, the WAF checks the request. Third, if the request is for /images, the edge serves it from its cache. Fourth, if the request is for /api, latency routing sends it to the Asia origin. Fifth, if the probes mark Asia unhealthy, the request goes to Europe instead.

A common mistake is picking Front Door for traffic that is not web traffic, such as database connections or remote desktop. It cannot carry that traffic. Azure Load Balancer handles any TCP or UDP traffic within a region. Application Gateway gives layer 7 features within a single region, including private, internal-only apps. Choosing wrongly leaves the app either unreachable or without the global failover it needed.

questions.prompt:
A software company runs a public help site and a web app behind Azure Front Door. The app origin group has a main origin in East US and a standby origin in West US. The standby must receive no traffic unless the main origin fails. Here is how a request from a user in Toronto is handled.

Step 1: Anycast sends the user to the nearest Front Door edge location.
Step 2: The web application firewall (WAF) checks the request for attacks.
Step 3: A request for /help is sent to the help-site origin group through path-based routing.
Step 4: A request for /app is sent to the app origin group. [MISSING STEP]
Step 5: If health probes mark East US unhealthy, the request goes to West US.

Which choice correctly fills in Step 4?
choices: The rules engine redirects the request to West US, because the rules engine decides which region is healthy.
Latency routing sends the request to whichever app origin answers fastest, so West US may serve Toronto users when it is quicker.
Weighted routing splits app requests 50/50 between East US and West US so both origins stay busy.
Priority routing sends the request to East US, and West US stays unused while East US is healthy.
questions.why: Priority routing is the method that keeps a standby origin unused until the main origin fails, which is exactly what the app origin group requires.

questions.prompt: Azure Front Door uses anycast. What does anycast mean here?
choices: Each user is given a different public address, depending on which country they are in.
Traffic is spread across origins by fixed percentages that the administrator sets.
Front Door copies every request to all origins at once and keeps the first answer.
One public address is announced from many edge locations at once, and each user reaches the nearest one.
questions.why: Anycast announces a single public address from all edge locations at the same time, so each user lands on the closest edge.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company has built a new version of its web app and placed it in a second origin. It wants 10% of users to reach the new version and 90% to stay on the current one while it watches for problems. Which Azure Front Door feature fits this requirement?
choices: Caching at the edge, so the new version is served from edge locations
Private Link, so only some users can reach the new origin
Weighted routing, with the two origins set to 90 and 10
Priority routing, with the new version set as the standby origin
questions.why: Weighted routing splits traffic between origins by percentages, which is exactly how a 90/10 split is achieved.

questions.prompt: A gaming studio runs multiplayer game servers that talk to players over UDP, not over web requests. It puts Azure Front Door in front of the servers in two regions, hoping to get global failover. What is the most likely result?
choices: Players cannot reach the game servers through Front Door, because Front Door only handles web traffic and cannot carry UDP game traffic.
It works, but only if caching at the edge is turned on for the game traffic.
It works, because Front Door forwards any network packets to the nearest healthy origin.
It works, but the WAF will block every UDP packet as an attack.
questions.why: Front Door is a layer 7 service for web requests, so non-web traffic such as UDP game traffic cannot pass through it, which leaves the app unreachable; Azure Load Balancer is the service that handles any TCP or UDP traffic within a region.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you decide that a requirement calls for Azure Front Door rather than Load Balancer or Application Gateway. Name the features you would map to the requirement, and name at least one limit of Front Door.
lessons.modelAnswer: Front Door is a global web entry point. Users hit the nearest Microsoft edge through one anycast address, and Front Door forwards each request to a healthy origin. So I reach for it when users are worldwide or the app runs in several regions and needs automatic failover. Then I map the details to features. Latency routing gives users the fastest origin, priority routing gives an active-standby setup, and weighted routing splits traffic by percentage. Path-based routing sends /api and /images to different backends. Edge caching speeds up static files. The WAF blocks malicious requests, Private Link keeps origins private, and the rules engine handles rewrites and redirects. The limit is that it only carries HTTP and HTTPS, and it is public-facing. For other TCP or UDP traffic within a region I'd use Load Balancer. For layer 7 features inside one region or for an internal app, Application Gateway fits better.
rubricPoints: Defines Front Door as a global, layer 7 entry point that reaches users through nearby edge locations.
Maps multi-region or worldwide needs to latency, priority or weighted routing with health probes.
Maps specific needs to path-based routing, caching, WAF, Private Link or the rules engine.
States that Front Door handles only HTTP and HTTPS and faces the public internet.
Contrasts it with Load Balancer for regional layer 4 traffic and Application Gateway for regional layer 7 traffic.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine exercises Front Door, and this objective is about reasoning from a requirement to the right feature, so working through exam-style scenarios teaches it best.

lessons.plain: Azure Front Door is Microsoft's global front entrance for websites and web APIs. Visitors do not travel all the way to your servers in one region. Instead, they connect to the nearest of many Microsoft sites around the world, called edge locations. From there, Front Door sends each request to the healthiest, closest copy of your app. It can also hand out saved copies of common files and block harmful requests before they reach you. Think of a hotel chain with a reception desk in every city: you check in at the desk near you, and staff send you to whichever hotel has rooms.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your shopping website runs in two Azure regions, one in Europe and one in Asia, and customers come from all over the world. Would you want one entry point that lives in a single region, or one that sits close to every customer and can choose between both regions? Why?
lessons.teach:
Azure Front Door is a global, layer 7 entry service for HTTP and HTTPS traffic. Layer 7 means it understands web requests, including URLs, paths, headers and cookies. Global means it runs at many edge locations, also called points of presence, which are Microsoft data sites spread around the world. An origin is the backend that holds your app, such as a web app, a storage account or an Application Gateway, in any region or even outside Azure.

Why it works: anycast networking gives every edge location the same public address, so each user reaches the nearest one. The user's connection and TLS handshake (the encryption setup) finish close to home. The request then crosses Microsoft's private backbone network to the best origin, which is faster than the public internet. Front Door checks origin health with probes and stops sending traffic to an origin that fails. It can also cache, meaning it stores copies of static files such as images at the edge. It can run a web application firewall (WAF), a set of rules that blocks common web attacks.

Worked example: a user in Singapore opens shop.example.com. Step one, anycast routes them to the Singapore edge. Step two, TLS ends there. Step three, the request asks for /images/logo.png, which is cached, so the edge answers immediately. Step four, a later request for /api/cart is not cached, so Front Door checks health and finds Southeast Asia healthy. Step five, it forwards the request over the backbone to that region. If that region goes down, the next request goes to Europe with no DNS change.

Compare: Azure Load Balancer is regional and layer 4, meaning it sees only IP addresses and ports. Application Gateway is layer 7 but regional.

Common mistake: choosing Front Door for non-web traffic, such as a SQL database port or remote desktop, or for an internal-only app. Front Door handles only public HTTP and HTTPS, so those designs simply will not work and need Load Balancer instead.

questions.prompt: A travel-booking company publishes its public website, trips.example.net, through Azure Front Door. It has two origins: a web app in the Brazil South region and a web app in the East US region. A user in São Paulo requests trips.example.net/search?city=lisbon. Step one: anycast sends the user to the nearest edge location, in São Paulo. Step two: the TLS handshake (the encryption setup) finishes at that edge. Step three: the search result is not cached, so the edge must contact an origin. Step four: the health probes show that the Brazil South origin is failing and the East US origin is healthy. Step five is missing. What does Front Door do next?
choices: It sends the request to Brazil South anyway, because that origin is closest to the user
It forwards the request over Microsoft's backbone to the healthy East US origin, with no DNS change
It tells the user's browser to connect straight to East US over the public internet
It returns an error until the company changes its DNS records to point at East US
questions.why: Front Door stops sending traffic to an origin that fails its health probes and forwards the request across the private backbone to a healthy origin, with no DNS change needed.

questions.prompt: Azure Front Door uses anycast networking. What does anycast achieve for a user connecting to an app behind Front Door?
choices: It gives every edge location the same public address, so the user reaches the nearest one
It spreads traffic across virtual machines inside a single region by IP address and port
It stores copies of static files such as images at each edge location
It encrypts traffic between the origin and the database behind it
questions.why: Anycast means every edge location shares one public address, so each user is routed to the closest point of presence, where the connection and TLS setup finish.

questions.prompt: A media company serves a public HTTPS video-catalogue site to viewers on three continents. The origins are in Japan East, West Europe and Canada Central. It wants one public entry point, automatic failover if a region goes down, cached thumbnail images near viewers, and a web application firewall (WAF). Which service fits best?
choices: Azure Load Balancer, because it can spread traffic across virtual machines
Application Gateway, because it understands URLs and can run a WAF
Azure Load Balancer in each region, with users told which region to use
Azure Front Door, because it is a global layer 7 entry with edge caching and WAF
questions.why: Only Front Door is both global and layer 7, so it can route web users to healthy origins in any region, cache files at the edge and apply WAF rules; Load Balancer is regional layer 4 and Application Gateway is regional.

questions.prompt: An engineering team lists four workloads they want to place behind a load-distribution service. Which one should NOT use Azure Front Door and needs Azure Load Balancer instead?
choices: A public HTTPS marketing site with images served to visitors worldwide
A public HTTPS blog whose origin is hosted outside Azure
A public REST API over HTTPS with origins in two Azure regions
A MySQL database that clients reach on TCP port 3306
questions.why: Front Door handles only public HTTP and HTTPS traffic, so a database port such as 3306 is non-web traffic that will not work through it and needs Load Balancer.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, when you would put Azure Front Door in front of an application, and name at least one situation where it is the wrong choice and what you would use instead.
lessons.modelAnswer: Front Door is the pick when we have a public website or web API whose users are spread across the world, especially if the app runs in more than one region. Users connect to the nearest Microsoft edge location, where their TLS connection ends. Front Door then sends the request over Microsoft's backbone to the healthiest, closest origin. If a region fails, it fails over automatically. It can also cache static files at the edge and run a WAF to block attacks before they reach us. Its limits are clear, though. It only handles HTTP and HTTPS, and it is public-facing. If we need to balance raw TCP or UDP, like a database or game server, we'd use Azure Load Balancer. If everything lives in one region and we just need path-based routing inside it, Application Gateway is the simpler regional choice.
rubricPoints: Front Door is a global, layer 7 service for public HTTP and HTTPS traffic.
Users connect at the nearest edge location and travel over Microsoft's backbone to the origin.
It routes to the healthiest, closest origin and fails over across regions.
It adds edge caching and a WAF at the entry point.
It is wrong for non-HTTP or internal traffic, where Load Balancer fits better.
For a single region, Application Gateway is the regional layer 7 alternative.

suggested.rationale: The skill is choosing Front Door over Load Balancer or Application Gateway from a stated requirement, which is best practised by reasoning through exam-style scenarios.

lessons.plain: Azure Front Door is a global service that receives web traffic at the edge of the internet and forwards it to your web apps wherever they run. It comes in tiers, which are bundles of features sold at different price points. Choosing a tier means asking which extra protections and private connections your situation needs, then paying only for those. A public website that needs fast global routing and caching can often use the cheaper tier. An app that must hide its backend servers behind private networks, or needs managed bot filtering, needs the higher tier. The skill is matching required features to the tier, not defaulting to the most expensive one.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company runs a public retail site in two regions and wants global routing with caching, but its backend servers must never be reachable from the internet directly. Without reading further, which tier would you guess is needed, and what single requirement makes you think so?
lessons.teach:
Azure Front Door is a global entry point for web traffic. Its edge locations sit close to users, and it forwards requests to your origins, meaning the backend servers or services that actually produce the responses. Front Door comes in tiers, which are sets of features bundled together. The two you need to know are Standard and Premium. Both handle the core job: global routing, health-based failover, TLS termination (decrypting HTTPS at the edge), caching and rules. Premium adds protections that the core job does not need. Two of them matter most here. Private Link to origins lets Front Door reach a backend over a private network, so the backend has no public address. Managed bot protection rules are curated rules in the web application firewall (WAF, a filter that inspects HTTP requests for attacks) aimed at automated traffic.

Why it works: each requirement either belongs to the core set or to the premium set, so the tier is decided by the most demanding requirement on your list. Worked example: the retail site needs (1) global routing with failover, which Standard covers; (2) caching, which Standard covers; (3) backends with no public address, which needs Private Link, a Premium feature. Step one: list the requirements. Step two: tag each as core or premium. Step three: one premium tag forces Premium. Result: Premium.

Common mistake: picking the tier by price, or assuming custom WAF rules alone give the same protection as private origins. Consequence in a running system: if the backend keeps a public address, an attacker can skip the edge entirely and hit the server directly, bypassing every WAF rule in front of it.

The tier is set by the strongest requirement on your list, not by the cheapest or most expensive option.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company lists three requirements: (1) global routing that fails over to a healthy origin when one region goes down, (2) caching of static files at the edge, and (3) managed bot protection rules that block scraper traffic. Step one is done: all three are listed. Step two is done: requirements 1 and 2 are tagged as core features, and requirement 3 is tagged as a premium feature. Step three is missing. Which tier should the company choose, and what rule decides it?
choices: Premium, because one premium requirement is enough to force that tier, since the strongest requirement sets the tier.
Standard, because bot protection is an optional add-on and cost should break the tie.
Premium, because every requirement on the list must be met by the most expensive tier to be safe.
Standard, because two of the three requirements are core and the majority decides the tier.
questions.why: The tier is set by the most demanding requirement on the list, so one premium tag forces Premium regardless of how many core tags there are.

questions.prompt: In Azure Front Door, what does Private Link to origins provide?
choices: A way for the edge to cache responses longer than the origin's own settings allow.
A way to terminate HTTPS at the edge so that the origin never sees encrypted traffic.
A managed set of WAF rules that block automated traffic before it reaches the origin.
A way for Front Door to reach a backend over a private network, so the backend has no public address.
questions.why: The teaching text defines Private Link to origins as letting Front Door reach a backend privately so the backend has no public address.

questions.prompt: A company keeps public addresses on its origin servers and relies only on custom WAF rules at the edge. Why is this a risk?
choices: The edge cache will serve stale content because the origin is reachable from the internet.
Custom WAF rules stop working whenever TLS termination is enabled at the edge.
An attacker can send requests straight to the origin's public address and skip the edge, bypassing every WAF rule in front of it.
Custom WAF rules can be bypassed because they only apply to Front Door's own rules engine.
questions.why: With a public origin address an attacker can skip the edge entirely, so the WAF rules in front of it never inspect that traffic.

questions.prompt: A company needs global routing with health-based failover, caching, and TLS termination at the edge, and nothing else. Which Front Door tier fits, and why?
choices: Premium, because TLS termination is always a premium feature that Standard cannot provide.
Standard, because all three requirements belong to the core set that Standard covers.
Standard, because the cheapest tier is always the correct choice for any requirement list.
Premium, because any site that uses global routing must be on the highest tier.
questions.why: Global routing, failover, caching, and TLS termination are all core features that Standard covers, and no premium requirement is on the list.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between the Front Door Standard and Premium tiers for a new public web app, and name one limit or tradeoff of choosing the cheaper tier.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by listing what the app actually needs: global routing, failover, caching, TLS, and any security demands. Most of those are covered by Standard. Then I check the premium-only items. If the backends must have no public address, Private Link to the origins is needed, which means Premium. If we need managed bot protection rules in the WAF, that also points to Premium. One premium requirement is enough to choose Premium, regardless of how many standard features we use. The main tradeoff of choosing Standard is that the backends stay reachable from the internet, so the edge cannot be the only way in. We would have to protect the origins another way, such as IP restrictions or network controls, and accept that the WAF can be bypassed if those fail. I would document that decision and revisit it when requirements change.
rubricPoints: Tier choice follows the strongest requirement, not price or habit
Core features such as global routing, caching and TLS are shared across tiers
Private Link to origins and managed bot protection are Premium features
Choosing Standard with public origins leaves a bypass path around the edge WAF

suggested.rationale: Choosing a tier is a scenario-based decision where weighing several requirements against each tier adds the most practice.

lessons.plain: Azure Front Door is a global front desk for web traffic. Clients connect to one public address, and Front Door, which runs at many locations around the world, decides which of your servers should answer. Those servers are called origins. Front Door checks that they are alive, sends each request to a healthy one, and can send different URL paths to different groups of servers. Because clients only ever see the public name, you can add, move, or replace backends without them noticing.
lessons.guessPrompt: A shop runs its web app in two regions and wants customers to use one address, with traffic moved to the second region if the first breaks. What does the single entry point need to know about each server, and what should it do when one stops answering?
lessons.teach:
An endpoint is the public hostname that clients connect to, such as a name ending in azurefd.net or your own custom domain. An origin is a real backend, such as a web server or app service, that actually holds the content. An origin group is a named set of origins that Front Door treats as one pool. Health probes are periodic test requests to a chosen path, used to decide which origins are answering. A route is the rule that ties these together: it matches an incoming request by hostname and URL path, then sends it to one origin group and sets how it is forwarded.

Why it works: Front Door receives the request at the location closest to the client, finds the route whose hostname and path pattern fit, then picks an origin from that route's group. Within a group, priority sets failover order. All priority 1 origins share traffic, and priority 2 is used only when every priority 1 origin is unhealthy. Weight splits traffic among origins at the same priority.

Worked example: an endpoint called shop.example.azurefd.net has a route for the path /api/* that points to an origin group containing east (priority 1, weight 50) and west (priority 1, weight 50). A request to /api/orders matches the route, the probes show both origins healthy, weight sends it to east, and east answers. If east fails its probes, requests go to west until east recovers.

Common mistake: sending traffic to an origin that rejects the host name Front Door forwards, so the origin returns 404 even though it is running. Check that the origin host header setting matches what the backend expects.

Consequence: if every origin in a group fails its probes, the edge has nowhere to send requests and clients receive errors. For that reason, the probe path should test something that really works, not a static page that always responds.

questions.prompt: A team runs a ticketing site at tickets.northwind-events.azurefd.net. The route for /checkout/* sends traffic to an origin group with three origins: alpha (priority 1, weight 70), bravo (priority 1, weight 30), and charlie (priority 2, weight 100). A customer requests /checkout/pay, and the trace goes like this. Step 1: the request reaches the Front Door location nearest the customer. Step 2: the route matches, because /checkout/pay fits the path pattern /checkout/*. Step 3: the probes show alpha, bravo, and charlie all healthy. Step 4: [MISSING] Step 5: weight 70 to 30 selects alpha for this request. Which statement correctly fills in step 4?
choices: Front Door sends the request to charlie because its weight of 100 is the highest of the three origins.
Front Door limits selection to the priority 1 origins, because at least one of them is healthy, so charlie is not used.
Front Door rewrites the host header to each origin's own name and then sends the request to all three origins.
Front Door sends the request to all three origins at once and returns whichever answer arrives first.
questions.why: Priority decides which tier of origins is eligible first, and since alpha and bravo are healthy at priority 1, the priority 2 origin charlie is excluded before weight is applied.

questions.prompt: An online course platform gives its learners the address learn.fernhill-academy.azurefd.net. In Front Door terms, which name describes that public address that clients type into a browser?
choices: Endpoint
Health probe
Origin group
Origin
questions.why: The endpoint is the public hostname clients connect to, while origins hold the content and are not what clients type.

questions.prompt: A media site uses endpoint store.bluefern.azurefd.net. The route for /media/* points to an origin group with: pan (priority 1, weight 20), quill (priority 1, weight 80), and rho (priority 2, weight 100). Both pan and quill now fail their health probes. A visitor requests /media/logo.png. Which origin receives the request?
choices: Pan or quill, chosen in a 20 to 80 split by weight, even though both are failing
No origin, so Front Door returns an error immediately without trying rho
Rho, but only if its weight is at least 50 percent of the group total
Rho, because priority 2 is used only when every priority 1 origin is unhealthy
questions.why: Priority 2 origins take traffic only when all priority 1 origins are unhealthy, so with pan and quill both failing, rho answers the request.

questions.prompt: A backend origin passes every health probe, yet requests forwarded through Front Door to it return 404 errors. Which setting should the team check first, and why?
choices: The origin's weight value, because a low weight causes the backend to reject forwarded requests
The length of the endpoint's public hostname, because long names cause the backend to misroute requests
The probe interval in seconds, because probes that run too rarely cannot detect the 404 errors
The origin host header setting, because it must match the host name the backend expects, and a mismatch causes 404 errors even when the origin is running
questions.why: A running origin can still return 404 when the host name Front Door forwards does not match what the backend expects, which the origin host header setting controls.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a request travels from a client through Azure Front Door to a backend. Name the parts you configure, and name one limitation or tradeoff of relying on Front Door as the single entry point.
lessons.modelAnswer: A client resolves the endpoint hostname and connects to Front Door at the nearest location. Front Door looks for a route whose hostname and path pattern match the request. That route points to an origin group, which is a pool of backend origins. Front Door uses health probe results and the priority and weight settings to pick one origin, then forwards the request, sending the origin host header the backend expects. The parts I would tell a teammate to configure are the endpoint, the routes, the origin groups, the origins with their priority and weight, and the probe path. The tradeoff is that Front Door becomes a dependency for every request. If its configuration is wrong, or if a backend stays reachable directly from the internet, clients may either be locked out or bypass the protection we intended. We should verify both the route matching and the origin lockdown, not just that the site loads.
rubricPoints: Describes the path from client to endpoint, route, origin group, and origin
Explains priority for failover and weight for splitting traffic
Names the health probe and why probe paths should test real function
Mentions the origin host header or host name mismatch as a common cause of errors
States a tradeoff, such as Front Door becoming a single dependency or origins being bypassed if not locked down

suggested.rationale: Front Door configuration is mostly product-specific settings and console steps that a reading lesson covers better than any listed mission or planned engine.

lessons.plain: When people visit a website over HTTPS, their browser and the server first agree on a scrambled connection called TLS, the successor to SSL. TLS keeps the traffic private and proves the server's identity with a certificate. TLS termination means one device is where that encrypted connection ends: it decrypts the request, reads it, and decides where to send it. End-to-end TLS means encryption continues all the way to the server that does the real work, so the middle hop is encrypted too. Azure Front Door is a global entry point in front of your apps, so you choose how much of the path needs encryption and where the certificates live. This lesson covers those choices.
lessons.guessPrompt: A customer's browser connects to a global entry point over HTTPS, and that entry point forwards the request to your app server over plain HTTP. Is the customer's data encrypted for the whole journey? Where would you expect it to be readable, and why?
lessons.teach:
Definitions first. A certificate is a signed file that binds a domain name, such as shop.example.com, to a public key, and it is issued by a certificate authority that browsers trust. TLS termination means the encrypted connection from the client ends at a given device, which holds the private key, decrypts the traffic, and reads it. Azure Front Door terminates TLS at its edge points of presence, the servers spread around the world closest to users, using a certificate for your custom domain. An origin is the backend where your app actually runs. The forwarding protocol is a per-route setting that decides how the edge talks to the origin: HTTP only, HTTPS only, or match the incoming scheme.

Why it works: the TLS handshake happens close to the user, so the slow part is short, and the edge can route requests after decrypting them. When forwarding is HTTPS, the edge opens a second TLS connection to the origin and checks that the origin certificate is trusted and covers the hostname it dialed. That check is what turns the chain into end-to-end encryption rather than encryption that stops at the edge.

Worked example: a browser requests https://shop.example.com/cart. Step 1: the edge presents the certificate for shop.example.com and completes the handshake. Step 2: it decrypts the request and matches the route for /cart. Step 3: the route forwards over HTTPS to the origin app.shop-backend.example. Step 4: the edge validates that origin's certificate against that name. Step 5: it sends the request, and the response returns encrypted on both hops.

Common mistake: enabling HTTPS forwarding against an origin with a self-signed, expired, or mismatched certificate, then blaming the edge when requests fail. The fix is a valid certificate on the origin, not switching the check off.

Consequence: with HTTP-only forwarding, the edge-to-origin leg is plaintext, which is a real exposure if that path crosses networks you do not control. Choose the forwarding protocol deliberately, because it decides whether encryption stops at the edge or continues to the origin.

questions.prompt: A media company serves map tiles through Azure Front Door. Its custom domain is maps.harbor-city.example, and the route for /maps/* uses HTTPS-only forwarding to the origin tiles-origin.harbor-city.example, which has a valid certificate. A visitor types http://maps.harbor-city.example/maps/12/3 into a browser. Step 1: the request arrives over plain HTTP, and the edge's redirect rule sends the browser to the https:// address. Step 2: the browser opens a TLS connection to the nearest edge, and the edge presents the certificate for maps.harbor-city.example and completes the handshake. Step 3: the edge is left to decide where the request goes next, so for this question, Step 3 is the missing step. Step 4: the edge forwards the request over HTTPS to tiles-origin.harbor-city.example. Which choice correctly fills the missing Step 3?
choices: The edge decrypts the request and matches it against the /maps/* route before any forwarding happens.
The browser checks the origin certificate directly, because the forwarding protocol applies to the client connection.
The edge sends the request to the origin in plaintext, because the earlier redirect already made the connection secure.
The origin presents its own certificate to the browser, and the browser checks it before the edge is contacted.
questions.why: The edge must decrypt the request before it can read the path and pick a route, and only after routing does the route's HTTPS forwarding setting apply to the origin leg.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does TLS termination at an edge service mean?
choices: The edge stops forwarding any requests to the origin after the handshake completes.
The origin deletes its certificate once the edge has taken over the domain name.
The client's browser stops encrypting data so the edge can cache responses more easily.
The encrypted connection from the client ends at the edge, which holds the key, decrypts the traffic, and reads it.
questions.why: TLS termination means the device that holds the private key is the one that ends the encrypted connection and reads the plaintext, which is what the edge does for the client connection.

questions.prompt: A team sets a Front Door route to HTTPS forwarding, but every request returns an error. The origin uses a certificate that expired last month. The team wants requests to work again without weakening security. What is the right action?
choices: Turn off certificate validation on the edge so it accepts any origin certificate.
Point the custom domain at a different origin that has no certificate at all.
Renew or replace the origin certificate with a valid one that covers the origin hostname.
Switch the route to HTTP-only forwarding so the expired certificate is never checked.
questions.why: HTTPS forwarding only works when the origin presents a currently valid, trusted certificate covering the hostname the edge dialed, so the fix is to correct the origin certificate rather than disable the check or lower the protection.

questions.prompt: A retailer's route forwards payment-related requests from Front Door to its origin using HTTP only. The origin sits behind a third-party network link the retailer does not operate. What is the main concern with this setup?
choices: The browser will refuse to load the checkout page because the origin lacks a certificate.
The edge will stop caching responses, which slows checkout for every shopper.
The edge-to-origin leg carries plaintext across a network the retailer does not control, so the data could be read in transit.
The custom domain certificate will expire sooner because the forwarding protocol is set to HTTP.
questions.why: With HTTP-only forwarding, the edge-to-origin hop has no encryption, so on a path crossing networks you do not control, anyone able to observe that path can read the traffic.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has never configured Front Door the difference between TLS termination at the edge and end-to-end TLS, and name one limit or tradeoff of making the origin leg HTTPS.
lessons.modelAnswer: Terminating TLS at the edge means the encrypted connection from the client ends at Front Door's edge server. That server holds the certificate for our custom domain, decrypts the request, reads it, and can route it. The edge is close to the user, so the handshake is fast. End-to-end TLS adds a second encrypted connection from the edge to the origin, so the traffic stays encrypted on every hop. The tradeoff is that the origin now needs a valid, trusted certificate that matches the hostname Front Door connects to. Each extra TLS hop also adds handshake latency and certificate upkeep, and a mismatched or expired origin certificate causes failed requests that look like edge problems. So I would enable HTTPS to the origin for sensitive traffic and check the origin certificate first.
rubricPoints: Defines TLS termination as ending the encrypted connection at the edge, where decryption happens
Explains that end-to-end TLS adds an encrypted edge-to-origin connection with the origin's certificate validated
Names a real tradeoff such as origin certificate management, handshake latency, or failures from mismatched certificates

suggested.rationale: Choosing between edge termination and end-to-end TLS is a scenario decision, so working through an exam-style situation adds the most.

lessons.plain: Caching means keeping a saved copy of an answer close to the people asking for it, so the next person gets it without the original server doing the work again. Think of a bakery that keeps a tray of today's bread by the door: most customers grab from the tray, and only a few need the back kitchen. In Azure, Front Door can keep copies of web responses at edge locations around the world. Configuring caching means deciding which responses may be stored, how long they stay fresh, and which parts of a web address make two requests count as the same item. Get that wrong and you either serve stale content or save nothing.
lessons.guessPrompt: A shop's product photos rarely change, but its product page shows different prices and a greeting for each logged-in customer. Which of these two would you expect a shared cache serving everyone to be safe to store and reuse, and why?
lessons.teach:
A cache is a stored copy of a response, kept so a later request can be answered without doing the full work again. Azure Front Door is a global entry point for web traffic, and its edge locations can hold copies of responses from your origin, which is the backend server or storage that actually produces the content. Configuring caching means choosing, per route, whether responses are stored, how long they stay fresh, and which parts of the request define the cache key, the label that decides whether two requests share one stored copy. The time a copy stays fresh is its time to live, or TTL. The origin can state it in a Cache-Control header, a line of metadata sent with each response, and you can override it at the edge.

Why it works: most traffic asks for the same public files again and again, so serving a stored copy cuts delay for the user and load on the origin.

Worked example: a route serves /images/logo.png, and the origin says max-age 3600, meaning one hour. Step 1: the first request misses, so the edge fetches from the origin and stores the copy with a one hour TTL. Step 2: a request ten minutes later hits the stored copy, and the origin sees nothing. Step 3: after sixty minutes the copy expires, and the next request is fetched from the origin again.

Common mistake: caching a response that differs per user, such as an account page. A shared edge cache can then hand one customer's private page to another. Only cache what is the same for everyone who asks for that address. Query strings matter too: if every query string is part of the cache key, each variant gets its own copy and the hit rate falls.

Consequence: a TTL that is too short saves little, and one that is too long keeps serving outdated content until the TTL ends or someone purges the copy. Load Balancer spreads connections across servers and keeps no copies of responses, and Application Gateway is a regional web router that does not offer a shared edge cache, so response caching for global web content belongs to Front Door. Caching is a per-route decision about what is safe to share and how long it stays true.

questions.prompt: A retail team routes /docs/handbook.pdf through Azure Front Door. Their origin sends Cache-Control max-age 900, so the time to live (TTL, how long a stored copy stays fresh) is 15 minutes. Step 1: the first request misses, so the edge fetches the file from the origin and stores a copy with a 15-minute TTL. Step 2: a request at minute 5 is answered from the stored copy, and the origin sees nothing. Step 3: a request arrives at minute 20. Which happens?
choices: The edge returns an error, because a cache cannot hold content beyond its TTL.
The edge serves the stored copy and then purges it, because any copy older than 15 minutes is removed automatically.
The edge serves the stored copy, because the hit at minute 5 renewed the TTL.
The edge fetches the file from the origin again, because the copy expired at minute 15 and a hit does not extend the TTL.
questions.why: The copy's TTL was set at minute 0 and ended at minute 15, and serving a hit does not reset that clock, so the request at minute 20 has to go back to the origin.

questions.prompt: In caching on Azure Front Door, what does the term time to live (TTL) describe?
choices: The length of time a stored copy of a response stays fresh before it must be fetched again.
The delay between a user's request and the first byte of the origin's reply.
The number of requests a single edge location can answer before it must refuse new ones.
The maximum size, in bytes, of a response the edge is allowed to store.
questions.why: The teaching text defines TTL as the time a copy stays fresh, which is the period before the edge needs to fetch a new copy from the origin.

questions.prompt: A team caches the response for a customer account page at the edge. Which outcome is the main risk of this choice?
choices: The account page loads more slowly for every customer because the edge adds delay.
The origin receives more traffic because each request bypasses the cache.
The edge stores a copy that is cut off after one hour, so customers see errors.
A shared edge cache can hand one customer's private page to a different customer who asks for the same address.
questions.why: A cache keyed on the address alone would serve the same stored copy to anyone asking for that address, so a page that differs per user must not be shared this way.

questions.prompt: A company wants responses for its global product pages stored close to users around the world so that repeated requests do not reach the origin each time. Which Azure service fits this requirement, and why?
choices: Azure Application Gateway, because it is a regional router that caches responses inside each region it serves.
Azure Load Balancer and Application Gateway together, because caching requires both a connection spreader and a regional router.
Azure Front Door, because its edge locations can hold copies of origin responses, while Load Balancer keeps no response copies and Application Gateway offers no shared edge cache.
Azure Load Balancer, because it stores copies of responses at each server it spreads traffic across.
questions.why: Front Door is the service that holds shared copies at global edge locations, which is the feature this requirement needs, while the other two do not provide that function.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how caching at the Front Door edge decides whether a request reaches your origin, and name one tradeoff of caching a response for a longer time.
lessons.modelAnswer: When a request arrives at a Front Door edge location, the edge checks whether it has a stored copy under the cache key for that route. If it has a copy that is still within its time to live, it returns that copy and the origin never sees the request. If not, it forwards the request to the origin, stores the response if the route allows caching, and returns it. The cache key is built from the address and whichever query string settings the route uses, so including more query strings splits one item into many copies. The main tradeoff of a longer time to live is freshness: users can keep getting an old version after the origin changes, so you either accept that delay or purge the copy when content changes. Caching should also be limited to content identical for every requester, because a shared copy of a personal page would be a data leak.
rubricPoints: Edge checks for a stored copy under the cache key before contacting the origin
A hit within the time to live is served without touching the origin; a miss goes to the origin and may be stored
Longer time to live trades freshness for fewer origin requests, so stale content is a risk
Only cache responses that are identical for all users; personal content must not be shared

suggested.rationale: Choosing whether a request is answered at the edge, the regional gateway, or the balancer is an exam-style reasoning task that builds the why-not comparison this objective needs.

lessons.plain: Traffic acceleration is a set of techniques that make a website or app feel faster for people far from the servers it runs on. Instead of every visitor's request travelling all the way to your one data centre, the request is picked up by a nearby entry point on a global network. That entry point handles the first part of the conversation locally and reuses open connections for the long trip. Content that repeats can be kept close to users too. Think of a national chain of shops that stocks popular goods in local branches, while the head warehouse only ships the rare items.
lessons.guessPrompt: A user on another continent says your site loads slowly, but the server itself responds quickly when you test it from your office. What is probably adding the delay, and what could you place closer to the user to reduce it?
lessons.teach:
Traffic acceleration means making requests from users reach your application faster and more reliably, without changing the application. The main cause of slowness is usually distance. Each round trip across the internet adds delay, and a secure connection needs several round trips before any data flows. A global edge network places entry points, called edge locations or points of presence, close to users around the world. Anycast is a routing method where the same public address is announced from many places, so internet routing sends each user to the nearest one. At the edge, the user's connection ends locally, and the edge keeps a pool of warm, persistent connections to your origin, meaning the backend server or service that holds the real content. This is split TCP: the user-side handshake is short because it is local, and the long-distance leg reuses connections that are already open. Edges can also cache static responses and compress them, so less data travels far. In Azure, this capability is provided by Azure Front Door. Regional load balancers and Application Gateway work inside one region and do not give you this global edge.

Worked example: a user in Sydney requests a page from an origin in Virginia. Without acceleration, the browser performs the TCP and TLS handshakes and sends the request across the Pacific, paying hundreds of milliseconds per round trip. With Anycast, the request lands at a Sydney-area edge. The TLS handshake finishes locally in a few milliseconds. The edge already has an open connection to Virginia and forwards the request over it. A cached image is served from the edge without touching Virginia at all.

Common mistake: assuming acceleration fixes slow backend code. It does not. If the origin takes two seconds to build a response, the edge only trims the network time. Uncacheable dynamic responses still wait for the origin.

Consequence: caching a response that contains one customer's personal data can show that page to another customer, so cache rules must match what is safe to share.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company, HarborSeat, keeps its origin server in Frankfurt. A customer in Nairobi loads a seat-map image and then submits a checkout form. The steps are: (1) the request reaches a nearby edge location because the public address is announced from many places; (2) the edge completes the secure handshake with the customer locally; (3) this step is missing; (4) the seat-map image is served from the edge cache, so Frankfurt never receives that request. Which choice correctly completes step 3?
choices: The edge forwards the checkout request over an already-open, persistent connection to the Frankfurt origin, which processes it.
The customer's browser abandons the edge and connects straight to Frankfurt, so the edge plays no further part.
The edge stores the checkout response in its cache so the next customer receives the same page without asking Frankfurt.
The edge opens a brand-new connection to Frankfurt and repeats the full secure handshake before forwarding the checkout request.
questions.why: The edge keeps warm, persistent connections to the origin, so the long-distance leg reuses an open connection, and a dynamic checkout response is not safe to cache and share.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes anycast as used in traffic acceleration?
choices: A method where each user is assigned one fixed server address that never changes.
A method that encrypts traffic between the user and the origin so intermediaries cannot read it.
A method where the same public address is announced from many locations, so internet routing sends each user to a nearby one.
A method that copies the origin's database to every edge so reads never leave the region.
questions.why: Anycast announces one public address from many places, and internet routing then sends each user to the nearest announcement point.

questions.prompt: A company's report page takes 1.8 seconds to build on its origin server. It turns on edge acceleration and expects the page to load in under 0.3 seconds for an uncached, per-user report. What is the most accurate expectation?
choices: The edge will generate the report faster because it runs a copy of the application code.
Acceleration will make the page load in under 0.3 seconds for every user, because the secure handshake is handled locally.
The edge only shortens network travel time, so the 1.8 seconds of origin processing still applies to an uncached page.
The edge removes origin processing time entirely once the page has been requested twice.
questions.why: Acceleration reduces network time and reuses connections, but it does not speed up slow backend code, and uncacheable dynamic responses still wait for the origin.

questions.prompt: A company serves customers in Brazil and Japan from one origin in Ireland. It wants each customer's connection to end at a nearby entry point worldwide, with static content cached close to users. Which kind of service fits best, and why do the regional options not?
choices: A regional load balancer that spreads traffic across virtual machines in a single region, because it keeps traffic inside one location.
A larger virtual machine size in the Ireland region, because more compute speeds up delivery to distant users.
A global edge service such as Azure Front Door, because it places points of presence near users, while regional services work only inside one region.
A web application firewall policy attached to a single regional gateway, because it filters requests before they reach Ireland.
questions.why: Only a global edge service places entry points near users around the world and caches content there; regional load balancers and gateways work inside a single region and do not provide that edge.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how traffic acceleration at a global edge differs from simply adding a bigger backend server, and name one limit or tradeoff of acceleration.
lessons.modelAnswer: A bigger backend server makes the origin compute responses faster, but the user still pays for every round trip across the internet to reach it. Traffic acceleration attacks the distance part. Users connect to a nearby edge entry point, the secure handshake completes locally, and the edge forwards requests over connections it already keeps open to the origin. Static content can be served from the edge without reaching the origin. The main limit is that acceleration does not speed up slow backend logic, so dynamic responses that take time to compute are still slow. There is also a tradeoff in caching: a cached response can be shared with the wrong user if the rules are careless, so you must decide carefully what is safe to cache.
rubricPoints: Acceleration reduces network distance by terminating user connections at a nearby edge.
A bigger backend improves server processing time but not the round trips to reach it.
Persistent connections from the edge to the origin avoid repeated handshakes on the long leg.
Acceleration does not fix slow backend code or uncacheable dynamic responses.
Caching gains speed but risks serving private content to the wrong user if misconfigured.

suggested.rationale: Choosing between acceleration at a global edge and regional load balancing is best practised through exam-style scenarios, which no listed mission covers.

lessons.plain: Imagine a receptionist at a large office building. A visitor asks for the billing department, and the receptionist either points them to the right door, tells them to walk to a different address, or quietly passes the paperwork along with a corrected label. In web traffic, a load balancer at the edge does similar work for HTTP requests. Rules decide where a request goes based on its host name or address path. A redirect tells the browser to go to a different address and try again. A rewrite changes the request or response inside the gateway, so the browser never notices. Knowing which of these tools fits a situation is the core skill here.
lessons.guessPrompt: A website moves its old page at /prices to a new page at /pricing. Should the gateway quietly serve the new page while the browser keeps showing /prices, or should the browser be told to ask again at /pricing? Which would you choose and why?
lessons.teach:
A listener is the part of an Application Gateway that accepts incoming web traffic on a given port and host name. A routing rule connects a listener to a backend pool, which is the set of servers that do the real work. A rewrite rule set is a named group of rules that change parts of a request or response while it passes through the gateway, such as the URL path or a header. A redirect configuration is different: it makes the gateway answer the browser with a 3xx status code and a Location header naming a new URL, so the browser makes a second request to that new address.

Why this matters: a redirect costs an extra round trip and the address bar changes, but the browser ends up on a URL you chose. A rewrite costs nothing extra and the address bar stays the same, but the browser cannot see what happened, and the backend receives the changed request.

Worked example. A browser sends GET http://shop.example.com/old-page to a listener on port 80. Step 1: the listener matches the host name shop.example.com. Step 2: a redirect rule sends a 301 response with Location https://shop.example.com/old-page. Step 3: the browser repeats the request over HTTPS. For a path change instead, a rewrite rule turns /old-page into /new-page before forwarding; the browser still shows /old-page, and the backend serves /new-page.

Common mistake: writing an HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect that also matches traffic already on HTTPS. The browser is sent to the same address again and again, producing a redirect loop, and the site becomes unreachable.

In a running system, a redirect loop takes the site down for every visitor, and a rewrite that changes the Host header can make the backend fail to match the site it serves. Choose redirect when the browser must learn the new address, and rewrite when only the gateway and backend need to agree.

questions.prompt: A small airline company runs an Application Gateway. Its listener (the part that accepts traffic on a given port and host name) is set to port 80 for the host name booking.skyroute.test. A browser sends GET http://booking.skyroute.test/fares/june to that listener. Step 1: the listener matches the host name booking.skyroute.test. Step 2: a routing rule (the rule that connects a listener to a backend pool, which is the group of servers doing the work) sends the request to the backend pool called fare-servers. Step 3: a rewrite rule (a rule that changes part of a request while it passes through the gateway) changes the path from /fares/june to /v2/fares/june before forwarding. Step 4 is missing: what does the browser's address bar show once the response arrives, and what does the backend receive? Choose the statement that completes step 4 correctly.
choices: The address bar shows /v2/fares/june, because the gateway tells the browser the new path in the response.
The address bar still shows /fares/june, because no 3xx redirect was sent, and the backend received /v2/fares/june.
The address bar still shows /fares/june, and the browser makes a second request to /v2/fares/june automatically.
The address bar shows /fares/june, and the backend also receives /fares/june, because rewrites only change the response.
questions.why: A rewrite changes the request inside the gateway without sending a 3xx response, so the browser keeps its original address while the backend receives the changed path.

questions.prompt: In a redirect configuration (the gateway setting that makes it answer the browser with a 3xx status code and a Location header naming a new URL), what does the browser do when it receives that response?
choices: It makes a second request to the URL in the Location header, so the address bar changes.
It caches the response and never contacts the gateway again for that path.
It passes the Location value to the backend pool, which then decides which page to serve.
It sends the same request again to the original address, and the gateway forwards it unchanged.
questions.why: A redirect works by having the browser make a second request to the new address named in the Location header, which is why the address bar changes.

questions.prompt: A company has moved its customer portal from portal.old-brandname.test to portal.newbrand.test and wants every visitor's browser to end up on the new address and keep it. Which approach fits, and why?
choices: A rewrite rule that changes the Host header, because the browser never sees the change.
A routing rule to a backend pool named after the new brand, because routing rules change addresses.
A redirect configuration returning a 3xx status with a Location header of the new address, because the browser must learn the new address.
A rewrite rule that changes the path, because the address bar keeps the original host name.
questions.why: Because the browser itself must move to the new address, a redirect is needed; a rewrite keeps the browser on the old address and only changes what the backend receives.

questions.prompt: A team creates an HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect (sending plain-HTTP visitors to the HTTPS version of the same address) on a listener for api.lumenpay.test, but the same rule also matches requests that already arrived over HTTPS. What is the most likely result, and why?
choices: Faster page loads, because the browser caches the redirect and skips the backend.
No visible effect, because the gateway ignores redirect rules for traffic that is already encrypted.
A redirect loop, because each HTTPS request is sent to the same HTTPS address again, so the browser never reaches a page and the site becomes unreachable.
A rewrite of the Host header, because the gateway changes the host name whenever a redirect matches.
questions.why: A redirect that matches its own destination keeps sending the browser to the same address, so the browser loops and the site fails for every visitor.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says, 'Just rewrite the URL in the gateway, the browser will never know.' Explain to them when that is the wrong choice, and name one limit or tradeoff of a rewrite compared with a redirect.
lessons.modelAnswer: A rewrite is useful when the change only matters between the gateway and the backend, because the visitor's address bar and bookmarks stay the same and there is no extra round trip. But that same invisibility is the limit. If an old address has moved for good, a rewrite keeps the old link alive forever, so search engines and bookmarks never learn the new address. A redirect fixes that, because the browser receives a response saying the page now lives somewhere else and updates itself. The tradeoff is an extra request for the browser and a visible URL change. So I would rewrite for internal path mapping, and redirect when the public address itself has changed or the scheme must change, such as HTTP to HTTPS.
rubricPoints: A rewrite changes the request inside the gateway and the browser's URL stays the same.
A redirect makes the browser make a new request to a different URL, which is visible to the client.
A rewrite cannot make search engines or bookmarks learn that a public address has moved.
A redirect costs an extra round trip, so it is slower than a rewrite.

suggested.rationale: Choosing between redirect and rewrite for a given situation is best practised by reasoning through exam-style scenarios, and no listed mission covers HTTP routing.

lessons.plain: Azure Front Door is a global entry point that accepts web traffic and forwards it to your backend servers, called origins. By default the origin still has a public address, so anyone who finds it can bypass the entry point. Private Link lets Front Door reach the origin over a private connection inside Azure, so the origin no longer needs to be open to the internet. Think of a building with one front desk: Private Link means the back door opens only for the desk's own courier, and the courier is let in only after the building owner signs off.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a backend server should accept requests only from one global entry point, what would you want to remove from that server's public exposure, and how would you still let the entry point reach it?
lessons.teach:
Private Link is a way to reach a service through a private endpoint, which is a network interface with a private IP address placed inside your virtual network. For Azure Front Door, the feature is called a Private Link origin. Front Door, on its Premium tier, creates a private connection from its own managed network to your origin, such as a web app, a storage account, or a service behind an internal load balancer. The origin owner must approve that connection request before traffic can flow. After approval, the owner can turn off public network access on the origin, so the only route in is the private one.

Why it works: the connection runs from Front Door's side to a private endpoint on your side. Traffic travels over Microsoft's backbone network rather than the open internet, and the origin never needs a public listener that attackers can probe.

Worked example: a team runs a web app origin with public access enabled. Step 1: they enable Private Link on the Front Door origin and select the app's private endpoint. Step 2: the request appears in the app's connection list as pending. Step 3: the owner approves it. Step 4: the team disables public network access on the app. Step 5: a direct request to the app's public address now fails, while requests through Front Door still succeed. Health probes, which are periodic checks Front Door sends to confirm an origin is alive, keep passing over the private path.

Common mistake: approving the connection but leaving public access on. The origin is still reachable directly, so the protection is only partial. A second mistake is assuming the private path works before approval; until the connection is approved, Front Door cannot reach the origin through it.

Consequence in a running system: if the approval is missed or the connection is removed, health probes fail, Front Door marks the origin unhealthy, and users see errors even though the application itself is running. The safe pattern is to make the private path the only path and to verify it with a direct request that must fail.

questions.prompt: A regional newspaper keeps its photo archive in a storage account and serves it through an Azure Front Door profile on the Premium tier. The team wants only Front Door to reach the archive. Here is their trace. Step 1: they add a Private Link origin that points at the storage account's blob endpoint and submit the connection request. Step 2: the request shows as pending on the storage account. Step 3: [MISSING STEP: the storage account owner approves the pending connection request.] Step 4: they turn off public network access on the storage account. Step 5: a direct request to the storage account's public address is refused, while a request through Front Door returns the photo. Which choice correctly fills the missing step?
choices: The team deletes the Front Door origin group and recreates it so the request is reset
The storage account owner approves the pending connection request
The team moves the profile from Premium to Standard so the private option appears
The team turns off public network access on the storage account before the request is submitted
questions.why: Until the owner approves the pending connection, Front Door cannot reach the origin through the private path, so approval must come before public access is turned off.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does a Private Link origin in Azure Front Door provide?
choices: A DNS rewrite that makes the origin's public name resolve to a Front Door address
A cache at edge locations that stores copies of the origin's pages to reduce wait times for users
A private connection from Front Door's managed network to a private endpoint on the origin's side, so the origin does not need a public listener
A custom certificate that encrypts traffic between the user's browser and Front Door
questions.why: A Private Link origin creates a private connection from Front Door to a private endpoint on the origin side, which removes the need for a public listener on the origin.

questions.prompt: A company runs an internal API behind an internal load balancer in its own virtual network. Its Front Door profile is on the Premium tier. The owner has already approved the Private Link connection. What should the team do next to make sure the only route in is the private one?
choices: Turn off public network access on the API origin, then confirm that a direct request to its public address fails
Remove the private endpoint so that only the public address is used for traffic
Leave public network access on, because the approved connection already protects the path
Change the health probe settings to zero so the origin is never checked over the public path
questions.why: Approval enables the private path, but public access must be disabled and a direct request must be shown to fail, otherwise the origin stays reachable directly.

questions.prompt: A team on the Premium tier removed the Private Link connection from a web origin while the web app kept running normally. Users now see errors when they browse through Front Door. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The web app crashed because its private IP address was reassigned when the connection was removed
Front Door can no longer send its health probes over the private path, so it marks the origin unhealthy and users see errors
Front Door switched automatically to the origin's public address, which is now blocked by the team
Users' local DNS caches still point to an old origin address that no longer responds
questions.why: Health probes depend on the private path, so when the connection is removed Front Door marks the origin unhealthy even though the application is still running.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how Private Link lets Azure Front Door reach a backend origin without that origin being open to the internet, and name one limit or tradeoff of this setup.
lessons.modelAnswer: Front Door is the public entry point, but without Private Link the backend still has a public address, so someone could skip Front Door and call it directly. With Private Link, Front Door creates a private connection to the origin through a private endpoint, and the origin owner approves that connection. The traffic travels on Microsoft's network rather than the open internet. Once the connection is approved, we turn off the origin's public access, so only the private path works. The tradeoff is that this requires the Premium tier, the origin has to support Private Link, and each connection and private endpoint needs ongoing management. If the approval is missing, Front Door sees the origin as down, so the approval step belongs in the deployment process rather than being an afterthought.
rubricPoints: Front Door reaches the origin through a private connection and private endpoint instead of the public internet.
The origin owner must approve the connection before traffic flows.
Public access on the origin should be turned off so direct calls fail.
A real limit: the Premium tier is required, and missed approvals cause the origin to look unhealthy.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style scenario about which exposure to remove and what approval step is needed adds the most beyond the facts.

lessons.plain: A private endpoint gives a cloud service, such as a storage account or a database, a private address inside your own virtual network. Instead of your servers reaching the service over the public internet, they connect to that private address, and the traffic stays within the cloud provider's network. Planning one means deciding where the address lives, which parts of your network can use it, and how names get resolved to it. Think of it as giving a shared office building a door that opens only from inside your company's floor, rather than from the street.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your application servers sit in a private subnet and need to read from a storage account. With no extra setup, would their traffic normally leave your network and cross the public internet? What would you need to change so that it does not?
lessons.teach: A virtual network (VNet) is your private network in the cloud. A subnet is a range of addresses inside it. A private endpoint is a network interface that receives a private IP address from one of your subnets and connects to one specific service resource, or one part of it. A private link is the connection that carries traffic from your network to that resource across the provider's backbone, not the public internet. The public endpoint is the service's normal internet-facing address, which stays open until you close it. Planning means deciding five things: which subnet holds the endpoint, which networks need to reach it, how many addresses to set aside, how names resolve to the private address, and whether the public endpoint is turned off. A subnet should be dedicated to endpoints where possible, because Azure reserves five addresses in every subnet and each endpoint consumes one more. Worked example: an application in spoke network A must read blobs from storage account st-orders. Step 1: choose a subnet, snet-endpoints, sized 10.1.2.0/27. Step 2: create one blob endpoint in it; it receives 10.1.2.4. Step 3: make names for st-orders resolve to 10.1.2.4 from spoke A. Step 4: disable public network access on the account. Only then is the public route closed. A common mistake is assuming that creating the endpoint blocks internet access.
