The public endpoint stays open, and name resolution can still send clients to it, so the application appears to work while still using the public path. A second mistake is leaving network policies off on the endpoint subnet by default, so NSG rules do not filter traffic to the endpoint unless that setting is enabled. In a running system, a missed DNS record makes the application fail or silently take the public route after a change. A private endpoint is planned as an address, a name and a closed public door, all three together.

questions.prompt: Harbor Clinic runs a key vault named kv-claims for its billing spoke network. The team plans a private endpoint for it. Step 1: they set aside subnet snet-pe at 10.4.16.0/28 and reserve it for endpoints only. Step 2: they create one vault endpoint in snet-pe, which receives 10.4.16.4. Step 3: they map the name kv-claims to 10.4.16.4 in the DNS zone the billing spoke uses. What final step is still needed before the public route is closed?
choices: Create a second vault endpoint in a different subnet so there is a backup private address
Attach a network security group to the billing spoke that blocks outbound port 443 to the internet
Turn on network policies for snet-pe so the vault endpoint can be reached through the subnet
Disable public network access on kv-claims
questions.why: Only disabling public network access on the vault closes the public route, because the endpoint and DNS mapping alone leave the internet-facing address open.

questions.prompt: A dedicated endpoint subnet is sized /29, which gives 8 addresses in total. Azure reserves five of those addresses in every subnet. How many private endpoints can this subnet hold?
questions.why: Azure reserves five addresses in each subnet and each endpoint uses one of the remaining three, so the subnet holds 3 endpoints.

questions.prompt: A team adds a deny rule in a network security group on the subnet that holds its private endpoint, expecting it to stop an application subnet from reaching a storage account through that endpoint. Traffic still gets through. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The endpoint subnet has network policies disabled, which is the default, so the rules do not filter traffic to the endpoint
The deny rule has to be placed on the storage account's firewall, not in any network security group
Storage accounts ignore network security groups entirely, so no subnet rule can filter them
The rule priority is too high and is being overridden by the default allow rule
questions.why: By default the endpoint subnet has network policies off, so network security group rules there do not filter traffic to the endpoint until that setting is enabled.

questions.prompt: A team creates a private endpoint for a document database account used by its app spoke. Clients in the spoke still connect to the account's public address, and the public endpoint remains open. Which planning item was most likely missed?
choices: Sizing the subnet to hold more addresses
Enabling a service endpoint on the same subnet
Mapping the account's name to the endpoint's private address in name resolution
Adding a route table entry that sends traffic to the public internet
questions.why: Clients still reach the public address because their name resolution points to the public endpoint, so the private address is never used even though the endpoint exists.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why we should use a private endpoint for our database rather than only restricting the database's public address by IP. Explain to them what planning a private endpoint involves, and name one limit or tradeoff we would have to accept.
lessons.modelAnswer: Restricting by IP still leaves the database on a public address, so traffic crosses the internet and the allowed list must be kept up to date as our servers change. A private endpoint gives the database a private address inside our own subnet, so our servers reach it without leaving the provider's network. Planning it means choosing a dedicated subnet with enough free addresses, since each endpoint uses one, making sure the database's name resolves to the private address from every network that needs it, and then turning off public access so the old route is closed. The tradeoff is that it adds work and cost: we must set up DNS correctly for each connected network, and anything outside the private network, including on-premises clients, cannot reach it until we arrange a path for them. We also need to decide how network policies apply to the endpoint subnet, since they are off by default.
rubricPoints: A private endpoint gives the service a private IP inside our own subnet.
Traffic stays on the provider's network instead of crossing the public internet.
Planning covers subnet choice and address capacity, since each endpoint uses an address.
Name resolution must point to the private address, or traffic still goes public.
Public access should be turned off after the endpoint is in place.
A tradeoff is added DNS and connectivity work, and off-network clients need a path.

suggested.rationale: An exam-style requirement that asks the learner to choose between a private endpoint and other options, and justify the choice, is the most useful practice for this planning objective.

lessons.plain: A private endpoint gives a cloud service a private address inside your own network. Normally, when your app reaches a storage account or database hosted in the cloud, the traffic travels over the public internet to a public address. With a private endpoint, the service gets a private address from a subnet you choose, so your machines reach it the way they reach any other machine on the local network. You can then turn off public access, which keeps the data off the open internet.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your app runs in a virtual network and reads files from a storage account. The security team says that traffic must never cross the public internet. Before reading anything else, what would you expect to change so the app reaches the storage account by a private route, and what would you need to choose to make that happen?
lessons.teach:
A private endpoint is a network interface with a private IP address, placed in a subnet of your virtual network. A virtual network is your own isolated private network in the cloud, and a subnet is a range of addresses inside it. The endpoint is linked to one specific resource through Private Link, the mechanism that carries traffic to a service without using its public address. Clients inside your network that reach the service then use the private address instead of a public one.

Creating one means choosing three things: the target resource (for example, a storage account), the sub-resource it exposes (such as blob, file or queue storage), and the subnet where the private IP should live. Azure allocates a free address from that subnet and creates the network interface. Approval can be automatic when you own the target, or pending until the resource owner approves the connection, which is common across subscriptions or tenants.

Worked example. Your subnet is 10.1.2.0/24 and your storage account is named contosodata. Step 1: create a private endpoint for its blob sub-resource in that subnet. Step 2: Azure reserves the first four addresses of any subnet, so the first free address is 10.1.2.4, and the endpoint's network interface takes it. Step 3: a virtual machine in the subnet looks up the blob name and connects to 10.1.2.4, so the traffic stays inside your network.

Common mistake: creating the endpoint but leaving the name pointing at the public address. Clients then keep using the internet path, and the endpoint sits unused. In a running system, the security team still sees public traffic in logs, and the endpoint looks broken even though nothing has failed.

A private endpoint is created per sub-resource, so a storage account that needs both blob and file access needs two endpoints. Creating the endpoint alone does not make traffic private; it is the combination of the endpoint, the name resolution and disabled public access that keeps data off the public internet.

questions.prompt: Northwind Freight has a subnet 192.168.40.0/27 and a storage account named northwindlogs. The team needs blob and file access over private addresses, so they create one private endpoint for blob and one for file, both in that subnet. Step 1: the blob endpoint takes 192.168.40.4, because Azure reserves the first four addresses of the subnet. Step 2: the file endpoint takes 192.168.40.5. Step 3 is not yet done. Which action completes the setup so that clients in the subnet actually use the private addresses?
choices: Create a third endpoint for queue storage so all sub-resources are covered
Enlarge the subnet from /27 to /26 so the reserved addresses no longer overlap the endpoints
Make the blob and file names resolve to 192.168.40.4 and 192.168.40.5 instead of the public addresses
Delete the blob endpoint and recreate it, because a second endpoint must be created after the first is approved
questions.why: Endpoints only carry traffic once clients look up the account names and receive the private addresses, so the name resolution must point to the endpoint addresses.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is a private endpoint?
choices: A firewall rule that blocks internet traffic to a storage account without changing how clients find it
A copy of a storage account placed inside a virtual network so that data is replicated for backup
A network interface with a private IP address in a subnet of your virtual network, linked to one specific resource through Private Link
A public IP address that a storage account is given so that clients on the internet can reach it
questions.why: The teaching text defines a private endpoint as a network interface with a private address in your subnet, linked to one resource through Private Link.

questions.prompt: A subnet is 10.60.5.0/24 and a team creates a private endpoint in it for a storage account's blob sub-resource. Which private IP address is the first one Azure can assign to that endpoint's network interface?
questions.why: Azure reserves the first four addresses of any subnet, so the first free address is 10.60.5.4.

questions.prompt: A company created a private endpoint for its storage account, and the connection was approved. Users inside the virtual network still reach the account over the public internet, and the security team sees public traffic in logs. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The endpoint needs its own public IP address before any traffic can use it
Private endpoints only work for accounts created after the endpoint was approved
The endpoint's subnet is too small, so Azure fell back to the public path
The endpoint was created but the account's name still points to its public address, so clients never use the private IP
questions.why: The endpoint existing does not make traffic private; clients must resolve the name to the private address, and otherwise they keep using the public path.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why we would not just allow the application's subnet through the storage account's public firewall rules instead of creating a private endpoint. Explain to them, in your own words, what a private endpoint changes and what limit or tradeoff they should weigh before choosing it.
lessons.modelAnswer: An allow rule on the public address still sends the traffic to a public IP, so the connection still uses the public path, and the service stays reachable from outside our network. A private endpoint instead gives the storage account a private IP inside our subnet, so traffic stays on private addressing, and we can disable public network access entirely. The tradeoff is that each endpoint adds cost and needs name resolution set up so the service name returns the private address; without that, clients quietly keep using the public route. Each sub-resource needs its own endpoint, and a connection to a resource owned by another team may wait for their approval, so we should plan that lead time. If the only goal is limiting which subnets can reach a public endpoint, a service endpoint may be enough, but when the requirement is no public path at all, the private endpoint is the better fit.
rubricPoints: A private endpoint is a network interface with a private IP in a chosen subnet, linked to one resource through Private Link.
Traffic stays on private addressing, so public access to the service can be turned off.
Each sub-resource (such as blob or file) needs its own endpoint.
Name resolution must return the private IP, or clients keep using the public path.
Cross-owner connections may need manual approval before they work.

suggested.rationale: Deciding and creating a private endpoint in an exam-style scenario, with the reasoning about public paths, adds the most value beyond a console walkthrough.

lessons.plain: A private endpoint gives a cloud service a private address inside your own network, so machines on that network can reach it without sending traffic across the public internet. Think of it as a dedicated door into the service that opens only onto your building's hallway. Configuring access means deciding who may use that door: whether the owner of the service must approve the connection, which network rules filter the traffic, and whether the service still answers on its public address at all. Getting these settings right is how you keep traffic private rather than just hoping it is.
lessons.guessPrompt: A storage account already accepts requests from the internet, and you add a private endpoint for it inside your own network. Does adding that endpoint by itself stop internet requests from reaching the account?
lessons.teach:
A private endpoint is a network interface that lives in a subnet you choose, and it receives a private IP address from that subnet's range. It links to one specific resource, such as a storage account or a database, through a connection that the cloud platform manages. Clients inside your network send requests to that private address and reach the resource without the traffic crossing the public internet.

Configuring access to a private endpoint involves three separate controls. First, connection approval: when the endpoint targets a resource owned by someone else, the owner can approve, reject or leave the request pending, and only approved connections carry traffic. Second, network rules on the subnet: a network security group (a set of allow and deny rules on traffic) and a route table apply to the private endpoint only when the subnet's private endpoint network policy is enabled, so you must switch it on deliberately. Third, public network access on the resource: setting it to disabled makes the resource refuse requests that arrive on its public address, leaving the private path as the only one.

Worked example: a storage account should accept uploads only from the application subnet 10.1.2.0/24. Step 1: create a private endpoint for the storage account in a subnet of the application network. Step 2: approve the connection if it is pending. Step 3: enable the subnet's private endpoint network policy and add an NSG rule allowing the application subnet to reach the endpoint on the service port, typically 443. Step 4: set public network access to disabled. A request from a laptop on the internet is now refused, and a request from the application subnet succeeds.

Common mistake: assuming the subnet's NSG already filters private endpoint traffic while the network policy is off. The deny rule then silently does nothing. In a running system, a security review may find that traffic which was supposed to be blocked was never blocked, and the fix is to enable the policy and confirm the rule with a test from outside the allowed subnet. Set each of the three controls deliberately, because one open setting can leave a private path with a public door beside it.

questions.prompt: Brightwater Clinics keeps patient records in a managed database called records-db. Its application runs in subnet app-tier at 172.20.4.0/24. The records-db private endpoint sits in subnet pe-tier at 172.20.8.0/24 and its connection is already approved. The worked steps are: Step 1, create the private endpoint in pe-tier. Step 2, confirm the connection is approved. Step 3 is missing and you must fill it in. Step 4, set public network access on records-db to disabled. Which choice correctly completes Step 3 so that only app-tier can reach records-db on TCP 1433?
choices: Create a service endpoint on app-tier so the database is reached privately, then skip the NSG
Add an NSG rule on app-tier denying 172.20.8.0/24 on port 1433, which filters traffic into the endpoint
Enable the private endpoint network policy on pe-tier, then add an NSG rule allowing 172.20.4.0/24 to reach TCP 1433
Add a route table on app-tier that sends all traffic to the internet, then leave the policy alone
questions.why: The NSG rule only applies to private endpoint traffic once the subnet's private endpoint network policy is enabled, and the rule must allow the application subnet on the database port.

questions.prompt: A private endpoint receives its IP address from which source?
choices: A shared pool the resource owner assigns per request
A public range owned by the cloud provider
The address range of the subnet where you place it
A link-local range chosen by the client machine
questions.why: A private endpoint is a network interface that takes its private address from the range of the subnet you choose for it.

questions.prompt: A partner company owns a database, and your private endpoint to it shows a pending connection. Your application's traffic to it fails. What must happen first?
choices: Increase the size of the application subnet
Turn on public network access for the database
The database owner approves the pending connection
Add a route table entry pointing the subnet at the database
questions.why: When the target resource belongs to someone else, the owner must approve the connection, and only approved connections carry traffic.

questions.prompt: After you set public network access on a storage account to disabled, a developer on a home laptop tries the public address. What happens?
choices: The request is served only if the subnet NSG allows it
The resource refuses the request arriving on its public address
The request succeeds because the laptop is outside the VNet
The request is redirected to a private endpoint automatically
questions.why: Disabling public network access makes the resource refuse requests arriving on its public address, so the private path becomes the only way in.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between configuring a private endpoint and simply leaving a resource on its public address, naming one limit or tradeoff of the private endpoint approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would first ask whether the traffic must avoid the public internet entirely. If it must, a private endpoint gives the service a private IP inside our network, so clients reach it over that private path. Then I configure access in three places. I approve the connection if the owner is a different team. I enable the subnet's private endpoint network policy so that NSG rules actually filter the traffic. I set public network access on the resource to disabled so the public address refuses requests. The tradeoff is that a private endpoint adds cost and a dependency on name resolution: every client must resolve the service name to the private address, so a DNS mistake can break access that worked before. Without the public-access change, the private path exists but the public door stays open.
rubricPoints: A private endpoint gives the service a private IP address inside the customer network.
Connection approval by the resource owner controls whether the endpoint carries traffic.
The subnet private endpoint network policy must be enabled for NSG rules to filter the traffic.
Disabling public network access stops requests arriving over the public address.
Each tradeoff, such as cost or name-resolution dependency, is named.

suggested.rationale: Choosing and configuring access is best learned by reasoning through a requirement where several settings interact, and no listed mission covers this.

lessons.plain: Imagine you run a useful service, such as an internal fleet-tracking API, and you want customers in other companies' networks to reach it without ever touching the open internet. A Private Link service is how you publish that service so that other networks can connect to it privately. You keep your service behind a load balancer inside your own network. Each consumer creates a private doorway, with a private address in its own network, that leads to your service. The traffic stays on the cloud provider's private backbone, and you decide who is allowed to connect.
lessons.guessPrompt: If your API runs inside your own private network and a customer in a different private network needs to call it, what would you need to avoid to keep the traffic off the public internet, and what would you put in front of the API so many callers can reach it?
lessons.teach:
A Private Link service is the provider side of private connectivity. You, the owner of a service, place it behind a standard load balancer in your own virtual network (VNet, a private address space you control, divided into subnets). Then you publish that frontend as a Private Link service. A consumer, meaning a customer in another VNet or subscription, creates a private endpoint: a network interface with a private IP address in its own subnet that connects to your published service. The consumer's applications call that private IP, and the traffic never crosses the public internet.

Some terms. A standard load balancer spreads incoming connections across backend machines. A NAT subnet is a subnet you designate so that connections arriving at your service carry source addresses from a range you control, which means your backends do not need to know the consumer's real address. Visibility settings control which subscriptions may find the service, and auto-approval controls which connection requests go through without a manual decision.

Why it works. The consumer gets no route into your network, and you expose no public endpoint. Every connection request appears as its own record on your side, so you can approve, reject or remove each consumer independently.

Worked example. A fleet-tracking API runs on two backend machines behind a standard load balancer in VNet A. Step 1: you publish that load balancer's frontend as a Private Link service and give it a NAT subnet. Step 2: a customer in VNet B creates a private endpoint pointing at the service. Step 3: the customer's app calls the private IP in VNet B. Step 4: the request reaches your load balancer, which passes it to a healthy backend. Step 5: you see a pending connection request, approve it, and the connection becomes active.

Common mistake. Trying to publish a service that is not behind a supported standard load balancer, or skipping the subnet setting that governs network policies for private link on the subnet hosting the service, so the setup fails. Another mistake is assuming consumers can see your backend addresses; they see only their own private endpoint.

Consequence. If you reject or delete a consumer's connection, that consumer loses access at once while other consumers keep working.

A Private Link service lets you offer one service to chosen consumers over private addresses, and you hold the approval switch for every connection.

questions.prompt: A payments company runs an invoice-scanning API on three backend machines behind a standard load balancer (a service that spreads incoming connections across backends) in its VNet named ledger-core, which uses the address space 10.40.0.0/16. The owner publishes the load balancer's frontend as a Private Link service and sets a NAT subnet of 10.40.9.0/24. A partner in a different subscription creates a private endpoint (a network interface with a private IP in its own subnet that connects to the published service) in subnet 172.16.3.0/27. The partner's app then calls the endpoint's private IP, 172.16.3.4. The step between creating the endpoint and the partner's first call is missing. What is it?
choices: The owner opens the backend NSG to the partner's subnet 172.16.3.0/27 so the connection can reach the machines.
The partner enables a service endpoint on subnet 172.16.3.0/27 so the traffic stays on the Azure backbone.
The partner asks the provider to attach a public IP to the endpoint so the call can be routed.
The owner sees the pending connection request on the Private Link service and approves it, so the connection becomes active.
questions.why: A new private endpoint sends a connection request to the service owner, and the connection stays pending and unusable until the owner approves it.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is the purpose of a NAT subnet on a Private Link service?
choices: It replaces the load balancer so that connections are spread across backends without a frontend.
It gives every consumer a public IP so the backends can reply over the internet.
It lets connections arriving at the service carry source addresses from a range the owner controls, so backends do not need the consumer's real address.
It makes the backend machines' addresses visible to each consumer so they can connect directly.
questions.why: A NAT subnet is a subnet the owner designates so that arriving connections use source addresses from a range the owner controls, hiding the consumer's real address from the backends.

questions.prompt: A team has a internal reporting API behind a basic load balancer, not a standard one. They try to publish it as a Private Link service. What is the most likely result?
choices: The service publishes normally, but consumers see the backend addresses.
The service is published but traffic is sent over the public internet to reach it.
The service publishes, and approvals happen automatically because the load balancer is basic.
The publish step fails, because a Private Link service must sit behind a supported standard load balancer.
questions.why: Private Link services require a supported standard load balancer, so publishing a service behind a basic load balancer fails.

questions.prompt: A provider holds a Private Link service with three consumers connected through private endpoints. The provider rejects one consumer's connection request. What happens next?
choices: Only the rejected consumer loses access right away, while the other two keep working.
The rejected consumer keeps access until its private endpoint is deleted by the consumer.
The rejected consumer is moved to a public endpoint so its traffic still avoids nothing.
All three consumers lose access until the provider re-approves them.
questions.why: Each connection request is handled separately, so rejecting one consumer cuts off only that consumer and leaves the others unaffected.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a Private Link service is and how it differs from simply putting the service on a public address, and name one limit or tradeoff of using it.
lessons.modelAnswer: A Private Link service is how we publish one of our own services so that other teams or customers can reach it over private addresses. We put the service behind a standard load balancer, publish that frontend, and give it a NAT subnet so connections arrive from addresses we control. Each consumer then creates its own private endpoint and calls a private IP in its own network. Compared with a public address, nothing is exposed to the internet and we approve each consumer individually. The tradeoff is that consumers reach only the one service we published, which is good for isolation but means they cannot use broader parts of our network. The limit is that the service has to sit behind a supported standard load balancer, and every consumer needs its own endpoint and our approval. If a consumer needs general network access, or the service is not built behind a load balancer, this is the wrong tool.
rubricPoints: Defines the provider side: a service behind a standard load balancer, published as a Private Link service.
Explains that consumers connect through their own private endpoint with a private IP in their network.
Contrasts the private model with a public endpoint, noting the provider approves each connection.
Names a real limit, such as the load balancer requirement or access limited to the single published service.

suggested.rationale: Explaining the provider and consumer roles and the tradeoff back to a teammate is the core skill, and no existing mission or planned engine covers Azure private connectivity.

lessons.plain: Normally, when your application reaches a cloud service such as a storage account or a database, the request travels across the public internet to a public address. Private Link is a way to give that service a private presence inside your own cloud network, so traffic can stay on private paths. A private endpoint is the concrete piece that does this: a network card with a private IP address taken from one of your subnets, connected to one specific service. Getting the private address is not enough on its own, because the name your software looks up must also resolve to that private address instead of the public one. This lesson explains how that name lookup has to be arranged.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose you give a database a private endpoint with the private IP 10.1.2.4, but your application still uses the database's usual hostname and the connection still goes out over the internet. Before any DNS setup is explained, what do you think is the most likely reason?
lessons.teach:
Definitions. A private endpoint is a network interface that sits in a subnet of your virtual network (VNet, your private network in the cloud) and holds a private IP address. It connects to one target resource, or one part of it such as the blob part of a storage account. Private Link is the broader feature that makes this connection possible. DNS, the Domain Name System, turns a hostname into an IP address. A private DNS zone is a DNS zone that answers only for clients inside the VNets linked to it. An A record is the DNS entry that maps a name to an IPv4 address.

Why it works. The service keeps its usual public name, for example contoso.blob.core.windows.net. The platform also publishes a matching name under a privatelink label, such as contoso.privatelink.blob.core.windows.net. When a client inside your network looks up the usual name, DNS answers with a pointer to the privatelink name. Your private DNS zone for that privatelink name holds an A record pointing to the endpoint's private IP. The client therefore receives the private address and never sees the public one.

Worked example. Your VNet uses 10.1.0.0/16. A private endpoint in subnet 10.1.2.0/24 receives 10.1.2.4. Step 1: an app in the VNet asks for contoso.blob.core.windows.net. Step 2: DNS returns a pointer to contoso.privatelink.blob.core.windows.net. Step 3: the private zone, linked to the VNet, answers with an A record for 10.1.2.4. Step 4: the app connects to 10.1.2.4 over the private path.

Common mistake. Teams create the endpoint but skip linking the private DNS zone to the VNet, or they leave a public DNS record in place. The lookup then returns the public address. If public access is disabled on the service, the connection fails. If public access is still enabled, traffic quietly goes over the internet, which defeats the purpose.

In a running system, the DNS link is part of the design, not an afterthought. Every VNet that needs access, including peered networks and on-premises DNS resolvers, must resolve the name the same way.

questions.prompt: Northwind's reporting app runs in a VNet (your private network in the cloud) that uses 172.16.0.0/16. Its private endpoint sits in subnet 172.16.5.0/24 and receives the private IP 172.16.5.7. The private DNS zone for the privatelink name is linked to that VNet. The app needs northwindreports.blob.core.windows.net. Trace the lookup. Step 1: the app asks DNS for northwindreports.blob.core.windows.net. Step 2: DNS returns a pointer to northwindreports.privatelink.blob.core.windows.net. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the app opens its connection to 172.16.5.7. Which completes step 3?
choices: The private DNS zone returns the subnet address 172.16.5.0, and the app connects to that address.
The app skips DNS and connects to the privatelink name directly, which resolves to the public address.
The public DNS zone returns the storage account's public IP address, and the app connects to that address.
The private DNS zone, linked to the VNet, answers with an A record (an entry that maps a name to an IPv4 address) pointing the privatelink name to 172.16.5.7.
questions.why: The linked private zone holds the A record that maps the privatelink name to the endpoint's private IP, which is what step 4 relies on.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is a private endpoint?
choices: A public IP address reserved for a storage account so that any client on the internet can reach it directly without any extra setup.
A DNS zone that answers for any client on the internet that looks up the name of a storage account, wherever that client is located.
A firewall rule that blocks public traffic to a subnet before the traffic can reach the service behind it, for every client.
A network interface in a subnet of your VNet that holds a private IP address and connects to one target resource or part of one.
questions.why: A private endpoint is a network interface in a VNet subnet with a private IP that connects to one resource or part of one, as defined in the teaching text.

questions.prompt: Litware created a private endpoint for its storage account in subnet 10.8.3.0/24, which gives the endpoint the private IP 10.8.3.4. It did not link the private DNS zone to its VNet, and public access on the storage account is disabled. An app inside that VNet looks up the storage account name. What happens?
choices: The app receives the public address and traffic goes over the internet, because the endpoint is not used for name lookups at all.
The app receives a private address from the DNS server automatically, without any zone link, because the endpoint registers itself.
The app receives the public address, and the connection fails because public access is disabled on the storage account.
The app receives 10.8.3.4 and connects privately, because creating the endpoint is enough for lookups to return its private address.
questions.why: Without the zone link the lookup returns the public address, and since public access is disabled, the connection fails.

questions.prompt: Tailspin has a peered VNet and on-premises DNS resolvers that need to reach a storage account through its private endpoint. Which statement must be true?
choices: Every network that needs access must resolve the service name to the private IP through the same private zone setup.
Only the VNet that contains the endpoint needs to resolve the name, because peered networks fall back to the public address automatically without any extra configuration.
On-premises resolvers can keep forwarding to public DNS unchanged, because the private endpoint handles the routing of those lookups for them.
The private endpoint must be moved into each peered VNet's subnet, with its own separate private zone, before any lookup can succeed for that network.
questions.why: The teaching text says every VNet that needs access, including peered networks and on-premises resolvers, must resolve the name the same way, to the private address.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a private endpoint together with its DNS setup keeps a storage account's traffic off the public internet, and name one limit or tradeoff of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: A private endpoint gives the storage account a network card with a private IP inside one of our subnets, so traffic from inside the VNet can reach it without leaving the private network. The endpoint alone is not enough. The account's normal hostname has to resolve to that private IP, and that happens because the public name points to a privatelink name, and a private DNS zone linked to our VNet holds an A record for it. If the zone is missing or not linked, clients get the public address instead. One tradeoff is that every network that needs access has to resolve names correctly, including peered VNets and on-premises DNS, so the setup takes more planning than a simple firewall rule. Also, the endpoint only covers the specific service it was created for.
rubricPoints: A private endpoint is a network interface with a private IP in a subnet that connects to one specific service.
The public hostname must resolve to the privatelink name and then to the private IP through a linked private DNS zone.
Without correct DNS, clients receive the public address, causing failures or traffic leaving the private network.
Each network needing access must resolve the name correctly, which adds planning effort.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a realistic DNS and endpoint situation where a connection goes to the wrong address adds the most, since the skill is tracing the lookup chain rather than memorising steps.

lessons.plain: A Private Link service lets one team offer its own application to other networks without putting that application on the public internet. The owner places the app behind a load balancer and publishes it. The customer then gets a private address inside its own network that leads to the app. When the customer is an office or factory running on premises, outside Azure, it connects over a VPN or a dedicated circuit. Its computers can then reach that private address as if the app were on the local network. The hard part is making sure the route and the name lookup work from the office side.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your office network needs to call a partner's API, which the partner has published as a Private Link service in Azure. The company wants no public internet exposure for this call. What do you think has to exist between the office and that API for the call to succeed?
lessons.teach:
A Private Link service is the provider side of a private connection. The provider puts its application behind an internal load balancer, which is a private traffic spreader with no public address, and then publishes that setup as a Private Link service. A consumer creates a private endpoint, which is a network interface with a private IP address inside the consumer's own virtual network. That private IP is linked to the published service, so consumer traffic never crosses the public internet.

On-premises clients sit outside Azure, so they need a hybrid path first. A site-to-site VPN or an ExpressRoute circuit connects the on-premises network to the Azure virtual network that holds the private endpoint. Routes must tell the on-premises network how to reach the endpoint's private IP, and firewalls on both sides must allow the traffic. Once the path exists, the client treats the endpoint like any other internal server.

Worked example. A plant's on-premises network is 10.50.0.0/16. The hub virtual network is 10.1.0.0/16, and the partner's private endpoint in the hub has the private IP 10.1.4.5. Step 1: the VPN links the plant network to the hub. Step 2: the plant's routing sends traffic for 10.1.0.0/16 across the VPN. Step 3: the plant app connects to 10.1.4.5 on the service port. Step 4: the packets cross the VPN, reach the private endpoint, and the endpoint forwards them to the published service.

Common mistake: assuming that because the private endpoint exists, on-premises clients can reach it. Without the route, or when the on-premises address range overlaps the Azure range, the connection simply times out. Name resolution, which decides whether the client's name leads to that private IP, is a separate topic covered in another objective.

Consequence in a running system: the on-premises app depends entirely on the hybrid link. If the VPN or circuit goes down, the app loses access to the service, because the design deliberately offers no public fallback.

questions.prompt: A freight company runs its warehouse network on 172.20.0.0/16. Its hub virtual network, which is the central Azure network that holds the shared connections, is 10.8.0.0/16, and a partner's private endpoint (a network interface with a private IP inside a virtual network, linked to a published service) in that hub has the private IP 10.8.2.9. An ExpressRoute circuit (a dedicated private line from the on-premises network into Azure) connects the warehouse network to the hub. The team has completed these steps: Step 1: the circuit links the warehouse network to the hub. Step 2: the warehouse routing sends traffic for 10.8.0.0/16 across the circuit. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the warehouse app connects to 10.8.2.9 on the service port, and the packets reach the published service. Which item correctly fills the missing Step 3?
choices: Both the warehouse-side and hub-side firewalls are opened for the app's traffic to 10.8.2.9 on the service port.
A second private endpoint is created in a different virtual network to share the load.
The private endpoint is given a public IP so the warehouse can reach it over the internet.
The warehouse app is switched to the partner's public DNS name so it uses the internet path.
questions.why: The hybrid path needs firewalls on both sides to allow the traffic, and opening them for the app's traffic to the private IP and service port is the step that makes the packets pass.

questions.prompt: A factory's on-premises clients need to use a partner's published service without sending traffic over the public internet. Which description best fits the private endpoint on the consumer side?
choices: A public load balancer that gives the service an internet address.
A DNS record that moves the client's name to a public address.
A VPN gateway that encrypts traffic between the factory and Azure.
A network interface with a private IP in the consumer's own virtual network, linked to the published service.
questions.why: The private endpoint is a network interface with a private IP inside the consumer's virtual network, and that IP is linked to the published service so traffic stays off the public internet.

questions.prompt: A clinic's on-premises network uses 10.1.0.0/16, and the Azure hub virtual network also uses 10.1.0.0/16. The VPN is up and the private endpoint exists, but the clinic's app times out when connecting to the endpoint's private IP. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The private endpoint was deleted and must be re-created as a public endpoint.
The Azure hub virtual network is too large for the VPN to carry its traffic.
The two address ranges overlap, so the routing cannot reliably send traffic for the private IP across the VPN.
The clinic's app must be changed to use a public IP address instead of the private one.
questions.why: When the on-premises range overlaps the Azure range, the routing cannot reliably direct traffic for the private IP across the link, so the connection times out even though the VPN and endpoint exist.

questions.prompt: A distribution center reaches a private endpoint over an ExpressRoute circuit. The circuit fails overnight. What happens to the center's app?
choices: It loses access to the service until the hybrid link is restored, because the design offers no public fallback.
The service itself moves into the on-premises network automatically.
The app switches to the service's public address so it stays online.
Only the center's DNS changes, and the app still reaches the service.
questions.why: The on-premises app depends entirely on the hybrid link, and the design deliberately has no public fallback, so losing the circuit means losing access to the service.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how an on-premises client reaches a Private Link service that another team published, and name one limit or tradeoff of this design.
lessons.modelAnswer: The partner publishes the service behind an internal load balancer and creates a Private Link service for it. Our network gets a private endpoint, which is a network interface with a private IP in our hub virtual network. The office reaches that IP through a site-to-site VPN or ExpressRoute, so traffic never touches the public internet. The office's routing must send that address range over the hybrid link, and the firewalls on both sides must allow the port. The main tradeoff is dependency: if the VPN or circuit fails, the on-premises app loses access, because there is no public fallback by design. Address ranges must also not overlap, or routing breaks. Name resolution is a separate step that decides which private IP a hostname returns.
rubricPoints: The provider publishes the service behind an internal load balancer as a Private Link service, and the consumer connects through a private endpoint with a private IP.
On-premises clients need a hybrid path such as VPN or ExpressRoute, plus routes and firewall rules that reach the private IP.
Traffic stays on private addresses and does not cross the public internet.
A named limit: loss of the hybrid link cuts off access, and overlapping address ranges break routing.

suggested.rationale: An exam-style scenario in which the learner must trace the route from an office to a private endpoint adds more than reading alone, and no listed mission covers hybrid private connectivity.

lessons.plain: Traffic to Azure services such as storage or databases normally travels over the public internet to a public address. A service endpoint is a setting on your own network subnet that says: when traffic from here goes to this kind of Azure service, send it over Microsoft's internal backbone and recognize it as coming from my subnet. The service can then accept requests only from that subnet. It is a simple, low-cost way to tighten who can reach a service, but the service keeps its public address. When you need the service to have a private address inside your own network, a different tool is used. Knowing which one fits a requirement is the skill here.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your app runs in one subnet and must reach a storage account. You want only that subnet allowed in, and you do not want to change any DNS names. After you turn this on, would you expect the storage account to still have a public address, or would it now have an address inside your network? Explain your guess in one or two sentences.
lessons.teach: A subnet is a range of addresses inside a virtual network, which is your private network in Azure. A public endpoint is the internet-reachable address of an Azure service, such as a storage account. A service endpoint is a feature you switch on for a subnet, for a named type of service. Once it is on, traffic from that subnet to the service travels over Microsoft's own backbone network instead of the general internet, and the service can recognize the request as coming from that subnet. You then add a firewall rule on the service that allows that subnet and denies other access. The service keeps its public address, and the names your apps use do not change. It works because the service checks the subnet identity of the caller rather than a single IP address. Worked example: a subnet 10.1.2.0/24 holds an app. Step 1: switch on the storage service endpoint for that subnet. Step 2: on the storage account, allow network access only from that subnet. Step 3: the app resolves the storage name to its usual public address, connects, and the request carries the subnet identity, so it is accepted. Step 4: a laptop on a home internet connection using the same name is refused. Common mistake: believing a service endpoint gives the service a private address in your network, or lets on-premises clients reach it privately. It does neither. Traffic from an on-premises network does not carry the subnet identity, so it is refused unless you allow its address separately. Consequence: because the service stays public, this is not enough when the requirement is that the resource has no public address at all. A service endpoint is the right choice when you need a low-cost lock-down of subnets to a service, with no change to name resolution.

questions.prompt: A company called Brightwater Labs has a reporting VM in subnet 192.168.40.0/24 that reads from an Azure SQL database. The team wants that subnet, and no other network, to reach the database over Microsoft's backbone. Step 1: the network team switches on the SQL service endpoint for subnet 192.168.40.0/24. Step 2 is missing. Step 3: the VM keeps using the database's usual public name, and the connection is accepted because it carries the subnet identity. Step 4: a developer's home laptop using the same name is refused. What is the missing Step 2?
choices: Change the reporting VM's connection string to use the database server's IP address
Create a new subnet for the database and move the server into it
On the database server's network rules, allow subnet 192.168.40.0/24 and deny other access
Give the SQL server a new private IP address inside subnet 192.168.40.0/24
questions.why: The service endpoint only identifies the subnet, so the database's own firewall rule must allow that subnet and deny other callers for the lock-down to take effect.

questions.prompt: An analytics subnet 10.60.4.0/23 in a virtual network has its service endpoint for a storage account switched on. Which statement describes the result accurately?
choices: The storage account is assigned a private IP address inside 10.60.4.0/23
On-premises clients reaching the network over VPN can use the storage account privately without any extra rule
Traffic from that subnet to storage travels over Microsoft's backbone, and the storage account's public name does not change
All internet access to the storage account stops automatically, with no rule needed on the account
questions.why: A service endpoint sends the subnet's traffic over the Microsoft backbone and keeps the service's public address and name unchanged; it does not give a private address or change access for other networks by itself.

questions.prompt: A team in a company with an office network 172.16.0.0/16 connects to Azure over VPN. Their app runs in a subnet that has a service endpoint for a Key Vault, and the Key Vault allows only that subnet. Office users get refused when they call the vault. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Office traffic does not carry the subnet identity, so the office address range must be allowed separately on the vault
The service endpoint was switched on in the wrong region
The VPN tunnel automatically blocks all traffic to any Azure service
The vault's public name was changed when the endpoint was enabled
questions.why: Traffic from an on-premises network does not carry the subnet identity the service checks, so it is refused unless its address range is allowed on the service explicitly.

questions.prompt: A finance company requires that its customer database has no public address at all, reachable only from inside its private network. A junior engineer proposes enabling a service endpoint for the application subnet and allowing that subnet on the database firewall. Is that enough to meet the requirement?
choices: No, because the database keeps its public address, so a different private-access option is needed
No, because service endpoints only work with storage accounts and never with databases
Yes, because allowing only the subnet removes the public address from the database
Yes, because the database name resolves to a private address once the endpoint is on
questions.why: A service endpoint restricts who can call a service but leaves the service's public address in place, so it cannot satisfy a requirement that the resource have no public address at all.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we should just use a service endpoint so our database stays off the internet. Explain to them when a service endpoint is enough, when a private endpoint is needed, and one limit of the service endpoint you would raise.
lessons.modelAnswer: A service endpoint is enough when the callers sit inside specific subnets of our virtual network and we only need to restrict which subnets can reach the service. It keeps traffic on Microsoft's backbone and lets us allow those subnets on the service's firewall, with no new IP address in our network and no DNS change. The limit is that the database still has a public address, so it stays reachable by its public name, and callers from on-premises or outside the allowed subnets are not recognized as inside. If the requirement says the resource must have no public address, or on-premises clients must reach it privately over VPN or ExpressRoute, we need a private endpoint. That gives the service a private IP in our subnet, and DNS must be set up so names resolve to that IP. I would read the requirement wording first, then pick the tool that matches it.
rubricPoints: A service endpoint keeps traffic on the Microsoft backbone and restricts access by subnet identity.
The service keeps its public address, so it is not private in the sense of having an internal IP.
A private endpoint gives the service a private IP inside the learner's subnet and suits on-premises access over VPN or ExpressRoute.
The choice depends on whether the requirement says no public address or private access from outside the subnet.

suggested.rationale: Choosing between two options in a short scenario is the core skill, so reasoning through a case adds the most beyond reading.

lessons.plain: A service endpoint is a setting you switch on for a subnet inside your private network so that traffic from that subnet to certain Azure services, such as storage accounts, travels across Microsoft's own backbone network instead of the public internet. The service keeps its public address, but you can then configure it to accept requests only from that subnet. Think of a company building with a private corridor to a shared office: people still use the same front door, but outsiders are kept out and the route stays inside the campus. It is the simpler of the two main ways to keep traffic off the public internet, and it is usually the first choice when the goal is to lock a service down to your own network.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a virtual machine in a private subnet reads from a storage account that has a public address. What would you expect to change, if anything, about the route its traffic takes, and what would you want to restrict on the storage account side?
lessons.teach: A virtual network (VNet) is your private network in Azure. A subnet is a range of addresses carved out of that network, and resources such as virtual machines sit inside subnets. A service endpoint is a feature you enable on a subnet for a specific Azure service, such as storage or a database. Once enabled, traffic from that subnet to the service is routed over Microsoft's backbone network rather than out across the public internet. The service still has its public name and public address. What changes is the route and the identity the service sees: requests arrive carrying the source's private address from your subnet, so the service can check that the request came from a network you trust. The service is then configured with a network rule that allows only listed subnets. Worked example: subnet A has the endpoint enabled and holds a virtual machine at 10.1.2.5. Step 1: the machine requests the storage account's public name. Step 2: because subnet A has the endpoint, the request travels over the backbone and carries source address 10.1.2.5. Step 3: the storage account checks its network rule, sees subnet A is allowed, and accepts the request. A machine in subnet B without the endpoint, or on the internet, is refused once the account allows only listed networks. Common mistake: enabling the endpoint but leaving the storage account open to all networks, which means the traffic is private but the service is still reachable from anywhere. Another mistake is expecting the service to get a private address inside your network; that is what a private endpoint does, not a service endpoint. Consequence in a running system: when a new subnet is added and the endpoint is forgotten, its calls fail as soon as the service is locked to listed subnets, and no DNS change is needed because the name still points to the public address.

questions.prompt: Harbor Cove Clinic keeps scanned records in a storage account and wants clinic traffic kept off the public internet. Its app VMs sit in app-snet (172.20.4.0/24), which has the service endpoint enabled. A tester VM sits in test-snet (172.20.9.0/24), which has no endpoint, and the account allows only app-snet. Trace one tester request. Step 1: the tester VM requests the storage account's public name. Step 2: [MISSING]. Step 3: the account checks its network rule, finds test-snet is not listed, and refuses the request. Which statement completes step 2?
choices: The request leaves over the public internet and arrives with a public source address, not an address from test-snet.
The account rewrites the source address to app-snet's range before it checks its rule.
The request travels over the backbone and carries source address 172.20.9.4, which the account then matches against app-snet.
The request is redirected to a private IP inside app-snet, because the public name now resolves to a private endpoint.
questions.why: Because test-snet has no endpoint, its traffic takes the public route, so the account sees a public source address that is not inside any listed subnet.

questions.prompt: A learner says that enabling a service endpoint on a subnet gives the storage account a private address inside that subnet. Which description is accurate?
choices: The account keeps its public name and address; requests from the subnet arrive over the backbone with a private source address.
The account is moved into the subnet and loses its public address, so only subnet members can reach it at all.
Traffic is wrapped in an encrypted tunnel, so the account's address is hidden from the subnet.
The subnet gets a new public address that the account uses to reach it.
questions.why: A service endpoint changes the route and the source address the service sees, but the service keeps its own public name and address.

questions.prompt: Harbor Dental adds imaging-snet (10.30.6.0/24) for new scanner VMs. The scanner VMs cannot reach their archive account, which allows only listed subnets, because imaging-snet was never added to the account's rule. Which fix is correct?
choices: Change the scanner VMs' DNS to a private address so they use a private endpoint.
Move the scanner VMs into an existing subnet that already works.
Open the archive account to all networks so the new subnet can reach it.
Enable the service endpoint on imaging-snet and add imaging-snet to the account's network rule.
questions.why: The subnet must have the endpoint enabled so its traffic reaches the service over the backbone, and it must be listed in the service's network rule so the request is accepted.

questions.prompt: Northwind Logistics wants traffic from warehouse-snet (10.8.0.0/22) to its order database kept off the public internet. The team enables the service endpoint on warehouse-snet but leaves the database's network rule set to allow all networks. Which statement is true?
choices: The database gets a private address in warehouse-snet, so its public name stops working.
Warehouse traffic is now encrypted end to end, so the open rule does not matter.
The database is now reachable only from warehouse-snet, so the rule change is unnecessary.
Warehouse traffic now takes the backbone route, but the database remains reachable from any network that can reach its public name.
questions.why: The endpoint changes the route for warehouse traffic, but an open network rule still lets requests from anywhere be accepted, so the service stays exposed.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, how a service endpoint keeps a subnet's traffic off the public internet, and name one limit or tradeoff compared with a private endpoint.
lessons.modelAnswer: A service endpoint is enabled on a subnet for a specific Azure service. Traffic from that subnet to the service then goes over Microsoft's backbone rather than the public internet, and the service sees the subnet's private source address. To actually restrict access, you also set the service's network rules to allow only that subnet, otherwise the service stays reachable from everywhere. The main limit is that the service keeps its public address and name; the traffic is private in route, but the endpoint is not brought into your network as a private address. A private endpoint gives the service a private IP inside your VNet, which also lets on-premises clients reach it privately, but it costs more and needs DNS changes. So for locking a service to your own subnets with minimal change, a service endpoint is simpler, and a private endpoint is the better fit when you need a private address itself.
rubricPoints: A service endpoint is enabled per subnet and routes traffic to the service over the Azure backbone, not the public internet.
The service keeps its public address; access control depends on the service's network rules allowing the subnet.
The service does not receive a private IP inside the VNet, which is the key difference from a private endpoint.
Enabling the endpoint without restricting the service's network rules leaves the service reachable from other networks.

suggested.rationale: Choosing between a service endpoint and a private endpoint from a requirement is an exam-style reasoning skill, and no current or planned OpsForge mission or engine covers Azure networking directly.

lessons.plain: A service endpoint policy is an allow-list attached to a subnet. Resources in a virtual network subnet can reach some Azure services over Microsoft's own network instead of the public internet. Without a policy, that subnet could reach any storage account or database of that service type, including ones owned by someone else. The policy names the specific resources the subnet may use, and calls to anything else of that type are refused. You can think of it as a guest list for outbound traffic from one subnet.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your app subnet can already reach Azure Storage without using the public internet. If that means it can reach every storage account in Azure, is that a security gap, and what would you add to close it?
lessons.teach: A service endpoint policy is a filter attached to a subnet that already has a service endpoint turned on for a service such as Azure Storage or Azure SQL Database. A service endpoint is a route that keeps traffic from that subnet to the service on Microsoft's backbone network rather than the public internet. The endpoint decides the path, but it does not decide which resource on that path is acceptable. The policy closes that gap. It holds a list of allowed resource IDs, which are the unique paths Azure uses to name each resource, and any call from the subnet to a resource of that service that is not on the list is refused.  Why it works: the check happens on the source side. Azure compares the destination resource against the policy before traffic leaves the subnet, so the subnet's own outbound traffic is what gets filtered. One policy can be shared by several subnets, so you maintain the list in one place.  Worked example: subnet app-snet has a service endpoint for Microsoft.Storage. Step 1: you create a policy and add the resource ID of storage account stfinance01. Step 2: you associate the policy with app-snet. Step 3: an app in app-snet calls stfinance01, and the call succeeds. Step 4: the same app calls stlegacyold, a storage account in another team's subscription. That call is refused, even though it is also reached through the same service endpoint.  Common mistake: assuming the policy alone secures the subnet. If the service endpoint is not enabled for that service on the subnet, the policy has no effect. A second mistake is forgetting to add a new storage account to the policy when the app starts using it.  Consequence: a missing entry breaks only that dependency, and the error usually looks like an access denial or failed connection. When a new dependency suddenly fails from one subnet, check the policy's resource list before blaming the application.

questions.prompt: Northwind Clinics runs a web app in subnet clinic-web-snet. The subnet already has a service endpoint turned on for Microsoft.Storage. The team wants the app to reach only their records account, stclinicrecords, and refuse every other storage account. They follow these steps. Step 1: create a service endpoint policy named pol-records. Step 2: (missing step, to be filled in by you). Step 3: associate pol-records with clinic-web-snet. Step 4: the app calls stclinicrecords and the call succeeds. Step 5: the app calls stclinicarchive in another subscription and the call is refused. Which step 2 completes the setup correctly?
choices: Create a network security group rule that allows outbound traffic on port 443
Enable a service endpoint for Microsoft.Sql on clinic-web-snet
Set the policy to allow every storage account in the clinic's resource group
Add the resource ID of stclinicrecords to the policy's allowed list
questions.why: The policy works by holding the resource IDs of the storage accounts the subnet may reach, so the resource ID of stclinicrecords must be on that list before the association produces the described results.

questions.prompt: When a subnet with a storage service endpoint sends a call through a service endpoint policy, what does Azure compare against the policy before the traffic leaves the subnet?
choices: The source IP address range of the subnet against the policy's list of subnets
The packet size of the call against a maximum size set on the policy
The application's login name against the storage account's access keys
The destination resource's unique resource ID against the policy's allowed list
questions.why: The policy filters by the destination resource's resource ID on its allowed list, and the check happens on the source side before traffic leaves the subnet.

questions.prompt: Two subnets share one service endpoint policy that lists storage account stfinance01. Subnet B has no service endpoint enabled for Microsoft.Storage. An app in subnet B calls stlegacyold, which is not on the list. What happens?
choices: The call succeeds, because the policy has no effect on a subnet without the storage service endpoint enabled
The call succeeds only if the app is in subnet A, because the policy is shared with that subnet
The call is refused and the policy automatically adds stlegacyold to its list
The call is refused, because the policy blocks every resource not on its list for any subnet that uses it
questions.why: A policy only filters traffic from subnets that have the matching service endpoint enabled, so with no service endpoint on subnet B the policy never applies to its calls.

questions.prompt: A team's app has been reaching storage account stbillingdaily from a subnet that already has a storage service endpoint and a service endpoint policy. The team starts using a new account, stbillingnew, from the same subnet, and the calls begin failing with access denied errors. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The app's storage account key has expired and must be rotated
stbillingnew was not added to the policy's list of allowed resource IDs
The service endpoint has been removed from the subnet by the platform
The subnet's address range is too small to hold the new storage account
questions.why: Because the policy refuses any storage resource not on its allowed list, the new account must be added to the list to restore access from the subnet.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why we need a service endpoint policy on the app subnet when the service endpoint already keeps traffic on Microsoft's backbone. Explain what the policy adds, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on it.
lessons.modelAnswer: The service endpoint already keeps traffic from our subnet to Azure Storage on Microsoft's network, but it does not say which storage accounts the subnet may reach. Any storage account reachable through that endpoint is reachable from our subnet, including one owned by someone else. A service endpoint policy adds an allow-list of specific resource IDs, so calls to listed accounts succeed and calls to anything else of that service are refused. That limits damage if an app is compromised and tries to copy data to an outside account. The tradeoff is operational: every new storage account the app needs must be added to the policy first, or the app fails with access errors. The policy also only governs traffic that uses the service endpoint, so it is not a full substitute for a private endpoint when we need the service on a private IP address.
rubricPoints: Service endpoint alone keeps traffic on the backbone but does not restrict which resources of the service are reachable.
A service endpoint policy is an allow-list of specific resource IDs applied to a subnet's outbound traffic.
Calls to resources not on the list are refused, which limits data exfiltration to unknown accounts.
Tradeoff: new dependencies must be added to the policy first, or they break with access errors.
The policy needs the service endpoint enabled on the subnet and does not replace a private endpoint.

suggested.rationale: An exam-style scenario asking the learner to decide which resource list a subnet should allow adds the most practice beyond reading the definition, and no listed mission covers Azure networking directly.

lessons.plain: Normally, when your app talks to a managed cloud service such as file storage or a database, the traffic travels over the public internet to the service's public address, even when the app runs inside your own private network. A service endpoint is a setting you turn on for one subnet of your network. It tells Azure to send that subnet's traffic to the service over Microsoft's own internal backbone instead of the open internet, and it lets the service's owner say that only that subnet may connect. The service keeps its public address. You are controlling who gets in and which path they use, not giving the service a private address inside your network.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your app runs in a private subnet and needs to read files from a managed storage service without that traffic crossing the open internet. Would you guess that the storage account gets a new private address inside your network, or that the subnet is given a better route to the storage service's existing public address?
lessons.teach:
A subnet is a range of IP addresses inside a virtual network, which is your private network in the cloud. A service endpoint is a setting on a subnet that does two things. First, it sends that subnet's traffic bound for a particular Azure service over Microsoft's backbone, the internal network that Microsoft runs, rather than the public internet. Second, it stamps the traffic with the subnet's identity, so the service can recognise where a request came from. The service itself also has a set of network rules, a list of allowed subnets plus a default action that says what happens to everyone else. You configure access in two steps. First, enable the service endpoint type on the subnet. Second, on the service, add that subnet to the allowed list and set the default action to deny.

Worked example. A subnet called app-subnet, with address range 10.1.2.0/24, hosts an app that stores files in a storage account. Step 1: enable the storage service endpoint on app-subnet. The app's storage traffic now crosses the backbone. Step 2: in the storage account's network settings, add app-subnet to the allowed list and set the default action to deny. Step 3: a virtual machine in a different subnet, db-subnet, tries to reach the storage account at its public address. The request is refused, because db-subnet is not on the list. The app in app-subnet succeeds, because its subnet is allowed.

Common mistake: enabling the endpoint on the subnet and assuming the service is now locked down. The subnet gets its backbone route, but the service still accepts public traffic until you add rules to it. The app keeps working, so the gap stays hidden, and a quick check suggests all is fine when the storage account is still open to the internet.

Consequence in a running system: if you set the default action to deny and forget to add a subnet, that subnet's app starts failing with access-denied errors right after the change, even though nothing in the app changed. Check the service's allowed list before you turn on deny.

A service endpoint keeps the service's public address. It restricts access by subnet, it does not give the service a private IP inside your network.

questions.prompt: Northwind Clinic has a subnet called ingest-subnet, with address range 10.8.4.0/22, that runs a sensor-logging service writing to a storage account named nwlogs. A subnet is a range of IP addresses inside a virtual network, which is the private network you own in the cloud. The team has done two things so far. First, they enabled the storage service endpoint on ingest-subnet, so its storage traffic travels over Microsoft's internal backbone. Second, they added ingest-subnet to the allowed list on nwlogs. The allowed list is the set of subnets the storage account accepts traffic from. The team's goal is that no other subnet can reach nwlogs. The one step still missing is the setting that decides what happens to every subnet that is not on the list. Which action completes the setup?
choices: Set the storage account's default action to deny
Remove the storage service endpoint from ingest-subnet
Add a second allowed subnet for the monitoring team's subnet
Create a private endpoint so nwlogs gets a private IP address inside ingest-subnet
questions.why: The default action is the setting that refuses everyone not on the allowed list, so changing it to deny is the step that makes the block take effect.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes what a service endpoint does to a subnet's traffic bound for an Azure service?
choices: It moves the service's public address into the subnet, so the service becomes private
It blocks all outbound traffic from the subnet until a rule is added to the service
It sends the traffic over Microsoft's backbone and stamps it with the subnet's identity
It gives the subnet its own dedicated public IP address for the service to trust
questions.why: A service endpoint does two things: it routes the subnet's traffic to the service over the backbone and tags the traffic with the subnet's identity, without changing the service's public address.

questions.prompt: A subnet named web-tier, with range 172.20.8.0/24, has the Azure SQL-style managed database service endpoint enabled and is on that database's allowed list. The database's default action is still set to allow. A virtual machine in batch-subnet, a different subnet, connects to the database at its public address and succeeds. What explains this?
choices: The default action is still allow, so requests from subnets not on the list are accepted
The batch subnet's traffic is automatically treated as coming from web-tier
The database has a private IP address that batch-subnet can reach through web-tier
The service endpoint on web-tier forwards batch-subnet's traffic over the backbone
questions.why: With the default action at allow, the service still accepts public traffic from any subnet, so putting web-tier on the list alone does not block batch-subnet.

questions.prompt: A reporting job runs in subnet 10.3.9.0/24 in a virtual network owned by Harbor Freight Logistics. The team enables the storage service endpoint on its own app subnet and sets the storage account's default action to deny, but forgets to add the reporting subnet to the allowed list. Right after the change the reporting job starts failing with access-denied errors, and nobody changed the job's code. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Enabling a service endpoint removes the subnet's ability to reach any storage account
The storage service endpoint must be enabled on the reporting subnet before the default action can change
The reporting job's code cached an old public address for the storage account
The storage account's allowed list does not include 10.3.9.0/24, so deny refuses it
questions.why: Once the default action is deny, only subnets on the allowed list get through, and the reporting subnet was left off, which is why its requests now fail.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a service endpoint does for a subnet that reaches a storage account, and name one limit or tradeoff compared with simply leaving the storage account publicly reachable.
lessons.modelAnswer: A service endpoint is enabled on a subnet, so that subnet's traffic to the storage service travels over Microsoft's backbone instead of the public internet, and the storage service can recognise the subnet as the caller. The storage account is still reached through its public name and address, so it is not private in the way a private endpoint is. Access control happens in the storage account's network rules, where we allow the subnet and deny everything else. The main limit is that the endpoint only restricts by subnet. Anything inside an allowed subnet can reach the service, and clients coming in from on-premises over a VPN are not covered just by enabling the endpoint; they arrive from other addresses and need their own rule. So it suits cases where subnet-level restriction is enough and a private address is not required.
rubricPoints: A service endpoint is enabled per subnet and routes that subnet's traffic to the service over the Microsoft backbone.
The service keeps its public address, so the endpoint restricts access but does not make the service private.
Access must be finished on the service side by allowing the subnet and setting the default action to deny.
Enabling the endpoint alone does not close public access, and on-premises clients need their own rules.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a requirement that must choose between a service endpoint and a private endpoint teaches the decision better than reading settings alone.

lessons.plain: A network security group is a list of filtering rules you attach to parts of a cloud network. Each rule says: for traffic of this kind, coming from here, going to there, on this port, allow it or block it. Think of it as a guard at a door with a checklist, not a wall around the whole city. Creating one is the easy part: you give it a name and a region, and it starts with a few built-in default rules. The real work is deciding which rules it holds and where it is applied. An empty group does nothing useful until you attach it to something.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web server should accept visitors on port 443 from anywhere on the internet, but nobody from the internet should reach its SSH port 22. Would a single allow rule for port 443 be enough to block port 22, or do you need something more? Explain your reasoning in a few sentences.
lessons.teach:
A network security group (NSG) is a container for security rules. It is the filter that decides which network traffic may enter or leave the resources it is attached to. Creating an NSG means making that container and then setting its rules.
