Each rule has a priority number (custom rules use numbers from 100 upward, and lower numbers are checked first), a direction (inbound for traffic arriving, outbound for traffic leaving), a source, a destination, a port and protocol, and an action of allow or deny. Rules are checked from the lowest priority number upward, and the first match decides the outcome, so a low-numbered deny overrides a higher-numbered allow. Every NSG also starts with default rules at very high priority numbers: traffic from inside the virtual network is allowed, inbound traffic from the internet is denied, and most outbound traffic is allowed. These defaults mean a new NSG is not an open door, but they also mean a public web server may be unreachable until you add an allow rule. NSGs are stateful: if an inbound connection is allowed, the reply traffic is allowed automatically.

Worked example: a web subnet should accept HTTPS on TCP 443 from the internet and nothing else from the internet. Step one, create the NSG. Step two, add rule 100: inbound, allow, TCP, source internet, destination port 443. Step three, add rule 200: inbound, deny, any protocol, any port, source internet. Now an HTTPS request from the internet matches rule 100 and is allowed. An SSH request to port 22 skips rule 100, matches rule 200, and is denied before the default rules are ever reached.

Common mistake: writing the deny rule at a higher priority number than the allow it was meant to override, which lets the allow win, or assuming a created NSG protects anything by itself. An NSG with rules has no effect until it is associated with a subnet or a network interface, which is a separate step.

Consequence in a running system: one overly broad allow rule for a management port exposes that port to the whole internet, and attackers scan for exactly that. Creating the NSG correctly is only half the job; its rule order and its attachment decide what traffic really passes.

questions.prompt: A logistics company has a build-agent subnet, 10.60.8.0/24, that must not send any traffic to the partner data range 203.0.113.0/24, but must keep its normal outbound access. The team creates an NSG named nsg-build and adds rule 100 with direction outbound, action deny, any protocol, any port, source 10.60.8.0/24, destination 203.0.113.0/24. The NSG is now complete as a set of rules, and the team stops there. Which step is missing so that the block actually takes effect?
choices: Change rule 100 to inbound, since outbound rules only filter traffic that arrives at the agents.
Raise rule 100 to priority 4096 so that it is checked after the default rules.
Add a rule with priority 50 that allows all outbound traffic, so the deny has something to override.
Associate nsg-build with the build-agent subnet, because rules have no effect until the NSG is attached to a subnet or network interface.
questions.why: An NSG with rules does nothing until it is associated with a subnet or network interface, so attaching nsg-build to the build-agent subnet is the step that makes rule 100 take effect.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes how an NSG chooses between its rules when more than one rule could match a packet?
choices: The rule with the highest priority number is checked first, so the largest number decides the outcome.
The allow rule always wins over a deny rule, regardless of priority numbers, because allows are checked before denies.
All matching rules are applied together, and a deny only wins if it has a lower priority number than every allow.
Rules are checked from the lowest priority number upward, and the first matching rule decides whether the traffic is allowed or denied.
questions.why: NSG rules are checked from the lowest priority number upward and the first match decides the outcome, so a lower-numbered deny overrides a higher-numbered allow.

questions.prompt: An NSG on a payments subnet contains rule 110, which denies inbound traffic on any port from the Internet source, and rule 120, which allows inbound TCP 8080 from the Internet source. A client on the public Internet sends a request to TCP 8080 on a server in that subnet. What happens, and why?
choices: Allowed by rule 120, because a specific port rule overrides a broader deny rule regardless of priority.
Allowed by the default rules, because the default rules are checked before any custom rule.
Denied by rule 110, because it has the lower priority number and matches the traffic first.
Denied by the default rules, because rule 120 is never reached when the NSG is attached to a subnet.
questions.why: Rule 110 has the lower priority number, is checked first, matches the Internet traffic on any port, and denies it, so rule 120 is never reached.

questions.prompt: An NSG on an application subnet has a single inbound rule that allows TCP 9000 from the partner range 192.0.2.0/24. A partner client connects and the application server sends a reply. A new engineer adds no outbound rule for the reply. Does the reply get through, and what principle explains it?
choices: Yes, but only if the reply uses port 9000 as its source port, which it always does by default.
Yes, because NSGs are stateful, so the reply to an allowed inbound connection is permitted automatically.
No, the reply is blocked until the default outbound rule is manually removed and recreated.
No, the reply is blocked because every outbound flow needs its own explicit allow rule.
questions.why: NSGs are stateful, meaning once an inbound connection is allowed the return traffic for that connection is allowed automatically, so no separate outbound rule is needed for the reply.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what happens when you create a network security group and add rules to it. Name one limit or tradeoff a beginner often misses when writing those rules.
lessons.modelAnswer: Creating an NSG gives you an empty filter that you then fill with rules. Each rule has a priority, a direction, a source, a destination, a port and protocol, and an allow or deny action. Rules are evaluated from the lowest priority number, and the first match wins, so the order matters more than the order you typed them in. The NSG also comes with default rules that deny inbound internet traffic and allow traffic within the virtual network, so a public service stays unreachable until you add an explicit allow. The tradeoff to name is that a broad allow rule placed at a low priority number can silently override a narrower deny you wrote later, and the NSG does nothing at all until it is associated with a subnet or network interface. A rule that looks correct on paper can therefore expose the wrong port in practice.
rubricPoints: An NSG is a container of rules, each with priority, direction, source, destination, port, protocol and action.
Rules are evaluated from lowest priority number, and the first match decides the outcome.
Default rules deny inbound internet traffic, so explicit allow rules are needed for public services.
An NSG has no effect until it is associated with a subnet or network interface.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a concrete allow-and-block requirement adds more than a menu walkthrough, because the learner must predict which rule matches first.

lessons.plain: An NSG, or network security group, is a simple filter that decides which network traffic is allowed in or out, based on a list of rules. Associating it means attaching that filter to something. You can attach it to a subnet, which is a section of a private network, so every machine in that section is covered at once. Or you can attach it to a network interface, the single connection point of one virtual machine, so only that machine is covered. Where you attach it decides how far its rules reach. When two filters apply to the same traffic, both must allow it for it to get through.
lessons.guessPrompt: You attach a filter to a subnet that blocks inbound port 22 from the internet. A web VM in that subnet has its own network-interface filter that allows port 22 from the internet. Do you expect SSH from the internet to reach that VM, and why?
lessons.teach:
An NSG (network security group) holds rules. Each rule has a priority number, a direction (inbound or outbound), a source, a destination, a port and protocol, and an action of allow or deny. Lower priority numbers are checked first, and the first matching rule decides the outcome. Associating an NSG means linking it to a subnet or to a network interface (NIC, the connection point that gives one virtual machine its network address). A subnet can have at most one NSG, and a NIC can have at most one, but one NSG can be linked to many subnets and NICs.

Why it works: the filter is applied where traffic crosses a boundary. When an NSG sits on a subnet, every packet entering or leaving that subnet is checked, which covers all machines in it. When it sits on a NIC, only that one machine's traffic is checked. Traffic that stays entirely inside one subnet never crosses the subnet boundary, so the subnet NSG does not evaluate it; only NIC-level rules filter that traffic.

Worked example: a web subnet has an NSG allowing inbound TCP 443 from the internet and denying other inbound internet traffic. A web VM in that subnet has a NIC NSG allowing inbound 443. Step 1: a request to port 443 arrives; the subnet NSG allows it. Step 2: the NIC NSG checks it and also allows it, so it is delivered. Step 3: an SSH request to port 22 arrives; the subnet NSG denies it, and the packet never reaches the NIC check.

Common mistake: assuming a NIC allow rule overrides a subnet deny. For inbound traffic the subnet NSG is checked first, so a subnet deny stops the packet before the NIC rule is considered. For outbound traffic the order reverses, with the NIC NSG checked first.

Consequence: a broad deny added to a subnet can silently cut off every machine in it, and the symptom looks like a broken VM rather than a filter change. Attaching an NSG is a choice of boundary, and traffic must pass every boundary it crosses.

questions.prompt: A billing VM sits in the 10.40.8.0/24 subnet. Its NIC has an NSG with an outbound rule at priority 150 that denies TCP 587 to the Internet. The subnet also has an NSG with an outbound rule at priority 100 that allows TCP 587 to the Internet. An application on the VM sends mail on port 587. Step 1: for outbound traffic the NIC NSG is checked first, and its priority 150 deny matches, so the packet is dropped at that point. Step 2 (the missing step you must supply): ___. Step 3: the mail stays blocked and never reaches the Internet.
choices: The subnet NSG is never evaluated for this packet, because the NIC NSG already denied it and the check stopped there.
The packet leaves the VM, and the NIC deny is only written to a log for later review.
The subnet NSG allow is checked and overrides the NIC deny because subnet rules have priority.
The subnet NSG allow at priority 100 is checked and the packet is delivered anyway.
questions.why: Once the first boundary's first matching rule denies a packet, the packet is stopped there, so the later subnet NSG never gets to evaluate it.

questions.prompt: A network team wants two different NSGs on one subnet, one for web rules and one for database rules. Which statement about associating NSGs is correct?
choices: Both NSGs can be linked to the subnet, and the lower-numbered one is ignored.
A subnet can hold only one NSG link, so the team must merge the rules into a single NSG or split the subnet.
Two NSGs are allowed on a subnet only when each one is attached to a different NIC in it.
A subnet can hold any number of NSGs, but the second one only applies to outbound traffic.
questions.why: A subnet can have at most one NSG, so the rules must live in one NSG or the design must change, which is why the team cannot link two to the same subnet.

questions.prompt: Two VMs, A and B, sit in the same subnet 172.16.4.0/24. The subnet NSG denies all inbound traffic from 172.16.4.0/24. The NIC NSG on VM B allows inbound TCP 9000 from any source. VM A sends TCP 9000 to VM B. What happens?
choices: The traffic is blocked by the NIC NSG because a deny rule on the subnet is checked before the NIC allow.
The traffic is delivered only if VM A also has an outbound allow on its own NIC NSG.
The subnet deny blocks the traffic because it covers every inbound packet in the subnet.
The traffic is delivered, because traffic that stays inside one subnet never crosses the subnet boundary, so only the NIC NSG filters it.
questions.why: Traffic that does not cross the subnet boundary is not evaluated by the subnet NSG, so only VM B's NIC NSG applies and its allow rule lets the traffic through.

questions.prompt: An administrator attaches a new NSG with a deny-all inbound rule to a subnet, intending to block one legacy VM. Within minutes, the other VMs in that subnet stop responding to their users. What best explains this?
choices: The deny-all rule was given a low priority number, so it was checked before the allow rules in the other NSGs.
The subnet NSG applies to every packet entering or leaving the subnet, so the deny-all blocks inbound traffic to all machines in it, not just the legacy one.
Azure Firewall took over the subnet and started denying all inbound requests automatically.
Each NIC NSG on the other VMs was overwritten, which removed their allow rules.
questions.why: A subnet NSG checks every packet crossing the subnet boundary, so a broad deny there cuts off all machines in that subnet, which looks like broken VMs rather than a filter change.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says: I allowed port 443 on the web VM's NIC NSG, but users still cannot reach the site. Explain to them what else could be blocking the traffic, and name one tradeoff of putting a filter on the subnet versus on each NIC.
lessons.modelAnswer: The most likely blocker is an NSG on the subnet, because inbound traffic to the VM is checked there before the NIC. The subnet NSG runs first for inbound traffic, so a deny on port 443 or a broad inbound deny there stops the packet, and the NIC allow never matters. I would look at the subnet NSG rules and their priorities, then check the combined effective rules for that NIC to see the final result. The tradeoff is that a subnet NSG is simple to manage, since one rule set covers every machine in the subnet, but a mistake hits all of them at once. A NIC NSG limits the damage to one VM and can be more specific, but the same rules must then be kept consistent across many machines.
rubricPoints: Identify the subnet NSG as checked first for inbound traffic, so it can block before the NIC rule matters.
Explain that a subnet NSG covers every machine in the subnet while a NIC NSG covers one machine.
State a tradeoff: subnet-level is simpler but has a wider blast radius; NIC-level is precise but harder to keep consistent.
Mention checking the combined effective rules for the NIC rather than reading one NSG in isolation.

suggested.rationale: Tracing which subnet and NIC NSG each packet hits, in order, is exactly what the planned virtual network path tracer would show.

lessons.plain: An application security group, called an ASG for short, is a label you give to a set of virtual machines that do the same job, such as all the web servers in one application. Security rules can then say 'allow web servers to talk to database servers' instead of listing each machine's address. When a machine is rebuilt or added, you only change its group membership, and the existing rules keep working. An ASG on its own blocks or allows nothing. It only matters when a security rule refers to it.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have ten web servers whose IP addresses change every time they are rebuilt. Why might writing one firewall rule per IP address become a problem, and what would you rather refer to in the rule?
lessons.teach: An application security group (ASG) is a named group of virtual machine network interfaces. A network interface is the virtual network card a virtual machine uses to connect to a network. You put interfaces that play the same role, such as web servers, into one ASG. The ASG does not filter traffic by itself. It is used as a source or destination inside a network security group (NSG), which is a list of allow and deny rules applied to a subnet or an interface. Why this works: IP addresses change when machines are rebuilt or scaled, but a role stays stable, so a rule written against a group keeps working as members come and go. Worked example. Put the web servers' interfaces in an ASG called web-servers and the database servers' interfaces in db-servers. Step 1: in the NSG, add an inbound rule that allows TCP port 443 from the Internet to web-servers. Step 2: add an inbound rule that allows TCP port 1433 from web-servers to db-servers. Step 3: add a new web server and attach its interface to web-servers. It is covered by the first rule immediately, with no rule edits. Common mistake: creating ASGs and assuming traffic is now controlled. Without an NSG rule that references them, an ASG does nothing. A key limit: every interface in an ASG used by a rule must be in the same virtual network as that NSG. In a running system, a machine that is missing from its group gets no traffic and nobody notices until a user reports a failure, and a wrong machine added to a group can quietly receive access it should not have.

questions.prompt: Harbor Foods runs API servers and Redis cache servers in one virtual network. Step 1: attach the API servers' network interfaces to an ASG called api-tier. Step 2: attach the cache servers' network interfaces to an ASG called cache-tier. Step 3 is missing from this list and is the step that makes the groups do anything. Step 4: add a new cache server, attach its interface to cache-tier, and confirm it receives API traffic on TCP port 6379 without any rule edits. Which step 3 completes the setup?
choices: Give each cache server a public IP address so the API servers can reach it
Add an inbound NSG rule that allows TCP port 6379 with api-tier as the source and cache-tier as the destination
Create a route table that sends traffic from api-tier to cache-tier through a gateway
Move the cache servers into their own subnet so the ASG applies to that subnet
questions.why: An ASG does nothing until an NSG rule references it, so the rule using api-tier as source and cache-tier as destination on port 6379 is the missing step that makes the group membership take effect.

questions.prompt: Which description best defines an application security group (ASG)?
choices: A routing table that decides which subnet a packet should leave the virtual network through
A list of public IP addresses that are allowed to reach a load balancer
A named group of virtual machine network interfaces that can be used as a source or destination inside NSG rules
A firewall appliance that inspects and filters packets on its own, without any rules
questions.why: The teaching text defines an ASG as a named group of VM network interfaces that is referenced as a source or destination inside an NSG, and it does not filter traffic by itself.

questions.prompt: A team creates an ASG called logs-servers, attaches the interfaces of three logging machines to it, and then assumes the logging machines are now protected from unwanted inbound traffic. No NSG rule in the network references logs-servers. What is the actual result?
choices: Azure automatically creates a deny rule for logs-servers in every subnet
The three machines are moved into a separate virtual network for protection
The ASG blocks all inbound traffic to the three logging machines by default
The ASG has no effect on traffic, because it only matters when an NSG rule names it
questions.why: The teaching text says that without an NSG rule that references an ASG, the ASG does nothing, so the logging machines are not controlled by it at all.

questions.prompt: An administrator wants an NSG in virtual network VNet-East to allow traffic from an ASG called app-tier. Some of the app-tier interfaces belong to virtual machines in VNet-West. What is the limit that applies here?
choices: The NSG can use the ASG only if the ASG holds exactly one interface, regardless of network
All interfaces in an ASG used by a rule must be in the same virtual network as that NSG, so the VNet-West interfaces cannot be used this way
The NSG will automatically copy the VNet-West interfaces into VNet-East when the rule is saved
An ASG can span any number of virtual networks as long as the rule uses port 443
questions.why: The teaching text states that every interface in an ASG used by a rule must be in the same virtual network as that NSG, so interfaces from another virtual network break this use.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what an application security group is, why we use it in an NSG rule instead of IP addresses, and one limit or tradeoff we must keep in mind when using it.
lessons.modelAnswer: An ASG is a label that groups virtual machine network interfaces by role, like web or database. We reference it as the source or destination in an NSG rule, so the rule says web tier to database tier on port 1433 instead of naming addresses. The main benefit is that new or rebuilt machines inherit the right rules as soon as they join the group, because the rule follows the role rather than the IP. The limit is that the ASG itself filters nothing; without an NSG rule referencing it, it has no effect. Another limit is scope: all interfaces in a group used by one NSG must be in the same virtual network as that NSG. The tradeoff is that group membership becomes a security control, so a wrong interface in the group can grant access it should not have, and someone needs to own that membership.
rubricPoints: Defines an ASG as a named group of network interfaces that share a role.
Explains that the ASG is used as a source or destination inside an NSG rule and does nothing alone.
Gives the benefit that rules follow roles, so IP changes and new machines need no rule edits.
States the same-virtual-network limit or the risk of wrong group membership.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style requirement, such as which group should be the source and what traffic the rule then allows, adds the most here, and no listed mission covers Azure networking.

lessons.plain: An application security group, or ASG, is a label you attach to a virtual machine's network card so that machines playing the same role can be named together. Instead of listing each server's IP address in a traffic rule, you write the rule once against the label. Associating an ASG with a network interface means attaching that label to the network card of one machine. Any security rule that names the label then covers that machine automatically, including machines you add later. The label by itself allows or blocks nothing. It only matters when a rule refers to it.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have a rule that allows web traffic to every machine labelled web-tier. You launch a new web server and attach its network card to web-tier. Does the rule start covering the new server automatically, and why or why not?
lessons.teach:
A network interface (NIC) is the virtual network card a virtual machine uses to join a virtual network. Its address settings live in an IP configuration, and an ASG is attached at that level. A network security group (NSG) is a set of allow and deny rules that filter traffic. Each rule has a source, a destination, a protocol and a port range. A rule can name an ASG in its source or destination field instead of an IP address range.

Why it works: rules are written against roles rather than addresses. When a NIC is associated with an ASG, every rule that names that ASG applies to that machine. When the association is removed, the rule stops applying. Addresses can change, but the role label stays stable.

Worked example: you have web servers web-1 and web-2, and an ASG called web-tier. An NSG attached to the web subnet has rule 100, which allows TCP 443 from the internet to destination web-tier. Step 1: for traffic to web-1, the NSG checks whether web-1's NIC belongs to web-tier. It does. Step 2: the traffic is TCP 443, which matches rule 100, so it is allowed. Step 3: you deploy web-3 and associate its NIC with web-tier. Step 4: you edit no rules, and web-3 is covered immediately. Step 5: a request to port 22 matches no allow rule, so it falls through to the default rules, which block inbound internet traffic that has not been allowed.

Common mistake: believing that associating a NIC with an ASG opens ports. It does not. The NSG rule does the allowing, and the ASG only decides which machines the rule covers. A second mistake is grouping NICs from different virtual networks under one ASG used by the same rule, which fails because all NICs referenced by a rule must sit in the same virtual network.

Consequence: if web-3's NIC is never associated with web-tier, the rule silently skips it. Clients reach web-1 and web-2 normally while requests to web-3 on port 443 time out.

questions.prompt: Northgate Clinics has a virtual network (VNet, a private network in Azure) with two application servers, app-1 and app-2, whose network interfaces (NICs, the virtual network cards) are associated with an application security group (ASG, a label that groups machines by role) named app-tier. Two database servers, sql-1 and sql-2, have NICs associated with an ASG named db-tier. A network security group (NSG, a set of allow and deny rules) on the database subnet has rule 210 that allows TCP 1433 with source app-tier and destination db-tier, and a built-in deny rule at the lowest priority. A packet from app-1 to sql-2 on TCP 1433 is traced: Step 1: app-1's NIC belongs to app-tier, so the source matches. Step 2: sql-2's NIC belongs to db-tier, so the destination matches. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the packet is allowed, and the deny rule is never reached. What must Step 3 establish?
choices: The packet uses TCP to port 1433, which matches rule 210's protocol and port range.
The deny rule is checked first because its rule number is the highest.
The NSG on the application subnet must also allow TCP 1433 outbound before rule 210 can apply.
sql-2 must be associated with app-tier as well as db-tier for the rule to apply.
questions.why: Rule 210 only allows a packet when its protocol and port match the rule, so Step 3 must confirm that the packet is TCP 1433; the other options invent requirements or misread how priority works.

questions.prompt: In Azure networking, what is the correct description of what happens when you associate a NIC with an ASG?
choices: It opens every port that is named in the ASG's label.
Any existing NSG rule that names that ASG starts applying to the NIC's machine, but the ASG itself does not open any port.
It changes the NIC's private IP address so it falls inside the group's range.
It gives the NIC its own allow rules that override the NSG.
questions.why: An ASG only decides which machines a rule covers; the NSG rule does the allowing, so association alone opens nothing.

questions.prompt: Brightwater Labs has batch worker machines, including worker-7, whose NIC is in an ASG named worker-pool. An NSG rule denies TCP 8080 from the internet to worker-pool. An administrator removes worker-7's NIC from worker-pool and makes no other change. What happens to inbound internet traffic to worker-7 on TCP 8080?
choices: The deny rule no longer matches it, so it falls through to the default rules, which still block unallowed inbound internet traffic.
It is allowed only if worker-7 has a public IP address.
It is still denied, because the ASG remembers earlier associations.
It is allowed, because removing the NIC removes the deny rule along with it.
questions.why: Removing the association stops the rule from covering worker-7, so the packet is judged by the defaults, and with no allow rule the default inbound internet block still stops it.

questions.prompt: A team at Harrow Freight puts NICs from two different VNets into a single ASG called trucks, then writes one NSG rule whose destination is trucks. What is the problem with this design?
choices: Nothing; ASGs work across virtual networks, so the rule covers both sets of NICs.
The NICs are automatically moved into one VNet, which breaks their routing.
Only the NIC that was added to the ASG first will be covered by the rule.
All NICs referenced by one rule must sit in the same VNet, so the rule cannot cover NICs from both networks.
questions.why: A rule that names an ASG requires every NIC in that group to be in the same virtual network, so mixing VNets makes the design fail.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what associating an ASG with a network interface does and does not do, and name one limit or tradeoff of using ASGs in NSG rules.
lessons.modelAnswer: Associating an ASG with a NIC puts that machine in the group. It does not open or close any port by itself. The NSG rule that names the ASG is what allows or blocks traffic, and it then applies to every machine in the group, including new ones. So the work becomes: attach the right NIC to the right group, and check that an NSG rule references that group. One limit is that the NICs a single rule refers to must all be in the same virtual network, so an ASG cannot span networks for one rule. Another tradeoff is that the rule is only as good as the membership. If a machine is missing from the group, it silently falls outside the rule, and the failure looks like a network fault rather than a configuration gap. Checking membership is part of verifying the rule.
rubricPoints: ASG association only adds the NIC to a group; the NSG rule does the allowing or blocking.
New NICs that join the ASG are covered by existing rules without editing them.
All NICs referenced by one rule must be in the same virtual network.
A NIC missing from the ASG silently falls outside the rule and causes timeouts.

suggested.rationale: A virtual network path tracer would let the learner test whether a flow is allowed when ASG membership changes, which is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: A network security group is a set of filter rules that sits in front of parts of a cloud network and decides which traffic may come in and which may go out. Each rule is a short instruction: look at where the traffic comes from, where it is going, which port and protocol it uses, and then either allow it or deny it. Rules are checked in order of a number you assign, and the first rule that matches decides the outcome. Inbound rules govern traffic arriving at a resource, and outbound rules govern traffic leaving it. Writing these rules well lets the right traffic through while keeping everything else out.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web server's subnet has a network security group with one inbound rule: priority 100, Deny, TCP port 443, source Internet, and no other custom rules. Will a visitor on the Internet reach the site over HTTPS, and why?
lessons.teach: Start with the terms. A network security group, or NSG, is a filter attached to a subnet (a slice of a virtual network), a network interface (the virtual network card of a machine), or both. A security rule is one line in that filter. Each rule has a priority, a whole number from 100 to 4096, where a lower number is checked first. Each rule also has a direction (inbound means arriving, outbound means leaving), a source and destination (an address range, a service tag such as Internet, or the whole virtual network), a port range, a protocol (TCP, UDP, ICMP or Any), and an action, Allow or Deny. Evaluation stops at the first match, so the priority numbers matter more than the order in which you typed the rules.  Why it works: the NSG reads each packet's header, the part that says who is sending and to which port, and compares it with the rules in priority order. NSG rules are stateful, meaning that if an inbound connection is allowed, the reply travels back without needing a matching outbound rule. Every NSG also has built-in default rules with priorities at 65000 and above. For inbound traffic from the Internet, the last default denies everything, so you must add an allow rule to open a port. For outbound traffic, the default allows Internet access, which surprises many beginners.  Worked example. A web subnet has inbound rules: priority 100 Allow TCP 443 from Internet, then priority 200 Deny Any from Internet, then the defaults. Step one: a browser sends a packet to port 443. It is checked against priority 100, matches, and is allowed. Step two: a scanner sends a packet to port 22. It skips 100, matches 200, and is denied. Step three: the server's HTTPS reply leaves the subnet and is allowed by state, not by an outbound rule.  Common mistake: giving the allow rule a higher number than a broad deny, so the deny matches first and the allow never applies. Consequence: the site looks down while the rule list looks correct, so always read the rules in priority order, top to bottom.  An NSG decides traffic by its first matching rule, and the priority numbers control that order.

questions.prompt: A bookings API subnet at a regional travel firm has these inbound rules: priority 120 Allow TCP 8443 from the Internet service tag; priority 180 Deny TCP 8443 from 203.0.113.0/24; priority 400 Allow Any from VirtualNetwork; then the defaults. Step one: a request from 198.51.100.7 to port 8443 is checked against priority 120, matches, and is allowed. Step two is missing: a request from 203.0.113.50 to port 8443 arrives and is checked by the NSG. Step three: the API's reply leaves the subnet and is allowed by state, not by an outbound rule. Which completion correctly fills in step two?
choices: It is denied by the default rule at 65500, because addresses in a listed range are blocked before any custom rule is read.
It is allowed only if an outbound rule also permits port 8443, because the inbound deny flagged the connection.
It is denied by priority 180, because a more specific deny rule overrides a broader allow rule.
It matches priority 120 first, is allowed, and evaluation stops, so the deny at 180 is never reached.
questions.why: The request comes from the Internet service tag, so it matches the first-listed rule at priority 120, and because evaluation stops at the first match, the deny at 180 is never checked.

questions.prompt: In a network security group, what does the priority number of a security rule control?
choices: The order in which rules were typed or created in the portal.
The bandwidth the rule is allowed to use before traffic is throttled.
The order in which rules are checked, where a lower number is checked first and evaluation stops at the first match.
Which direction, inbound or outbound, the rule applies to.
questions.why: The text defines priority as a whole number from 100 to 4096 where lower numbers are checked first, and evaluation stops at the first matching rule.

questions.prompt: A virtual machine in a logistics company's subnet has an outbound rule at priority 200 that denies TCP 443 to the Internet. No other custom outbound rules exist, so only the built-in defaults apply after it. The VM tries to load an HTTPS page on the Internet. What happens to that outbound packet?
choices: It is allowed, because the default outbound rule allows Internet access and the priority 200 rule cannot override a default.
It is allowed, because the reply coming back is stateful and so the outbound packet is exempt from rules.
It is denied by the priority 200 rule, which is checked before the default outbound allow, so the default never applies.
It is denied only if an inbound rule on the same subnet also blocks port 443.
questions.why: Rules are checked in priority order and the first match decides, so the custom deny at 200 is reached before the default outbound allow at 65000 and above.

questions.prompt: A retail company's web subnet has an inbound Deny Any rule from Internet at priority 400, and an inbound Allow TCP 8080 from Internet at priority 500. Customers report the site is unreachable on port 8080, although the rule list looks correct when read top to bottom in the portal. What best explains this?
choices: Stateful rules do not apply to inbound traffic, so the allow at 500 needs a matching outbound rule to take effect.
The Deny Any at priority 400 matches Internet traffic first, so the allow at 500 is never reached for those packets.
The default rule at 65500 denies all traffic before any custom rule is read, which is why the allow at 500 is ignored.
NSG rules only apply to network interfaces, so the subnet-level deny is ignored and the allow should be working.
questions.why: Because a lower number is checked first and evaluation stops at the first match, the deny at 400 catches the Internet traffic before the allow at 500 is considered.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we can fix a connectivity problem by adding one NSG rule that allows everything inbound, and the NSG will handle the rest. Explain to them how NSG rules are evaluated, what stateful means here, and one limit or tradeoff of that approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: An NSG checks each packet against its rules in priority order, starting with the lowest number, and the first rule that matches decides whether the packet is allowed or denied. So a broad allow rule only helps if no lower-numbered deny rule catches the same traffic first. Rules are stateful, which means that when an inbound connection is allowed, the reply is allowed back automatically without a separate outbound rule. The tradeoff with an allow-everything inbound rule is that it removes the protection the default deny gives, so every port on every machine in scope becomes reachable from wherever the rule's source allows. A better fix is to allow only the specific port and source that the application needs, and then confirm the rule's priority sits above any deny that would block it.
rubricPoints: Rules are evaluated in ascending priority order and the first match decides
Stateful means return traffic for an allowed connection needs no matching outbound rule
An allow-everything inbound rule removes the default protection and widens exposure
A narrower rule with a suitable source, port and priority is the safer fix

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through exam-style rule scenarios about priority, direction and statefulness adds more than reading alone, and no listed mission covers NSG rules directly.

lessons.plain: A virtual network flow log is a running diary of the network conversations inside a private network in the cloud. Each entry notes who talked to whom, on which port, over which protocol, and how much data moved, but not what was said. You switch it on for a virtual network, which is your isolated slice of cloud networking, and the cloud writes the diary to a storage account, a file store. Engineers read it afterwards to answer questions like what was talking to a database during an outage, or whether a sudden spike came from one server.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a web server suddenly sends far more data than usual to an address outside your network, which single piece of information would most quickly tell you which server, which destination and roughly how much traffic, without reading the contents of the messages?
lessons.teach:
A virtual network flow log is a record, kept by Azure's Network Watcher toolkit, of the network conversations that pass through a virtual network. A virtual network is your private, isolated address space in the cloud. Network Watcher is the built-in set of tools for observing and diagnosing networks. Each record is a flow tuple: a compact entry holding the source and destination IP addresses, the ports, the protocol, the direction, and counts of packets and bytes. It holds metadata only, never the contents of the traffic.

Why it works: the platform observes traffic at the network layer and writes these summaries out on a schedule, so you can answer questions later, such as which servers talked to a database last Tuesday or whether a spike came from one address. The logs are written to a storage account, a cloud file store, and you set a retention period so that old files are deleted rather than piling up.

Worked example: you want to see whether a web server at 10.1.1.4 is calling an outside API. Step 1: choose a Network Watcher in the same region as the virtual network. Step 2: enable a virtual network flow log on that network and point it at a storage account. Step 3: wait for traffic, then open the log file covering the hour you care about. Step 4: find entries where the source is 10.1.1.4 and the destination port is 443. Step 5: count them to see the volume. You now have evidence rather than a guess.

Common mistake: assuming the log explains everything. It shows what flowed, not the rule that stopped a packet, and it never shows payload. Engineers also forget that storage costs grow with traffic.

Consequence: on a busy network with no retention limit, the storage account can fill up and quietly cost real money, so set retention and estimate the volume before enabling logs widely.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm has a virtual network with the address range 10.40.0.0/20 in Canada Central. Its depot sync server at 10.40.2.9 should never accept remote desktop connections from outside the network on port 3389, and the team wants evidence about last night. Their method is below. Step 1: confirm that a virtual network flow log is already enabled on that network and writes to a storage account, using a Network Watcher in the same region. Step 2: open the log files covering 22:00 to 06:00 UTC. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: count the matching entries and report the total. Which choice fills the blank?
choices: Restart the sync server so that its open connections are written to the log file
Filter for entries going to 10.40.2.9 on port 3389 from a source outside 10.40.0.0/20
Raise the retention period to 365 days so that last night's file is kept
Look up the network security group rule that allows port 3389, since the log records which rule stopped each packet
questions.why: The log holds flow records, so the blank is the filter that isolates inbound flows to that server on port 3389 from outside the network, while checking rules, restarting the server, or changing retention does not produce the count.

questions.prompt: What is a flow tuple in a virtual network flow log?
choices: A compact record of source and destination addresses, ports, protocol, direction, and packet and byte counts, without the traffic contents
A firewall rule that the platform writes into a storage account whenever traffic is blocked
A full copy of every packet's payload, stored so that engineers can read application data later
A summary of CPU and memory use for each virtual machine attached to the network
questions.why: The teaching text defines a flow tuple as a compact metadata entry with addresses, ports, protocol, direction and counts, and states that it never contains traffic contents.

questions.prompt: A team enables a virtual network flow log on a busy network and leaves the retention period unset. What is the most direct consequence they should expect?
choices: Packets are blocked once the storage account reaches its size limit, cutting off the network
The flow log stops recording as soon as the first file is written, until retention is configured
Old log files keep accumulating in the storage account, so storage cost grows as traffic grows
The log begins to store payload contents, which breaks their data-handling rules over time
questions.why: Without a retention period old files are not deleted, so the storage account fills and costs rise with traffic, which the teaching text names as the consequence of skipping retention.

questions.prompt: An engineer sees repeated connection attempts from 10.60.3.5 to a database on port 1433 that never succeed, and asks the flow log to name the rule that blocked them. Which use of the flow log is correct?
choices: Read the log entry to find the name of the rule that denied each attempt, then copy that rule into the report
Conclude that the database is down, because a flow log always shows the cause of a failed connection
Open the payload of each attempt to see the login request the client sent to the database
Use the log to confirm which flows occurred between 10.60.3.5 and port 1433 and how much traffic they carried, then check the rules separately for the cause
questions.why: The teaching text says the log shows what flowed and its volume but not the rule that stopped a packet, so the rules must be checked separately for the cause.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a virtual network flow log records, what it does not record, and one limit or cost tradeoff you would weigh before turning it on for a busy production network.
lessons.modelAnswer: A flow log records the network conversations crossing a virtual network: source and destination addresses, ports, protocol, direction, and packet and byte counts. It is metadata, so it tells us who talked to whom and how much, but not the content of the messages and not the specific security rule that allowed or blocked a flow. To use it, we enable it on the virtual network, point it at a storage account, and read the files it writes. The main tradeoff is cost and retention. On a busy network the volume of records grows quickly, so before enabling it broadly I would estimate the daily size, set a retention period so old files are deleted, and consider whether traffic analytics is needed for the level of detail we want. Logs answer what happened; they do not replace checking the rules that governed it.
rubricPoints: Defines a flow log as metadata about traffic on a virtual network, not payload
Names key fields such as addresses, ports, protocol and byte or packet counts
Explains that the logs are stored in a storage account and read from there
States a limit: logs do not show which rule allowed or blocked a flow
Names a cost or retention tradeoff for busy networks

suggested.rationale: Choosing what a flow log can and cannot prove in a realistic incident is better practised as a reasoning scenario than as a catalogue read, and no listed mission covers cloud network flow records.

lessons.plain: A virtual network flow log is a record kept by Azure of the traffic moving through a virtual network, which is your private network inside the cloud. Think of it as a phone call log: it does not capture the conversations, only who connected to whom, on which port, when, and roughly how much data moved. Engineers read these logs after something goes wrong, to answer questions like whether a server ever reached a database or why connections keep dropping. Reading them well means knowing what each field means and what the log cannot tell you.
lessons.guessPrompt: A client in one subnet cannot get responses from a server in another subnet. The flow log shows a begin record for the client's connection, but no continuing or end records. What do you think happened, and what would you check next?
lessons.teach:
A flow is one conversation between two endpoints, identified by a five-part key called the flow tuple: source address, source port, destination address, destination port, and protocol (such as TCP or UDP). A flow log is a stream of records, written as traffic is observed, and each record describes one flow at one moment. A record carries a timestamp, the tuple, a direction (inbound or outbound, relative to the resource being logged), a flow state, and counters for packets and bytes.

The flow state marks where the flow is in its life. A begin record appears when a new flow starts. Continuing records appear while the flow stays open and report counters so far. An end record closes the flow. The counters in continuing and end records are totals for that flow, so you read the latest record for a flow rather than adding every record together.

Worked example: a web server at 10.1.0.4 receives a request from 10.2.0.7 to port 443 over TCP. First you see a begin record with the client's source port, destination 10.1.0.4 port 443, direction inbound. A continuing record shows 40 packets so far. The end record shows 58 packets and about 9 kilobytes. You now know the connection opened, carried data, and closed. Compare that with having only a begin record, which tells you the connection started but nothing more.

Common mistake: treating a missing record as proof that traffic was blocked. A gap may mean no traffic was attempted, the packets never reached the point where they were recorded, or logging was not enabled for that period. Flow logs show what was observed, not what a rule intended.

Consequence: during an outage, the flow log is often the only evidence of whether packets reached their destination, so the first question is whether the expected begin and end records exist for that exact tuple.

questions.prompt: A database VM at 172.16.8.20 accepts SQL connections from an application server at 172.16.3.9 over TCP to port 1433. An engineer is reading the flow log for one connection, whose flow tuple is 172.16.3.9, source port 51822, 172.16.8.20, destination port 1433, TCP. Step 1: confirm the tuple matches exactly on all five parts. Step 2: note the direction, which is inbound for the database VM. Step 3: list the records for this tuple in time order. There is a begin record at 14:00:05, a continuing record at 14:02:40 showing 18 packets, and a continuing record at 14:03:10 showing 31 packets. The connection is still open. Step 4: the packet count to report for this flow is taken from which value?
choices: 31, from the most recent record for this tuple
18, from the earlier continuing record
49, by adding the two continuing records together
It cannot be read until an end record appears
questions.why: Counters on continuing and end records are running totals for the flow, so the latest record gives the current total, and adding records together double-counts.

questions.prompt: In a virtual network flow log, what does an end record indicate?
choices: That the flow was allowed by a rule and will not be logged again
That the flow was blocked before any packets were counted
That the flow has closed, and its counters are the final totals
That the flow has started and no data has been sent yet
questions.why: An end record closes the flow, and the counters it carries are the totals for that flow.

questions.prompt: A support engineer checks the flow log for a payment API at 10.20.5.12 during a two-minute window when customers reported timeouts. No records exist for the expected tuple. Which conclusion is justified?
choices: The NSG blocked the traffic, so the rule must be fixed
The missing records do not prove blocking, because no attempt, a packet that never reached the recording point, or logging being off could explain them
The packets reached the API and the app caused the timeouts
The API never failed, because the logs prove there was no traffic
questions.why: A missing record is not proof of a block, since flow logs only show what was observed and not what a rule intended.

questions.prompt: A client at 192.0.2.44 opens two separate TCP connections to a web server at 198.51.100.10 on port 80, one after the other. The second connection uses a different source port than the first. How should these be treated in the flow log?
choices: As duplicate records of the same flow, so one should be discarded
As two separate flows, because the source port is part of the five-part key
As one flow, because the client address and server address are the same
As one flow with combined counters, because they share a destination port
questions.why: Each flow is identified by all five parts of its tuple, so a different source port means a different flow that must be looked up separately.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would read a virtual network flow log to decide whether a connection reached its destination, and name one limit of the log that could mislead you.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would filter the log to the flow tuple for that connection: the client's address and source port, the server's address, the destination port, and the protocol. Then I check which records exist. A begin record shows the connection was seen starting. Continuing and end records with packet and byte counts show it carried data. If only a begin record exists, the server may not have replied, or the reply may never have arrived, so I would look at the server side, routing, and rules next. The limit I would raise is that the log only shows what was observed. A missing record does not prove a rule blocked the traffic, and the log cannot explain why, so I would confirm with a second source before blaming a specific rule.
rubricPoints: Identifies a flow by its tuple: addresses, ports and protocol.
Explains begin, continuing and end records and what each one implies.
Reads counters from the latest record for a flow instead of double-counting.
States that a missing record is not proof that traffic was blocked.
Names at least one limit, such as the log showing observations rather than intent.

suggested.rationale: That mission builds the same habit of reading log records for a specific connection pattern and drawing a careful conclusion from them.

lessons.plain: When an application cannot connect, a useful first question is whether the network rules would let one specific piece of traffic through at all. Verifying IP flow means asking the cloud network to check a single hypothetical packet, described by its source address, destination address, port and protocol, and getting back allowed or denied along with the name of the rule that decided. The check uses the configured rules and sends no real traffic, so it is a quick way to narrow down a connection problem before you change anything.
lessons.guessPrompt: A virtual machine's web app responds from inside its own subnet but not from the internet. Before you read any settings, what would you check first to decide whether the network rules are the problem, and how could you test that without changing anything?
lessons.teach:
A packet is one small unit of network data, carrying a source address, a destination address, a port and a protocol. A network security group, or NSG, is a set of allow and deny rules that Azure attaches to a subnet or a network interface, the virtual card of a virtual machine. Each rule has a direction (inbound means traffic coming in, outbound means traffic going out), a priority number, and match conditions such as source, destination, port and protocol. Rules are checked in priority order, lowest number first, and the first rule that matches decides the outcome. Verifying IP flow is a test that takes one hypothetical packet, with a given direction, source, destination, port and protocol, and reports whether the rules allow or deny it and which rule matched. Because the test reads the rules rather than sending traffic, it is fast and safe to run.

Worked example. A virtual machine has the address 10.0.1.5. Its NSG contains rule 100, which allows inbound TCP on port 443 from the internet, and the default rule at priority 65500 that denies inbound traffic from the internet. Test one: inbound TCP 443 from 203.0.113.10 to 10.0.1.5. Rule 100 is checked first, its conditions match, so the result is allow. Test two: inbound TCP 22 from the same source. Rule 100 does not match the port, so the check moves down the list and reaches the deny rule, and the result is deny.

A common mistake is treating an allow result as proof that the application works. The check only looks at rules. It does not confirm that the service is listening on the port, that the operating system firewall permits the traffic, or that routing and other appliances in the path are correct. A deny result, however, tells you the rules themselves are blocking the packet, which is useful evidence.

In a running system this matters because a deny rule added in a hurry can cut off production traffic immediately. Running the check before and after a rule change shows exactly which traffic is affected.

questions.prompt: A company called Harbor Dental has a virtual machine at 10.20.3.8 in a subnet with an NSG. The NSG has rule 150, which denies inbound TCP on port 8080 from the address 192.0.2.44, and rule 300, which allows inbound TCP on port 8080 from 192.0.2.44. An engineer runs verify IP flow for inbound TCP 8080 from 192.0.2.44 to 10.20.3.8. Step 1: the check orders the rules by priority, lowest number first, giving rule 150 before rule 300. Step 2: rule 150 is the first rule examined, and its conditions match the direction, source, destination, port and protocol. Step 3 is missing. What is the result of the check, and which rule is reported?
choices: Deny, reported by rule 150, because the first matching rule decides the outcome and its action is deny
Allow, reported by rule 300, because a later allow rule overrides an earlier deny rule for the same traffic
Deny, reported by the operating system firewall on the virtual machine, because verify IP flow only reports the NSG default rules
Allow, reported by rule 300, because the check always prefers the rule whose number is larger
questions.why: Rules are checked lowest priority number first and the first match decides, so rule 150 matches and its deny action is the result, with rule 300 never reached.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does a verify IP flow test tell you about a hypothetical packet?
choices: It checks whether the application on the virtual machine is running and listening on the requested port
It changes the NSG rules temporarily so that the packet is allowed through and then restores them
It sends a real test packet across the network and measures how long the destination takes to reply
It reads the NSG rules for a described packet and reports whether they allow or deny it, along with the rule that matched
questions.why: The test reads the rules without sending traffic and reports the allow or deny result and the matching rule for the packet you describe.

questions.prompt: A team sees an allow result from verify IP flow for inbound TCP 443 on a web server and concludes that users can now load the site. Which statement best explains what is wrong with that conclusion?
choices: Port 443 is not a valid port for web traffic, so the allow result must have come from a misconfigured rule
The check cannot report allow for inbound traffic unless the virtual machine has a public address
An allow result is only valid for outbound traffic, so the team must run the check again in the outbound direction
The check only examines the NSG rules, so an allow result says nothing about whether the service is listening, whether the operating system firewall permits the traffic, or whether routing is correct
questions.why: Verify IP flow only evaluates NSG rules, so an allow result is necessary evidence but not proof that the application works end to end.

questions.prompt: A subnet NSG contains rule 210, which allows inbound UDP on port 53 from the address 172.16.8.9, and rule 4096, which denies all inbound UDP from any source. An engineer runs verify IP flow for inbound UDP 53 from 172.16.9.9 to a host in that subnet. What result should the engineer expect?
choices: Allow, because port 53 is listed in rule 210 and the check ignores the source address
Deny, because rule 210 does not match the source 172.16.9.9, so the check moves on to rule 4096, which denies it
Allow, because rule 4096 only applies when no other rule exists in the NSG
Deny, because the check always reports deny for UDP traffic regardless of the rules
questions.why: Rule 210 requires the source 172.16.8.9, so it does not match 172.16.9.9, and the lower-priority deny rule 4096 is the first match.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says: the rule check came back allowed, so the connection problem is solved. Explain to them in your own words what a check of this kind does and does not prove, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on it.
lessons.modelAnswer: The check takes a hypothetical packet, with a direction, source, destination, port and protocol, and runs it through the rules attached to the network interface and subnet in priority order. It reports whether the first matching rule allows or denies it, and which rule that was. That is useful because it answers a narrow question quickly, without sending real traffic or touching anything. What it does not prove is that the connection will succeed. The service may not be listening, the operating system firewall may block the port, or routing may be wrong. The main tradeoff is that you only test the packets you describe. If you check port 443 and the problem is on port 8443, the result tells you nothing about the real failure, so you still need to test the path that users actually take.
rubricPoints: Explains that the check evaluates a described packet against NSG rules in priority order and reports allow or deny with the matching rule.
States that an allow result does not prove the application is listening or that the whole path works.
Notes that the check tests only the packet described, so the scenario chosen has to match real traffic.
Mentions that the check sends no real traffic and is safe to run before or after a rule change.

suggested.rationale: The planned virtual network path tracer would let the learner test hypothetical packets along a path and see which rule decides each one, which is the skill this objective needs.

lessons.plain: A network security group is a list of allow and deny rules that a cloud network uses to decide which traffic may reach a virtual machine. When you need to manage a server remotely, the risky choice is opening the admin port, such as SSH on port 22 or RDP on port 3389, to the whole internet. A safer pattern is to allow admin ports only from a trusted source, or to skip opening them entirely and reach the machine through Azure Bastion, a managed jump service you open in a web browser. This lesson covers how to set those rules so only the right people can get in.
lessons.guessPrompt: A virtual machine has no public IP address, and its network security group allows nothing from the internet. An administrator still needs a remote shell on it. Before reading on, name two ways they could get in safely, and say what each one exposes to the internet.
lessons.teach: A network security group, or NSG, is a set of rules that the cloud network checks before letting traffic reach a subnet or network interface. Each rule has a direction (inbound or outbound), a source, a destination, a port and protocol, an action (allow or deny), and a priority number. Lower numbers are checked first, and the first matching rule wins. Remote administration means reaching a machine's shell: SSH on TCP port 22 for Linux, or RDP on TCP port 3389 for Windows. The design question is who may send those ports, and by what path. Azure Bastion is a managed jump service. You open it from a web browser over HTTPS, and it opens the SSH or RDP session to the target's private IP address from inside the virtual network. The target needs no public IP and no admin port open to the internet. Bastion must sit in a subnet named AzureBastionSubnet, sized at least /26. That subnet has its own NSG requirements set by the platform, which you should check in the current documentation. Worked example: a Linux VM sits in subnet 10.1.2.0/24 with private address 10.1.2.4, and Bastion lives in 10.1.3.0/26. The VM's NSG has rule 100 allowing TCP 22 from source 10.1.3.0/26, and rule 4096 denying inbound TCP 22 from the Internet. Step one: the engineer's browser reaches Bastion over HTTPS. Step two: Bastion opens TCP 22 to 10.1.2.4 from its own address. Step three: the VM's NSG matches rule 100 and allows it. A scan from the internet to port 22 matches rule 4096 and is dropped. Common mistake: assuming default rules are enough. Azure includes a default rule that allows traffic originating inside the virtual network, so any machine in that network can reach SSH unless you deny it. Set explicit rules and keep the deny in place. Consequence: an admin port open to the internet gets scanned and brute-forced constantly, which fills authentication logs and risks a compromised login. Restricting the port to a bastion source removes that exposure.

questions.prompt: Harbor Dental runs a Windows server VM at 192.168.20.8 in subnet 192.168.20.0/24, with no public IP. Its Bastion host sits in AzureBastionSubnet at 192.168.21.64/26. The VM's NSG has two inbound rules for TCP 3389: rule 200 allows it from source 192.168.21.64/26, and rule 300 denies it from source VirtualNetwork. Step 1: an administrator's browser reaches Bastion over HTTPS. Step 2: Bastion opens TCP 3389 to 192.168.20.8 from its own address in 192.168.21.64/26. Step 3: the VM's NSG checks its rules in order of priority number to decide what happens to that RDP connection. What is the result of step 3?
choices: Denied, because rule 300 blocks all traffic that originates inside the virtual network, including Bastion
Allowed, because rule 200 matches first as the lower priority number, and the session comes from the Bastion subnet
Denied, because Bastion's session must come from a public IP address to pass the NSG
Allowed by the default rule at 65000, because priority numbers only affect deny rules
questions.why: The NSG checks lower priority numbers first, so rule 200 matches the Bastion source and allows the session before rule 300 is reached.

questions.prompt: An NSG on a subnet holds two inbound rules for TCP 22 from the same source, 203.0.113.0/24. Rule 140 denies it and rule 150 allows it. A connection from 203.0.113.9 arrives. What happens and why?
choices: Denied, because rule 140 has the lower priority number, so it is checked first and its action wins
Allowed, because the allow rule always beats a deny rule regardless of priority
Allowed, because rule 150 is a higher priority number and the NSG keeps checking until it finds an allow
Denied, because the NSG reads every matching rule and a deny in any of them blocks traffic only if it has no priority
questions.why: Rules are checked from lowest priority number upward and the first matching rule decides the outcome, so rule 140's deny applies.

questions.prompt: A VM in a virtual network has an NSG with no custom rules at all, only the platform defaults. Another VM in the same virtual network tries to open an SSH session to it. What is the likely outcome?
choices: Blocked, because SSH uses TCP 3389 inside a virtual network
Allowed to connect only if the connecting VM has a public IP address
Blocked, because the default rules deny all inbound traffic unless a custom rule allows it
Allowed, because a default rule permits traffic that originates inside the virtual network, so the connection goes through unless an explicit deny is set
questions.why: The default rule allows traffic from inside the virtual network, which is why an explicit deny is needed to stop it.

questions.prompt: A team wants Bastion in a new virtual network, with AzureBastionSubnet to be created. Which address range is a valid size for that subnet?
questions.why: Bastion's subnet must be at least /26, and /26 meets that minimum while /27 and smaller do not.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would let one engineer administer a Linux server in a private subnet without opening SSH to the internet. Name the NSG rule you would write, and state one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would not open port 22 to the internet at all. The server gets a private address only, and I would put Azure Bastion in its own AzureBastionSubnet. On the server's NSG I would add an inbound rule with a priority number below the default deny, allowing TCP 22 from the Bastion subnet's address range and denying TCP 22 from Internet. The engineer then connects through the Bastion portal in a browser, and Bastion opens the SSH session to the private address. The tradeoff is cost and setup: Bastion is a billed service with its own subnet and its own NSG requirements, so for a single small lab it can be more than needed. A second limit is that Bastion only moves the front door. If someone can sign in through it with a weak password or a shared key, the risk is still there, so access still needs proper credentials and logging.
rubricPoints: Admin ports should not be open to the internet; the server is reached over a private address
Azure Bastion is the browser-based jump path, and it needs its own dedicated subnet
The NSG rule allows the admin port only from the Bastion subnet, and an explicit deny covers other sources
Default rules allow traffic inside the virtual network, so explicit rules are needed to tighten access, and Bastion adds cost and setup

suggested.rationale: Choosing which source may reach an admin port, and tracing what that rule allows or blocks, is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style scenario.

lessons.plain: Imagine a company with dozens of separate office networks, each run by a different team. Head office wants one rule that says no office may accept remote-login traffic from the internet, no matter what local managers configured. Azure Virtual Network Manager is a service that groups many virtual networks together and pushes a central set of security rules to the whole group. Those central rules are checked before the local rules, so the head-office policy wins where they conflict. This lesson covers how that layering works and what it means when traffic is blocked.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a local firewall rule in one virtual network allows inbound traffic on port 3389 from the internet, but a central rule applied to that network says deny for the same traffic, which one do you think decides whether the traffic gets through?
lessons.teach: Azure Virtual Network Manager, often shortened to AVNM, is a central management service for many virtual networks (VNets, which are isolated private networks in the cloud). Its security feature is built from three pieces. A network group is a named set of VNets or subnets, either listed by hand or selected by a rule. A security admin configuration is a bundle of central rules that you apply to network groups. Each security admin rule has a priority number from 1 to 4096, where lower numbers are checked first, and an action. The action Allow passes the traffic on to the local network security group (NSG), the filter that teams attach to subnets and network interfaces. Deny blocks the traffic immediately. Always Allow lets the traffic through even when a local NSG would block it. Why it works: AVNM security admin rules are evaluated before NSG rules. A central Deny cannot be undone by a local Allow, and a central Always Allow cannot be undone by a local Deny. Only traffic that matches no central rule, or matches a central Allow, reaches the NSG for its own decision. Worked example: a security admin rule with priority 100 denies inbound TCP 3389 from the Internet to every VNet in a network group called prod. An application team has an NSG rule allowing 3389 from the Internet on their subnet. A remote login attempt arrives. AVNM checks priority 100 first, matches the Deny, and drops the packet. The NSG rule is never reached. Common mistake: editing a central configuration and assuming it is live. Changes must be deployed, which AVNM calls committing, to each region where the VNets sit before they take effect. Consequence in a running system: a central deny can break a workload while the owning team sees a correct-looking NSG and no error, so troubleshooting must start with the central layer.

questions.prompt: Harbor Ledger Co. has a network group called finance-vnets that holds three VNets. Its central security admin configuration has a rule at priority 60 with action Deny for inbound TCP 3389 from any source to all members. A second rule at priority 210 has action Always Allow for inbound TCP 1433 from 172.16.8.0/24 to the subnet db-tier. The local NSG on db-tier has a Deny rule for inbound TCP 1433 from 172.16.8.0/24. A client at 172.16.8.10 opens a connection to port 1433 on db-tier. Step 1: AVNM checks priority 60 first. Its port is 3389, which does not match 1433, so the rule is skipped. Step 2: AVNM checks priority 210. The client is in 172.16.8.0/24 and the port is 1433, so the rule matches with action Always Allow. Step 3 (not shown): what happens to the packet, and does the NSG on db-tier decide its fate? Complete step 3.
choices: The packet is held until the Harbor Ledger team removes the NSG Deny rule, because AVNM cannot override a local NSG.
AVNM returns an error to the client and the packet is dropped, because a central Always Allow conflicts with a local Deny.
The NSG Deny rule drops the packet, because the local NSG is always checked after any central Always Allow.
The packet is delivered without the NSG on db-tier making a decision, because Always Allow lets it through even when a local NSG would block it.
questions.why: Always Allow lets the traffic through even when a local NSG would block it, so the NSG on db-tier never gets to decide on this packet.

questions.prompt: Gulf Print Works wants one central rule to cover its staging VNets. Which description of a network group in AVNM is accurate?
choices: A single NSG shared by every VNet in a region.
A rule that assigns priority numbers to the NSGs attached to each subnet.
An action such as Allow or Deny attached directly to one network interface.
A named set of VNets or subnets, either listed by hand or selected by a rule.
questions.why: A network group is a named collection of VNets or subnets, built by hand or by rule, and central security rules are applied to it.

questions.prompt: Riverstone Clinic has a central security admin rule at priority 500 with action Allow for inbound TCP 443 from any source to its web-tier network group. The configuration has been committed. The web-tier subnet has a local NSG rule that denies inbound TCP 443 from any source. An internet client sends an HTTPS request to the web tier. What happens to the request?
choices: It is allowed, because any central Allow overrides a local NSG Deny.
It is allowed only if the clinic removes the central rule first.
It is blocked by the local NSG Deny, because a central Allow passes the traffic on to the NSG, which makes its own decision.
It is blocked by AVNM with an error message, because the two layers disagree.
questions.why: A central Allow only passes traffic to the local NSG, so the NSG's Deny still applies and blocks the request.

questions.prompt: A security admin rule at priority 90 with action Deny and a rule at priority 120 with action Always Allow both match SSH traffic from 203.0.113.0/24 to a VNet in the same network group. Which outcome is correct?
choices: The packet goes to the local NSG, which decides whether it passes.
The priority 90 Deny is checked first and drops the traffic, so the priority 120 rule is never reached.
Both rules apply together, and the traffic is dropped only if the local NSG also denies it.
Always Allow at priority 120 wins, because Always Allow overrides every Deny in the configuration.
questions.why: Lower priority numbers are checked first, so the priority 90 Deny matches and blocks the traffic immediately before the priority 120 rule is considered.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how an AVNM security admin rule and a local NSG rule combine when they disagree, and name one limit or tradeoff of managing security centrally this way.
lessons.modelAnswer: Traffic is checked against the central security admin rules first, in priority order, so a lower number is checked earlier. If a central rule says Deny, the traffic is dropped and the local NSG never sees it. If a central rule says Always Allow, it passes even if the NSG would block it. If a central rule says Allow, the decision falls through to the NSG on the subnet or network interface, which then applies its own rules. The tradeoff is that central control is powerful but less flexible: a broad deny can break a team's application, and the owning team may not see why. Also, a change does nothing until it is committed to each region. So when I troubleshoot, I check the central configuration and whether it has been deployed before I look at the local NSG.
rubricPoints: Central security admin rules are evaluated before local NSG rules.
Lower priority numbers are checked first.
Deny blocks traffic outright, Always Allow passes it regardless of the NSG, and Allow defers the decision to the NSG.
A central deny can break a workload whose NSG looks correct, which is the main tradeoff of reduced local flexibility.
Configuration changes must be committed to each region before they take effect.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a conflicting central and local rule scenario builds the precedence judgement this objective depends on more than reading steps would.

lessons.plain: Azure Firewall is a managed firewall service that sits at the edge of a group of cloud networks and decides which traffic may pass. Think of it as a security guard at a building's gate who checks not only where a visitor is heading, but which door they want and what they are asking for. Mapping a requirement to this firewall means taking a plain sentence, such as 'our servers may only reach the software update sites', and choosing the feature that enforces it: filtering by address and port, by domain name, or by inspecting content. Getting this match right is the core skill, because the wrong feature either lets risky traffic through or blocks something the business needs.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your application servers in a private network need to download operating system patches from a fixed list of vendor websites, and nothing else on the internet. Which would you expect to control this more precisely: a rule that lists IP addresses for each vendor, or a rule that lists the website names themselves? Why?
lessons.teach:
Definitions first. A firewall is a device or service that inspects network traffic and allows or denies it against a set of rules. Azure Firewall is Microsoft's managed firewall: you deploy it into its own subnet inside a virtual network, and you do not run or patch the underlying machines yourself. Stateful means it remembers the connections it has allowed, so reply traffic for an allowed request passes without a separate rule. Egress means traffic leaving your network. East-west means traffic moving between your own networks. A fully qualified domain name (FQDN) is the complete host name of a site, such as one specific website.

Why it works: the firewall offers several kinds of rule, and each one looks at a different layer. Network rules match source and destination IP addresses, ports, and protocols. Application rules match FQDNs and, on some tiers, web categories. Threat intelligence can block known malicious addresses and domains. Premium tiers add TLS inspection, which decrypts and re-checks encrypted traffic, and intrusion detection and prevention (IDPS), which looks for known attack patterns. The mapping question is therefore: which layer does the requirement describe?

Worked example. The requirement says the servers may reach only the update sites of one vendor, over HTTPS. Step 1: the requirement names destinations by host name, and vendor IP addresses change, so an application rule fits better than an IP rule. Step 2: the rule allows the listed host names on port 443 from the server subnet. Step 3: all other outbound traffic matches no allow rule and is denied by the firewall's default behaviour. Result: a server asking for an unlisted site is blocked, and listed sites succeed.
