Common mistake: expecting Azure Firewall to stop attacks such as SQL injection against a public web application. Azure Firewall works at the network and destination level and does not read a web request the way an application does. That job belongs to a Web Application Firewall. The consequence of getting this wrong is that a team believes an app is protected when its attack surface has not changed, or that an update job fails silently because one host name is missing from the allow list.

Azure Firewall, with the right rule type, gives you a tight and auditable allow list for outbound traffic, and it is the right tool whenever the requirement is about where traffic may go rather than what a web request contains.

questions.prompt: Harbor Dental runs a records server at 10.60.1.10 inside a virtual network. A branch office at 192.168.20.0/24 must reach that server on TCP port 1433 and nothing else. Worked so far: Step 1, the requirement names a fixed IP address and port rather than a host name, so a network rule fits better than an application rule. Step 2, the rule allows source 192.168.20.0/24 to destination 10.60.1.10 on TCP 1433. Step 3 is missing and is the one you must supply: how does the firewall treat the reply packets sent from 10.60.1.10 back to the branch? Which completion of step 3 is correct?
choices: Nothing extra is needed: the firewall is stateful, so replies to the allowed connection pass without their own rule.
Turn on TLS inspection so the firewall can decrypt and recheck the replies before they return to the branch.
Add a second rule allowing the server's replies on every high port, because the firewall treats each direction as a brand-new connection.
Add an application rule listing the branch office's host name, since replies are matched by FQDN.
questions.why: Because Azure Firewall is stateful, it remembers the connection it allowed and lets the matching replies through without a separate rule.

questions.prompt: A threat feed lists one IP address as known malicious. The team wants that address blocked from reaching anything behind Azure Firewall, without writing an allow-list entry for each service. Which firewall feature fits this requirement?
choices: An application rule matching the address's FQDN on port 443
TLS inspection enabled on the outbound rule collection
A custom rule in a Web Application Firewall on the public listener
Threat intelligence set to block known malicious addresses
questions.why: Threat intelligence can block known malicious addresses and domains directly, whereas application rules match host names and TLS inspection only decrypts and rechecks traffic.

questions.prompt: A public web application is hit by SQL injection hidden in a query string. The team has Azure Firewall with network rules only and believes the app is now protected. Which statement is accurate?
choices: Stateful inspection drops the request because it does not match a previously allowed connection.
An application rule with the application's FQDN will stop SQL injection carried in the query string.
Azure Firewall works at the network and destination level and does not read the web request content, so a Web Application Firewall is needed for that job.
The firewall blocks it because the source address is unknown, so the application is protected.
questions.why: The firewall matches addresses, ports and protocols and does not read the content of a web request, which is the job of a Web Application Firewall.

questions.prompt: A finance subnet at 172.20.8.0/24 must reach one file server at 172.20.30.5 over TCP port 445 and nothing else. Which rule definition fits this requirement best?
choices: A network rule with source 172.20.8.0/24, destination 172.20.30.5, and protocol TCP on port 445
An application rule allowing the file server's host name on port 445
A threat intelligence rule that blocks the file server's address
A network rule allowing any source to 172.20.30.5 on all ports, followed by a deny for everything else
questions.why: The requirement names fixed addresses, a protocol and a port, which is exactly what a network rule matches, and the default deny already blocks everything else from that subnet.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says Azure Firewall will stop SQL injection attacks against our public web app, so we can skip a WAF. Explain to them what Azure Firewall can and cannot map to, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you would recommend instead.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would correct that. Azure Firewall controls which networks, IP addresses, ports, and domain names traffic may reach. On Premium tiers it can also inspect encrypted traffic and match known attack patterns at the network level. It does not analyse the content of a web request the way a web application would, so it is not the right control for SQL injection or cross-site scripting against a public site. That is the job of a Web Application Firewall, which sits in front of the web app and inspects HTTP requests against managed rule sets. For this app I would put a WAF in front of it and keep Azure Firewall for outbound allow lists and traffic between networks. The tradeoff is cost and operations: two components to configure and monitor, and WAF rules can block legitimate users, so the rules need tuning over time.
rubricPoints: Azure Firewall maps to network, address, port, and domain-name rules, plus threat intelligence and Premium inspection features.
It is a stateful, centrally managed service, most useful for controlling outbound traffic and traffic between networks.
Web application attacks such as SQL injection are the job of a WAF, not Azure Firewall.
A good answer names a limit or tradeoff, such as cost, rule maintenance, or false positives.

suggested.rationale: Choosing the right firewall feature for a scenario is best practised by reasoning through exam-style requirements, and no listed mission covers network firewalls.

lessons.plain: An Azure Firewall is a managed firewall that sits in a network and inspects traffic moving between networks or out to the internet. It comes in tiers called SKUs (stock-keeping units, a term for a product edition). Each tier includes a different set of inspection features and handles a different amount of traffic, and the tiers cost different amounts. Choosing a tier means matching the features you need, such as filtering by web address or inspecting encrypted traffic, plus the volume you expect, against the cheapest tier that still does the job. A tier that is too small misses protections or runs out of capacity, while one that is too large wastes money.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company needs a firewall that only blocks traffic to a short list of known IP ranges and handles a few megabits a day. Another team wants the same firewall to also inspect encrypted web traffic for hidden malware and filter by website category. Would you expect both needs to be met by the same tier, and why or why not?
lessons.teach:
A firewall is a device or service that allows or blocks network traffic based on rules. In Azure, Azure Firewall is a managed firewall, meaning Microsoft runs the underlying hardware and software for you. A SKU (stock-keeping unit) is the edition or tier you deploy. Azure Firewall offers Basic, Standard and Premium tiers. Each tier adds inspection features on top of the one below it, and each has a different ceiling on how much traffic it can handle. Basic is aimed at small workloads. Standard adds richer filtering, such as allowing or blocking by fully qualified domain name (the full host name of a site, like a web address without the path) and by web category. Premium adds deeper inspection, including TLS inspection (decrypting, checking and re-encrypting HTTPS traffic) and intrusion detection and prevention.

Worked example. Requirement: outbound web traffic must be filtered by website category, and encrypted content must be inspected for malware. Step 1: category filtering is not available in Basic, so the tier must be at least Standard. Step 2: inspecting encrypted content requires TLS inspection, which is a Premium feature. Step 3: the answer is Premium, and you still check the expected throughput against that tier's limits.

Common mistake. Learners often pick the highest tier by default, or pick the lowest tier to save money without listing the required features first. Start with the requirement list, then choose the cheapest tier that covers every item.

Consequence. In a running system, an undersized tier can drop or delay traffic at peak times, or quietly skip an inspection you assumed was happening. Changing tiers later is usually disruptive, so the decision belongs in the design stage.

questions.prompt: A regional bank runs a hub network with Azure Firewall. Requirement: outbound traffic may reach only a short list of named host names (fully qualified domain names, the full host name of a site), and traffic crossing between spoke networks must be checked against known attack signatures (intrusion detection and prevention). Step 1: host-name filtering is not in Basic, so the tier must be at least Standard. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: the answer is Premium, and the expected peak of 4 Gbps must be checked against that tier's throughput ceiling.
choices: Web category filtering is included in Basic, so Basic covers the requirement.
Intrusion detection and prevention is a Premium feature, so the requirement forces the Premium tier.
Basic supports host-name rules, so Standard is unnecessary.
Throughput limits only matter for Basic, so Premium needs no capacity check.
questions.why: Intrusion detection and prevention is listed as a Premium feature, so it is the step that rules Standard out and makes Premium the required tier.

questions.prompt: Which Azure Firewall tier adds TLS inspection, meaning decrypting, checking and re-encrypting HTTPS traffic?
choices: Standard
Standard and Basic together
Premium
Basic
questions.why: TLS inspection is described as a Premium feature, added on top of Standard, which in turn adds host-name and web category filtering.

questions.prompt: A small development team has about 200 Mbps of traffic and needs outbound access only to two named host names, with no deep inspection. Which tier should they choose, using the cheapest tier that covers every requirement?
choices: Premium, because it is the most capable tier available
Basic, because it is designed for small workloads and host-name rules are a Basic feature
Premium, because the team wants room to grow later
Standard, because it adds host-name filtering that Basic lacks
questions.why: Host-name filtering is a Standard feature not present in Basic, and the workload is modest, so Standard is the cheapest tier meeting the requirement.

questions.prompt: A team deploys Azure Firewall on the Basic tier for a branch whose expected peak is well above that tier's ceiling. What is the most likely consequence in the running system?
choices: Premium inspection features switch on to handle the load
Azure automatically upgrades the tier and no traffic is affected
Traffic may be dropped or delayed at peak times
All traffic is blocked permanently until the tier is changed
questions.why: Each tier has a throughput ceiling, and an undersized tier can drop or delay traffic at peak, so the consequence is degraded delivery rather than automatic upgrade or total blockage.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose an Azure Firewall SKU for a new workload. Name one tradeoff between cost and capability, and one limit you would need to check before committing.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start by listing what the workload needs the firewall to do, such as filtering by domain name, filtering by web category, or inspecting encrypted traffic. Each need points to the lowest tier that supports it: domain and category filtering push us to Standard, and TLS inspection or intrusion detection pushes us to Premium. Then I check the expected traffic volume against that tier's throughput limit, because a tier that inspects well but cannot keep up at peak will cause delays. The tradeoff is cost: Premium costs more per hour and per data unit, so paying for features nobody uses is waste. I would also flag that changing tiers later is disruptive, so I want the choice settled before deployment.
rubricPoints: Matches each required feature to the lowest Azure Firewall tier that includes it
Checks expected traffic volume against the tier's throughput limit
Names cost as a tradeoff against extra inspection features
Notes that changing tiers later is disruptive, so the choice belongs in design

suggested.rationale: Choosing a tier means reasoning from a requirement list to features and traffic limits, which is best practised through exam-style scenarios rather than a single listed mission or engine.

lessons.plain: A firewall is a checkpoint on the road between networks that decides which traffic may pass. Azure Firewall is Microsoft's managed version of that checkpoint: you do not patch or run the hardware, you place it in your network and send traffic through it. Designing a deployment means deciding where the checkpoint sits, which traffic is forced through it, how it gets its own subnet and address, and how it stays available. If placement and routing are right, every chosen flow is inspected. If they are wrong, the firewall exists on paper while traffic walks around it.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose you add a firewall to a hub network, but the spoke networks have no routing changes at all. Do you think traffic from a spoke heading to the internet passes through the firewall? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
A virtual network (VNet) is a private address space in Azure that you divide into subnets. A hub-and-spoke design places shared services such as a firewall in a central hub VNet, while workload VNets (spokes) connect to the hub. A route is an entry that tells traffic which next hop to use. A user-defined route (UDR) is a route you create yourself to override Azure's default routing. The firewall needs its own dedicated subnet, named AzureFirewallSubnet and usually sized at /26 or larger, and a public IP address if it must reach the internet.

Why it works: a firewall only inspects traffic that is actually routed to it. So for each spoke subnet you attach a route table with a route for 0.0.0.0/0 (meaning all internet-bound traffic) whose next hop is the firewall's private IP. Azure Firewall is stateful, meaning it tracks each connection, so replies must return through the same firewall. Routes must therefore be designed for both directions.

Worked example: the hub subnet AzureFirewallSubnet is 10.0.1.0/26 and the firewall gets private IP 10.0.1.4. Step 1: a VM in spoke A (10.1.0.0/24) sends a packet to the internet. Step 2: the route table on spoke A's subnet says 0.0.0.0/0 goes to 10.0.1.4. Step 3: the packet reaches the firewall, which applies its rules and allows or denies it. Step 4: the reply comes back through the firewall, because the route tables on the return path also point to it.

Common mistake: deploying the firewall but skipping the route tables. The firewall then sees no spoke traffic, its logs stay quiet, and internet-bound traffic leaves directly as if the firewall were absent.

In a running system, a missing or one-directional route creates two failures: traffic that should be blocked gets through unseen, or connections break because replies bypass the firewall and stateful tracking loses the session. A correct design makes the firewall both the enforcement point and the only path.

questions.prompt: Northwind Logistics has a hub VNet 10.20.0.0/16 with a dedicated firewall subnet AzureFirewallSubnet at 10.20.4.0/26. The Azure Firewall gets private IP 10.20.4.4. A workload VNet spoke B uses subnet 10.30.2.0/24, and its route table has a 0.0.0.0/0 route whose next hop is 10.20.4.4. Trace one HTTPS session. Step 1: a VM at 10.30.2.15 sends a packet to a public website. Step 2: the spoke B route table sends it to 10.20.4.4. Step 3: the firewall receives the packet, applies its rules, and allows it to the internet. Step 4 is missing. Which statement correctly completes step 4 so the session stays intact?
choices: The firewall forwards the reply straight to the VM and skips the spoke route table because it already knows the destination.
The reply travels back through the firewall because the return-path routes also point to 10.20.4.4, so the firewall can match it to the session it tracked.
The reply is sent to the firewall's public IP and then the firewall copies it into a new session with the VM, which means the original connection is not reused.
The website's reply is delivered directly to 10.30.2.15 because public internet traffic ignores private route tables.
questions.why: Azure Firewall is stateful, so the reply must pass through the same firewall that tracked the outbound connection, and that requires the return-path routes to point to the firewall.

questions.prompt: A planner reserves the subnet 10.50.0.0/27 and names it AzureFirewallSubnet for a new Azure Firewall in a hub VNet. Which statement best describes the problem with this plan?
choices: The subnet name is wrong, so the firewall must be placed in a subnet called FirewallSubnet instead.
The subnet is fine, but the firewall needs a route table with 0.0.0.0/0 attached to the subnet itself.
The subnet is smaller than the /26 or larger size the design usually calls for, so it should be resized.
Nothing is wrong, because the firewall only needs a /27 when it has no public IP address.
questions.why: The teaching text says the firewall subnet is usually sized /26 or larger and must be named AzureFirewallSubnet, so a /27 falls short of the usual sizing.

questions.prompt: A hub firewall is deployed and healthy. Spoke C's subnet has a route table with 0.0.0.0/0 pointing to the firewall private IP, but the firewall logs show no outbound traffic from a VM in spoke C, and that VM reaches the internet normally. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The route table exists but is not associated with the spoke C subnet, so default routing sends traffic directly to the internet.
The firewall is stateful, so it does not log traffic that starts from a spoke VM.
The firewall subnet is too large, which stops it from receiving packets from other VNets.
The VM needs its own public IP address before any firewall can see its traffic.
questions.why: A route table only affects traffic from the subnet it is attached to, so an unattached route table leaves the spoke using default routing and the firewall never sees the traffic.

questions.prompt: In a hub-and-spoke design, the outbound route from spoke D sends internet traffic to the firewall, but the return route on the other side is missing, so replies reach the spoke by a different path that skips the firewall. What happens to the connection?
choices: The firewall blocks the outbound request by default because it cannot confirm the route.
The connection breaks, because the firewall cannot match the reply to the session it tracked, so the reply is not part of a known connection.
The connection works normally and the firewall logs it twice, once for each direction.
Azure automatically reroutes the reply through the firewall, so nothing breaks.
questions.why: Because the firewall is stateful, a reply that bypasses it cannot be matched to the tracked session, so the connection fails.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says the Azure Firewall design is finished once the firewall is deployed in the hub. In your own words, explain to them what else must be designed so the firewall actually inspects spoke traffic, and name one limit or tradeoff of routing everything through a central firewall.
lessons.modelAnswer: Deploying the firewall is only the first step. Every spoke subnet that should be inspected needs a user-defined route, typically a 0.0.0.0/0 route for internet traffic and routes for spoke-to-spoke traffic, with the firewall's private IP as the next hop. The firewall needs its own AzureFirewallSubnet, a public IP if it serves internet traffic, and routes for the return path so replies pass through it too, otherwise the stateful inspection breaks. The main tradeoff is that the firewall becomes a central point of traffic and cost: its throughput limits, its availability, and the added latency of every hop all have to be sized and planned. Teams often add zone redundancy or capacity planning for that reason.
rubricPoints: Spoke subnets need user-defined routes pointing at the firewall's private IP, not just a firewall in the hub.
The firewall needs a dedicated AzureFirewallSubnet of adequate size and, for internet traffic, a public IP.
Return traffic must also route through the firewall because it is stateful.
A central firewall is a throughput, availability, and latency tradeoff that must be planned for.

suggested.rationale: Tracing the hop-by-hop path of a packet through hub and spoke routes is the core reasoning skill this objective needs and the planned path tracer would practice it directly.

lessons.plain: A cloud firewall is a managed security checkpoint that sits at the edge of a group of networks and decides which traffic may pass, based on rules you write. Azure Firewall is Microsoft's version: you deploy it into your network as a managed service rather than running a device yourself, then steer traffic through it. Deploying it means choosing where it sits, giving it a public address for outbound and published inbound traffic, and making sure the traffic you care about actually goes through it instead of around it. Placement and routing matter as much as the rules, because a firewall that nothing is routed through protects nothing.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you place a firewall inside a virtual network but leave every subnet's default routing unchanged, do you think traffic leaving a subnet will pass through the firewall? Why or why not?
lessons.teach: Azure Firewall is a managed, stateful firewall: a service that inspects traffic as connections open and remembers each connection so that return traffic is matched to it. A virtual network is your private address space in the cloud, and a subnet is a slice of that space. To deploy the firewall, you first need a virtual network containing a subnet named exactly AzureFirewallSubnet, sized at least /26 and reserved for the firewall alone. You then create the firewall in that subnet and attach a public IP address, which it uses for outbound connections and for inbound rules that publish services. Rules are grouped into rule collections with priorities. The firewall evaluates translation rules (DNAT, which map an incoming public address and port to a private one) first, then network rules (matching source and destination IP address, port and protocol), then application rules (matching fully qualified domain names such as a web host name). Lower priority numbers are evaluated first, and the first matching allow or deny decides the outcome for that rule type. Worked example: a spoke subnet 10.2.0.0/24 may reach a storage endpoint on TCP 443 only. Step one, create a network rule allowing source 10.2.0.0/24 to that destination on TCP 443. Step two, create a route table with a default route, 0.0.0.0/0, whose next hop is the firewall's private IP, and attach that table to the spoke subnet. Step three, check the firewall logs to confirm the connection matched the rule. Common mistake: creating the firewall and its rules but skipping the route table, so the spoke's traffic never reaches the firewall and no rule runs. In a live system this looks healthy because traffic still works, yet it leaves no firewall log entries, so nothing was inspected. A firewall only protects the traffic that is routed through it.

questions.prompt: Harbor Point Logistics runs a parcel-tracking app in spoke subnet 10.30.2.0/24 that may reach only the host updates.parcel-track.example over HTTPS. Their hub virtual network is 10.30.0.0/22, with AzureFirewallSubnet at 10.30.0.0/26, and the firewall is deployed there with public IP 198.51.100.44. An application rule at priority 300 allows source 10.30.2.0/24 to that host name on TCP 443. Step four has not been done yet. Which action must be completed so this app's traffic actually passes through the firewall?
choices: Resize AzureFirewallSubnet to a /24 so the firewall can inspect spoke traffic.
Raise the application rule to priority 50 so it is evaluated before network rules.
Create a route table with a default route 0.0.0.0/0 whose next hop is the firewall's private IP, and associate that table with subnet 10.30.2.0/24.
Add a DNAT rule mapping 198.51.100.44 port 443 to 10.30.2.0/24 so the outbound call is translated.
questions.why: Traffic only reaches the firewall's rules if a route table sends the spoke subnet's default traffic to the firewall's private IP, and that table must be attached to the spoke subnet.

questions.prompt: What does it mean that Azure Firewall is described as stateful?
choices: It keeps its configuration saved so the rules survive a restart of the virtual network.
It checks each packet on its own and forgets it once the rule has been applied.
It remembers open connections so that return traffic is matched to the connection it belongs to.
It decides only from the host name in a web request, ignoring addresses and ports.
questions.why: Stateful means the firewall tracks each connection as it opens, so replies are recognised as part of an allowed connection rather than being judged as brand-new traffic.

questions.prompt: A firewall has a network rule collection at priority 200 that denies source 10.40.1.0/24 to destination 192.0.2.10 on TCP 22. A second network rule collection at priority 500 allows the same source, destination and port. A connection attempt from 10.40.1.0/24 to 192.0.2.10 on TCP 22 arrives. What happens?
choices: Denied only after the application rules have also been checked.
Allowed, because allow rules always override deny rules in Azure Firewall.
Allowed, because the allow rule is the more specific match.
Denied, because priority 200 is evaluated first and its deny matches.
questions.why: Lower priority numbers are evaluated first and the first matching allow or deny decides the outcome, so the priority 200 deny is reached and applied before the priority 500 allow.

questions.prompt: A team plans a new virtual network and creates AzureFirewallSubnet with the address range 10.60.0.0/27, intending to place other workloads in the same subnet beside the firewall. What is the problem with this plan?
choices: Nothing is wrong, since /27 is a valid size for any subnet and sharing with workloads is fine.
The subnet must be /24 or larger because a firewall needs a full /24 of addresses.
The subnet is fine, but the firewall's public IP must also be sized /27 to match.
The subnet is smaller than the minimum; it must be at least /26 and hold only the firewall.
questions.why: The firewall subnet must be named exactly AzureFirewallSubnet, sized at least /26, and reserved for the firewall alone, so a /27 shared with other workloads breaks the deployment requirement.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what must be true, beyond creating the firewall itself, for it to filter a subnet's outbound traffic, and name one limit or tradeoff of this setup.
lessons.modelAnswer: Creating the firewall is not enough. The firewall has to sit in its own subnet named AzureFirewallSubnet with a public IP attached, and the subnet you want filtered needs a route table with a default route pointing at the firewall's private IP. Without that route, the subnet's traffic goes straight out and skips the firewall, so none of the rules apply. Rules then decide what is allowed, by IP, port and protocol for network rules, or by domain name for application rules. One tradeoff is cost and sizing: the firewall is a billed, always-on managed service, and everything routed through it adds a hop and depends on its capacity. A second limit is that rules only see what is routed through the firewall, so routing mistakes can silently remove protection.
rubricPoints: Explains that the firewall must sit in a dedicated AzureFirewallSubnet with a public IP.
States that traffic must be routed to the firewall, usually with a default route in a route table.
Describes how network rules and application rules match traffic differently (IP, port, protocol versus domain name).
Names a real tradeoff such as cost, added hop, or the risk that a routing mistake silently bypasses inspection.

suggested.rationale: Deployment steps and portal settings are reference facts best learned by reading, and no listed mission or planned engine has the learner build a firewall deployment.

lessons.plain: Azure Firewall is a managed firewall that checks network traffic against a list of allow and deny rules. Think of it as a security guard at a building entrance with a clipboard. The guard can check who is calling by address and door number, or by the name of the company they are visiting. Rules tell the guard what to let through. Anything not on an allow list is turned away by default, so a missing rule is usually the first suspect when a connection fails. This objective is about writing those rules well: choosing the right kind of rule, the right order, and the right scope.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web server in a private subnet must download updates from one vendor's website but must not reach any other internet site. Would you write a rule using that website's IP addresses or a rule using its host name? Why?
lessons.teach:
Azure Firewall is a managed, stateful firewall that sits at the edge of a virtual network or hub and inspects traffic routed through it. You do not patch or size a box yourself. Its rules are grouped into rule collections, and each collection holds rules of one kind. A network rule matches on source and destination IP addresses, the destination port, and the protocol such as TCP or UDP; it is the generic layer-4 check. An application rule matches on the fully qualified domain name (FQDN, the full host name of a site, such as a website name) and on web protocols, so it can allow one specific site without you tracking that site's changing IP addresses. A DNAT rule (destination network address translation) forwards an inbound connection arriving at a public address to a private address behind the firewall. Each rule collection has a priority number between 100 and 65000; lower numbers are evaluated first, and each rule's action is either allow or deny.

Why it works: the firewall evaluates in a fixed order. DNAT rules come first, then network rules, then application rules. When a flow matches an allow rule, evaluation stops for that flow. When nothing matches, the traffic is denied by default. Writing a rule therefore means choosing the right kind of rule and the right place in that order.

Worked example: a web server in the subnet 10.1.0.0/24 needs to call api.example.com over HTTPS. Step one: the firewall sees an outbound connection from 10.1.0.0/24 to port 443. Step two: no DNAT rule matches, because this is outbound. Step three: a network rule allowing any destination on port 443 would work, but it is broader than needed. Step four: the better choice is an application rule with source 10.1.0.0/24, target FQDN api.example.com, and protocol https on port 443. It matches, so the flow is allowed. Any other site falls through to the default deny.

Common mistake: pinning a rule to the IP addresses of a SaaS endpoint. Those addresses change, the rule silently stops matching, and traffic is blocked at the firewall while nothing on the server looks wrong.

Consequence in a running system: an overly strict rule shows up as timeouts or failed package downloads, so the firewall logs are the first place to check.

questions.prompt: A logistics company has a monitoring agent at 192.168.10.25 on the subnet 192.168.10.0/24 that must reach a partner's API. The partner's API is reached at public address 203.0.113.50 on port 8443, and the firewall should forward it to the private server 10.20.3.7 on port 443. Step one: an inbound connection arrives at 203.0.113.50 on port 8443. Step two: a DNAT rule (destination network address translation, which rewrites a public destination to a private one) matches and rewrites the destination to 10.20.3.7 on port 443. Step three: [missing; work it out]. Step four: the translated flow is allowed and evaluation stops for that flow.
choices: A DNAT rule applied a second time, to rewrite the port back to 8443.
An application rule with target FQDN api.partner-example.com, because the agent uses a host name.
The default deny, because inbound traffic is never evaluated after a DNAT match.
A network rule that matches the translated flow by destination IP 10.20.3.7, destination port 443, and protocol TCP, because the destination is a fixed private address and port.
questions.why: After DNAT, the translated flow has a fixed private IP and port, so the generic layer-4 check, a network rule matching IP, port and protocol, is the kind that fits this step.

questions.prompt: Which kind of firewall rule matches on a fully qualified domain name (the full host name of a site) and web protocols, so you do not have to track the site's changing IP addresses?
choices: A network rule
An application rule
A priority rule
A DNAT rule
questions.why: Application rules match on the FQDN and web protocols, which lets them allow a named site without tracking its IP addresses.

questions.prompt: Two rules in the same firewall both match one flow. One is an allow rule with priority 500 and the other is a deny rule with priority 200. Which one decides the outcome, and why?
choices: Neither, because a conflict makes the firewall skip both rules.
The deny rule at 200, because lower numbers are evaluated first and evaluation stops at the first matching allow or deny.
Whichever rule was written first, because priority numbers only matter between rules of the same kind.
The allow rule at 500, because a higher number is evaluated first.
questions.why: Lower priority numbers are evaluated first, so the deny at 200 is reached before the allow at 500 and decides that flow.

questions.prompt: A server in 10.4.0.0/16 sends traffic to port 8080 on a destination that no rule in the firewall matches. What happens to that flow, and what should you check first if the application reports timeouts?
choices: It is allowed, because the firewall is managed and permits unmatched traffic by default; check the DNAT rules first.
It is denied only if an explicit deny rule exists, so check the application's DNS settings first.
It is denied by default, because nothing matched; check the firewall logs for the denied flow.
It is allowed after the network rules run out, so check the priority numbers of the application rules first.
questions.why: Unmatched traffic falls through to the default deny, and the firewall logs are the place to confirm that a flow was blocked.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how Azure Firewall decides whether to allow a connection, and name one limit of IP-based rules compared with name-based rules.
lessons.modelAnswer: Azure Firewall checks each new connection against rule collections in a fixed order: address translation rules for inbound traffic first, then network rules that match source and destination IP address, port and protocol, then application rules that match the host name and web protocol. Lower priority numbers in a collection are checked first. The first matching allow rule lets the flow through; if nothing matches, the connection is denied. The main limit of IP-based rules is that a service's addresses can change, so a rule that worked last month can silently stop matching and block legitimate traffic. Name-based application rules avoid that for web traffic, because the firewall matches the requested host name. The tradeoff is that application rules only cover web-style protocols, so other traffic still needs network rules, which cannot match on names.
rubricPoints: Describes the fixed evaluation order: translation rules, then network rules, then application rules
States that lower priority numbers are evaluated first and that no match means default deny
Names the limit of IP-based rules: the addresses behind a service can change and silently break the rule
Explains that application rules match host names for web protocols, and that other protocols still need network rules

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style scenario about which rule type fits a requirement adds the most here, since the skill is choosing the right control and predicting what it allows or blocks.

lessons.plain: Azure Firewall Manager is a central place to set up the firewalls that guard a cloud network and the rules those firewalls follow. Instead of logging into each firewall and typing the same rules again, you write a rule set once, and many firewalls can use it. Think of a head office that publishes one security rulebook for every branch building. Each branch can add its own local rules, but the head office rules still apply everywhere. This lesson covers how that shared rulebook is built, how it is applied, and what can go wrong when it is not connected to anything.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose you run ten firewalls across three regions and want all of them to block the same list of known-bad destinations. Would you rather edit the rules on each firewall separately, or write the rule once and share it with all of them? Why?
lessons.teach:
Azure Firewall is a managed network firewall that filters traffic moving between networks and out to the internet. Azure Firewall Manager is the central control point for creating, grouping and applying these firewalls and their rules across many subscriptions and regions. The rules themselves live in a firewall policy, a separate reusable object that one or more firewalls can reference. Inside a policy, rules are grouped into rule collection groups, and each group holds rule collections. Every rule collection has a priority number, and lower numbers are evaluated first.

Why it works: a policy can have a parent policy. A child policy inherits the parent's rules, so a security team can set a baseline once, such as blocking known bad destinations, and every child applies it automatically. A child can add its own rules on top, but it cannot remove what the parent enforces.

Worked example: a parent policy denies outbound traffic to a list of malicious addresses at priority 100. A child policy for the production hub adds an allow rule for a payments API at priority 200. Traffic to the payments API arrives. The engine checks the parent's deny rule first: the destination is not on the list, so it does not match. It then reaches the child's allow rule at priority 200 and passes. Traffic to a listed bad address matches the parent's deny at priority 100 and is blocked before any allow rule is reached.

Common mistake: creating a policy but never associating it with a firewall or a virtual hub, then assuming traffic is filtered. An unassociated policy enforces nothing.

Consequence: one bad rule in a shared parent policy changes behaviour in every child at once, so changes to parent policies need the same review as production changes.

questions.prompt: A retail company has one firewall policy with a single rule collection group containing two rule collections. Collection X has priority 400 and allows outbound HTTPS to any destination for its web team. Collection Y has priority 150 and denies outbound traffic to the 192.0.2.0/24 range, a partner's test network. A request arrives on HTTPS for 192.0.2.44. Step 1: the engine sorts the rule collections by priority, so it reaches Y before X. Step 2: 192.0.2.44 falls inside 192.0.2.0/24, so Y matches. Step 3: the engine has found a match at Y, and the question is what happens to the request and whether X is ever checked.
choices: Allowed, because the HTTPS allow in collection X at priority 400 also matches and allow rules override deny rules
Blocked by collection Y at priority 150, and collection X is never reached
Allowed, because a deny rule only takes effect when the policy has a parent policy
Blocked only after both collections are evaluated, with the higher priority number winning
questions.why: Lower priority numbers are evaluated first, so Y matches and stops the evaluation before X's allow rule is reached.

questions.prompt: In a firewall policy hierarchy, what is the correct description of how a child policy relates to its parent?
choices: A child policy replaces the parent's rules entirely once it is created, so the parent has no effect afterwards
A child policy only applies rules that are copied manually from the parent, so later parent changes do not reach it
A child policy overrides the parent whenever its rule priority number is lower than the parent's
A child policy inherits the parent's rules and can add its own, but cannot remove rules the parent enforces
questions.why: A child inherits the parent's rules automatically, may add rules on top, and cannot take away what the parent enforces, so the lower-number option is wrong because priority numbers do not let a child override a parent.

questions.prompt: A network engineer writes a deny rule in a firewall policy for traffic from a set of spoke networks, then assumes the traffic is being blocked. The policy has never been attached to a firewall or a virtual hub. What is the actual state of the traffic?
choices: The traffic is blocked, because deny rules take effect as soon as they are saved in a policy
The traffic is blocked at the priority number the rule was given, but only during business hours
The traffic is blocked only for the spoke networks that have a parent policy
The traffic is not filtered by this policy at all, because an unassociated policy enforces nothing
questions.why: A policy only takes effect once it is associated with a firewall or hub, so until then the deny rule is never applied to any traffic.

questions.prompt: A security team adds a new deny rule at priority 100 to a parent firewall policy that three child policies inherit from. What is the most important consequence the team should plan for?
choices: The change applies only to traffic that originates in a region the parent policy was created in
Only the child policy the team edits will change, since children do not read the parent after creation
The change takes effect in every child policy at once, so it needs the same review as a production change
The change is ignored by children whose own rules have lower priority numbers than 100
questions.why: Children inherit from the parent, so one change to the parent alters behaviour in every child at the same time, which is why parent changes need production-level review.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says, 'Let's put every rule in one shared Firewall Manager policy so we never have to touch individual firewalls again.' Explain to them how parent and child firewall policies with inheritance work, and name one limit or tradeoff of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: Firewall Manager policies are reusable rule objects. A parent policy holds rules that every child policy inherits, and each child attaches to one or more firewalls or virtual hubs. Rules are grouped into rule collection groups, and priority numbers decide which rule is checked first, with lower numbers first. This means a baseline, like blocking known bad destinations, is written once and applied everywhere. The tradeoff is that a child cannot remove a parent rule, so a mistake in the parent spreads to every child at once. A change to a shared parent needs careful review and staged rollout. Also, a policy does nothing until it is associated with a firewall, so the link has to be checked as part of any deployment.
rubricPoints: Explains that a firewall policy is a reusable rule object that firewalls or hubs reference.
Explains parent and child inheritance, and that children add rules but cannot remove parent rules.
Explains that lower priority numbers are evaluated first.
Names a tradeoff, such as one parent mistake affecting every child at once.
Notes that a policy enforces nothing until it is associated with a firewall or hub.

suggested.rationale: An exam-style scenario about which rule set wins and what breaks when a parent policy changes adds more than reading alone, and no listed mission or planned engine teaches firewall policy directly.

lessons.plain: Imagine a large office building where every tenant's hallway connects to a central lobby. Instead of letting people walk freely between floors, you put a security desk in that lobby and make everyone pass through it. This lesson is about putting that kind of checkpoint inside a managed central network. Azure Virtual WAN gives you a central hub that joins your branch offices and your cloud networks. Azure Firewall is a managed filter that inspects traffic and allows or blocks it by rule. Deploying the firewall inside the hub means traffic crossing the hub can be checked at one place, instead of trusting every network to guard itself.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company has three branch offices and ten cloud networks all connected to one central hub. If you place a firewall in that hub but do nothing else, do you think traffic between two cloud networks will pass through the firewall? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
Definitions. A virtual hub is the central, Microsoft-managed network inside Azure Virtual WAN that connects branch sites, VPN and ExpressRoute links, and virtual networks (called spokes) to one another. Azure Firewall is a managed stateful firewall: it tracks each connection and applies rules that allow or deny traffic by source, destination, port and protocol. A secured hub is a virtual hub with an Azure Firewall deployed into it. Traffic that matches no allow rule is denied by default.

Why it works. Once the firewall sits in the hub, the hub can be told to send chosen kinds of traffic through it. The setting that does this is called routing intent: you choose which traffic class, private traffic between branches and spokes, or internet-bound traffic, must go to the firewall. Without that choice, the hub routes spoke-to-spoke traffic directly and the firewall never sees it.

Worked example. A branch office uses 10.10.0.0/16. A spoke virtual network 10.2.0.0/16 holds a SQL database subnet. Step 1: the firewall is deployed into the hub. Step 2: routing intent sends private traffic to the firewall. Step 3: a branch host opens a connection to 10.2.1.4 on TCP port 1433. Step 4: the hub forwards the packet to the firewall first, not straight to the spoke. Step 5: the rule 'allow branch subnet to database subnet on TCP 1433' matches, so the packet continues. Step 6: a connection from the same branch on TCP 3389 matches no allow rule and is dropped.

Common mistake. Deploying the firewall and assuming it protects everything. If routing intent is not set, traffic bypasses the firewall, and its logs show nothing for that flow.

Consequence. In a running system, a missing routing setting means a compromised spoke can reach another spoke freely while the team believes it is filtered. The hub's address range must also not overlap any connected network, or routing becomes ambiguous.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm has a secured virtual hub in Azure Virtual WAN (a managed hub that joins branches, VPNs and virtual networks), with an Azure Firewall deployed in it and routing intent set to send private traffic through the firewall. Its order-API spoke network is 10.60.0.0/16 and its reporting spoke is 10.70.0.0/16. Step 1: a reporting host at 10.70.3.9 opens a connection to 10.60.1.5 on TCP port 8443. Step 2: the hub sends the packet to the firewall before it reaches the order-API spoke. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: a second attempt from the same host on TCP port 22 reaches the firewall and is dropped, because no allow rule covers it. Which statement correctly completes step 3?
choices: The firewall forwards the packet because no deny rule exists, so unmatched traffic is allowed by default.
The firewall rewrites the destination to the hub's address range, so the order API never receives the packet.
The firewall finds the rule 'allow reporting subnet to order-API subnet on TCP 8443' matches, so it forwards the packet on to 10.60.1.5.
The hub sends the packet straight to 10.60.1.5, because the firewall only inspects traffic bound for the internet.
questions.why: The firewall is stateful and default-deny, so a flow that matches an allow rule is passed on to its real destination, which is what step 3 must say.

questions.prompt: In a secured Azure Virtual WAN hub, what does routing intent control?
choices: Which private or internet-bound traffic classes are sent through the firewall
The password policy for administrators who manage the hub
The public IP addresses the firewall may use for outbound traffic from each spoke
How many branch sites are allowed to connect to the hub at the same time
questions.why: Routing intent is the hub setting that chooses which traffic classes, such as private traffic between branches and spokes or internet-bound traffic, must be forwarded to the firewall.

questions.prompt: A team deploys Azure Firewall into its secured hub and writes allow rules for the branch-to-database path. A compromised spoke can still reach another spoke on TCP port 445 with no log entries on the firewall. Routing intent for private traffic has never been set. What best explains this?
choices: Spoke-to-spoke traffic bypasses the firewall, because no routing intent steers it through the firewall
The firewall logs have been turned off, so the traffic is being filtered but not recorded
The firewall rule needs an explicit deny for TCP 445 before the firewall will inspect that port
Azure Firewall only inspects traffic that originates from on-premises branch sites
questions.why: Without routing intent the hub routes spoke-to-spoke traffic directly, so the firewall never sees those packets and cannot log or filter them.

questions.prompt: A hub uses the address range 10.5.0.0/24, and a spoke virtual network is connected that uses 10.5.0.0/20. What is the main problem with this design?
choices: The firewall will automatically translate the overlapping range into a new one
The spoke will run faster because the two address ranges are effectively merged
Routing becomes ambiguous because both networks claim the same addresses
Only the spoke's rules are applied, and the hub's rules are skipped
questions.why: When the hub's range overlaps a connected network, the routing table cannot tell which network a packet belongs to, so the hub's address range must not overlap any connected network.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what it means to deploy Azure Firewall inside a Virtual WAN hub, and name one limit or tradeoff of a secured hub compared with giving each spoke its own firewall.
lessons.modelAnswer: A secured hub puts the firewall in the middle of the central network, so traffic between branches, the internet and attached virtual networks can be inspected at one place and managed once. The firewall alone does not do the job. We also have to set routing intent so the hub sends the traffic classes we care about through it, otherwise spoke-to-spoke traffic goes around it. The tradeoff is that everything crossing the hub now depends on one central control point: it adds cost, it can become a bottleneck, and a rule change affects many teams at once. Each spoke with its own firewall gives teams independence, but the rules end up scattered and harder to audit. Before relying on it, I would confirm the routing setting and test a blocked port from a branch to check that it is actually dropped.
rubricPoints: Defines a virtual hub and a secured hub, with Azure Firewall deployed inside the hub.
Explains that routing intent must send chosen traffic through the firewall, or it is bypassed.
Describes firewall rules as allow or deny by source, destination, port and protocol, with unmatched traffic denied.
Names a tradeoff such as a central control point, cost, or shared rule changes versus per-spoke independence.
Recommends verifying with a test of a blocked flow rather than assuming protection.

suggested.rationale: The planned virtual network path tracer would let the learner see whether a spoke-to-spoke flow actually passes through the hub firewall.

lessons.plain: A web application firewall is a filter that sits in front of a website or web API and reads the web requests themselves: the page address being asked for, the query text, the form fields and the headers. A basic network filter only sees where traffic comes from and which port it targets. This kind of filter understands the messages inside the traffic and can recognise common attacks, such as someone trying to slip database commands into a search box. Think of it as a guard who reads the letter rather than just checking the return address. Mapping a requirement to it means asking whether the problem is about the content of web requests, or only about who may connect at all.
lessons.guessPrompt: A login form on your public website is receiving thousands of requests whose username field contains fragments of database commands. Before reading anything, which kind of control would you reach for first, and why would a rule that only looks at source addresses and port numbers not be enough to stop it?
lessons.teach:
A web application firewall (WAF) is a layer 7 filter, meaning it inspects HTTP and HTTPS requests: the web messages that carry the page path, query parameters, headers and body. In Azure it is attached to a delivery point such as Azure Front Door or Application Gateway, so it examines requests before they reach your application. Its main features map to requirements. A managed rule set is a prepared collection of detection rules, usually based on the OWASP Top 10 categories of web attacks such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting; you switch it on rather than writing patterns yourself. A custom rule is one you write, with match conditions (for example a client IP range, a country, a header value or a URL path) and an action such as allow, block, log or rate-limit. Rate limiting counts requests from a client over a time window and acts when a threshold is crossed. Custom rules are checked in priority order, and a terminating action such as allow or block ends evaluation. A WAF policy can run in detection mode, which logs matches but lets them through, or in prevention mode, which blocks them. An exclusion tells a rule set to ignore a named field that legitimately contains text that looks like an attack, such as a rich-text comment box.

Worked example: a public site must block SQL injection, but the team fears blocking real customers. Step 1: enable the SQL injection managed rules. Step 2: set the policy to detection mode. Step 3: review logs and find that a search parameter called q matches attack patterns on ordinary searches. Step 4: add an exclusion for that single field. Step 5: switch the policy to prevention mode.

Common mistake: switching straight to prevention mode on day one and blocking legitimate users. Consequence: a running checkout can start returning 403 errors to customers within minutes of the change, which is why the detection-then-prevention path exists.

A WAF does not replace a network security group, which filters by address and port and cannot read web content. When a requirement is about what a web request says, the WAF is the control that fits; when it is about which addresses or ports may reach a resource at all, a network control is the right choice.

questions.prompt: A ticket-resale site runs behind Azure Front Door, with a web application firewall (WAF) policy attached. The team wants to slow password guessing on the sign-in page /account/signin without blocking shoppers who log in normally. Step 1: add a custom rule whose match condition is that the URL path contains /account/signin. Step 2: set the rule's action to rate-limit, with a threshold of 15 requests per client IP address in a one-minute window. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: after a week of logs shows that no normal shopper crossed the threshold, switch the policy to prevention mode. Which step belongs in place of Step 3?
choices: Add an exclusion on the path /account/signin so the rate-limit rule ignores it
Move the rule to a priority below the managed rules so it is checked after them
Change the rule's action from rate-limit to block so the threshold is enforced immediately
Keep the policy in detection mode while the rule runs, so matches are logged but not blocked, and review those logs
questions.why: Detection mode logs matches without blocking them, which lets the team confirm that the rate-limit threshold does not catch normal shoppers before prevention mode is turned on, as the staged path in the teaching text requires.

questions.prompt: What does it mean that a WAF works at layer 7?
choices: It inspects the content of HTTP and HTTPS requests, such as the path, query parameters, headers and body
It filters traffic only by source IP address and destination port
It counts packets at the network interface before they reach any application
It encrypts traffic between the client and the delivery point
questions.why: Layer 7 means the filter reads the web request itself, which is what the teaching text describes; address-and-port filtering is the job of a network security group instead.

questions.prompt: A company has two requirements. Requirement A: only the office range 10.20.0.0/16 may open remote desktop (port 3389) to a virtual machine. Requirement B: requests to its order API must be blocked when the query string contains SQL fragments such as a quote followed by OR 1=1. Which control fits Requirement B?
choices: A network security group rule that denies port 3389 from all sources
An Azure Firewall rule that allows only the office address range
A WAF managed rule set for SQL injection, in prevention mode, attached to the delivery point
A network security group rule that blocks the API's public IP address
questions.why: Requirement B is about what the web request says, and only a WAF reading the request content with a SQL injection rule set can match that text; the other options are address-and-port controls that cannot read the query string.

questions.prompt: A WAF policy has two custom rules. Rule X is a block action that matches requests from one country. Rule Y is an allow action that matches requests from the same country. Rule X is checked first. A request arrives from that country. What happens?
choices: It is blocked, because Rule X is checked first and its terminating block action ends evaluation
It is logged and then passed to Rule Y, which decides the final outcome
It is rate-limited, because the two conflicting rules cancel each other out
It is allowed, because allow rules always override block rules
questions.why: Custom rules are checked in priority order and a terminating action such as block ends evaluation, so Rule Y is never reached and the request is blocked.

lessons.explainPrompt: A colleague says we should put our public web app behind a WAF and drop the network security group rules because the WAF is more advanced. In your own words, explain what a WAF inspects that an NSG cannot, name one tradeoff of starting a new WAF policy in detection mode, and say why you would still keep network-level controls.
lessons.modelAnswer: A WAF works at the HTTP layer, so it can read the request path, query parameters, headers and body, and match them against attack patterns or custom conditions. An NSG works at layers 3 and 4, filtering by source and destination address, port and protocol, so it cannot tell a normal search from an injected SQL fragment sent to the same port. The tradeoff of detection mode is that it is safe for customers because nothing is blocked, but attacks still reach the application until we review logs and move to prevention mode. We keep NSG rules because a WAF only protects the web endpoints it is attached to; restricting which networks can reach databases, management ports and other services is a separate job that only network-level controls do well.
rubricPoints: A WAF inspects HTTP request content such as paths, parameters and bodies, while an NSG filters only by address, port and protocol.
Detection mode logs matches without blocking, and prevention mode blocks them; the switch is made after tuning false positives.
Managed rule sets cover common web attacks, and custom rules handle specific conditions such as IP ranges, countries or rate limits.
Network-level controls remain needed for non-web services and for limiting which sources can reach resources at all.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or engine covers WAF policy, so reasoning through an exam-style requirement-to-feature mapping is the most useful practice.

lessons.plain: A web application firewall is a checkpoint that sits in front of a website or web API and reads each web request before it reaches the application. Ordinary network filters only look at addresses and ports, but a web application firewall looks inside the request itself, at the address being asked for, the query text, and the body, and checks it against known attack patterns. Designing one means deciding where the checkpoint stands, which attacks it should watch for, and how strictly it should act at the start, so that real customers are not turned away by mistake.
lessons.guessPrompt: A public shop website already sits behind a network firewall that allows traffic on port 443 (the standard secure web port). Why might an attacker still get through to the website, and what kind of filter would be needed to catch the attack?
lessons.teach:
A web application firewall, or WAF, is a filter that understands HTTP, the language browsers and web apps use to talk. Each request has parts: the host name, the path, the query string, headers, and the body. A WAF inspects those parts and matches them against rules. A managed rule set is a prebuilt collection of rules covering common attacks, such as SQL injection (hiding database commands inside ordinary input) and cross-site scripting (injecting script into a page). A custom rule is one you write yourself, for example limiting how many requests one address can make per minute.

Why it works: web attacks travel inside allowed traffic on port 443, so a network filter that checks only addresses and ports cannot tell a malicious request from a normal one. The WAF reads the content. Two design decisions matter. The first is placement. Azure Front Door applies the WAF at a global edge close to users, which suits public traffic arriving from many regions. Application Gateway applies it as a regional layer 7 load balancer inside a virtual network, which suits an app that runs in one region. The second is mode. Detection mode logs matches and lets requests through. Prevention mode blocks them.

Worked example: an API behind Application Gateway receives a request whose query text is id=1' OR '1'='1. Step 1: the request reaches the listener, the entry point that accepts traffic. Step 2: the WAF parses the query string. Step 3: the SQL injection rule matches. Step 4: in detection mode the match is logged and the request continues to the backend; in prevention mode the WAF returns a 403 Forbidden response and the backend never sees it.

Common mistake: switching to prevention on day one, so a legitimate search containing an apostrophe is blocked. The safer path is to start in detection, review the logs, add exclusions for false positives, and only then enable prevention. Consequence: a WAF in prevention mode without tuning turns false positives into real customer errors, so it needs ongoing operational attention rather than being set once and forgotten.

questions.prompt: A travel booking site runs a public API in one Azure region behind an Application Gateway with a WAF. A custom rule, which is a rule the team writes itself, allows at most 100 requests per minute from each client IP address. Step 1: client 198.51.100.23 sends its 101st request within one minute, and the request reaches the listener, the entry point that accepts traffic. Step 2: the WAF counts that address's requests in the current one-minute window. Step 3: the count of 101 is above the limit of 100, so the rate-limit rule matches. Step 4 is left for you: the WAF is running in detection mode. State what happens to this 101st request.
choices: The rule switches itself off, and every later request passes without a log entry.
It is blocked with a 403 Forbidden response and the API never sees it.
It is logged as a rule match and then forwarded to the API backend.
It is dropped silently by the subnet's NSG before it reaches the WAF.
questions.why: In detection mode the WAF records the match and lets the request continue to the backend, because only prevention mode blocks matched requests.

questions.prompt: Which description best defines a managed rule set in a web application firewall?
choices: A list of IP addresses that your team maintains by hand and blocks outright.
A prebuilt collection of rules covering common web attacks such as SQL injection.
A network filter that checks only source addresses and destination ports on each packet.
A rule you write yourself, such as a per-address request limit for your own app.
questions.why: A managed rule set is a prebuilt collection of inspection rules for common attacks, while a custom rule is one you write yourself and the other options describe different controls.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm serves customers in thirty countries through one public web application. The firm wants web attacks inspected close to users rather than in a single data centre region. Which placement fits this requirement, and why?
choices: Azure Front Door with its WAF, because the WAF runs at a global edge close to users arriving from many regions.
Azure Firewall with threat intelligence, because it inspects HTTP request bodies for cross-site scripting by default.
An NSG rule on port 443 that blocks requests containing SQL keywords, because network filters can read request content.
Application Gateway in one region, because a regional layer 7 load balancer is cheaper to run for a global user base.
questions.why: Front Door applies the WAF at a global edge close to users, which suits public traffic from many regions, whereas the other options either lack HTTP content inspection or fit a single-region app.

questions.prompt: A shop turns its WAF to prevention mode on the first day and without any tuning. Customers searching for names like O'Brien then receive 403 errors. Which response best fixes the problem while keeping protection in place?
choices: Permanently allow every request containing an apostrophe through a custom rule, without reviewing any logs first.
Keep prevention mode and turn off WAF logging, so the search errors stop appearing in the team's reports.
Remove the managed rule set entirely and rely only on NSG port rules to stop web attacks.
Run the WAF in detection mode, review the logs, add exclusions for the false positives, and then move to prevention mode.
questions.why: Detection mode shows which legitimate requests match, exclusions remove those false positives, and only then does prevention mode become safe to enable.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who runs the company's web shop where a WAF should sit, and why you would start it in detection mode. Name one limit or tradeoff of a WAF.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would put the WAF where public traffic first arrives. If customers come from many countries and we want filtering at the edge, Azure Front Door with a WAF policy is the fit. If the app runs in one region inside a virtual network and traffic enters through a regional load balancer, Application Gateway with a WAF is the fit. I would start in detection mode so the logs show what would be blocked, because managed rules can flag legitimate things such as search text with apostrophes or unusual headers. Once we add exclusions for those false positives and the logs look clean, we move to prevention. The limit is that a WAF only checks what its rules recognise. It does not fix flaws in the application code, and it does not replace network filtering such as NSGs, which control traffic by address and port.
rubricPoints: Places the WAF at the right entry point: Front Door for global edge traffic, Application Gateway for regional traffic in a virtual network
Explains detection mode versus prevention mode and why to start in detection
Mentions tuning or exclusions to handle false positives before blocking real traffic
States a real limit: a WAF does not fix application code and does not replace NSG network filtering

suggested.rationale: The core skill is choosing placement and mode and explaining the tradeoff back, and no listed mission or planned engine covers web application firewalls.

lessons.plain: A web application firewall, or WAF, sits in front of a website and inspects each web request before it reaches the app. It checks for patterns that look like attacks, such as someone sneaking database commands into a form field. A WAF has two working styles. In detection mode it watches and writes down what it would have blocked, but lets everything through. In prevention mode it actually stops the requests that match. Choosing between them is about how much risk you accept while you learn what normal traffic looks like.
lessons.guessPrompt: A newly added WAF rule starts matching a few requests from real customers on the first day. Would you switch the WAF to blocking right away, or first watch what it would have blocked? Explain your reasoning in a few sentences.
lessons.teach:
Mode is the setting that decides what a web application firewall (WAF) does when a request matches one of its rules. A WAF policy is the named bundle of rules and settings attached to a gateway or edge service that receives web traffic. Each policy has one of two modes. Detection mode means the WAF inspects traffic, logs every match, and still forwards the request. Prevention mode means the WAF inspects, logs, and blocks the matching request, returning an error response to the caller instead of passing it on.

Why this matters: rules are pattern checks, and pattern checks make mistakes. A legitimate request can look like an attack, for example a product note that happens to contain a quote character and a database keyword. Such a wrongly matched request is called a false positive. Detection mode lets you measure false positives in logs before they cost real customers anything. Once you have reviewed the logs and added an exclusion, which tells the WAF to ignore a specific field for a specific rule, you switch to prevention so the rules actually protect the app.

Worked example. A shop's checkout sits behind a WAF in detection mode. Step 1: a customer submits a note containing a quote character and a SQL keyword. Step 2: the rule matches, the WAF logs it, and the request reaches checkout normally. Step 3: the team reviews a week of logs and sees that every match came from the note field. Step 4: they add an exclusion for that field. Step 5: they switch to prevention. Now a real injection attempt matching the rule is blocked with an error response, typically 403.

Common mistake: leaving a new policy in detection mode indefinitely and assuming it protects you. Detection mode blocks nothing, so attacks succeed while the log fills up. The opposite mistake is switching to prevention without reviewing logs, so real customers get blocked.

Consequence: switching to prevention without tuning can cause a sudden drop in successful checkouts. That shows up as a business alarm, such as falling order completions, before anyone looks at the WAF itself.

questions.prompt: A ticket marketplace called Harbor Tickets puts its search endpoint behind a WAF policy that starts in detection mode. Step 1: a seller's event description contains an apostrophe and a SQL keyword, so a rule matches. Step 2: the WAF logs the match and the request reaches the search service normally. Step 3: the team reviews two weeks of logs and finds every match came from the description field. Step 4: they add an exclusion that tells the WAF to ignore the description field for that rule. Step 5: [missing]. Afterwards, a crafted injection attempt that matches the same rule against the description field is still allowed through, and the logs show it was recorded but not stopped. What step 5 must be for the WAF to block matching attacks?
choices: Switch the policy mode from detection to prevention so matching requests are blocked with an error response.
Create a second policy in detection mode and send the search traffic to it as well.
Raise the log retention period so reviews can cover a longer window.
Remove the exclusion so that every field is checked by the rule again.
questions.why: Detection mode only logs and forwards matches, so the policy must be switched to prevention before the WAF blocks matching requests.

questions.prompt: In a web application firewall, what does detection mode do when a request matches a rule?
choices: It blocks the request and returns an error to the caller.
It inspects and logs the match, then still forwards the request.
It rewrites the matching field so the rule can no longer match.
It drops the request silently without writing a log entry.
questions.why: Detection mode inspects and records every match but forwards the request unchanged, which is why it cannot stop an attack.

questions.prompt: A legitimate customer's request is being blocked by a prevention-mode WAF because a rule matches a harmless comment field. Logs confirm this is the only field triggering the block. Which control fits best?
choices: Switch the policy to detection mode permanently and leave it there.
Remove every rule from the policy so that the comment field can never match.
Turn off the whole WAF policy so that no request is inspected at all.
Add an exclusion that tells the WAF to ignore that specific field for that specific rule.
questions.why: An exclusion targets one field for one rule, fixing the false positive while keeping the rest of the protection in place.

questions.prompt: A team creates a new WAF policy, leaves it in detection mode for several months, and assumes the application is protected. An attacker sends requests that match the rules. What is the most likely outcome?
choices: The requests are blocked and the attacker receives a 403 response.
The requests are logged and forwarded to the application, so the attacks can succeed.
The policy automatically switches itself to prevention after a set time.
The requests are held in a queue until a human approves each one.
questions.why: Detection mode records matches but never blocks them, so the attacks reach the application while the log fills up.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between WAF detection mode and prevention mode, and name one limit or tradeoff of running detection mode for a long time.
lessons.modelAnswer: Detection mode and prevention mode both run the same rules against every web request. The only difference is the action taken on a match. In detection mode the WAF records the match in its logs and lets the request through, so nothing is blocked. In prevention mode it records the match and also stops the request with an error response. The tradeoff of detection is that it gives you no protection while it runs, so an attack matching a rule still reaches the app. Its benefit is that it exposes false positives, which are legitimate requests that match a rule by accident, before they hurt customers. So the usual approach is to run detection, review the logs, add exclusions for known-good traffic, and then switch to prevention. I would also keep reviewing logs after the switch, because new application features can create new false positives.
rubricPoints: Detection mode logs matches but forwards every request, so it blocks nothing.
Prevention mode logs matches and also blocks the request with an error response.
Detection mode lets the team find false positives before real users are affected.
Staying in detection mode indefinitely leaves the application unprotected.
Switch to prevention only after reviewing logs and tuning exclusions.

suggested.rationale: Choosing a mode means reasoning through a situation about what traffic gets blocked and what risk remains, which an exam-style scenario practises better than reading alone.

lessons.plain: A web application firewall is a checkpoint that reads the contents of web requests, not just where they come from, and stops ones that look like attacks, such as text crafted to inject database commands or scripted probes. Azure Front Door is a global entry point that receives web traffic close to users and forwards it to your applications. Its firewall protection is organised into rule sets, which are prepackaged collections of checks maintained by the platform for common attack types, plus any custom rules you write yourself. Configuring rule sets means choosing which collections apply and tuning the few checks that wrongly block real customers. Think of it as choosing which security guards stand at the door and adjusting the instructions of the ones who turn away honest visitors.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your web application blocks a legitimate customer search because the search text happens to contain a word that a protection check treats as suspicious. Before reading anything, which would you guess is the safer fix: turning the whole protection off for the site, or narrowing only the one check that fired? Explain your reasoning in a sentence.
lessons.teach:
A web application firewall (WAF) inspects the content of HTTP requests, the messages browsers and apps send to a website, and blocks those that match known attack patterns such as SQL injection, where text is crafted to smuggle database commands, and cross-site scripting, where a page is tricked into running a foreign script. Azure Front Door is a global entry point that accepts web traffic near users and forwards it to your back ends. A WAF policy is the object you attach to it to apply these checks.

A WAF policy holds two kinds of checks. Custom rules are your own conditions, such as blocking an IP range, and they are evaluated first in priority order. Managed rule sets are collections of checks maintained by the platform vendor, grouped by attack family and covering OWASP-style threats. A bot protection rule set is a third managed option aimed at automated clients. You configure a managed rule set by choosing its version, then enabling or disabling whole rule groups, or overriding the action of individual rules.

Why does this work? Each managed rule looks for a signature in a specific part of a request, such as the query string, headers, or body. Because checks are narrow, you can keep broad protection on and carve out only the one check that misfires.

Worked example: a search page sends the word select, and a SQL injection rule fires. Step one, read the log entry to find the exact rule identifier and the request field it matched. Step two, confirm the traffic is legitimate. Step three, disable or change the action of only that one rule for the search route, leaving the rest of its group active. Step four, retest the search and also a known attack payload, expecting the search to pass and the attack to remain blocked.

Common mistake: disabling an entire rule group or the whole rule set to silence one false positive. That removes protection for every endpoint, not just the one that misfired.
