Consequence: a broad exclusion can quietly expose the application to the attack class it covered, and the gap often goes unnoticed because normal traffic still works. Narrow changes keep the protection meaningful.

questions.prompt: A travel company runs a hotel booking API behind Azure Front Door with a WAF policy, and guests' free-text remarks are being blocked. Step one: the log shows managed rule 41207 in the SQL injection group matched the remarks field on the route /api/bookings. Step two: the team confirms the remarks are genuine guest text. Step three: [missing]. Step four: retest with a normal remark and a known attack payload, expecting the remark to pass and the attack to stay blocked. Which action completes step three?
choices: Disable the entire SQL injection rule group across every route in the profile.
Add a custom rule at top priority that allows all traffic from the guest's country.
Turn off the whole WAF policy on the endpoint until the next release.
Set rule 41207 to log only, scoped to the /api/bookings route.
questions.why: Changing the action of only the one misfiring rule, and scoping it to the affected route, removes the false positive while the rest of the group keeps blocking attacks elsewhere.

questions.prompt: Which description best fits a custom rule in a WAF policy?
choices: An NSG rule that filters packets by IP address and port number at the subnet boundary.
A managed collection of checks, maintained by the platform vendor and grouped by attack family, that you can switch on per rule group.
A switch that turns Azure Front Door off during a planned maintenance window.
Your own condition, such as an IP range block, evaluated before managed checks.
questions.why: Custom rules are conditions you write yourself, such as blocking an IP range, and they are evaluated first in priority order, ahead of managed rule sets.

questions.prompt: A retailer sees a scraping bot copying its product prices from the catalogue pages, while human shoppers are unaffected. Which WAF control fits this requirement best?
choices: A bot protection rule set on the WAF policy, which is aimed at automated clients.
An NSG rule on the back-end subnet that blocks port 443 from all sources.
Disabling the SQL injection rule group, since scrapers send database commands.
A custom rule that blocks every request whose header names a standard browser.
questions.why: The bot protection rule set is the managed option aimed at automated clients, so it targets the scraper without changing protection against other attack families.

questions.prompt: A team disables the entire cross-site scripting rule group to stop one false positive on a comments form. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: Custom rules are moved behind managed rules, so the comments form becomes rate limited.
Cross-site scripting protection disappears for every endpoint, and the gap may go unnoticed because normal traffic still works.
The WAF policy begins blocking every HTTP GET request across all applications on the profile.
Azure Front Door stops accepting traffic near users, so requests are routed to a distant region.
questions.why: Disabling a whole group removes that attack class from every endpoint, not just the comments form, and ordinary requests keep succeeding so the exposure is easy to miss.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would keep WAF protection on for a Front Door application when one managed rule blocks a legitimate form submission. Name the tradeoff of the narrower fix you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would not turn the WAF off or drop the whole managed rule set. First I would check the WAF log for the rule identifier that fired and the exact request field it matched, so I know which single check is misfiring. Then I would confirm the submission really is a legitimate customer request and not an attack in disguise. If it is, I would override the action of that one rule or disable that one rule, scoped as narrowly as the policy allows, and leave the rest of its group active. The tradeoff is that this rule no longer inspects that field, so the narrower the scope the better. I would then retest the form and a known attack payload to confirm the form works and the attack is still blocked everywhere else.
rubricPoints: Use the WAF logs to identify the specific rule that fired rather than guessing.
Narrow the change to one rule or one route instead of disabling a whole group or set.
Name the tradeoff: the exempted check no longer protects that input.
Verify both that the legitimate request passes and that a real attack is still blocked.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a false-positive scenario and choosing the narrowest rule change adds the most, since no listed mission practises WAF configuration directly.

lessons.plain: A web application firewall is a checkpoint that reads the content of web requests, not just their address and port, and decides whether each one may reach the website. On Azure's Application Gateway, which is a load balancer for web traffic, the checkpoint's behaviour comes from rule sets. Think of a rule set as a long checklist of known attack patterns, such as injected database commands or malicious scripts, that each request is checked against. Configuring rule sets means choosing which checklists to use, switching off individual items that cause false alarms, and deciding whether matches are only logged or actually blocked.
lessons.guessPrompt: A shop's website receives a comment from a customer that happens to contain the text of a database command. Why might a security checkpoint block that comment even though the customer did nothing malicious, and what would you change first?
lessons.teach:
Definitions first. A web application firewall (WAF) inspects the HTTP requests that reach a web app and matches them against rules. Application Gateway is Azure's layer 7 load balancer for web traffic, and its WAF is attached to it through a WAF policy. A rule set is a group of rules. A managed rule set is a pre-built collection maintained by the provider, commonly based on the OWASP Core Rule Set, which covers attack families such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting. A rule group is a subset of rules inside a set, such as those for one attack family. An exclusion tells the firewall to skip inspecting a particular part of a request, such as one form field. A rule group override changes the action or enabled state of individual rules. A custom rule is one you write yourself, with conditions and an action such as allow, block or log.

Why it works: the firewall does not understand your application. It only recognises suspicious shapes in requests, so the same set that protects the site can also block legitimate content that happens to look like an attack.

Worked example: a managed set is active and blocking. A customer posts a comment containing a database command as a code snippet. Step 1: the comment body matches an SQL injection rule. Step 2: because the set is blocking, the request is refused with a 403 response. Step 3: you add an exclusion for that one body field, or disable only that single rule, then re-test. The rest of the set keeps protecting the site.

Common mistake: disabling a whole rule group, or turning the firewall off, to stop one false alarm. That silently removes protection for every page, not just the one that caused the problem.

Consequence: a blocked legitimate request looks like an outage to the user, so tuning is usually done while matches are only logged, and blocking is enabled once the false positives are understood.

questions.prompt: A helpdesk portal runs behind an Application Gateway whose WAF policy uses a managed rule set in Prevention (blocking) mode. Agents paste ticket text that includes the HTML tag urgent into the Subject field, and the gateway returns 403 for those requests. The team's logs show the match is on a cross-site scripting rule in the Subject field, and they confirm the agents are legitimate users. Step 1: they keep the WAF in Prevention mode so every other page stays protected. Step 2: they confirm from the logs that the match is only on the Subject field, not on the rest of the request. Step 3 is the one missing step. Which action completes the tuning?
choices: Switch the WAF to Prevention mode with logging turned off so the 403 responses stop appearing
Add an exclusion scoped to the Subject field only, keep the rule group enabled, then re-test
Disable the entire cross-site scripting rule group for every page behind the gateway
Turn the whole WAF policy to Disabled until the helpdesk tickets are fixed
questions.why: An exclusion scoped to one field skips inspection of only that field, so the rest of the request and the rest of the site remain protected by the active rule group.

questions.prompt: In Application Gateway's WAF, which term describes a pre-built collection of rules maintained by the provider and commonly based on the OWASP Core Rule Set?
choices: A custom rule
An exclusion
A managed rule set
A rule group override
questions.why: A managed rule set is the provider-maintained, pre-built collection; a custom rule is one you write yourself, an exclusion skips inspecting part of a request, and a rule group override changes the action or state of individual rules.

questions.prompt: A travel booking site sits behind an Application Gateway WAF in Prevention mode. A shopper searches for the phrase 'DROP the fare' and the request is refused with 403. The shopper is legitimate, and the team wants to stop this false alarm without weakening protection elsewhere. Which change is the most targeted fix?
choices: Disable the WAF policy for the whole gateway until the search feature is redesigned
Turn off the entire SQL injection rule group so no search request is ever inspected
Add an exclusion for the search query argument only, then re-test the search page
Move the search page to a separate gateway that has no WAF attached
questions.why: Scoping an exclusion to the one query argument removes inspection of only that part of the request, keeping the rest of the rule set active across the site.

questions.prompt: A team gets a false alarm on a feedback form behind an Application Gateway WAF and turns off the entire cross-site scripting rule group to stop it. What is the direct consequence for the running system?
choices: Cross-site scripting protection is removed for every page behind that WAF policy, not just the form
Nothing changes, because the managed rule set re-enables the group automatically after a day
Only the feedback form loses protection, because rule groups apply per form
Requests are still inspected, but the 403 responses are replaced with silent drops
questions.why: A rule group applies across all matching requests the policy inspects, so disabling it removes that attack-family protection site-wide, which is why targeted exclusions or single-rule overrides are preferred.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would configure WAF rule sets on an Application Gateway protecting a public shop site, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you chose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with a managed rule set on the WAF policy, since it covers common attack families like SQL injection and cross-site scripting without us writing those patterns ourselves. Before any blocking, I would let it log matches so we can see what it would stop. When a legitimate request gets flagged, such as a product review containing code-like text, I would add a narrow exclusion for that one field or disable that single rule, not the whole group. The tradeoff is that managed rules are generic: they cannot know our application, so some false positives will always need tuning, and an exclusion that is too broad can leave a real gap. Each exclusion should be reviewed regularly.
rubricPoints: Managed rule sets cover common attack families but cannot know the application's own traffic.
Tune in logging mode first, then move to blocking once false positives are understood.
Fix false positives with narrow exclusions or single-rule overrides, not by disabling whole groups or the firewall.
Name a tradeoff: broad exclusions can open real gaps, so each one needs review.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers WAF rule sets, and a short exam-style scenario asking which rule, exclusion or mode fits a false-positive problem would test the reasoning this objective needs most.

lessons.plain: A web application firewall (WAF) is a filter that sits in front of a website or web API and reads each HTTP request before it reaches the application. Think of a security guard at the door who checks each visitor against a list of known tricks, such as database-attack text hidden in a form field or scripts tucked into a web address. A WAF policy is the written set of rules that guard follows, along with a decision about whether to only log suspicious visitors or actually turn them away. Attaching that policy to the entrance it protects is what makes it active. This lesson explains what a policy is made of and how to reason about what it lets through.
lessons.guessPrompt: A shop wants to stop customers from typing harmful text into its search box, but it worries that blocking too eagerly will turn away real shoppers. Before any teaching: what two decisions would you want to make first about the filter, and why?
lessons.teach:
A WAF policy is the set of rules a web application firewall uses to judge each HTTP request, the message a browser or app sends when it asks a website or API for something. A rule is a single test, such as whether a query string contains keywords typical of an injection attack. A managed rule set is a large, prebuilt group of rules maintained by the cloud provider, usually based on the public OWASP core rule set. A custom rule is one you write yourself, for example blocking requests from a region you do not serve, or limiting how often one address may call a login path. Each policy has a mode. In detection mode the WAF matches rules and writes the matches to logs but forwards every request. In prevention mode it blocks matching requests, normally returning an HTTP 403 response. A policy does nothing until it is associated with the entry point it protects, such as an Azure Front Door profile or an Application Gateway.

Why it works: the WAF reads request content, which a network filter that only sees addresses and ports cannot do. Matches can also be scored, so a request is blocked only when enough signals add up.

Worked example: a login form sends a POST whose username field contains an injection string. The request reaches the edge node. The WAF evaluates the managed rule set and one SQL injection rule matches. The policy is in prevention mode, so the WAF returns 403 and never forwards the request. In detection mode the same match would be logged with its rule ID and the request would reach the app.

Common mistake: turning on prevention mode on day one. Legitimate traffic, such as a search containing a quoted phrase, can match a rule (a false positive), and real customers get 403 errors. The safer path is detection first, review the logs, add exclusions for known-good fields, then switch to prevention.

In a running system a blocked checkout looks like an outage to customers, so changing the mode is a release decision, not a formatting tweak.

questions.prompt: A small recipe site runs behind an Azure Front Door profile. The team's WAF policy is in detection mode. Their rollout runbook has four steps. Step 1: associate the WAF policy with the Front Door profile so it inspects live traffic. Step 2: review two weeks of WAF logs and note every rule match, with its rule ID. Step 3: find that the search box's quoted-phrase queries match a SQL injection rule and add an exclusion for that search field. Step 4 is missing from the runbook. The team's goal is to start returning 403 responses for real attack requests while keeping ordinary searches working. Which step should come next, to finish the sequence?
choices: Attach the same policy to a second Front Door profile before making any other change.
Change the policy mode from detection to prevention, then watch the logs for new 403 responses on search and checkout paths.
Delete the managed rule set so that no further matches are logged.
Convert the search exclusion into a custom rule that blocks all quoted text.
questions.why: After logs are reviewed and false positives are excluded, the policy is switched to prevention so matching requests are blocked with 403, and the new 403s are watched because a blocked path looks like an outage to users.

questions.prompt: In a WAF policy, a rule is set to run in detection mode for one site. What happens to a request that matches that rule?
choices: The request is forwarded to the app, and the match is written to logs with its rule ID.
The request is held in a queue until an administrator reviews the match.
The request is dropped silently at the network layer before the WAF reads it.
The request is blocked and the client receives an HTTP 403 response.
questions.why: Detection mode matches rules and records them in logs but still forwards every request, which is why it is the safer first step.

questions.prompt: A public API's login path receives password-guessing traffic from a few client addresses. The team wants each address limited to 10 login requests per minute, without changing rules that protect the rest of the site. Which WAF feature fits this requirement best?
choices: A custom rule that counts requests per client address on the login path and blocks addresses over the limit.
An NSG inbound rule that allows only port 443 from the internet.
Switching the whole policy to detection mode so that the limit is logged instead.
A larger managed rule set that covers all HTTP methods.
questions.why: A custom rule can express a per-address request limit on one path, whereas managed rule sets are prebuilt generic groups and an NSG works on addresses and ports, not request content.

questions.prompt: A team builds a WAF policy in prevention mode with a tested SQL injection rule, but attacks still reach the application. The policy shows as healthy. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The policy has not been associated with the entry point, such as the Front Door profile or Application Gateway, that receives the traffic.
HTTP 403 responses are sent by the application instead of the WAF.
The managed rule set does not support POST requests.
Prevention mode only blocks requests that come from outside the region.
questions.why: A WAF policy does nothing until it is associated with the entry point that protects the app, so unassociated traffic never reaches its rules.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a WAF policy does, how detection mode and prevention mode differ, and name one limit or tradeoff of switching to prevention mode too early.
lessons.modelAnswer: A WAF policy is the rule set a web application firewall applies to each HTTP request before it reaches the app. It holds managed rule sets, which are prebuilt groups of rules for common attacks, and custom rules that you write for your own traffic. The policy's mode decides what happens on a match. Detection mode logs the match and forwards the request, so you can see what would have been blocked. Prevention mode blocks the request, usually with a 403 response. The tradeoff is false positives. A rule can match legitimate input, such as a search phrase that looks like an attack, so turning on prevention without a detection period can block real customers. The usual approach is to run detection, review logs, add exclusions for known-good fields, and then enable prevention. The policy also only protects what it is attached to, so an unattached policy protects nothing.
rubricPoints: A WAF inspects the content of HTTP requests, unlike a filter that only checks addresses and ports.
Managed rule sets and custom rules are the two kinds of rule in a policy.
Detection mode logs matches and forwards traffic, while prevention mode blocks matching requests.
A policy must be associated with an entry point such as Front Door or Application Gateway to take effect.
Turning on prevention too early risks false positives that block legitimate users.

suggested.rationale: Choosing between detection and prevention, and which rules to keep, is best practised by reasoning through a realistic traffic scenario rather than by memorising settings.

lessons.plain: A web application firewall, or WAF, is a filter that sits in front of a website and inspects the web requests coming in, blocking the ones that look like attacks. Writing the filter's rules is only half the job. A WAF policy is the saved set of rules and settings, and associating it means attaching that policy to the specific entry point it should guard, such as a load balancer for web traffic or a global edge service. Until the policy is attached to something, it protects nothing. Think of an instruction sheet for a security guard: it only matters once it is handed to the guard posted at a particular door.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have written a WAF policy that blocks SQL injection attempts, but those attacks still reach your application. What is the most likely thing you forgot to do, and why would that explain the result?
lessons.teach:
A WAF (web application firewall) inspects HTTP requests, the messages web browsers and apps send to a web server, and decides whether to allow, block or log each one. A WAF policy is the named resource that holds the rule sets, custom rules, exclusions and the mode. Mode is either detection, which logs matches but lets them through, or prevention, which blocks them. Association is the act of attaching a policy to a target. On Application Gateway, a regional web load balancer with a WAF feature, the target can be the whole gateway, a listener (one hostname and port), or a single URL path. On Azure Front Door, a global edge service, a security policy links a WAF policy to chosen domains or endpoints.

Why it works: a policy does nothing on its own. The platform checks each incoming request against the policy linked to the entry point it arrived through. Attachments can exist at several levels, and the most specific one wins. A policy linked to one URL path overrides one linked to the listener, which overrides one set for the whole gateway.

Worked example: a gateway has a global policy in prevention mode. A legitimate upload is blocked, so the team adds a path-level policy for /api/uploads in detection mode. A request to /api/uploads arrives. The gateway finds the path-level association, uses its detection mode, logs any match and forwards the request. A request to /checkout finds no path-level association, uses the global prevention policy, and is blocked if it matches.

Common mistake: creating and tuning a policy, then never associating it, so no traffic is inspected. A related error is forgetting that a narrow override silently weakens protection for that path.

Consequence: an unattached or wrongly scoped policy lets attacks reach the application while the policy itself still looks correct on paper.

questions.prompt: A regional retailer runs an Application Gateway with one gateway-wide WAF policy in prevention mode. It also has a listener for partner.example.net on port 8443, and that listener has its own WAF policy in detection mode. No URL path under that listener has a policy attached. A request for partner.example.net:8443/orders/status arrives. Step 1: the request came in through the partner.example.net:8443 listener, so the platform finds the listener-level association. Step 2: the platform has to decide which mode to apply. Your task is to name the step-2 result that the platform reaches.
choices: Prevention, because the platform uses whichever policy has the strictest mode among all attachments
Prevention, because the gateway-wide policy always takes precedence over listener policies
Detection, because the listener-level association is the most specific one that applies to this request
No inspection at all, because listeners cannot hold WAF policies and only the gateway can
questions.why: The most specific attachment wins, so the listener association is used and its detection mode applies, meaning matches are logged but not blocked.

questions.prompt: A team on Azure Front Door builds a WAF policy in prevention mode with a set of custom rules, then deploys it, but never links it to any domain in a security policy. What happens to incoming requests for that domain?
choices: They are blocked anyway, because a prevention-mode policy protects every domain in the subscription
They are forwarded and logged, because a policy that exists but is unlinked falls back to detection mode
They are forwarded without being checked against the team's policy, so the policy has no effect
They are inspected by the default platform rules, but not by the team's policy
questions.why: A policy only acts on requests whose entry point is linked to it, so an unlinked policy leaves that traffic uninspected.

questions.prompt: An Application Gateway has a gateway-wide WAF policy in prevention mode. The path /reports/* has a path-level association using a policy in detection mode. A request containing a suspicious pattern arrives at /reports/q3. Which outcome follows?
choices: The request is blocked, because the platform combines both policies and applies the stricter mode
The request is forwarded to the backend, and the match is logged, because the path-level detection mode is the one that applies
The request is rejected with an error, because a path cannot have a different mode than its gateway
The request is blocked, because the gateway-wide prevention policy is always enforced as a floor
questions.why: The path-level association is the most specific one, so its detection mode decides the outcome: the match is logged and the request still reaches the application.

questions.prompt: A shop runs an Application Gateway. The listener for shop.example.org on port 443 has a listener-level WAF policy in prevention mode. The path /media has its own path-level policy in detection mode, and the whole gateway has a policy in prevention mode. A request arrives for shop.example.org/media/banner.png. Which policy governs this request?
choices: The path-level detection policy, because it is the most specific association that matches the request
The listener's prevention policy, because it is the only one tied to the hostname
The gateway-wide prevention policy, because it sits at the top of the hierarchy
All three policies, applied in sequence, with the first block stopping the request
questions.why: When several attachments apply, the most specific one wins, and the path-level association for /media is more specific than the listener or the gateway.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a WAF policy and its association, and what happens when a path-level policy in detection mode sits under a gateway-wide policy in prevention mode. Name one limit or tradeoff of scoping a policy narrowly.
lessons.modelAnswer: A WAF policy is the object that holds the rules, exclusions and mode, but it only takes effect when it is associated with a target such as a gateway, a listener, a URL path or a Front Door domain. The most specific association wins for a given request. So if a path-level policy is in detection mode under a gateway-wide prevention policy, requests to that path are logged rather than blocked, while everything else stays blocked. The tradeoff is that a narrow override can quietly weaken protection on that path, and it adds one more place to check during an incident. I would review every path-level override regularly and record why it exists, so it stays temporary and deliberate.
rubricPoints: A WAF policy holds rules and mode, and it has no effect until it is associated with a target
Association can be made at gateway, listener, or path level, or on a Front Door domain or endpoint
The most specific association wins for a given request
Detection mode logs matches while prevention mode blocks them
A narrow override can silently reduce protection, so it needs review

suggested.rationale: Choosing the right association scope for a described situation is best practised by reasoning through a scenario, since no listed mission covers WAF.

scenarios.title: Larkspur Clinic Supplies: Fixing Bastion, Private DNS and Fixed Outbound Access
scenarios.scenario:
Larkspur Clinic Supplies is a fictional company that runs an online ordering app. The app servers sit in one virtual network (VNet), which is a private, isolated address range you define in Azure. Inside that range, a subnet is a smaller slice you assign to a group of resources. The team has three problems this week.

First, an administrator needs to manage the app servers without giving them public IP addresses. Azure Bastion is a managed jump service that lets you connect to a VM through a browser over secure HTTPS. It must sit in a subnet with the exact name AzureBastionSubnet, and that subnet must not hold application servers.

Second, the orders database is reached through a private endpoint, which is a network interface with a private IP address that connects your VNet privately to a platform service. The app servers look up the database by name, but the name resolves to a public address and the connection fails. The team has a private DNS zone, which is a name lookup zone that only answers for networks linked to it, but it is not linked to the VNet.

Third, a partner requires all outbound traffic from the app servers to come from one fixed public IP address. Today the servers use outbound access that can change. The team plans to use a NAT gateway, which is a managed outbound translator that gives a subnet a fixed public address.

Complete these tasks:
1. Name the subnet requirement for Azure Bastion and explain why the Bastion host should not share the app server subnet.
2. Explain why the app servers resolve the database name to a public address, and name the specific Azure control that fixes it.
3. Describe how a NAT gateway and a public IP address give the subnet a fixed outbound address, and state which subnet setting must be applied.
subParts: Fixed outbound address with NAT gateway
modelAnswer: Azure Bastion must be placed in a dedicated subnet named exactly AzureBastionSubnet, sized to the size the service documentation specifies (typically /26 or larger if you use standard features). The name must match exactly or deployment fails. It should not share the app server subnet because the Bastion subnet is a reserved, purpose-built space for the service's components, and keeping it separate keeps management access paths and security rules clear. A common mistake is naming it something like bastion-subnet, which Azure will not accept for the Bastion host.

The private endpoint gives the database a private IP address inside a subnet, but the database's normal name is published in public DNS, which returns the public address. Without a private DNS zone linked to the VNet, the app servers' lookup goes to public DNS and gets the public address. If public network access to the database is disabled, that connection is blocked and fails. The specific fix is to create the matching private DNS zone for the service (for example the privatelink zone for that service type), add a DNS record for the database pointing to the private endpoint IP, and create a virtual network link that connects that zone to the app VNet. After this, lookups from the app VNet return the private IP. A common mistake is linking the zone but forgetting to create the record, or creating the zone without linking it to the VNet.

A public IP address resource gives you a fixed IPv4 address. Attach that public IP to a NAT gateway, then associate the NAT gateway with the app server subnet. Outbound connections from VMs in that subnet are translated to the NAT gateway's public IP, so the partner sees one stable address. Inbound traffic is not affected by this association. The subnet setting that must be applied is the NAT gateway association on the app server subnet. A common mistake is attaching the public IP to individual VM network interfaces, which does not give one fixed outbound address for the whole subnet, or associating the NAT gateway with the AzureBastionSubnet, which is not needed for this requirement.

scenarios.title: Warehouse site-to-site VPN for Harbor Lane Logistics
scenarios.scenario: Harbor Lane Logistics is a fictional company with a head office and a distribution warehouse. Its inventory application runs in an Azure virtual network (VNet, a private network inside Azure) with address space 10.1.0.0/16. The warehouse network uses 10.20.0.0/16 and sits behind a firewall device at its edge. The company needs a site-to-site VPN, which is an encrypted tunnel carried over the public internet that joins two networks as if they were one. The tunnel must keep working if one Azure gateway instance fails, and the team wants routes exchanged automatically using BGP (Border Gateway Protocol, a routing protocol that shares which network paths exist). In Azure, the virtual network gateway is the resource that terminates the VPN, and the local network gateway is the Azure object that describes the warehouse device and its address ranges. A junior engineer has proposed a policy-based VPN on a Basic gateway SKU because it looks simpler. Please answer the following. 1. Recommend a gateway SKU and high-availability setup for this requirement, and justify your choice. 2. Explain whether a route-based or policy-based VPN fits this requirement, and why. 3. The tunnel now shows as connected, but warehouse staff still cannot reach the inventory application. Name the two most likely configuration causes and how you would check each one.
modelAnswer: Recommend a zone-redundant VpnGw SKU such as VpnGw2AZ, configured in active-active mode. A SKU is the tier that sets throughput, the number of tunnels and features available. Zone-redundant means the gateway instances are spread across availability zones (separate data centre groups within one Azure region), so one zone failing does not take the gateway down. Active-active means Azure runs two gateway instances, each with its own public IP address. The warehouse device then builds two tunnels, one to each address, so if one instance is lost the other keeps the link up. The Basic SKU is wrong here because it does not support BGP and does not offer the zone-redundant, active-active high-availability design. Choose the SKU whose rated throughput covers the expected warehouse traffic, and confirm that figure in current Azure documentation before buying.

Use a route-based VPN. A route-based VPN treats the tunnel as a route target: any traffic whose destination matches a route through the tunnel is sent into it, and the tunnel supports BGP and multiple tunnels. A policy-based VPN uses fixed traffic selectors (lists of exact source and destination ranges) and is normally limited to one tunnel with static settings, so it cannot run active-active and cannot use BGP to share routes. Because this company needs failover between two gateway instances and automatic route sharing, the policy-based design fails the requirement even though it looks simpler. The common mistake is choosing the simpler-looking option without checking whether it supports the high-availability and routing features the business asked for.

Two likely causes. First, the local network gateway may not list the warehouse subnet 10.20.0.0/16 (or the specific warehouse ranges) in its address prefixes, or it may list the wrong public IP for the warehouse device. Check the local network gateway's address space and its public IP against the warehouse device settings. Second, the VNet or the subnet routing and network security rules may block traffic, or the return path is missing: the inventory subnet's network security group may not allow traffic from 10.20.0.0/16, or the warehouse side may lack a route back to 10.1.0.0/16. Check the network security group effective rules for the target subnet and confirm the warehouse device routes 10.1.0.0/16 into the tunnel. A tunnel can show connected while traffic is silently dropped by either cause, so the connected status alone does not prove the link works end to end.

scenarios.title: Harbor Parcel Co. traffic routing decisions
scenarios.scenario: Harbor Parcel Co. is a fictional company that runs a parcel tracking website. Several terms first. A load balancer spreads incoming connections across a group of servers, called a backend pool, and uses a health probe, a regular check on each server, to stop sending work to one that is down. A layer 4 load balancer decides using network details only, such as IP address and port, and cannot see the web request itself. A layer 7 service reads the web request, including the URL path and host name, so it can send /api to one group of servers and /static to another. TLS (Transport Layer Security) is the encryption behind HTTPS. TLS termination means the service decrypts traffic at its entry point before passing it on. A regional service runs in one Azure region, while a global service runs at many locations around the world. Harbor has three requirements. (a) Customers in one region connect over HTTPS to one hostname. Requests to /api must go to an API pool and requests to /static must go to a separate pool. (b) Warehouse staff use an internal tracking service on TCP port 8080. It must have a private address inside the company network and must not be reachable from the internet. (c) A global marketing site serves static files to customers worldwide from the nearest location. If one of two regional origins (the servers the global service fetches content from) fails, traffic must move to the other automatically. Complete the following. 1. For requirement (a), name the Azure service that fits, name the feature that makes path-based routing possible, and explain why Azure Load Balancer and Azure Front Door are not the best fit for this single-region requirement. 2. For requirement (b), name the load balancer type you would choose (public or internal) and explain what would go wrong if you chose the public option. 3. For requirement (c), name the Azure service that fits, name the caching and failover features it would use, and explain why Application Gateway alone is not the right answer.
modelAnswer: Azure Application Gateway is the regional layer 7 service that fits. Its feature for this job is listeners with routing rules, which match the host name and URL path and send /api and /static to different backend pools. It can also terminate TLS with a certificate. Azure Load Balancer is layer 4, so it sees only IP address and port. It would send both paths to the same pool and could not split them. Azure Front Door can route by path too, but it is a global service built for many regions and edge caching. For one-region traffic it adds scope the requirement does not ask for, so Application Gateway is the closer fit.

An internal load balancer, which receives a private IP address from a subnet inside the company network. That keeps the tracking service reachable only from inside the network, which meets the requirement. A public load balancer gets a public IP address that anyone on the internet can reach. If the company chose it, anyone could send traffic to port 8080 on the tracking service, which breaks the requirement and exposes an internal tool. Application Gateway is not the choice here because the service is plain TCP, not web traffic that needs URL routing, and Azure Front Door is a public entry point rather than an internal one.

Azure Front Door is the global service that fits. Caching stores copies of static files at edge locations near customers, so repeat requests do not go back to the origins. Failover uses origin groups, where each origin has a health probe and a priority, so traffic moves to the second origin when the first one fails. Traffic acceleration carries requests over the provider's network from the edge location to the origin. Application Gateway alone is regional. It runs in one Azure region and does not cache content at locations around the world. If that region fails, it cannot send customers to the other region. Azure Traffic Manager could switch between regions using DNS, but it does not cache or proxy the content, so it does not fully meet the caching requirement.

scenarios.title: Keeping Clinic Records Off the Public Internet
scenarios.scenario: Harbor Lane Clinics is a fictional company with 12 sites. Its booking app runs on virtual machines in an Azure virtual network named vnet-app-prod, in a subnet called snet-app. Patient documents are stored in a storage account named stharborrecords, and visit data is in an Azure SQL database. The security team has ruled that this traffic must not cross the public internet, even though Azure services have public addresses by default. Clinic staff also reach the storage account from an on-premises network connected over a VPN. Your manager, Priya, asks you to plan the change and explain it to the team. Work through these tasks: 1. Decide whether a private endpoint or a service endpoint fits the storage account requirement, including the on-premises staff, and say why. 2. Explain how the booking app should resolve the storage account name so that it reaches a private address, and what happens if that DNS setup is missing. 3. Explain how you would stop the app subnet from reaching any other storage account on the internet, while still allowing stharborrecords.
subParts: Choose private endpoint or service endpoint and justify it, including on-premises access
Explain DNS resolution to a private address and the failure if it is missing
Restrict subnet access to only the approved storage account using a policy
modelAnswer: A private endpoint is a network interface that gets a private IP address from your own subnet and connects to one specific resource, such as one storage account. Traffic from the app and from on-premises clients travels across your private network to that IP, so it never needs the public address of the storage account. A service endpoint, by contrast, is a setting on a subnet that sends traffic to the Azure service over the Azure backbone and tags it with the subnet identity, but the destination is still the service's public address. Because the requirement is to keep traffic off the public internet for the storage account, and because on-premises staff must reach it too, a private endpoint fits. A service endpoint would not give on-premises clients a private path, since they are not inside the subnet. Worked example: the app subnet is 10.20.1.0/24. Creating a private endpoint for stharborrecords assigns, say, 10.20.1.5 from that subnet. Traffic from the app to the storage account now goes to 10.20.1.5 and stays inside the network. Common mistake: assuming the subnet setting alone is enough for on-premises users. Consequence: on-premises users would still be sent to the public address and may be blocked or may reach the public path, breaking the rule.

The private endpoint only works if the name stharborrecords.blob.core.windows.net resolves to the private IP, not the public one. This is done by linking a private DNS zone named privatelink.blob.core.windows.net to the virtual network, with a record mapping the storage name to 10.20.1.5. The DNS name for the account is a standard public name, and without the private zone the lookup returns the public address. Worked example: the app asks for the storage name. With the private zone linked, the answer is 10.20.1.5 and traffic goes privately. Without it, the answer is the public IP, so the app reaches the storage account over the internet, or fails if the public path has been disabled. Common mistake: creating the private endpoint but forgetting the zone link or on-premises DNS forwarding, so on-premises clients still get the public address. Consequence: the traffic appears to work but is not private, or it breaks for on-premises users who cannot resolve the name correctly.

A service endpoint policy is an allow-list attached to a subnet that limits which specific Azure resources the subnet may reach through its service endpoint. Without it, a subnet with a service endpoint for Azure Storage can reach any storage account in the region, including ones outside your company, which is a data-leak risk. You would create the policy, add the storage account stharborrecords as the only allowed resource, and attach the policy to snet-app. Worked example: the app subnet tries to reach a storage account named stexternal01 that is not on the list. The policy blocks the connection, while stharborrecords still succeeds. Common mistake: enabling the service endpoint but not attaching a policy, which leaves the subnet able to reach every storage account. Consequence: a compromised app or a misconfigured script could send patient data to an unapproved account without any network rule being broken. Note that a policy is about the service endpoint path; for private endpoints, access is controlled by the private connection itself and by the resource's own network settings.

scenarios.title: Harbor Lantern Logistics: Locking Down a Three-Tier Web Application
scenarios.scenario:
Harbor Lantern Logistics is a small fictional shipping company that runs its order-tracking website on Azure. The setup has three tiers placed in separate subnets. A subnet is a smaller address range carved out of a virtual network, which is a private network inside Azure. The web servers sit in a web subnet, the SQL database sits in a data subnet, and administrators reach the servers for maintenance. A network security group (NSG) is a list of allow and deny rules that Azure checks against traffic entering or leaving a subnet or network interface, where a network interface is the virtual card attached to one server. Each rule has a priority number, and lower numbers are checked first. An application security group (ASG) is a named label you attach to servers so that rules can refer to a group of machines by role rather than by IP address. The security team has three requests. First, only the web servers may talk to the database, and only on the SQL port. Second, administrators must not expose remote-login ports such as RDP or SSH to the public internet. Third, the public website must be protected against common web attacks such as SQL injection. A web application firewall (WAF) is a filter that inspects the content of web requests and blocks suspicious ones. It can run in detection mode, which only logs matches, or in prevention mode, which actively blocks them. Please answer the following.

1. Name the NSG control you would use to limit database access to the web tier, explain how ASGs help you write that rule, and state exactly which traffic the rule allows and which it blocks.

2. Describe how administrators should reach the virtual servers without any public remote-login port, naming the Azure service that provides browser-based or secure tunneled access and explaining which NSG rule change supports it.

3. The team wants to tune the WAF before turning it on fully. Explain what detection mode and prevention mode each do, recommend which to start with and why, and describe how the team would confirm later that a blocked request was a genuine attack and not a legitimate customer.
subParts: NSG rule and ASG design for web-to-database access
Administrator access without public remote-login ports
WAF detection versus prevention mode rollout
modelAnswer: Create an ASG for the web servers, named for example asg-web, and another for the database servers, named asg-db. Attach each server's network interface to the matching ASG. Then write an inbound rule on the database NSG with a low priority number, for example 100, that allows TCP traffic on port 1433 (the standard SQL Server port) with asg-web as the source and asg-db as the destination. Because rules are checked in priority order, a later deny-all rule catches everything else. The result is that a web server's SQL connection is allowed, while the same port from any other source, such as an admin workstation or an internet address, is blocked. The ASG approach matters because if the team adds a third web server, they only attach it to asg-web, and the rule still applies without editing IP addresses.

A safe pattern is to avoid giving virtual servers public IP addresses for administration and to use Azure Bastion, a managed service that lets an administrator open a remote session through the Azure portal over a secure encrypted connection. Bastion itself runs in a dedicated subnet with its own required NSG rules, and the administrator never connects directly from the internet to the server. On the server-side NSG, you remove or deny any inbound rule for RDP (port 3389) or SSH (port 22) whose source is the internet, and you allow those ports only from the Bastion subnet's address range. The consequence of skipping this is that port scanners on the internet find the open remote-login port and attempt password guessing, which is a common path to compromise. A common mistake is to add an allow rule for port 3389 from any source and assume the default rules will protect it; default rules allow traffic from the virtual network but do not stop a broader allow rule you added yourself.

Detection mode means the WAF inspects each request and writes a log entry when a rule matches, but it still lets the request through to the website. Prevention mode means the WAF inspects the request and actually blocks it when a rule matches. The team should start in detection mode because legitimate customer traffic, such as a search query containing quotation marks or a long form submission, can accidentally match an attack rule. Running detection mode for a period lets the team see which rules fire on normal traffic and add exclusions for those false positives before blocking anything. To confirm a later block was a real attack, the team reviews the WAF logs, checks the rule that matched, the request path, the payload pattern, and the client address, and compares the pattern against known attack shapes. If the matched content was a normal customer action, the rule or exclusion needs tuning rather than leaving the block in place. Skipping this step can lock real customers out of checkout during the first day of prevention mode.
